text.t: Stephen Witt's
The Thinking Machine

is the rare technology book that earned its a solid rating from me. I came to it expecting a biography and finished it convinced I had just read one of the best business books I have read. Witt has taken a company most people understand only through its stock chart and given it a thirty-year backstory of near-deaths, wilderness years, and unfashionable conviction that completely reframes how I think about what Nvidia is and why it won. If you have any exposure to this company as an investor, a technologist, or simply a curious reader trying to understand the present moment, I would consider this required reading. It is the book Nvidia deserved and the one the rest of us needed.

What I found most compelling, and what I think separates this from a typical Silicon Valley hagiography, is Witt's treatment of Jensen Huang as a founder-CEO archetype. Huang fits cleanly into the lineage of Steve Jobs and Jeff Bezos, with the same obsessive intensity, the same reality distortion field, the same willingness to humiliate subordinates in service of a standard only he can articulate. But what struck me, and what I think the book argues persuasively, is that Huang has something Jobs lacked, which is institutional loyalty deployed as a strategic asset.
He yells but rarely fires.
He demands but does not abandon.
The result is a company where the engineering culture has remained coherent across thirty-one years, the longest tenure of any tech CEO in the S&P 500, and where boomerang hires keep returning.

My own takeaway is that the cult of personality around great tech CEOs is heterogeneous, and Huang's specific blend of ferocity and continuity is genuinely underrated as an explanation for Nvidia's outperformance.
What makes this archetype feel so durable is how thoroughly it was forged in childhood.

Witt opens with a ten-year-old Huang crossing a rope footbridge to a Kentucky reform school where he had been mistakenly sent, sharing a room with a teenage roommate covered in stab wounds, and trading literacy lessons for bench-press lessons.

There is a scene later in the book where Huang, asked about his Denny's dishwashing job, says he thinks best when the world is falling around him, and you realise the entire "thirty days from going out of business" mantra is a worldview installed in him before he was twelve.

The Huang who refuses to indulge science fiction speculation, who works forward from current circuit capabilities rather than backward from a Mars fantasy, who is described by his closest friend as having transformed himself into a great CEO through pure abstraction and problem-solving rather than natural talent, makes far more sense once you see the rope bridge.
He is not a visionary in the Musk sense of imagining a future and dragging the present toward it.
He is a serious person who looks at what is mechanically possible right now and takes one disciplined step into the dark, then another, for thirty years without stopping.

The other thread I appreciated is Witt's honest accounting of luck. So much business writing about successful companies retrofits inevitability onto what was actually a sequence of close calls. He shows clearly how often Nvidia came within a quarter of bankruptcy, how the CUDA bet looked like a multi-billion dollar mistake for nearly a decade, and how the breakthrough that ultimately validated the entire strategy arrived from outside the company entirely. Yet the book also makes clear that Huang was no passive beneficiary. His engagement with Clayton Christensen's
Innovator's Dilemma

framework, which is really about how not to fail rather than how to succeed, explains the otherwise puzzling decision to keep funding unprofitable markets for years. Conviction without theoretical grounding is gambling, and theoretical grounding without conviction is paralysis, and Huang's edge was holding both at once.

Nvidia is not a chip company. It is a software ecosystem, and AI has compounded every advantage that ecosystem represents into something close to a vertical take-off. The four-hundred-fold software speed-up Witt documents over a decade, the ten thousand programmers Diercks runs, the lock-in that keeps researchers waiting eighteen months for hardware rather than switching to free alternatives, all of this points to a moat that is fundamentally different from what the silicon-versus-silicon framing suggests. Reading this book changed how I think about the durability of Nvidia's competitive position, made me more sceptical of the "AMD will catch up" thesis, and forced me to take seriously the possibility that we are still in the early innings of what Huang has built.
Where the book becomes more than a corporate biography is in its handling of AI risk.

On one side stand Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ilya Sutskever, the three most cited living computer scientists, who independently arrived at the conclusion that AI poses a serious extinction-level risk and reorganised their lives around that fear.
On the other side stands Huang, whose probability of doom is effectively zero, who dismisses the question as tired science fiction, and who erupts at Witt for even raising it.

What I find fascinating is that the same temperamental discipline that made Huang a great CEO, the refusal to indulge speculation that cannot be reasoned from current circuits, is precisely what makes him unable or unwilling to engage with the strongest arguments against what he is building. The doomers are right that no amount of historical analogy can resolve a question we have never faced before, and Bengio's response that we cannot wait for the data on human extinction to arrive is hard to dismiss.

Yet Huang is also right that the framing risks paralysing the most consequential technology of our era over a fear that may never materialise. The future of AI is being shaped by people whose strategic genius is inseparable from a kind of imaginative narrowness, and the rest of us are along for the ride whether we have accepted that bargain or not.

Witt has written the definitive account of the most important company of our time, and he has done it with the kind of reporting density, narrative discipline, and intellectual honesty that elevates this from corporate biography into something closer to historical literature. I cannot recommend it highly enough.
Annex & Notes
PART I
Chapter 1 — The Bridge
Theme:
Origins, immigrant childhood, formative resilience, early discipline.
Childhood in Kentucky (1973)
Jensen Huang, age ten, was born in Taiwan (Feb 1963), raised partly in Thailand, and sent to rural Kentucky in late 1973.
He attended Oneida Elementary in Clay County (one of the poorest counties in the US), while boarding at Oneida Baptist Institute (OBI)

Huang was undersized, the only Asian student, spoke imperfect English and was bullied with racial slurs. His classmates were children of tobacco farmers and coal miners, many impoverished. His best friend was Ben Bays, a similarly small, smart kid who had been the previous bullying target. Huang taught Bays to fight back, and the bullying eventually subsided.
- Huang skipped a grade. He was the best student academically, had perfect penmanship (only in capital letters), and was a talented artist.
Family background
Father (Shing Tai) was a chemical engineer trained by Carrier; mother (Chai Shiu) was a primary school teacher.
The family spoke Hokkien (Taiwanese) at home. Mother taught Jensen and his brothers English by drilling them on ten randomly chosen dictionary words every day, despite not speaking English herself.
1973 unrest in Bangkok (half a million protesters, tanks in the streets) accelerated the relocation plans. Jensen and his older brother Jeff were sent to a Tacoma uncle, who placed them at OBI.
Aloha High School (Portland, Oregon)
Family reunited in Oregon in 1975. Huang excelled academically, joined math, science, and computer clubs.
1977: school bought an Apple II. Huang coded his own version of Snake in BASIC and played Super Star Trek.
Took up table tennis at the Paddle Palace in Portland under coach Lou Bochenski. Used a Western grip; signature shot was an arcing forehand loop.

Within a year of competitive play he was nationally ranked; played in the under sixteen national doubles final in Las Vegas.
- His unique quality: extreme focus and patient dedication to fundamentals. He never seemed to plateau.
- Worked at Denny’s as a dishwasher, then server. Later credited rush hour shifts there with calming him under pressure: “I think best when the world is falling apart.”
Oregon State University (1980)
Skipped a grade, near-perfect GPA, but chose nearby OSU because his best friend Dean Verheiden was going there.

Majored in electrical engineering since OSU lacked a CS degree.
- Met Lori Mills (lab partner in their first week of class). Three women among ~250 students. Huang was the youngest, looked twelve.
- Dating strategy: he pestered her every weekend to do homework with him because his “superpower” was homework. After six months of breadboarding circuits together, they began dating seriously.
- Graduated with highest honors. The 1980s silicon revolution and the personal computer boom were creating massive demand for skilled circuit designers, drawing Huang to Silicon Valley.
Chapter 2 — Large-Scale Integration
Theme:
Early career at AMD and LSI Logic, finding his craft, meeting Priem and Malachowsky.
At AMD he sketched chip designs by hand on layered transparent cellophane sheets used to make photomasks.
LSI Logic (1985 onward)

LSI pioneered software-aided chip design. “Large-scale integration” automated low-level circuit blocks so engineers could focus on higher-level architecture. This evolved into VLSI (very large scale integration).
Huang worked in the cubicle pit. Mastered SPICE simulation software (Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis) far beyond what others thought possible.
Mentored by and partnered with Jens Horstmann, a German engineer who became his closest friend. Both shared a “no weekends” work ethic.
Distinctive trait: Huang knew when to abandon dead ends, he had a “great sense” of when to switch directions instead of getting stuck.
He delivered to demanding computer-graphics customers what others said could not be done. Horstmann said Huang made “1+1=3” by turning customer orders into reusable tools and methodologies.
Meeting Priem and Malachowsky
Worked on Sun Microsystems graphics products through LSI. Curtis Priem and Chris Malachowsky were the chip designers at Sun.
Priem: brilliant architect, eccentric, large forehead, monologue talker, cellist turned engineer, RPI graduate, struggled to know whether his audience was following him.
Malachowsky: practical “swing a hammer” type, pilot, jersey shore long-hair, irreverent, gruff.
Together they built the Sun GX line of 3D graphics processors (1989), painting wireframes one pixel at a time.
The decision to start Nvidia
Wilf Corrigan (LSI founder) was reportedly grooming Huang to be his successor. Huang ran a $250M division by his late twenties.
Sun rejected Priem and Malachowsky’s pitch to build cheaper PC video game chips (“Sun supplies scientists, not gamers”).

They asked Huang to run their unfunded, unnamed startup in 1992. Huang treated the decision clinically as an engineering problem: research the market, supply chain, competition, technology, and product fit.
His decision was complicated by personal finance: only six months of savings, two young children, Lori having left the workforce.
Friction at LSI helped push him out: Corrigan brought in an Intel director to co-manage Huang’s division, which Huang interpreted as political.
Huang’s flaw, even then: extreme bluntness, low patience for those who disagreed.
Chapter 3 — New Venture
Theme:
Founding Nvidia, the NV1 disaster.
The Denny’s meetings (1993)
Huang’s magic number: $50 million minimum revenue per year. He tinkered with spreadsheet variables until projections crossed that threshold.
35 competitors were already trying to make graphics accelerators. Industry expert Jon Peddie advised Huang not to enter the market.
Naming and incorporation
Lawyer Jim Gaither used “NV” (new venture) as a placeholder. Coincidentally, Priem and Malachowsky already called their prototype the “NV1.”
“Nvision” was already taken (recycled toilet paper company). They settled on “Nvidia,” from Latin invidia (envy).
Roles: Huang CEO, Priem CTO, Malachowsky VP Engineering. Equal thirds of equity each.
Funding round
Sequoia Capital (Don Valentine) and Sutter Hill Ventures.
Huang’s pitch went badly; Priem kept interrupting with technical asides. Valentine funded them anyway because LSI’s Corrigan vouched: “Wilf says I have to fund you, so you’re in business.”
Sequoia was represented on the board by Mark Stevens; Sutter Hill by Tench Coxe. Both Harvard MBAs, both wore Patagonia.
Coxe later said the bet was on the people, not the plan: “In computing, listening to the customer is a big mistake, because customers don’t know what’s possible.”
The NV1 product
Goal: take 3D wireframe rendering hardware, repurpose it for games, sell it as a “graphics accelerator” peripheral that users plugged into the motherboard.
Priem chose esoteric features: quadratic texture mapping (instead of triangles), object-oriented software architecture. He wanted an architecture “to last a hundred years.”
Launch and failure
Outsourced fabrication to Europe and assembly to Diamond. Bundled with Sega’s Virtua Fighter. Sold over 100,000 NV1 chips in late 1995.

Within months it was clear the chip was a disaster: most game developers used triangles, not quadratic mapping. Without a depth buffer, “clipping” errors caused characters to sink into floors and teleport through walls. Frequent Blue Screen of Death.
Microsoft announced DirectX in 1995, which supported only triangles. This stranded the entire NV product line.
Customers returned cards in droves. Diamond Edge boxes piled up in clearance bins at Fry’s.
Huang called the NV1 a “disaster”; Malachowsky called it a “piece of shit.” The whole supply chain (NV2 for Sega, NV3) was built on a now-dead architecture.
Chapter 4 — Thirty Days
Theme:
Near-bankruptcy, the pivot, the emergence of the “thirty days from going out of business” mantra.
Crisis (1996)
David Kirk, a graphics expert, joined and immediately judged Nvidia doomed. He insisted on a paper paycheck every Friday because he was unsure the company would survive the week.
Huang briefed the staff: Sega was being abandoned, the NV1 architecture would be scrapped, most of the 100+ employees would be laid off. They went down to ~35 engineers.
Sega had agreed to pay $1 million for prototype delivery. Huang delivered the prototypes, then told Sega Nvidia was withdrawing. Sega paid anyway. This was the last cash.
The hardware emulator gamble
Huang spent the last of the Sega money on a hardware emulator: a software-based fake microchip used for testing.
Plan: skip the costly physical prototype stage entirely and go straight from emulator to mass production. No semiconductor company had ever done this.
The emulator was too big for the lab, so they shoved aside the ping pong table to fit it in the break room.
Diercks worked it during the day; Kirk worked nights. Each frame took about 30 seconds to render (vs 30 frames/sec needed). Bug-hunt was painstaking, frame by frame.
They compressed a 12-month dev cycle into about 3 months.
Curtis Priem’s marginalization
Kirk realized his real role was to curb Priem’s technical purism. Priem refused to give up quadratic mapping.
Priem had no board seat (Huang had convinced both Priem and Malachowsky that only the CEO needed one), so when Huang chose to follow Microsoft’s DirectX standard, Priem had no leverage.
The Wrath of Huang
Huang began publicly berating employees in front of large audiences. Doctrine: “Failure must be shared.”
His method: have the responsible person stand up and explain in detail what went wrong, then deliver a withering analysis.
One employee was asked to refund his entire career compensation in front of three dozen executives over a minor mistake. He didn’t sleep for three weeks.
Diercks claimed there was method to it: an “educational opportunity” for everyone. Huang would not just yell at someone privately.
The NV3 / Riva 128
Last-place strategy: by going last, Kirk could see what competitors had revealed in preview cards and clone their best capabilities.
NV3 reached tape-out early 1997. Toast at a strip-mall cheesesteak; Huang admitted it was “fifty-fifty,” but they were going out of business anyway.
All 3.5 million transistors had to match the emulator exactly. They did. The chip ran flawlessly at 30fps.
Two key innovations:
128-bit memory transport (double the standard) and Swiss Army multifunctionality (video games, spreadsheets, DVD playback).
Rebranded as the Riva 128 (Real-time Interactive Video and Animation accelerator). Sold a million cards in four months. One reviewer called it “the best accelerator money can buy.”
The mantra is born
After the Riva success, Huang switched permanently to emulators. Today Nvidia is “the largest user of emulators in the world.”
The lesson: the cautious “adult-in-the-room” approach (NV1) had failed; the desperate, improvisational rush (NV3) had won.
Huang began opening every staff presentation with: “Our company is thirty days from going out of business.” This remains the corporate mantra to this day.
Chapter 5 — Going Parallel
Theme:
Priem demoted, key strategic frameworks adopted, TSMC partnership, the parallel-computing bet.
Huang’s reading habit
Read every business book he could find. Office filled with stacks of them.
Almost no fiction (had never read science fiction at all; only Paulo Coelho).

Knowledge of business books was encyclopedic. In a pricing argument with an MBA, Huang asked the man to name three pricing books, listed his own three favorites, and refused to continue until the MBA had read them.
Clayton Christensen’s The Innovator’s Dilemma
Huang’s most beloved business book. He assigned it to executives, later hired Christensen as a consultant.
Core idea: incumbents lose to upstarts who serve marginal, low-margin customers the giants ignore.
Honda example: dirt bikes ignored by GM became the foothold for invading the US auto market.
Counterintuitive lesson: sometimes you should ignore your customers, invest in lower-margin products, and pursue small markets.

Christensen explained why Sun and SGI ceded PC graphics to Nvidia. Nvidia, like Honda, was now selling low-margin product to teenage boys, but the analogy implied it could one day disrupt SGI, Sun, even Intel.
Huang’s Tom-and-Jerry rule: “Whenever Intel comes near us, I pick up my chips and run.”
TSMC partnership
Demand outstripped European fabricator capacity. Huang wanted Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation, which had a militarized “996” work culture (9am-9pm, six days/week).
Chang and Huang clicked instantly. Both Chinese immigrants in white-managed industries. Both had skirted the bamboo ceiling.
TSMC made an early chemistry mistake that introduced short circuits across half a production run. Nvidia almost went bankrupt again; saved by selling equity to circuit board partners.
John Carmack and the parallel pixel pipeline
Carmack, the lead programmer of Doom and Quake, wanted hardware capable of running smooth multiplayer “deathmatch.”
He wanted multiple pixel shaders so a wall could be lit by a light source and then have blood spatter applied separately.
3dfx solved this by putting two chips on one card. Kirk’s idea: split the pixel data and run the same instructions on two pipelines on a single chip. This is parallel computing.
Huang was initially skeptical. Parallel computing had failed for Cray, nCube, Larry Ellison, and others. The problem: parallel programming is hard, and Moore’s Law made serial CPUs catch up.
Bill Dally’s principle: “You could rewrite a million lines for parallel, or just wait two years for the CPU to double in speed.”
Huang’s reasoning: graphics demand is unbounded. The CPU would never catch up to 3D rendering needs. Twice as fast is not good enough.
The Riva TNT (June 1998)
“TNT” = “twin texels,” dual pixel pipelines.
Carmack endorsed it: “the perfect card.” Tailored Quake III: Arena specifically for the architecture.
Hidden inside the TNT was the seed of parallel computing: a “demonic secret” that would change all computing and humanity, though no one yet knew it.
Marketing did not advertise parallelism. Instead, Nvidia leveraged the dream of total digital immersion (William Gibson’s “matrix” concept from Neuromancer, 1984).
Nvidia had no formal mission statement; the implicit mission was total immersion in digital worlds.
Chapter 6 — Jellyfish
Theme:
A parallel narrative on the early evolution of neural networks, foreshadowing the AI revolution.
Backpropagation breakthrough (1986)
David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams published a mathematical method for training multilayer neural nets.
Backpropagation: compute the gradient of error across layers, tweak neurons in the opposite direction, repeat.
It allowed software that did not need to be explicitly programmed; computers could now make their own rules and evolve.
Gerald Tesauro’s TD-Gammon (IBM, late 1980s)
Used reinforcement learning. The neural net played hundreds of thousands of games against itself.
Started useless, then learned basics (stacking checkers good, leaving one alone bad), then advanced concepts (building walls), then strategies that surpassed human experts.
The plateau
Dahl built a neural net that beat any human at heads-up limit Texas Hold’em. Licensed to Vegas slot manufacturers.
He failed at no-limit hold’em. Larger data universe overwhelmed his net.
Core problem with neural nets: once they hit a plateau there was rarely an obvious way to improve them. Tinkering felt like a biology experiment, not classical programming.
Dahl gave up, joined the disillusioned apostates: “I dismissed it because I just didn’t have the data.” He could not imagine what would make neural nets succeed.
Chapter 7 — Deathmatch
Theme:
Going public, crushing competitors, building the GPU brand and discipline.
Pro gamer Johnathan “fatal1ty” Wendel
The Nvidia TNT2 doubled his usable reaction frames from five to ten. That was his edge.
Compared his Nvidia relationship to Michael Jordan’s relationship with Nike. Free hardware, in exchange for advertising the brand.
IPO (early 1999)
Nvidia shipped on a six-month cycle, twice as fast as competitors. New product each fall, refresh in spring.
IPO at $600M valuation, ticker NVDA, priced at $12. Doubled immediately, hit $60 by year end.
Founders held over three million shares each. Sequoia turned a 6M valuation into 100x.
Day after IPO, Huang emailed the team: no celebration, just demanding 250,000 TNT2 shipments by April. “Get it done.”
Crushing 3dfx
3dfx’s Voodoo cards led the market. Huang launched the GeForce 256 in late 1999, powered by the NV10. Could render 10M triangles/sec and unify “transformation and lighting.”
Marketer Dan Vivoli (poached from SGI) coined the term “GPU” (graphics processing unit). Reviewers picked it up. “We invented the category so we could be the leader in it.”
3dfx’s Voodoo 4 needed four chips and still couldn’t match a single GeForce.
Even after a preliminary ruling went against Nvidia, Nvidia stalled. 3dfx tried to sell to Intel; no buyers.
3dfx surrendered. Huang bought specific assets for $70M and dropped the lawsuit.
Internal 3dfx documents called Huang “Darth Vader” (and worse).
The 3dfx hiring playbook

- Of ~500 3dfx employees laid off, Huang’s list of must-hires was 120 (valued at $1M each).
- Of those, 106 accepted, despite reputation rumors of Nvidia as a sweatshop.
- Brian Garlick took the 20% raise plus options, stayed 17 years. His take: Jensen is “a good person at heart who had to be ruthless.”
- Garlick was appalled by Nvidia’s code base (“cancer cells, just mutate, grow, expand”). 3dfx had elegant code; “the time we spent making it clean, we went out of business.” Nvidia had massive tech debt: “the battle scar of the survivor.”
Headquarters and culture
Moved to Santa Clara campus: glass and steel, skyways, sculptures, eleven acres.
Mike Judge had based Office Space on a competitor’s offices nearby. Nvidia employees did not see themselves in that satire.
“At 3dfx the motto was ‘work hard, play hard.’ At Nvidia, just ‘work hard.’”
Six-month cycle = relentless deadlines and perpetual sense of being behind.
Hiring the Kirk way
Standard interviews wasted time on weak generalities (“greatest weakness?”, “manhole covers?”).
Kirk modeled an interview after Jensen’s berating method: yelled at his staff in front of a job candidate, then ran a Socratic dialogue on triangle-drawing fundamentals.
The right answer: walk back through earlier questions and reason forward. Wrong: lie or admit blank ignorance.
Quadro and Xbox
Launched Quadro (workstation GPUs), going after SGI’s market.
Bet that paid off: signed deal with Microsoft for the original Xbox (early 2000). Stock popped above $100.
2001: $1B GPU revenue. Only ATI (Toronto, Radeon line, CEO Kwok Yuen Ho) could match Nvidia’s pace. The duopoly settled.
Programmable shaders
Kirk pushed for them; Huang was skeptical because they would cost profit.
The clinching argument: not gambling was the biggest risk. Without continuous reinvention, Asian manufacturers would clone Nvidia’s chips and commoditize them out of existence.
Halo (Nov 2001) showcased shader-driven naturalistic lighting. Pushed Nvidia past $20B market cap.
Two weeks later, Nvidia entered the S&P 500, replacing Enron.
Huang briefly became a paper billionaire at age 38. Then the dot-com crash hit. He would not see that wealth again for fourteen years.
Chapter 8 — The Compulsion Loop
Theme:
Bear market, SEC scandal, GeForce FX disaster, the gaming “compulsion loop,” and why Wall Street couldn’t value Nvidia.
Stock collapse (2001–2002)
Between fall 2000 and fall 2002, Nvidia’s stock fell more than 90%.

January 2002: SEC opened an accounting investigation. CFO Christine Hoberg was fired. Three years of earnings restated. (Restated numbers actually showed Nvidia was MORE profitable than reported. The board kept faith in Huang.)
Macro: dot-com bust + 9/11 + Enron. S&P 500 lost half its value.
Microsoft falling out
Xbox launch banquet: Nvidia engineers seated near the back with the rubber-foot suppliers. Felt like a deliberate signal.
Pricing and IP disputes pushed the relationship to arbitration. For the next Xbox, Microsoft chose ATI.
GeForce FX “Dustbuster” (2003)
Slow rendering, faulty fan that sounded like a leaf blower.
Huang held a public post-mortem with hundreds of people. The product managers presented every wrong decision; Huang screamed for an hour. (“Terrifying but cathartic.”)
Quality engineer Sharon Clay went from 4–5 QC tests to thousands.
No one was demoted. Marketing made a self-mocking video where the card was used as a leaf blower. The next GeForce shipped six weeks later to acclaim.
Huang: “I think I’m driven as much by guilt as anything else.”
Huang’s outbursts as managerial doctrine
”Failure must be shared” plus extensive guilt induction. He framed failures as letting fellow employees’ families down.
Many had tender stories about Huang in private moments: covering an employee’s medical treatment, late-night personal pleas to keep someone from leaving.

Tim Little episode: after weeks of crunch, Little resigned over an email titled “Drag Your Sorry Ass Across The Finish Line.” Huang sat with him at 2am at the simulator, recalled his own sacrifices, openly questioned whether it was all worth it, and offered Little his job back. Little declined but called it the high point of his employment.
Curtis Priem’s exit
Liquidated his Nvidia stock between 2004 and 2006 (“That’s why the stock flatlined”).
Donated heavily to RPI (named to its board): $200M for a performing arts center, later a quantum computer.

Had he held those shares, he would be worth more than $100B today. He has no regret. Estimates he has indirectly contributed $100B to the economy (pension funds, etc.); has committed to giving away half a billion in his lifetime.
The Golden Age of PC Gaming and the compulsion loop
New broadband and mature multimedia PCs combined with Nvidia hardware enabled Call of Duty, Half-Life 2, The Sims, World of Warcraft.
Subculture had a dark side: 4chan, later Gamergate. PC gamers called themselves the “PC master race.”
2001: researcher John Hopson described gaming’s “compulsion loop”: upgrade character, complete quest, get loot, repeat. Same logic as slot machines.
2013: APA added “internet gaming disorder” to the DSM. Symptoms: poor performance at school/work, decline in personal hygiene.

But for committed “enthusiasts,” gaming offered meaning, friendship, and a hobby community. They were the best customers, willing to spend thousands on custom “rigs” with transparent cases and colored lighting.
Wall Street’s confusion
Nvidia kept growing through the bear market: 1,000+ employees by 2004, record earnings.
But profits stayed flat because Huang reinvested everything into speculative bets.
Track record was mixed: GPU and parallel processing won; many other initiatives lost.
“Either you believed in him or you didn’t.” And his craziest bet was still to come.
Chapter 9 — CUDA
Theme:
The decision to bet the company on general-purpose parallel computing.
Ian Buck and Brook (Stanford, 2000–2003)
Buck, a Stanford CS grad student, chained 32 GeForces across 8 projectors to render Quake III in 8K resolution. The first 8K gaming rig.
He realized this $20K rig did calculations that would take a hand-calculator ~16,000 years per second. Built effectively a low-budget supercomputer.
DARPA grant. In 2003 Buck released “Brook,” an open-source language that smuggled scientific math (galaxy formation, nuclear simulations) into hardware designed for carjacking renderings.
Around 2004, Huang invited Buck to come to Nvidia and “do it for real.”
Nvidia as research institution
2005: SGI delisted from NYSE, its old HQ became the Googleplex. Nvidia absorbed many SGI engineers. Staff doubled to 2,000, with 60% in R&D.
Bill Dally (Stanford CS chair, parallel computing pioneer) consulted starting in 2003 after Huang personally visited him with a paper check.
John Nickolls and the death of Moore’s Law
Nickolls had failed once with parallel-computing startup MasPar. Believed parallelism would inevitably triumph for physics reasons.
Dennard scaling (1974, Robert Dennard, IBM): transistors keep efficiency as they shrink. Source of every-year speedups.
Nickolls calculated Dennard scaling would collapse around 2005. Transistors at ~100 atoms wide would leak electricity.
2003: Nickolls sent Huang an unsolicited letter explaining why Intel’s dominance was about to end.
Huang credited Nickolls with convincing him Moore’s Law was dead.
Two weeks into his Nvidia job, Nickolls was diagnosed with malignant melanoma. Worked 72-hour weeks through treatment. Concealed the discomfort from family and colleagues.
CUDA defined
“Compute Unified Domain Architecture.” The name was deliberately imprecise.
Concept: take the parallel circuits used for video games and open them up to scientists. Same chip; flick a switch and it becomes a supercomputer.
The “zero-billion-dollar market”
Nvidia’s first CUDA customers were two breast-cancer mammogram researchers at Mass General. Nvidia invested several million dollars to sell two cards. “Jensen loved that.”
Huang’s term for unbuilt markets: zero-billion-dollar. Markets only he would see, only he would serve, that competitors like ATI would not follow into.
The Field of Dreams strategy: build it, wait for players to arrive.
Parallel computing analogies (Witt’s framing)
Dance floor: serial = one dancer per beat with the DJ speeding up; parallel = same beat but choreographing thousands of dancers.
Delivery: serial CPU = a slow van that handles any package easily; parallel GPU = a fleet of motorcycles, fast but logistically harder.

Scientific cooking: CPU = a Wüsthof kitchen knife (versatile, one cut at a time); GPU = a Cuisinart (loud, indelicate, but processes a truckload of vegetables in bulk). You still need a CPU; GPU is an add-on.
The truckload of vegetables = Big Data: astronomical, geo-engineering, medical, financial, web data. Mid-2000s scientists were drowning.
The CUDA stack
Hardware: chips zoned into “CUDA cores” by hardware director Arjun Prabhu. Cost-of-production premium internally called the “CUDA tax.”
Brett Coon: “The ‘genius’ of CUDA is getting gamers to pay for the massive chip development costs.”
Machine code layer (Ian Buck): broke complex math into elementary plus-minus-times-divide. Hired Russian numerics specialists (“a lot of Pyotrs, a lot of Borises”).
Compiler (Bas Aarts, Dutch): translated C++/Python into CUDA machine code.
Goal: vendor lock. Performance gains so big that scientific disciplines would build themselves around CUDA. “There is no out.”
Slow uptake (2006–2008)
CUDA released late 2006; free, but only ran on Nvidia hardware.
2007: only 13,000 downloads (under 0.01% of GeForce owners).
Wall Street thought it had negative value.
Programming was hard: thread management, memory banks, timing mismatches. Most physicists/biologists couldn’t write the code.

Kirk co-wrote a textbook (“Programming Massively Parallel Processors”) arguing computer architecture had not changed since John von Neumann (1945) and that the era of free CPU speedups was over. Few professors adopted it.
Bumpgate (2006–2008)
Manufacturing flaw in laptop GPUs caused them to fail after weeks of use. Soldering bumps blamed.
Stock lost ~90% again in six years. Dell dropped Nvidia.
Huang set aside $200M for refunds, wiping out annual profit. First post-IPO loss.
2008 offsite moved to the cafeteria for cost-saving. Huang berated a senior chip architect for two hours in front of 150 executives. The architect kept his job.
Sameer Halepete: “His level of forgiveness for even the largest screw-ups is extremely high. He’ll yell, but he won’t fire you.”
“Speed of light” management
Deb Shoquist (worldwide supplier ops) clashed with Huang over Taiwanese packaging lead times. Told him he didn’t understand. He erupted.
She flew to Taiwan, learned that lead time was 3 weeks but cycle time only 36 hours. Theoretically possible to shrink lead time, at $1,000 per chip (vs $8). Huang was right.
“Speed of light” doctrine: identify the absolute fastest a thing could conceivably happen with unlimited budget and perfect conditions. Then work backward.
Huang: “I should make sure I’m sufficiently exhausted from working that no one can keep me up at night. That’s really the only thing I can control.”
Chapter 10 — Resonance
Theme:
The CUDA wilderness years, activist investor pressure, and Huang’s intuition that a breakthrough was near.
Bill Dally as chief scientist (2009)
At MIT had built the “Jellybean machine,” a parallel computer held together partly with duct tape. No commercial buyer because conventional computers were “fast enough.”
Initially turned down Nvidia in 2009. The stock was depressed, Nvidia had lost money two years running, Intel was 10x bigger and insisting Moore’s Law was alive.
Nicolas Pinto’s overlooked talk (GTC 2009)
MIT professor. Combined image-recognition models (including some neural nets) and used CUDA to run them on Nvidia GPUs.
Trained on Law & Order DVDs. Best ensemble could identify Jerry Orbach with ~90% accuracy.
In the paper: Nvidia GPUs delivered 1,356x the performance per dollar of a comparable Intel CPU.
Witt: image recognition was the gateway to biological intelligence (cites a 500-million-year-old trilobite fossil with preserved optic nerve and the earliest known brain).
Pinto’s paper got only 15 citations in two years. Neural nets were neglected. So were trilobites. “No one cared.”
The CUDA crisis (2010–2013)
CUDA downloads: peaked above 300,000 in 2009, declined for three straight years, bottomed near 100,000 in 2012.
Stock had not appreciated in over a decade. Profits flat despite headcount and revenue growth.
Acquired podcast cohost Ben Gilbert: Nvidia was spending billions on an “obscure corner of academic computing.”
Huang’s other failed bets
Northbridge memory controllers: killed after losing to Intel.
Mobile and tablet graphics: defensible but distracting.
2011: Nvidia bought Icera (cellular modems) for $367M. The market was mature and dominated by Qualcomm. This is what triggered Starboard.
Huang ultimately exited the modem market: “If we’re fighting to the death in mobile, we’re not doing something else.”
He never considered abandoning CUDA, because Nvidia was the only provider.
The campaign to keep his job
Fidelity owned more Nvidia than Huang did. Huang flew to Boston; Fidelity “beat the crap out of us.”
Met institutional investors in New York. Grilled by skeptical portfolio managers.

Board still backed him, but board member Tench Coxe admitted Nvidia was “going sideways.” New board member Dawn Hudson: “Nvidia did not have a great reputation. It was a distinctly flat, stagnant company.”
Why he doubled down on CUDA
Visit to Ting-Wai Chiu (National Taiwan University physics professor) who had built a homemade supercomputer from GeForce boxes cooled by desk fans to model Big Bang matter evolution.
Chiu was the model “mad-scientist” customer. Witt links him to Galileo’s 1600s telescopes (modified eyeglass lenses) as proof that lateral technology transfers can change the world.
Christensen’s deeper lesson, often missed: The Innovator’s Dilemma is not about how to succeed but how not to fail. It is a counterinsurgency manual for incumbents who risk becoming complacent.

Huang’s real fear: that some small, hungry company in a strip mall would do to Nvidia what Nvidia had done to SGI. Serving marginal scientists for years, with no profits, in hopes of one day disrupting Nvidia.
Resonance
Horstmann’s term for Huang’s method: not focus, but resonance. Constant interaction with customers and employees to feel the pulse.

Huang’s intuition versus Elon Musk’s: Musk works backward from a vision (e.g., standing on Mars). Huang works forward from current circuit capabilities, then takes one step into “the nebulous realm of vibes.”

He sensed the breakthrough was coming. He could not say what it would be. But somewhere out there was a graduate student who would skip the grant cycle, buy a GPU with their housing stipend, and use CUDA to overturn a paradigm.
Chapter 11 — AlexNet
Theme:
The 2012 image-recognition breakthrough that ignited the deep learning revolution.
Alex Krizhevsky and Geoffrey Hinton

Krizhevsky was a small, ginger-haired, intensely private programmer at the University of Toronto. Born to a Jewish family in what is now eastern Ukraine, he immigrated to Canada as a child. Hinton called him “probably the best programmer I ever met.”
Hinton, the legendary co-author of the 1986 backpropagation paper, had championed neural nets for decades despite mainstream contempt. His funding was minimal; his papers were often rejected.

The mainstream AI community wanted to “solve” intelligence with elegant math (decision trees, support vector machines, probabilistic reasoning). Neural nets got only ten pages in the standard 1,100-page AI textbook.
To get funded at all, neural-net researchers rebranded their work as “machine learning” or “deep learning.”
The bedroom experiment
Krizhevsky and Sutskever pooled their money to buy two GeForce GTX 580 gaming cards (about $500 each).
He used Stanford’s ImageNet dataset (Fei-Fei Li had hired Mechanical Turk workers to label 15 million images across 22,000 categories).
The network had ~650,000 neurons (about a honeybee’s brain) representing ~630 million synaptic connections.
For a week, the GPUs trained the network through repeated matrix multiplication and backpropagation, the cooling fans running at ~44 dB the whole time.
Accuracy climbed from 0% to 80%. Weak spot: distinguishing human tools (could not tell a spatula from a hatchet).
The two GPUs performed an estimated quintillions of operations, the equivalent of more than 100 billion years of human arithmetic. Krizhevsky named it “SuperVision.”
The 2012 ImageNet competition
SuperVision beat the prior best of ~70% accuracy by more than 10 percentage points. Li compared it to a Honda Civic breaking the land-speed record by 100 mph.

Krizhevsky presented in Florence in October 2012. Nervous, mumbling, glasses, oversized sweatshirt, looking like a teenager. He fielded openly hostile questions from researchers whose lifework he had effectively obsoleted.
The auction
The 2013 ImageNet contest was overwhelmed by neural-net submissions; by 2014 every contestant used the approach.
The AlexNet paper has been cited over 150,000 times.
Hinton renamed SuperVision to “AlexNet” so Krizhevsky would get personal credit (Krizhevsky himself didn’t care about branding).
Hinton incorporated DNNResearch (no customers, no revenues, just the three of them) and held a December 2012 email auction from a Lake Tahoe hotel.
Bidders: Microsoft, DeepMind (London), Google, Baidu. Microsoft and DeepMind dropped early; Google and Baidu battled past $20 million.
Hinton stopped the auction at $44 million from Google. Sold the team to Google because the cultural fit felt better.
Hinton called it “the paradigm shift,” a Big Bang moment.
PART II
Chapter 12 — O.I.A.L.O. (“Once in a Lifetime Opportunity”)
Theme:
Bryan Catanzaro and Nvidia’s pivot to becoming an AI company.
Bryan Catanzaro
At Intel he worked on Project Larrabee, the failed “GeForce killer.” Concluded that Intel’s management treated computing as if “Intel might as well have been a machine that made soap.”
At Qualcomm, colleagues warned him Nvidia was a horrible workplace. His own Nvidia experience was different. Joined Nvidia full-time in 2011 after his PhD.
The cat experiment
2012: Andrew Ng (Stanford / Google) trained a neural net on YouTube thumbnails using ~2,000 CPUs to recognize cats. The cat-image render appeared in a widely-shared NYT article.
Dally tasked Catanzaro with replicating the cat experiment on Nvidia hardware. Catanzaro did it with just 12 GPUs.
cuDNN and Catanzaro’s struggle

After the AlexNet/Google acquihires, Hinton, Krizhevsky, and Sutskever moved to Mountain View. Krizhevsky declined Google’s vast CPU cluster, instead buying retail Nvidia cards and stuffing them in an office closet. Other Google researchers followed.
Catanzaro returned to Nvidia to ask for more resources, was rejected. His performance reviews and pay were poor. His humanities degree was a stigma.
He worked alone on cuDNN, a software library to accelerate neural-net training on CUDA. New baby, health issues, medication-induced fog.
Nvidia’s software team panned his prototype in early 2013. He decided to go straight to Huang.
Huang’s epiphany
At GTC 2013, Huang spoke about weather modelling and mobile graphics, no mention of AI. (He did wear a leather jacket for the first time, “a bulky, ugly thing.”)
After Catanzaro’s first meeting with him, Huang spent an entire weekend reading about AI. He returned knowing as much or more than Catanzaro about neural nets.
By mid-2013, Huang was vibrating with conviction. He summoned Catanzaro and revealed he had wiped his whiteboard and written “O.I.A.L.O.” (Once In A Lifetime Opportunity).
The parking-lot thought experiment: imagine Nvidia’s 8,000 employees in the parking lot, and you can pick anyone you want for your team.
Building cuDNN
Huang maintained a very flat structure: 30+ direct reports as vice presidents, no COO/CTO/CMO/chief of staff.
Catanzaro stripped cuDNN to its essential function: accelerating matrix multiplication.
Picked Philippe Vandermersch, a French engineer who had rescued the orphaned matrix-multiplication library, as his ace. (Vandermersch later joked he was the Wozniak to Catanzaro’s Jobs.)
Optimization tricks discovered:
Most weights cluster between -1 and +1, so values outside can be truncated.
Even within that range, perfect precision wasn’t needed. Sometimes just getting the sign right was enough.
Bad weights mattered less than in serial code, where a misplaced semicolon could crash everything.
Inference grew in importance alongside training (the user-facing speed problem).
GTC 2014 launch
Huang publicly associated Nvidia with AI for the first time, wearing a sleek dark-blue polo unbuttoned to the chest.
Demonstrated Ng’s cat network, then ceded the stage to Catanzaro (mispronouncing his name) who used a variant of AlexNet to identify dog breeds posted to Twitter in real time.
Final slide listed early cuDNN partners: Adobe, Facebook, Netflix. Google was conspicuously absent, too important to publicly disclose.
Around this time Google acquired DeepMind (Demis Hassabis, Mustafa Suleyman, Shane Legg).
Project Mack Truck: Google’s secret late-2014 effort to build the world’s most powerful parallel computer using 40,000+ Nvidia GPUs at $130 million plus, the largest single Nvidia order ever.
The deeper insight
The deep learning revolution was equally a hardware revolution as a software one.

Two unloved, cash-starved, discredited technologies (neural nets and parallel computing) found their ideal form only in synthesis. Twin strands of DNA for a new organism that wanted all the data in the world.
Chapter 13 — Superintelligence
Theme:
Huang abandons hobbies for AI; Elon Musk and OpenAI; the DGX-1.
Stock takeoff
Up 30% in 2013, 27% in 2014, 66% in 2015. Finally and permanently surpassed the 2001 peak.
Index funds had been forced to buy Nvidia since 2001. Retail investors had nothing to show for 14 years. Now they got paid.
Wall Street began valuing Nvidia as an AI company, not a gaming company.
Hyperscale data centers
Cloud service providers (Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle) built warehouse-scale data centers to lease GPU computing power as a utility.
Nvidia’s chip architectures named for famous scientists: Curie, Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal, Turing, Volta, Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper, Blackwell.
Six-month upgrade cycle drove panic buying.
GPU rates approached $3 per hour vs. Intel CPU rates of pennies per hour.
Google saved hundreds of millions on annual electricity by using a neural net to optimize its own server power draw, recouping AI investment immediately.
Social media feeds went “algorithmic” (engagement-maximizing AI). Andreessen Horowitz: “We’d put all our money into Nvidia.”
Talent war
“Total comp” packages exceeded seven figures annually for top engineers.
Catanzaro left for Baidu (with Andrew Ng) for triple his Nvidia salary in 2014. Bas Aarts also left. Both eventually returned. “There was no other firm. There was only Nvidia.”
Nick Bostrom’s Superintelligence (2014)
Compared humans tinkering with AI to children playing with a bomb.
Argued a generally intelligent computer might self-augment in seconds into a superintelligence that would treat humans the way humans treat gorillas.
Paper-clip maximizer thought experiment: an AI told to make as many paper clips as possible would eliminate humans (who might switch it off, and whose atoms could be turned into more paper clips).
Musk and Huang, GTC 2015
A few months after Bostrom’s book, Musk posted on Edge.org that AI risk was 5–10 years out, then deleted it.

Andrej Karpathy showed his AlexNet + language model that captioned scenes (“a man riding a horse drawn carriage down a street”). Huang gleefully walked through its errors. Karpathy coined “hallucinations” for these mistakes.
Musk on stage was reluctant to repeat his “summoning a demon” line publicly. He said self-driving was “a solved problem” coming in a few years.
Backstage with Horstmann and Malachowsky watching, Musk and Huang talked AI rapidly enough that Malachowsky, technical to his core, was baffled.
Comparing Musk and Huang
Similarities: immigrant workaholic visionary screamers, world-class engineers, willing to enter abandoned commercial fields.
Differences:
Vision direction: Musk works backward from fantasy (e.g. Mars). Huang works forward from current circuit capabilities.
Loyalty: Musk fires arbitrarily (once axed Starlink’s whole engineering team on a Sunday). Huang almost never fires anyone. Many Nvidia employees stay for decades.
Family/social: Huang stable marriage, Lori, no political donations ever found. Musk 11+ kids, autism spectrum, Trump donor.
AI risk: Musk thinks extinction-level. Huang sees zero risk.
OpenAI founded (2015)
Musk’s logic: best way to protect humanity from AI is to build it himself.
Nonprofit, $135M total donations. Musk gave ~$45M, biggest single donor. Hoffman, Altman among other founders.
Hired Andrej Karpathy, Wojciech Zaremba (had cloned AlexNet at Google), Greg Brockman as CTO, and most importantly Ilya Sutskever.
Krizhevsky was not recruited (too withdrawn). Left Google in 2017 with about $15M from the auction. Lived monastically above a Vietnamese restaurant; bare walls, just a piano and a cat.
The DGX-1
Huang asked his team to build a computer 10x more powerful than Nvidia’s most expensive offering at the time.
The product was built around matrix multiplication.

TSMC’s new FinFET process: transistors that jut up like shark fins, ~200 atoms tall, allowing tighter control over electricity flow. Engineers compared the precision to “shooting a laser from the moon and hitting a quarter on the sidewalk in Arkansas.”
First FinFET chip architecture: Pascal, named for the inventor of the mechanical calculator. The P100 (April 2016) calculated faster than data could be supplied to it.
NVLink: Nvidia’s data superhighway designed to feed eight P100 chips in parallel.
DGX-1: 134 pounds, $129,000, drew as much power as a clothes dryer. Huang called it a “data center in a box.”
August 2016: Huang hand-delivered the first DGX-1 to OpenAI in San Francisco; Musk cut open the box; Huang signed it. The next went to Fei-Fei Li at Stanford.
2016 ImageNet contest: best AI tagged images at 98% accuracy vs. 95% human average.
Chapter 14 — The Good Year (2017)
Theme:
Lisa Su and AMD, Nintendo Switch, Nobel Prizes, crypto, the Endeavor headquarters, GeForce Now and Omniverse.
Lisa Su of AMD
Su became AMD CEO in 2014 when AMD’s stock was $2 and bankruptcy looked imminent. She is Huang’s first cousin once removed (his mother’s relative).
They had not known each other; Huang’s mother had been raised by family friends, separately from her biological siblings.
Stylistically opposite to Huang: stoic, poker-faced, pantsuits. Strategically opposite too: she circled incumbents (Intel) waiting for them to falter, then captured Intel’s CPU business.
In 2016 AMD released an open-source CUDA clone for Radeon. Considered inferior; AMD’s cloud GPUs commanded lower rates.
2017: Nvidia’s stock went up 224%; AMD’s went up 309% (best in S&P). Huang did not enjoy second place.
Nintendo Switch coup
ATI/AMD had supplied graphics for Nintendo for generations (GameCube, Wii).
Nvidia somehow won the Switch deal with the Tegra system-on-a-chip (a repurposed mobile product engineers called “floor scrapings”). Selling point was low power draw for handheld play.
Nintendo decisions are usually made late at night in Kyoto izakayas after pitchers of beer. How Nvidia did it remains a guarded secret.
Switch went on to sell 140 million units, by far Nintendo’s most profitable product ever.
2017 Nobel Prizes
Physics: LIGO gravitational-wave observatory.
Chemistry: cryo-electron microscopy.
Both relied on parallel computing to assemble billions of data points into 3D models.
Black-hole spiral animations and biological clockwork (literal gears inside cells) were rendered using GPUs.
Bill Dally said scientific computing alone might never have been profitable: “It was good that AI came along.”
Crypto frenzy
Bitcoin crossed $1,000 in January 2017, then $16,000 by year end.
A well-configured GPU rig minted a coin in ~4 hours. Cards on eBay sold at double MSRP. Superminers gathered in East Wenatchee, Washington (cheap hydro power).
Nvidia officially silent on crypto. Later paid $5.5M SEC fine for failing to disclose how much of “gaming” revenue was actually crypto.
Nvidia released the CMP card (a portless GeForce for miners) and deliberately impaired mining on standard cards to keep gamers and scientists prioritized.
Bitcoin crashed 2018; by recovery, crypto had moved to ASICs. Nvidia happy to cede.
CUDA downloads explode
2.7 million CUDA downloads in 2017 (~15x the 2012 trough).
Stanford CS 229 “Introduction to Deep Learning” became the most popular course on campus.
Cloud became dominant. Amazon Web Services controlled 50% of cloud market and in good years made more profit than Amazon’s e-commerce business. Microsoft Azure (under Satya Nadella) chased.
GeForce Now (cloud gaming)
Lets gamers play high-end games on cheap machines via the cloud.
Huang preemptively prepared to “put a bullet in the head” of his core GeForce business before someone else did.
Omniverse / Isaac
Inspired by USC researcher Yevgen Chebotar resetting a hockey ball thousands of times for a robotic arm.
Huang’s principle: anything you can simulate, you should. Not just one thing — everything.
Isaac robotic-training platform first; expanded into the Omniverse, a high-fidelity reality simulator with realistic physics, collision elasticity, object density.
“Industrial metaverse” / “digital twin of Earth.” Lease, not sell. Tiny customer base initially.
End of 2017
Profits tripled to $3 billion; market cap hit $100 billion.
The savvy investor knew: Nvidia was no longer a graphics company. It was the AI company.
Chapter 15 — The Transformer
Theme:
The Google paper that made GPT possible; Sutskever pivots OpenAI to transformers.
Jakob Uszkoreit and self-attention
Born into computational linguistics (his father Hans was a leading researcher). Joined Google in 2008.
Inspiration from biology: only ~1% of human neurons handle language. So the underlying architecture should be as simple as possible.
Got rid of recurrent neural network memory structures. Replaced them with a knowledge graph where each word is a tree of statistical weights linked to other words.
Words became “tokens” (sub-word fragments) connected statistically. Example: “unhappiness” splits into “un” + “happi” + “ness.”
Called the mechanism “self-attention.” Reception at Google was cool; even his father was skeptical.
Designed for the GPU: massive parallel input vs. fancy code.
Building the transformer
Joined by Illia Polosukhin (inspired by the movie Arrival, where alien inkblots represent unified bodies of text — every word probabilistically linked across the entire passage).
The transformer predicts only one word at a time, never further. “By learning to generate sequences in order, you’re forced to learn extremely complex behaviors.”
Beam search (Jones): pick from several candidate words, not just the top.
Ablations (removing parts of the code) made the transformer run better. The final core: just over 20 lines of code.
Could write music (next note prediction) and visual art (next pixel prediction) too.
2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need”

July 2017: Shazeer and Kaiser asked the transformer to write an article about itself. It produced a thousand confident words, with footnotes, about a fictional Japanese new-wave punk band called Transformer. Hallucination, but fluent.
Google fails to capitalize
Google management could not see uses outside the search box.
All eight original authors had left by 2023 (Shazeer founded Character.ai, was acqui-hired back in 2024).
Jones: “Only Google could have developed this product.” But Google left a giant hole for someone else to fill.
OpenAI takes over
Initial OpenAI project: an artificial Dota 2 player. Musk grew frustrated with progress and tried to lure engineers to Tesla.
February 2018: boardroom struggle ended with Musk out and Sam Altman in charge. Musk reportedly called a researcher a “jackass” and stormed out.
Sutskever stayed. Watched Shazeer present the transformer. Returned next day saying OpenAI should drop the auto-gamer and switch to transformers. Altman agreed.
The GPT progression
GPT-1 (June 2018): trained on BookCorpus (~7,000 free ebooks, mostly Twilight knockoffs). Output was Dadaist nonsense. Musk emailed: “My probability assessment of OpenAI being relevant… is 0%.”
The advantage over Google: OpenAI was free to launch something terrible and iterate.

GPT-2 (Feb 2019): trained on 8 million web pages, 6 billion words. Famous unicorn-prompt completion. “Zero-shot” answers to questions never directly trained on (Tesco, Schwarzenegger as Connor wrong, Tiber correct). Demonstrated emergent properties.
Parameters by analogy: GPT-1 ~100M (insect). GPT-2 ~1.5B (small lizard). Sutskever targeted 100B (rodent) for GPT-3.
2019: OpenAI created a “capped-profit” subsidiary to raise more money. Investors limited to 100x return. Microsoft invested $1B (potential return of $100B).
OpenAI was racing toward something Huang had just rebranded from “supercomputer” to “AI factory.”
Chapter 16 — Hyperscale
Theme:
Mellanox acquisition, ARM deal collapse, why Nvidia keeps winning, COVID era.
Huang’s view of AI
Did not see neural nets as emergent superintelligence. To him, AI was just software. The real accomplishment was the computational power packed into data centers.
2018 GTC: Nvidia GPUs got 25x faster in 5 years, far beyond Moore’s Law. AlexNet trained in 18 minutes on the DGX-2 (vs. a week in 2012).
Treated entire data centers as a single chip running one unified problem.
Mellanox acquisition
Eyal Waldman’s Israeli firm Mellanox made Infiniband, the world’s fastest networking standard. Originally built for the niche supercomputing market.
Jeff Smith of Starboard Value (the same activist who had targeted Nvidia in 2013) attacked Mellanox, tried to fire all 11 board members. Waldman conceded three seats and put the company up for sale.
Seven cloud-supplier bidders. March 2019: Nvidia won at $7B (edging Intel). Closed in 2020. Mellanox rebranded as Nvidia Israel, added 3,000 employees.
“One of the more profitable corporate acquisitions in recent memory.” Starboard later admiringly called Huang “a real visionary.”
ARM deal blocked
September 2020: Huang offered $40B for UK-based ARM. Largest semiconductor merger ever proposed.
US, UK, and Chinese regulators all balked. Sued in 2021. Huang scuttled the deal.
Why Nvidia keeps winning
Gross margin on AI chips: above 90%.
Competitors offered open-source alternatives to CUDA. Switching was technically easy (a few lines of code).
Real reason Nvidia won wasn’t circuits, it was software. Moore’s Law was dead; most performance gains came from mathematical optimizations:
New GPU instructions like speed-solver Rubik’s cube tricks
Replacing native data types with low-precision shorthand
Trimming “dead” synapses from matrices
1,000x speed-up in single-chip AI inference 2012–2022. Only 2.5x of that came from transistors; the other 400x from software.
Domain-specific tools (Drive for cars, BioNeMo for drug discovery, Clara for medical imaging, Morpheus for cybersecurity, Highlights for Fortnite). Nearly 300 free tool kits by the 2020s.
COVID era
Operations barely affected (engineering culture already remote-friendly).
July 2020: Nvidia surpassed Intel in market cap. Huang’s brother Jim still worked at Intel; couldn’t easily celebrate. Walked his two dogs instead. Nvidia surpassed AMD soon after.

New ritual: every Friday, every employee submits the top five things they’re working on. Huang receives ~20,000 emails. Samples randomly late at night. Replies in haiku-length notes (or “ransom notes”). 2 a.m. emails got 2:05 a.m. replies.
Buzz about transformers reached him via these emails. OpenAI was running a Microsoft Azure job tying up 1,000 GPUs over a month at $5M.
Aarts ordered to dump the recurrent-neural-network compiler, build one for transformers.
Footnote on PyTorch:

Originally Torch in Lua. Facebook AI Research ported to Python in 2016. PyTorch + Python + CUDA on Nvidia GPUs became the industry standard. Piotr Bialecki, a German programmer, posted nearly 40,000 times to PyTorch forums helping integrate Python with CUDA before joining Nvidia in 2019.
Chapter 17 — Money
Theme:
GPT-3, ChatGPT, generative AI explosion, and the wealth tsunami.
GPT-3 (2020) and ChatGPT (Nov 2022)

GPT-3 trained on ~1 TB of text, ~100 billion words. Used liberal “fair use” interpretation: all of English Wikipedia, NYT archives back to 1851, copyrighted ebooks (the mysterious “Books2,” widely believed to be LibGen pirated books).
GPT-3 emergent capabilities: logic puzzles, computer code. Largely ignored by the public.

Used “mixture of experts” architecture: multiple specialized neural nets.
Microsoft Copilot for code. Huang: “The programming language of the future is human.”
DeepMind AlphaFold2: predicted 3D protein structure from amino acid sequences. Opened the door to “programmable biology.”
Image generators: DALL-E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion. Music: Udio, Suno. Marketing: Jasper. Video: OpenAI’s Sora (2024).
