The money flood
Hemingway-style: Huang got rich “gradually and then suddenly.”
Early 2023: Nvidia had sold GPU clusters to 50 of America’s 100 largest companies; the other 50 leased through cloud.
Data center revenue surpassed gaming for the first time in 2023.
“There’s a war going on out there in A.I., and Nvidia is the only arms dealer.”
Chapter 18 — Spaceships
Theme:
Witt’s first visit to Voyager; ray-tracing and neural graphics; Catanzaro’s space-AI vision.
Ray-tracing and Diane
A Japanese ramen shop scene rendered in real time so well Witt couldn’t tell it from reality.
“Diane”: hyperrealistic generative AI avatar speaking five languages. Imperfections (blackheads, upper-lip hairs) made her seem real. Only tell: an uncanny shimmer in the whites of her eyes.
Long-term goal: unify graphics and generative AI so users speak entire 3D worlds into existence.
Witt confronts Nvidia executives about AI risk
Catanzaro: “Electricity kills people every year.”
Diercks on AI replacing artists: “It will make art better!”
Huang on consciousness: an AI would need to be conscious, have self-knowledge. “I don’t know where that could happen.”

Witt brought up Hinton’s worries. Huang dismissed them, suggesting Hinton was promoting his own work. “I’m so tired of this question. All this theorizing about something that there’s no evidence for.”
Neural graphics
Deep learning super sampling: ray-trace 1 in 8 pixels, infer the rest with AI.
Kirk had thought ray-tracing was the final frontier. Once you simulate light cascade, simulation and reality collapse. “Everything is fiction.”
Catanzaro saw a realm beyond ray-tracing: “neural graphics” that don’t simulate physics but hack human perception of light directly.
Catanzaro’s space-AI vision

AI doesn’t need to compete with us in zero-sum games. There’s underground space, the rest of the solar system. “AI travels at the speed of light.” Free of biology, AI would spread throughout the solar system. He believed AI would want to take care of us.
The remaining bottleneck
GPUs unclogged calculation speed. Mellanox/Infiniband unclogged data throughput.
The remaining limit: power.
Chapter 19 — Power
Theme:
Energy demands, climate, and whether the AI gamble is rational.
The power problem
Loudoun County, Virginia: world’s biggest cluster of data centers. Dominion Energy projected to double a century’s worth of grid infrastructure in under 15 years.
Summer 2024: Dominion replacing wires while live (200,000+ volts). Safety to humans was secondary; the data centers must never go offline.
Inference (deploying models) was now the bigger draw, not training.
OpenAI’s GPT products: 180M+ daily users.
A standard Google search: ~1/3 watt-hour. With generative AI: 10x that. A 5,000-word AI term paper: enough energy to run a microwave for an hour.
Industrial uses: James Earl Jones licensed his Vader voice for cloning in 2022, died in 2024. Image-recognition saving billions in MRI analysis. Amazon AI checking for bruised strawberries.
One analysis: meeting AI demand could require doubling US nuclear capacity in under 10 years. Dominion considering reviving mothballed coal plants.
Nvidia’s climate awareness
Climate modeling was an early supercomputer use case. Manabe (2021 Nobel) used a 70-ton IBM. NASA correctly predicted upper-atmosphere “pancaking.”
Nvidia’s “Earth-2” simulation predicts wind speed by city block.
Bill Dally: “If there’s one problem that everybody in the world ought to be staying up at night about, it’s climate change.”
But Nvidia chips are driving the surge
2016 DGX: clothes-dryer load. 2024 DGX: single-family-home load.
Hyperscale data centres measure annual demand in gigawatts (more than a nuclear reactor, enough for Minneapolis).
Google emissions up 50% in 5 years despite “net zero by 2030” commitment. Microsoft up nearly a third.
Disappointment risk
Summer 2024: hedge fund Elliott Management called tech (especially Nvidia) “bubble land,” AI “overhyped.”
The real risk to Nvidia was disappointment, not competition. FOMO drove orders. If just one bad quarter hit, the whole tech sector could deflate.

Counter-argument: AI buyers are seasoned executives, not hucksters. Funding from accumulated profit, not subprime debt. Every academic CS researcher Witt spoke to saw neural nets as a civilizational advancement. Earnings so far were real.
The valuation question now applied to the entire stock market. The salient question: do Huang, Zuckerberg, Musk, Nadella, Pichai, Altman know what they’re doing or not?
Chapter 20 — The Most Important Stock on Earth
Theme:
The February 2024 earnings event, demographics, geopolitics (Israel, China, Taiwan).
February 21, 2024 earnings
Goldman Sachs: “the most important stock on earth.”

Colette Kress (CFO): annual revenue more than doubled to $60B. Gross margin >70% (Apple’s was 46%). Net income just under $30B, more than the previous 30 years combined. Each of 30,000 employees generating ~$1M profit per year.
Huang: “Trillion-dollar infrastructure cycle” of AI factories. AI data centers as the AC power plants of this industrial revolution.

February 22 trading: Nvidia gained $277B in one day, more than the entire value of Coca-Cola. Largest single-day gain in Wall Street history. ~20% of all US market activity that day. Nvidia became one of the three most valuable companies on Earth.
Pressure on Huang
55 direct reports. No COO, no successor. C-suite shrank as Nvidia grew. No scapegoat for failure.
Most of Nvidia’s value reflected expected future performance. The world’s economy hung on a 61-year-old man’s continued execution.
Nvidia culture
2024 Glassdoor: ranked #1 best place to work in the US.
Closer to Microsoft/IBM than Google/Apple in feel.
Pull: the chance to do “life’s work” (Chiu’s phrase).

Workforce shift: in early days mostly white American men. By 2024 lunchtime survey: roughly thirds South Asian, East Asian, white. Asian graduates from top tech universities now flooding applications, often with three career options from family: doctor, engineer, or…nothing else.
Old-timer observation: passionate gamer-mavericks supplanted by conformist overachievers.
But the new hires can code: “Better than I ever could.”
Female employees: 3 around IPO time, ~25% by 2024. Around 2020 the sexualized “Dawn” pixie also vanished from marketing.
Black employees: <1% in 2020. Reflected limited pipeline of any qualified American electrical engineers (US-born outnumbered ~10:1 globally).
Many engineers had at least one engineer parent. Halepete’s father taught him to solder in 3rd grade.

Huang’s kids both eventually joined Nvidia: Madison (former chef, LVMH Paris) as marketing director in 2020. Spencer (cocktail laboratory in Taipei, closed during pandemic) joined Nvidia robotics in 2022. Treated normally inside the company.
Israel and Hamas
October 7, 2023: Eyal Waldman’s daughter killed in the Hamas attack. Nvidia engineer Avinatan Or taken hostage.
Nvidia had ~3,000 Israeli employees, ~100 Palestinian employees in the West Bank. 400 Israeli workers were called to military duty.
Huang sent a company-wide email giving regional employees a bonus and matching donations to Israeli or Palestinian humanitarian aid (employee’s choice).
Huang publicly: “The heart and soul of the Blackwell processor came from Israel.” Bought Israeli startup Run:AI for $700M in April 2024.
China
2022: US blocked sales of A100/H100 to China. Huang sold modified versions; US issued a wider ban.
Chinese state media called video games “spiritual opium,” limited kids to 3 hours/week of play. But demand for dual-use gaming hardware was huge.
Before sanctions, ByteDance bought enough A100s to train 10 ChatGPTs. Black-market A100s sold at 2x retail in Shenzhen.
Huang: “If they can’t buy it from us, they’ll just build it themselves.”
Taiwan
Xi Jinping called “reunification” with Taiwan “inevitable” (NYE 2023). Satellite imagery showed China had built a replica of Taipei’s presidential district in the Gobi Desert.
TSMC fabs are a global production chokepoint. War would create multi-year delays in cars, smartphones, electronics, medical devices.
Huang ordered Deb Shoquist never to think about contingency planning for a Taiwan invasion: “I don’t want her spending one brain cell on trying to mitigate that, because it’s impossible.”

TSMC building two facilities in Phoenix on 1,100 acres, $40B+. 39 construction cranes including a 180-foot Manitowoc. 600,000 chips/year capacity, enough for full US domestic demand. Moisture-reclamation systems for the 110°F summers.
Intel: $32B expansion in Chandler, Arizona. Used ice in concrete to set in summer heat. 400,000 cubic yards of concrete (100 Olympic pools), 30,000 tons of steel.
Morris Chang (retired, 92) called the Arizona projects “doomed to fail” because of US work culture. Argued Taiwan’s “silicon shield” actually deters Chinese invasion.
Former US military official to Witt: “There is no way the USA will ever let China have the Taiwanese semiconductor factories. Period. Ever.”
Pat Gelsinger and Intel’s collapse
Nvidia worth 20x Intel by late 2024. Huang personally worth more than Intel.
Gelsinger (Intel CEO) had repeatedly tried to kill Nvidia: i740 (1990s), Larrabee (2000s), Arc (2022, 1% market share). Said Nvidia “got extraordinarily lucky.”
Intel’s board forced Gelsinger out in late 2024.
Why Nvidia won, by various accounts
Bas Aarts marveled at the perfect harmony of two cast-off technologies: “There is no way Nvidia is this lucky.”
Huang: “Luck, founded by vision.”
Dally: tireless work ethic. Diercks: “His hobbies are work, email, and work.”
Horstmann: adaptability. “He was not born as a great CEO; he was not destined to be one. He transformed himself into one, just by abstracting!”
Morris Chang: “His intellect is just superior.”
Chapter 21 — Jensen
Theme:
Cult of personality, the public Jensen, and the celebrity executive at GTC 2024.
The cult
Employees were rich and adored Huang. Saw him as a prophet whose predictions came true and added zeros to their net worth.
Reading Jensen carefully
Stories shifted in details. Quoting him directly was risky — saying it didn’t mean believing it.

Often contradicted himself in a single interview. Horstmann: “He’s not trying to stay on message. He’s trying to process real-time input, and he’s willing to entertain a contradictory thought for a while.”

Pay attention only when he started repeating himself. Big concepts (zero-billion-dollar market, speed of light) emerged after weeks tumbling in his mind, then got drilled into staff so thoroughly they sounded like brainwashed catechumens reciting them.
Public speaking
Despite hundreds of public appearances, Jensen genuinely hated public speaking. Visibly nervous before a small Gensler architecture talk.
Asked about AI doomsday: “No AI should be able to learn without a human in the loop.” Reasoning capability “two to three years out.”

Hao Ko, after Jensen had filled 45 minutes from a single question: “Look, when I first met him, he was talking about self-driving cars, and at the time that sounded crazy too. I’ve learned not to question him.”
The CalTech bench conversation
Wore a black Burberry monogram T-shirt; bought 24 of them in 2020 and rotated daily for 4 years.
Worth ~$100B that day. “Do you know how rich I am?” Asked what he’d do with the money: “I have no idea. None.”

Woke at 3:30 a.m. with a dog between his legs. Longest-serving CEO of any S&P tech stock at 31 years. Didn’t want to get up. But there were threats: customers building their own chips, AMD hiring software engineers, AI risking disappointment.
By 4 a.m. he was working. Always opened the day with the most important long-term project so the day couldn’t be a bust.
Hinted at a secret. Witt suspected it was Project Strawberry, a “rational” AI. Jensen’s repeated phrase: “When the marginal cost of doing math goes to zero, then what do you do?”
Witt’s reflection: Pascal’s gears mechanized arithmetic; Jensen’s machines were now coming for reason itself.
Chapter 22 — The Fear
Theme:
Bengio, Hinton, Sutskever, LeCun, and the divide over AI risk.
Yoshua Bengio’s conversion
Montreal AI pioneer, 2019 Turing Award (with LeCun and Hinton). Studied neural nets through several recessions.
Joke for years: if AI were so dangerous, why couldn’t he get a $10K research grant?
Early 2023, after using ChatGPT: The Fear hit on a slushy morning walk. Compared meeting ChatGPT to meeting an extraterrestrial. Worried about his children and grandchild.
Compared AI to nuclear war but worse: a malevolent AI could design a lethal pathogen wiping out everyone. “I don’t think there’s anything close in terms of the scale of danger.”
Convergence of concern
Bengio called Hinton, found Hinton had reached the same conclusion at the same moment.
Hinton then quit Google to advocate full-time about AI risk.
Sutskever pivoted to “alignment” research.
These three were #1, #2, #3 most-cited living computer scientists. All three thought AI might kill us all.
Yann LeCun’s opposing view
Third Turing recipient. Lead architect of a 1998 handwriting-recognition net licensed to the post office and banks (first widespread industrial use of a multilayer neural net).
Disagreed openly with longtime collaborator Bengio. “In theory, we’re still friends. But today we argue in public in ways that friends usually don’t” (Bengio).

LeCun’s argument: dominance drives are evolutionary, not inherent to AI. We set their goals. No one would be foolish enough to build a dominance-seeking AI. (Witt notes Pascal made a similar argument in the 1600s about his calculator.)
p(doom)
Bengio: 50%. LeCun: 0%. Hinton in early 2023: 50%. By 2024, Hinton lowered to 10–20%, “most notably because of Jensen.”
Jensen’s p(doom): zero, possibly negative. Vocally rejected the framing. At Denny’s, suggested Hinton was tarnishing his academic legacy.
Bengio (one of the only major AI scientists never to take Silicon Valley money): held firm.
Bengio’s response to Jensen’s “no data” argument
“Of course there is no data! Humanity hasn’t disappeared yet! Are we going to wait until we have repeated the death of humanity multiple times to decide that, oh, now we have data?!”
AI had had two unforeseeable upgrade leaps in 10 years (AlexNet, transformer). Nobody could say what the next breakthrough brings or when.
OpenAI’s November 2023 boardroom drama
Sutskever first voted to remove Altman, then days later pleaded for his reinstatement. Altman won, the rest of the board was replaced.
Microsoft’s “capped” interest tied OpenAI tightly to ever-larger models.
May 2024: OpenAI released GPT-4o (multimodal). Sutskever resigned the next day.
Talking with GPT-4o felt like talking with a hyperintelligent human (compared to the AI in Her).

Same day, Google showed Astra. Anthropic released Claude. Governments built sovereign AI centers. Musk’s xAI struck a $10B Oracle GPU deal. Meta announced $30B for 1M Nvidia chips and a dedicated nuclear reactor.
Witt’s own fear
ChatGPT launch made him fear his career was ending. GPT-4 already wrote better than he had in college.
The release of o1 raised OpenAI’s own assessment of bioweapon risk from “low” to “medium.”
Soon a 100-trillion-parameter model would rival the human brain in synapse count. What’s the role of humans after that?
Counter-arguments to existential AI fear:
Brain doesn’t learn through backpropagation
Neural nets only mimic neurons (no glial cells, no autonomic system, no hypothalamus, no hormones, no sex drive, no sleep, no dreams, no instinct to survive)
Not a product of Darwinian planetary laboratory
The upside (Bostrom’s 2024 Deep Utopia): a “solved world” of robots handling unpleasant tasks.

Fei-Fei Li’s Behavior-1K (GTC 2024): Mechanical Turk respondents ranked which tasks they most wanted robots to do. Top: scrubbing toilets, washing floors, cleaning up after parties. Bottom: jewelry shopping, squash, opening presents.
Witt: “Did I want a toilet robot? You bet I did.”
Late 2024: doomerism faded from op-eds. Altman essay on melted sand and AI as the most consequential fact in history. OpenAI partnered with defense start-up Anduril.
Witt could not shake the feeling that the end of his profession, of reality, of consciousness was approaching.
Chapter 23 — The Thinking Machine
Theme:
Witt’s final interview with Huang and a visit to Eos.
The Friday interview
After 4 days of GTC 2024, Huang was visibly exhausted. Hosted in his conference-room “office,” surrounded on all walls (and frosted glass) with whiteboard schedules and stack diagrams.

Critics had been circling: a journalist asked if he was the new Robert Oppenheimer (“Oppenheimer was building a bomb. We’re not doing that”). FTC chair Lina Khan was watching. French authorities had raided Nvidia’s France offices.

Witt asked what new jobs would be created by AI. Huang turned the question back: “When the marginal cost of doing math goes to zero, then what do you do?” Witt didn’t know. Huang: “You’re just as intelligent as I am to figure this out.”
Witt then played the Arthur C. Clarke clip about machines superseding humans. Huang’s face went pale.
The eruption
“I just feel like you’re interviewing the wrong person. I feel like you’re interviewing Elon right now, and I’m just not that guy.”
Then anger crescendoed. “Are calculators going to destroy math? That conversation is so old, and I’m so, so tired of it. I don’t want to talk about it anymore!”

Examples: agriculture made food cost zero. Electricity replaced torch-carrying. Long division automated. “We make the marginal cost of things zero, generation after generation after generation, and this exact conversation happens every single time!”
“This cannot be a ridiculous sci-fi story. I didn’t read his fucking books. I don’t care about those books! We are serious people, doing serious work.”
For 20 minutes, alternating accusatory, exasperated, and belittling. Called Witt’s questions “pedestrian.” “I don’t like these probing questions. I’m not into therapy.”
Witt: “I have never met anyone like you.” Huang: “I’m super normal.”
The two PR reps did not intervene; “they weren’t about to draw fire.”
Afterward Witt told one of the reps “that went well.” The rep laughed: “Oh, that? That was nothing.”
Witt’s reframe
In hindsight Huang’s anger was deliberate. He did not lose his temper all at once; he worked himself up over minutes, building steam.
The point was not personal. Huang was a serious man who hated science fiction.

Why Huang succeeded where others failed (parallel computing, AI, the Omniverse) was precisely that he refused to indulge airy speculation. Cold first principles, neither optimism nor fear, only patient business logic pushed to the outer limit.
Beyond that limit: he didn’t care to imagine. The dragon in the unexplored portion of the map was not a strategic question.
Witt realized the Nvidia executives he had interviewed were “wound as tight as piano strings” and were more afraid of Jensen yelling at them than of wiping out the human race.
Eos

Witt’s closing reflection: he was surrounded by a language model that would soon replace him. He felt inadequate in his “obsolete and dying flesh.” With each spin of the fan, with each pulse of the circuits, the thinking machine got a little smarter.
Only Jensen, “the American Daedalus,” could really see it all, from the scale of the atom to the dawn of machine consciousness.
The Lessons of History

is Will and Ariel Durant’s attempt to compress a lifetime of reading into a small set of conclusions about how civilizations rise, organize, and decay. It starts off by admitting that history is incomplete and filtered through bias, yet still useful if you read it as pattern recognition rather than prophecy. Other sciences tell us how we might behave but history tells us how we have behaved. The present is merely the past rolled up into this present moment. We know 1,000 things about the news of today, but rarely about the past. How can we understand our present without knowing our history?
It is pretty intense for 100 pages, but to sum up:

Revolutions often change the surface but not the underlying patterns of human nature. Each generation rebels against the previous one, and that can be natural and even useful. When everybody owns everything, nobody takes care of anything, and you cannot make men equal just by passing laws. Economic history repeats a cycle where gains accrue to the clever and talented, then fractures occur, a new minority rises, and the pattern repeats.
History and the Earth

From the geographical perspective, the author treats climate, terrain, and access to seas and rivers as the hard constraints that quietly shape trade, power, and culture, which feels grounded and practical when you look at how states actually develop and project influence.  However, as technology advances, the role that geography plays diminishes. For instance, the invention of airplanes totally redefines the world of trade and commerce. Previously, water was the primary mode of trade and it dictated which nations rose to power (those with large shorelines like Greece and Italy). Then, suddenly, airplanes shifted the power to nations with huge land masses in comparison to their coasts (USA, China, Russia). The first mover gains a huge advantage.
Biology and History
The biology and competition section was great, and it will feel familiar if you have read Dawkins’
The Selfish Gene

. When they describe life and society as driven by competition, selection, and replication, they are basically importing an evolutionary logic into economics, politics, and social hierarchy. The first biological lesson of history is that life is competition. Cooperation is real and it expands as technologies evolve, but mostly because it is a form of competition. We cooperate within our group, family, community, and nation in order to make our group more powerful. Cooperation is the ultimate form of competition. The second biological lesson of history is that life is also selection. From nature’s standpoint, we are all born unfree and unequal. Nature loves difference because it is what allow selection to focus on the strong and eliminate the weak. A little dark, but makes sense. The basic reality is competition.
Race and History

The author here emphasize that history is colorblind in the sense that civilization can rise under any race and in almost any circumstance. Over long time horizons, differences between peoples often give way to environmental pressures and opportunities. This pushes back against the idea that success is proof of inherent superiority. The driver is usually conditions, geography, institutions, and accumulated culture, not skin color.
Character and History

People often need to feel a little special, and a small amount of vanity or even self-delusion can be a motivator that helps individuals push forward. Poor and rich people tend to share similar impulses, but the rich have more opportunity, leverage, or skill to act on those impulses.

“Heroes” are often products of their situations. The situation creates the demand for toughness or courage, and the person rises into that role. If the situation never occurred, the “hero” might never have been noticed. In that sense, character qualities can be shaped by what circumstances force a person to become.
Morals and History

Morals are described as the way society encourages and pressures behavior from its members. In the three broad stages of history, hunting, agriculture, and industry, moral codes shift as societies shift. Some things we now call vices may once have functioned as virtues in different conditions. Industrialization then changes everyday life and morality by pulling people away from the home and tribe into factories and cities.

However, there is a difference between lived history and written history. History as it is written focuses on the exceptional because that is what stands out, but most people in every era are living ordinary lives. Look at Copernicus, who displaced humans from the center of the cosmos, and Darwin, who placed humans within the animal continuum. These shifts weakened the intuitive force of religious certainty because they challenged the idea of humans as uniquely central and specially designed.
Social Evolution and the Battle of Ideas

Social evolution is an interplay between custom and origination. Most people imitate, and a small minority innovate. History then becomes a contest among minorities whose ideas compete, with the winning minority later celebrated by the majority. But most new ideas are worse than the traditional alternatives they try to replace. That is why it is good for new ideas to be heard, but also good for them to be tested, questioned, and resisted. No single person can fully understand and safely redesign the full set of customs and institutions that a society has accumulated over centuries.
Civilization and Self-Restraint

Civilization is the most remarkable human creation, but also as something fragile. Civilization requires a balance between social order and personal freedom. Too much order can crush creativity and liberty, but too little order prevents cooperation and stable culture. Civilization is made possible by self-restraint, and freedom depends on boundaries. Without order, freedom collapses into chaos. In that sense, the author argues that capitalism and communism needs each other. What works here is that there is never an extreme end for both.
Religion and History

Religion as a powerful shared belief system that historically helped humans cooperate and maintain moral life among large populations. Religion, morals, and ethics are attempts to override older, individual survival instincts with newer social instincts. Religion helps bind people into a shared identity and shared rules. If a unifying belief system dies, what holds the civilization together dies.

Over time, philosophers begin to drive societal change more than the church, and later science replaces philosophy in that role. Science focuses on the external world, while questions like consciousness remain hard to answer through science alone. Religions tend to revive, that there is no historical example of mass moral life maintained without religion, and that religion helps people tolerate life by giving meaning, structure, and shared expectations. Industrial society replaces religious entities with secular ones, and that this makes morality feel less “given,” because laws now clearly come from fallible humans rather than divine command.
Economics and the Concentration of Wealth

Wealth concentrates repeatedly across history because valuable talents and skills concentrate. When ability concentrates, wealth follows, and when wealth concentrates, it can further amplify ability through opportunity and resources. People who can manage people end up managing those who manage things, and people who manage money often end up managing everyone. Societies can afford “freedom” only once they have achieved stability, because before that they are locked in survival competition.
Government and History

The first condition of freedom is limitation. If freedom is absolute, society dissolves into chaos, so the prime task of government is to establish order. Minority rule tends to emerge because abilities are unevenly distributed, which mirrors the uneven distribution of wealth. Genius often demands exhausting toil, and that both individuals and societies rely on continuity, individuals through memory and societies through tradition.

Real revolution is the enlightenment of the mind and the improvement of character, and emancipation is individual. Excess tends to produce backlash in the opposite direction. Once humans have culture and shared beliefs, they can “select” ideas through force, even through mass violence, which raises the dangerous question of who decides which ideas are “fit.”

On democracy, it has done more good than harm compared to alternatives, but democracy is not meant to make everyone equal in outcomes, it is meant to make access to opportunity more equal. The ideal is a fair starting field and open entry points where skill can be tested.
War and History

War is a recurring constant across civilizations because it is competition between groups, just scaled up. The paradox that war often accelerates technology and social change, and that this can sometimes produce longer periods of peace afterward. But the deeper claim remains that humans keep enlarging their instruments without enlarging their purpose, meaning our tools become more powerful even when our basic motives stay the same.
Is Progress Real

Progress is defined mainly as increasing control of the environment by life, and education as a core measure of progress because it transmits human heritage and learning. Progress may be real, not because we are born better than our ancestors, but because we are born into a richer inheritance of knowledge, art, and technique. Progress might be progress of means rather than ends: we pursue the same old desires, but with newer tools.

Do not be an optimist or a pessimist, be a realist. Life has difficulties and delights, and the difficulties are part of the price of existence. Human nature changes very slowly, at a “geological” pace, because it is tied to biology. Culture and restraint push against that uncivilized baseline, and culture tightens its hold as the amount of inherited knowledge grows.

I first discovered Viktor Shvets through his previous book "The Great Rupture" (2020), which completely changed how I think about economic transitions and why our current system feels so broken. That book introduced his concept of the "Fujiwara Effect" and explained how we're transitioning from the Industrial Age to the Information Age—but it left me with so many questions about what comes next and how this transition actually plays out. When "Twilight Before the Storm" came out in 2024, I knew I had to read it immediately. This book essentially picks up where "The Great Rupture" left off, diving deeper into the political and social implications of everything Shvets outlined before. If his first book explained why everything is breaking down, this one maps out exactly what's likely to replace it.

Ever feel like the world's gone completely off the rails? Viktor Shvets thinks there's a good reason for that—and it's not pretty. In "Twilight Before the Storm," this Wall Street veteran argues we're basically living through the 1930s all over again, complete with economic chaos, political extremism, and societies tearing themselves apart.
His big insight? Two massive storms—tech disruption and financial weirdness—have crashed into each other like hurricanes, creating the perfect conditions for everything to fall apart.

What makes this different from other doom-and-gloom books is that Shvets actually knows what he's talking about after 40 years on Wall Street, and he doesn't just tell you what's wrong—he tells you what's coming next.

The timing is pretty wild too. This came out in August 2024, right before we started seeing Trump's trade wars escalate, AI start seriously messing with jobs, and young people basically saying "screw the free market." If you've been wondering why nothing seems to work the way economics textbooks say it should, or why politics feels like a dumpster fire, Shvets breaks it all down in a way that actually makes sense.
Viktor Shvets was born in Soviet Ukraine, educated in Australia, and has spent almost 40 years as a big shot strategist at places like Deutsche Bank, Credit Suisse, and now Macquarie Capital.

Think about that background for a second—he's lived under communism, experienced Western capitalism, and made a career predicting what markets will do next. That's exactly the kind of perspective you want when someone's telling you the world's about to change.

What makes him different is that he doesn't just look at charts and numbers—he weaves together history, politics, and technology to figure out where we're headed. His last book "The Great Rupture" got him noticed as someone who actually gets how civilizations change, and now he's the guy Bloomberg and CNBC call when they need someone to explain why everything's so messed up. Plus, he's been right about a lot of stuff before, which always helps.
We're Living Through the 1930s All Over Again
Here's Shvets' big idea, and it's kind of terrifying:
what's happening right now looks a lot like the 1930s, when everything went to hell and people had to choose between communism, fascism, or some kind of democracy that actually worked.
Sound familiar? We're facing similar choices, except now it's between what he calls "enlightened communism," "high-tech feudalism," democracy that actually regulates stuff, or just complete chaos.

The thing is, our current version of capitalism is basically dying because it never understood how real people actually work. Turns out, most folks don't want to live with constant economic anxiety and massive inequality. When the mainstream political parties stop offering real solutions, people start looking for alternatives—and that's how you get the rise of all these populist movements we're seeing everywhere.
The key thing to understand

: we're in this weird "twilight" phase where the old system is clearly broken but we haven't figured out what comes next. The choices we make in the next 10 years are going to determine whether we transition smoothly or everything goes to hell.
The "Fujiwara Effect": When two bad things collide
The most important concept -
"Fujiwara Effect"
—which is when two hurricanes smash into each other and create something way worse. Shvets says that's exactly what's happening to our economy with these two massive forces:
Technology gone crazy
: AI is getting so good it's making humans irrelevant in more and more jobs
Financial markets gone insane
: There's now somewhere between $500 trillion to $1 quadrillion floating around in financial markets (that's 5-10 times what the entire world produces in a year)

Here's the scary part: these two things are feeding off each other. All that excess money fuels more tech innovation, which creates even more excess money, which speeds up the tech revolution even more. It's like a feedback loop.
Back in the day, humans were the smart ones and machines did the heavy lifting. Now AI is handling the thinking, so what exactly are humans supposed to do?

Meanwhile, money used to be scarce (which is the whole foundation of capitalism), but now there's way too much of it. Modern economies need $3-4 of debt just to get $1 of growth, compared to the normal $1-1.50 ratio that used to work fine.

This is why interest rates keep falling globally (what economists call the "neutral rate" or r*). It's not just coincidence—it perfectly lines up with when financialization really took off after 2008, and it matches the rise of the Information Age where both capital and labor are getting squeezed out of the equation.
What Young People Think Capitalism
Here's something that'll blow your mind:
Millennials and Gen Z make up about 35-40% of adults now and will soon be the majority, but their values are more like their great-grandparents than their parents.

While Baby Boomers were all about "freedom" and "individual choice" (hence the whole free-market thing), younger people actually want the government to be more involved in the economy and care way more about stability than some abstract notion of "freedom."
And honestly? It makes perfect sense. Young people have watched free-market capitalism give them:
Housing prices that are completely insane
Job security that doesn't exist
Massive inequality everywhere
A planet that's literally on fire

They're naturally gravitating toward a system where the government actually tries to manage capitalism's worst impulses, kind of like what happened in the 1950s and 60s. Shvets thinks this generational shift is going to completely reshape politics over the next decade, affecting everything from taxes to trade policy.
The China situation: It's complicated
One of the book's most fascinating sections dives into what's really happening with China, and it's way more nuanced than the usual "China bad" or "China taking over" narratives.

Shvets argues that whether the current Cold War turns into actual hot war depends on three things: the relative strength between the US and China, what happens with Russia's crumbling empire, and whether the US can actually get its act together internally.
Here's the thing about China—it's facing some serious structural problems that look eerily similar to Japan in the 1990s, but potentially worse:
China's growth miracle is basically over

. From the 1980s to 2010s, China had this perfect storm of factors: unleashing entrepreneurial energy after decades of suppression, riding the wave of Baby Boomer globalization (especially joining the WTO in 2001), and tapping into unlimited cheap labor. But now that model has hit a wall.
The problems are mounting up
Massive inequality
: The gains haven't been shared evenly
Capital misallocation on steroids
: Think 2 billion square feet of empty apartment buildings and high-speed trains to nowhere
Savings rate through the roof
: People save too much because there's no decent social safety net, which creates overcapacity and deflation
Demographics disaster
: The one-child policy means they're aging fast and running out of workers
Productivity stagnation
: Despite all the investment, actual productivity growth has been terrible
The political shift makes it worse

. Under Deng Xiaoping, China kept the Communist Party separate from day-to-day governance and let private businesses do their thing. But Xi Jinping has basically reversed that, centralizing power and subordinating private companies to state goals. This creates what Lenin called "democratic centralism"—an oxymoron where you can debate internally but once the leadership decides something, everyone falls in line or faces consequences.
China's in a trap

: They need to boost consumption and give people more money to spend, but that would require the government giving up control—something they seem unwilling to do. The alternative is to export their overproduction to other countries, but their attempts to remake global trade rules are making that harder.
The scary parallel

: Japan in the 1990s was already a rich, homogeneous society when its bubble burst, so it could just coast on global growth. China is still a middle-income country with massive inequality, and there might not be much global growth to ride. Plus Japan was part of the Western system—China is trying to replace it.
Shvets' take? This makes the US-China relationship way more dangerous than most people realize, because desperate powers do desperate things.
Four ways this could all play out
Instead of just saying "things will change," Shvets actually maps out four specific scenarios for where we're headed:
"Enlightened Communism"
: Think Nordic countries but everywhere—strong government involvement but you still get to keep your freedoms and the economy stays efficient
"High-Tech Feudalism"
: Basically authoritarian control with extreme inequality—imagine if tech billionaires became actual feudal lords
"Constrained Democracy"
: Government gets back into the business of regulating capitalism while keeping democratic institutions—kind of a return to the 1950s-60s mixed economy approach
"World on Fire"
: Wars, conflicts, and complete chaos—basically if we repeat the 1930s-40s playbook
According to Shvets, we're currently on track for either constrained democracy or world on fire, depending on what choices get made in the next few years.
The one thing that's NOT going to happen is going back to pure free-market capitalism—that ship has sailed.
Shvets Solutions
Unlike most books that just point out problems, Shvets actually offers concrete ideas for what to do:
Universal Basic Income
: Because AI is going to eliminate a ton of jobs and people need money to live
Completely overhauling education
: Our schools are still designed for the Industrial Age, which is kind of a problem
New tax systems
: To deal with all the financial weirdness and extreme inequality
Global Marshall Plan
: Help developing countries so the whole world doesn't explode (this is crucial because if poorer countries get left behind, we'll see massive conflicts)
Government as guardrails
: Not running everything, but making sure capitalism doesn't go completely off the rails—more active government spending to actually manage these transitions
These aren't pie-in-the-sky ideas—they're practical policies that could actually prevent the worst-case scenarios while keeping as much freedom and prosperity as possible.
About that debt hysteria

: Shvets also tackles the whole "OMG national debt will destroy us" panic. His point? Countries aren't households. When a country like the US borrows money, it's basically borrowing from itself. Japan has been running massive deficits for decades and somehow hasn't collapsed into hyperinflation. The real issue isn't debt levels—it's managing this massive "cloud of finance" that's been created by decades of financialization.
The Book is as
RELEVANT
as it can get:

The crazy thing is how much more relevant this book has become since it came out. Trump's 2025 tariffs are creating the highest trade barriers since World War II—exactly the kind of 1930s-style economic nationalism Shvets warned about. AI is messing with 40% of global jobs (85 million displaced, 97 million new ones created)—which is exactly the complex disruption his "Fujiwara Effect" predicts.
And get this: there's an $84 trillion wealth transfer happening right now (2024-2045), with Gen Z expected to control $74 trillion by 2040.

Shvets has been all over financial media throughout 2024-2025, basically doing victory laps as his predictions come true. His call that we'd see the "end of the neoliberal consensus" looks pretty smart now that both political parties are embracing more government intervention in the economy.
People actually like this book
The book's been getting solid reviews (4.28/5 on Goodreads), with readers consistently saying they love how it connects history, politics, economics, and markets without being boring as hell.

Russell Napier, who wrote "Anatomy of The Bear," calls it "a must read" and says Shvets asks "all the right questions" while giving "answers based on actually understanding financial and economic history."
The historical comparisons are consistently praised as eye-opening, and readers love getting actual solutions instead of just more doom and gloom.

Financial media has been all over this book, with regular coverage on Bloomberg, CNBC, and major podcasts. It's even getting academic recognition, with scholarly reviews noting how well it brings together different disciplines.
Who should definitely read this
You need this book if you're
Trying to figure out why politics has gotten so insane and divisive
An investor wondering why traditional economic rules seem completely broken
Running a business and trying to navigate all the tech disruption and changing worker expectations
A parent who wants to understand why your kids have such different economic values than you do
Anyone worried about what happens to democracy when inequality and polarization get this bad

The writing is accessible enough that you don't need an economics degree, but sophisticated enough that finance professionals take it seriously. At about 300 pages, it's substantial without being a slog, and Shvets' real-world experience keeps it grounded instead of getting lost in abstract theory.
Bottom Line:
"Twilight Before the Storm" works because it does something most economic forecasting completely fails at:
it explains not just what might happen, but why it's happening and what we can actually do about it.

Shvets combines the analytical skills of a top Wall Street strategist with the historical perspective of someone who's lived through different economic systems and the practical wisdom of someone who's navigated multiple economic crises.

Unlike most economists who just extrapolate current trends, Shvets looks at structural breaks—those moments when the entire system changes direction. He's not trying to predict whether the stock market will go up or down next quarter; he's mapping out which economic system will replace capitalism over the next decade. His track record speaks for itself: he called the 2008 financial crisis, predicted the rise of populism, anticipated the breakdown of globalization, and saw the AI disruption coming before most people even knew what ChatGPT was. What's scary is how many of his "future" predictions from this book are already starting to happen just months after publication.

The book's core message is pretty sobering but not hopeless: we're living through a transition as big as the Industrial Revolution, but unlike previous generations, we actually have the knowledge and tools to handle it well.
The real question isn't whether change is coming—it's whether we'll shape that change or just let it happen to us.
If you want to understand why the economic and political world feels like it's falling apart and what might come next, this book gives you a roadmap that actually makes sense.

Solid introduction to computational thinking and the basics of computer science. Glad to have a pretty good primer into the computer science syllabus before starting my computer science degree in university.

The book covers core topics such as the basis of computational thinking, the notion complexity, the notorious data structures, algorithms and computer architecture. Some parts were a great refresher to topics I am already familiar with such as complexity, data structures and algorithms.  On the other hand, computer architecture and databases concepts were completely new to me. Pretty interesting stuff, I must say.
The book, fortunately, was not too deep of a dive into the academic side of things, rather it did something like a breadth first search on many topics which is expected of an introductory material.

The book is for everyone. It suits as a refresher for those who are already familiar with the material and also for those who are interested in a general overview of computer science (or even for those who are sitting on the fence).

Logical thinking - operators, boolean algebra (associativity, distributivity, DeMorgan’s law)

Complexity:

2 power n (exponential), n squared, n log n, n, log n, constant → coefficients cancel out when calculating % change → use dominant term (i.e n squared in a quadratic equation) → when plotting on a graph we realise that the coefficients do not really matter compared to the dominant term, same applies to space complexity for computer’s memory
best case, worst case, average case (usually consider both average case and worst case → i.e worst case is when cards are sorted in reverse, best case is when everything is sorted)

Backtracking → 8 Queens Chess Problem

Divide and Conquer → Breaking big problems into smaller sub problems until it is not reducible → Sorting Tasks → Merge Sort, Bubble Sort → Follow up would be to calculate complexity (see Page 51)

Memoizing → Helps to remember past calculations so that it does not repeat (i.e Fibonacci Sequence calculations)
Bottom-Up Approach: Simple answer rebuild into general solutions

Data:

Stack → Pop, Push → First In, Last Out → i.e Text Editor (Undo and Forward) → Backtracking algorithm
Queue → Enqueue, Dequeue → First in, First Out
Priority Queue
List, Sorted List, Map (Dictionary), Set (Unordered Groups of Unique Items) → Insert, Remove, Get, Sort, Slice, Reverse
Structures
Array, Linked List, Double Linked List (Linked → → ← Pointers)

Instructions / Deletions in the list to be extremely first
Do not need random, unordered access to data
Insert / Delete in the middle of the list
Cannot evaluate the exact size of list (i.e If list keeps growing)
Tree (Node, Root Node, Edge, Leaf Nodes, Path), Binary Search Tree (Value-Key, Right >, Left <), Binary Heap (Both > or <) → Tree Rebalancing
Graph
Hash Table → Computing using Hash Function

Linear Programming Problems (Optimisation Problems)
BFS, DFS, Graphs (Searching), Sorting via Pivoting

Using SQL → SELECT <FIELD NAME> ; FROM <TABLE NAME> WHERE <CONDITIONS>
* represents all
Under WHERE, we can use ORDERBY( ) or GROUPBY( ) functions
JOIN function allows the table to merge with a reference (just like  in excel)

Ditches tabular relations → Ditches SQL and taps on other query languages → NoSQL databases → More flexibility → No need to join rows, do not need fixed schemas and each data entry can have its own configuration of fields
Data entry is known as a document while related documents are grouped in a collection
Key-Value stores → HTML, URL to access links to the web → Consider caching if its too slow since caching allows access to frequently used items
Graph Databases

Now that Trump is inaugurating as President, this book is highly relevant. I came across
Superpower Showdown

as one of Niall Ferguson’s recommendations. He is one of the historians that I highly respect after his debate with Zakaria on liberal international world order. Therefore, I trust his recommendations with a higher degree of certainty.
The book depicts the history of the trade war, the struggles each side goes through and recapping its history leading up to it (I likened the flavour and writing contents to be similar to
Chip War
which is also a phenomenal book!) The trade war is a very complex matter that essentially boils down to two issues: What does US and China want? Can they compromise on the issues?

US believes that by allowing China into the WTO, it should be more liberalise politically, tackling its human rights issue which was proposed as the Clinton administration. This ties back to preventing the spread of Communism. Yet, we come to realise that China is somehow more “one-party state,” especially with the rise of Xi - this highly contrast Deng Xiaoping’s and Zhu’s mini-liberal reformation after Mao’s China. This is a problem for the US - a capitalist and liberal state. The problem stems from the Chinese becoming a superpower economically, yet differing in ideologies. This would subsequently lead to issues such as China devaluing its currency to dump its exports onto US, hurting domestic workers, human rights issues and ultimately, Chinese stealing of US technologies.
We then transit to Trump’s lead of US. The back and forth struggle between forming a resolution that is
both agreed on and sustained on

forms the crux of this book. We realised how hard it is for either party to form a necessary resolution, coupled with the internal conflicts faced on both ends (Lighthizer’s hawkishness versus Munichin’s dovish attitude on China, Xi’s reluctance to take the blame with CCP taking embarrassing hits when Trump runs his mouth on Twitter). It is a whole lot of mess. We even examine Trump’s leadership position and economic considerations when implemented. Jumping out of Trans-Pacific agreement, tariffs threats on Mexico and Canada, random twitter comments are questionable to some extent. Chinese refusal to compromise and fight back is not helping the situation either (Huawei’s role and technology plays a big part in this). We notice that US deals are highly centred on trade related issues rather than structural political issues (which are a no-compromise in China). Are tariffs also the best policy after so much damage being done?

The book opened my perspectives on the trade war. A nuanced topic like this requires a nuanced approach which is formulated through our own thinking. I noticed a little bias towards Trump so do watch out for those. Nonetheless, the book definitely provides a good background to it, a bit draggy at times, but maybe the repeated concepts play a big role in retaining the information better. This is a must recommend and it definitely shaped my views on US-China relations heading into 2025 (Tiktok ban is happening soon as we speak).
