A lot of issues were b not addressed (i.e Opening up of American credit card firms, cutting China’s steel exports etc.), every time they were close to reaching a deal, the plan would be scrapped. Trump fired Ross due to the fact that there were too many troubles producing a joint-statement - but the delay was due to other complicated factors such as combination of legal, regulatory and political decision making which was outside of the business deal making stuff. After Lighthizer (a hardcore nationalist) took over Ross, he was brutal towards China, accusing them on stealing technology and having no response the liberalization, unlike Trump’s soft approach, trying not to single out China and blaming the whole China situation on past US leadership. The question China is trying to find out was: Is Lighthizer speaking for Trump? Who is the main aggressor here? When China opened up their markets from a 49% to 51% skate, US did not show any gratitude.

The fight between US and China resembled a schoolyard brawl - the two relentlessly circled each other determined to settle old scores. To Trump, China had been cheating the US for decades and it was time to smack down the cheaters. To Xi, America was a bully and was jealous of China’s ascent. America was trying to clobber China before it grew too powerful to challenge. It was time for someone to show the bully he would not back down. Each side thought it was more resilient than it really was; each side exaggerated the weakness of the other.
More Miscalculations

China plans for a fast victory as its usually reliable engines of growth - exports, real estate and industrial outputs - were all slowing down. The last thing they wanted another problem, especially when Trump slapped them with tariffs on solar panels (a dominated China industry). He did not want to diminish his political standing due to the tariffs before his China reformation meeting (removing presidential term limit). Liu, Xi’s advisor, proposed a 5 point deal with the US (which is strange because it is usually US that proposes a deal and China scaling back on it), which included cutting of tariffs on autos, boost imports and increased funding in commercial deals. Yet, the offer barely registered with US. The pledge of financial liberalisation was a rehash of previous offers, they believed. Liu also did not make offer on what US considered to be the greatest economic sin: Dumping and stealing of US intellectual property. At the same time, internal divisions amongst US would undermine and hamper the US efforts which also reflected the views of trade and Trump:
Was he blue-collar Trump - making good on his campaign promise to stop the pillage of America by Chinese imports?
Was he wall-street Trump - worried about the market reaction to a deepening trade dispute?
He was both but it was hard to tell which side he was ascending at a particular time.
Problems faced by the US should they place tariffs on steel:
Rising prices on US consumers of steep - a much larger industry than producers of steel
Cost of production would rise for producers
Timing could be wrong - why anger Europe, Japan, Canada and others when you want to present a solid front against China

The problem US faced was China’s excess steel capacity whereby China could offshore the steel to other countries which would then be imported to US. This would not count as Chinese exports. That leaves the US with two options:
Stop the transshipments
US hits everyone with tariffs

Trump decided to hit the 25% tariff on steel and 10% tariff on aluminium. The North Korea argument did not work anymore- China seemed to be cozying up to Kim Jong Un. Confronting China on trade would make the situation with North Korea worse. Trump wanted tariffs no matter what and it was clear what the outcome would be.

Section 301 report - the US was filing a brief accusation on China for being the world’s biggest trade criminal and providing evidence of Beijing’s crimes and under US laws, the US did not have to prove the case, it could judge China and punish it.

The point of this is for US audience to ultimate back American actions - convincing China was up to no good and use Section 301 report as a resource. China, unlike Japan, did not rely on US military. Thus, China thought they ought to be treated with more respect unlike 1980s Japan and Washington dealings. China is an equal to the US and it will not yield to pressure tactics.

US Treasury Secretary, Paulson and his protege, Mnuchin, had good ties with Liu. Meanwhile, Navarro and Lighthizer were opposed to their trading friendliness and insisted on tariffs to force China to change. There is a clear definition between nationalist and globalist wings of the administration. Not only was the Trump administration tangling with China; it was tangling internally. In the end, US created an eight-part demand (not only they had to reduce US trade deficit by 200 billion in 2 years, they had to end pressure on US firms to transfer technology, stop cyber-spying, strengthen intellectual property and slash tariffs; furthermore, no retaliation is allowed), which was a “surrender or die” proposal. In response, China also presented a tough framework (drop Section 301 and cease tariff threats, better treatment of Chinese technology companies etc, The tough US demands provoked a similar Chinese response, and the divided US team made it impossible for Beijing to know who it could turn to for help in Washington. The negotiations also went terribly. Both sides could not agree to a joint statement. The “wall-street” Mnuchin and his soft approach backfired when the media said that “Trump is putting the trade war on hold,” with some calling him weak. Mnuchin received a lot of criticisms and blue-collar Trump is now in full swing, adamant on putting the first blow on China. To prevent tariffs, China would have to pledged to purchase large sum of exports from the US such as soybeans and electronics to reduce the trade deficit. There was some flaws in keeping track of the spending - double-counting, China did not include any signed deals and did not commit on multi-year purchases. Beijing was disappointed by the plan’s failure. There is not a way to design a system without a series of loopholes that are easy to exploit or where well intentioned investment that intends to seek out profits is not allowed in the US. Despite being able to freeze all assets and lumping ISIS and China, “Trump has never been that we should cut off investment from China.” Senior economic officials tried to convince Trump that trade surplus or deficit - especially with one country - is not a measure of economic success as neither economic growth nor job production depended on whether exports outpaced imports. Furthermore, economic prosperity in America has been strongly positive correlated with trade deficits and not surplus (Trump did not heed). To Trump, it is about structural changes that create fair market access, he believed deficits gave the other party more money which makes them stronger. But by that same logic, Chinese purchases of US bonds would make US more powerful at Chinese expense because of the money flooding into the Treasury’s coffers. Trump never brought that argument because Beijing could threaten to dump securities and drive up interest rates. Trump philosophy on this was simple: Retaliate and more tariffs would be slammed - forcing its opponents into submission.
Reducing deficits is not as good compared to focusing on Section 301 complaints:
China would increase US imports by reducing their sales
Concentrating on structural issues like subsidies and forced technology transfer could unite allies who had similar complaints against China
Convincing China to reduce tariffs and other barriers was also a winner because it would encourage China to boost imports long-term, not just short-term fix to get the US off its back

Trade war started with constant back and forth with tariffs. Many of the Chinese firms and USA agricultural business suffered. Beijing was after US most valuable technology and would steal it either through spying or through arm-twisting. That had to stop as US would lose its edge economically and military while Beijing denied it was engaged in such outrageous practices. The clash was at the heart of the US-China trade war. China believed that the accusations made by US about “technological theft” was disgusting. They could date it back to Deng Xiaoping, opening up their domestic economy in exchange for some form of technology. A joint venture between US and China in the 1990s had to include technological sharing by default. “China is effectively making an offer multinationals cannot refuse,” firms benefited greatly from its domestic market (GE, aviation companies). US companies accused of China’s stealing of technology but it lands in Chinese court and is ultimately dismissed. Companies are now just suing one another to no end. It got so bad that the countries is banning their home-grown companies to do business internationally (i.e Micron, AMD, Qualcomm banned products in China).

2019 Hong Kong prodemocracy protests brought back the human rights issue. Trump reluctantly signed the bill to reestablish a trade-human rights linkage - he had little stomach to pick a fight with Beijing over human rights. A battle could hurt corporate America which often chose Hong Kong as a gateway to Asia. Usually, China would rely on US Business CEOs to convince the president to back off, however, this time, they gave China the cold shoulder and fed Trump administration officials the information they needed to launch an offensive against Chinese economic policies. The change in attitude did not have a single cause:
American business faced a steady acceleration of practices they found offensive that accelerated global financial crisis in 2008
Beijing’s “Made in China 2025” report laid out goals in 2015 for China to become number one in advanced technology sparked concerns
Western firms figured the only way to achieve point 2 was to steal technology

Xi’s increased reliance on state-owned firms and government power, together with cybersecurity law that required foreign firms in China to store sensitive data in the country’s and favour Chinese network equipment over foreign products
China has put in place an expansive system for monitoring company behaviour, known as social credit system, which could blacklist firms that did not yield to government demands.

Trump wanted for US firms to leave China and move back to the US but his advisers realised a large-scale exodus to the US was unrealistic given America’s higher wages and short-age of skilled blue-collar labor. The administration renegotiated North American FTA to give Trump’s blessing to Mexico as a low-wage haven for China corporate refugees - tariff free access to US markets. At the same time, Trump used trade to squeeze Mexico on immigration.
Everyone decided to renew ties again:

“The lack of meaningful implementation of reforms for the last many years is a source of deep frustration for the US business community. The latest five year plan has further thrown into doubt the trajectory of reforms. There is a major trust gap right now in our relationship. By taking further action to liberalise the economy, this old put a floor under the current situation and we could begin to build trust.”
China defended by stating that “
the pace of China’s reform and opening up is very rapid and faster than that of any developing country.”
China assured to wait a while more, but American business executives were tired of waiting,

“how can it be that those who know China best, work there and do business there are among those now arguing for more confrontation? The answer lies in the story of stalled competition policy and slow pace of opening which has discouraged and fragmented the American business community.”

The solution was to go through “couples therapy” with Beijing relying on US big business (i.e Blackstone CEO etc.) to let the White House listen. It then leads to a lot of internal conflict on both ends which ties back to the question of “Does Trump really want a deal or just attacking China and controlling their economy?” Trump and Mnuchin agreed so have a 10% tariff first below rising it to 25%. When 10% was first implemented, China also fired back tariffs on selected items. Surprisingly, the Dow Jones tanked. China and US is now becoming more desperate of their economy especially before the deadline of 25% tariffs. Industrial production, consumer consumption and investor’s sentiment were all weakening, blue-collar Trump would transit to wall-street Trump. China would follow suit as well to save their own economy, trying to calm jittery investors. They tried to reconcile again but there were a host of issues dividing the two nations:
United States wanted China to make a formal offer, not simply hint what it would do
China wanted to have talks first before making an offer
Two sides did not trust each other’s leadership

Trump was erratic and unpredictable and Chinese officials feared that he would make public, through a tweet or an off-the-cut statement, any offer China made as a way to box in Xi or misrepresent what Xi said.

The US worried that the more disciplined and experienced Xi would get Trump to make commitments on issues that the president did not understand or had not bothered to study. Trump might fight for Chinese purchases of goods, rather than fight for structural changes in the Chinese’s economy.

China subsequently agreed to buy more of US imports to decrease its trade surplus with US, but we note later on the agreed upon 30% of goods purchased was unsustainable. Nonetheless, China agreed to buy more agricultural goods, crack down on fentanyl sales and help negotiations with North Korea over nuclear weapons. But we realised how vague the deal was (Chinese said they would open markets and prevent technology theft but only in accordance with policies already approved by the government and the party. No mention of any US requests and the coverage of state media that is highly censored was so effective that the Chinese population thinks that US has caved). It will then lead to the cycle of “if the deal is not in time, launch the tariffs again (even thought deadline has been extended by 90 days).” At the same time, US arrested the daughter of Huawei and news of her arrest produced a nationalist backlash in China, threatened once again to derail trade negotiations. Despite Trump saying tariffs will not cost Americans anything, markets were plummeting and Chinese suppliers did not cut their prices for the goods they exported to the US. Thus, tariffs added to the prices Americans paid. Business investment and international trade. Over time, that was bound to reduce employment and wages and cut into consumer spending, traders feared. “Trade policy concerns went from a virtual non-factor in US volatility to one of its leading sources in recent decades.” Because of Trump’s ignorance of trade policy, stocks dropped but Trump believed markets will always rebound and that China’s deal is more important. Market did not reverse and Trump’s administration had to reassure that Jerome Powell’s job is safe.

China would then bounce back and forth with its trade deals with no resolution. China wants US to remove the tariffs as the economy is turning down, while US wants to target structural issue that China does not want to compromise (only willing to compromise on trade). China has to concede a lot which made them realise maybe a deal with American terms was not worth it as there is nothing in for them. Xi soon turned down all plans and Trump launched his 25% tariffs.

Now China is not holding back, thinking of ways to attack the US hegemony. Political democracy protests in Hong Kong made the situation worse, indicating a new era of Cold War. After lots of tariffs which boosted the prices for consumer goods, Trump would not be dissuaded and believed that China rejected his peace offerings, thinking that he was a weak man. He would show them how wrong they were. “Our great American companies are hereby ordered to immediately start looking for an alternative to China, including bringing your companies
home and making your products in the USA

. The same day Beijing announced retaliation, worried that losing American multinationals would impact the economy further. Trump might not have the power to force MNCs out of China but he had untested authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to block financial transactions, acquisitions, exports, imports and many other business activities during a “national emergency.” This was the law that Treasury used to sanction terrorist groups and nations like North Korea and Iran.
National Security Council’s Asia chief, Pottinger, believed that US before Trump had been complacent about China in three different ways:
Assumed that deeper economic ties between China and the West would inevitably lead Beijing to liberalise politically and economically.
China experts downplayed ideology as a fundamental driver of Beijing’s heavier Under Xi, ideology was becoming as important as it was Mao.
Experts believed that CCP was simply interested in survival but Pottinger believed the party had global geopolitical designs.

“There are consequences when Chinese are in your networks. It is like saying we need the China market so badly that we need to deprioritise our national security - it is analogous to say let the KGB build all our telecom networks and computer systems because they are offering a great discount during the Cold War. Despite Pottinger’s argument, there were some push backs:
US were losing ground in China as US pressure forced Chinese companies to become more efficient and less dependent on them.
The Chinese would turn to European and Japanese suppliers instead.

As for Huawei, Washington would not be able to kill off Huawei since its technology was so embedded in European telecommunication networks which are linked to American ones. At the same time, Wall Street Trump was in full swing - election was coming, his ace card was the economy and the trade imbroglio with China was the Joker that could screw everything up. Xi also needed to showcase at the 70th year progress of CCP anniversary but was facing with trade war with US that was sinking the economy, unrest in Hong Kong for democratic protests. These setbacks formed criticism of Xi from political, business and academic elites who believed power in one person was not the way to progress. Thus, getting a trade deal with US could reinforce his standing.

Huawei, however, was able to branch out into Europe and US suppliers were reluctant to lose Huawei (as they were a big customer). Trump’s trump card of using Huawei as leverage was slowly fading, despite Huawei being very dependent on American semiconductor chips.

In the past, US used a 40-40-20 deal (40% could be discussed and solved now, 40% would need further negotiations and 20% would be off-limits), now Trump was looking for a complete deal, not a partial one that was used in the past. These 20% was always related to National Securities matters. They decided to do negotiations by blocks and in conclusion, the details were, in exchange of a modest reduction of US tariffs:
In exchange for modest tariff reductions, China would aggressively buy more products and services and nearly doubling spending on farm products from pre-trade war levels.
Beijing would also once again agree to tighten intellectual property protection and open further its market for financial services

Finally, they agreed on a truce. However, sustaining it was another issue. US essentially gave 3 chances of negotiations before it imposed back its tariffs and US had accessed to the WTO as an arbiter. China’s timing for the “one-sided truce” was also questionable, especially with the new outbreak of the coronavirus. Economy was weakening, together with poor management of the virus, leading to domestic and international tensions. On the US side, Trump was facing impeachment and he needed to score this trade victory before his elections, showing that he could still get things done despite unfavourable circumstances. It is a constant vicious cycle where the deals resembled the beginning of the trade war.
In some surprising ways, the Trump administration began to resemble the Clinton administration on China trade:
The only way to change China was to line up with reformers and try to help them with their internal battles.

Chinese leaders had to believe that change was in their interest and was not being forced upon them from outside - that was what Chinese thought of Lighthizer and his gamble on a transformative deal which came up short.

China needs a Zhu Rongji - the Chinese premier who used US pressure during WTO talks to remake the Chinese economy instead of centralised power and wanted to expand the power of the state to control the economy. Despite Zhu’s tenure being remembered for a short-term suffering of layoffs, uncertainty and rising inequality, there has been no one since who could convince the Chinese bureaucracy into accepting what was necessary for China’s long term success.

China is now staring to increase its decoupling initiative and is challenging the notion that private enterprises coupled with democracy is the way to lead a successful economy. Their state-led models that features bureaucratic direction, heavy censorship and a flood of cash, combined with competition at the local level makes it not obvious that America or China will prevail. Niall Ferguson who coined the term “Chimerica” and publicised the notion that the two nations’ futures are intertwined, now thinks that the coupling is dead and is because of the trade war. “It has now gone from trade war to Cold War. Having an American enemy helps Xi Jinping consolidate power and justify his Mao-like tendencies. Likewise, having a Chinese enemy gives Trump political traction too.” Both countries’ citizens are also increasing polarised against one another. An external enemy will help unify fractious Americans, as the Cold War against the Soviet Union did and it will rally to Congress to spend what is needed to contain China and ultimately prevail.

Economic research now provides with an in depth review of tariffs - studies have come to realised that tariffs did more harm than good through increased prices and rising inequality. This is due to retaliation and increased prices of imports.

The book argues that trade war was more harmful than good. Besides the economic backlash, the book notes that Chinese stealing rate of US technologies has stayed the same, together with the trade deficit (US switch to other countries for imports due to increased Chinese product costs, but these other countries’ factories are owned by China).

Even in China, the Chinese one-state model is increasingly demanding which might lead to its struggle trying to be a world superpower. Note on the increased lending and spending on domestic companies as a high percentage of the companies’ revenue. In fact, US opening of China’s markets might be good for them. However, for now, there seems to be no sign (when observing US silicon’s valley - ShenZhen).

US should rejoin and re-ally WTO’s nations. Currently, US is ahead of China and if US is able to pull in stronger economic ties with other nations. It is able to combat China without putting more trade war tensions. Trump’s mistaken was to pull out of trade organisations and wanting to implement tariffs immediately. Combination of alliance building, reinforced by sanctions and tariffs, is the most sensible way moving forward, not the other way around. Note that policies such as the Montreal Agreement was backed by tariffs and sanctions if countries did not comply (it can be useful when done in moderation). Unlike Soviets when they launch the first satellite, US R&D spending tripled to compete. That is not that same sense of urgency in the White House today - Trump is proposing to cut R&D budget year after year. The increased spending enables US to be placed ahead of other countries, whilst boosting the economy.

In the first Cold War, US relied heavily on allies to share the military, political and psychic burden of the confrontation. The winner of a new Cold War will also need allies to lead the world in the twenty-first century.
One of the hardest questions of philosophy: Does Consciousness Exists? This is one of the most difficult subjects that philosophers and scientists have been debating about for centuries.
I am a tad bit disappointed by the book as it is by no means a neutral review of the field as one might expect from Oxford’s 'Very Short Introduction' series. Firstly, this is not an
introduction to the subject – it is an introduction to particular theory of consciousness

. History of scientific and philosophical research on the subject is largely ignored, and competing theories are presented only so that they can be refuted. Susan Blackmore promotes her own thesis, sympathetic to the work of Daniel Dennett, in which a single inner self with subjective experience, holding opinions and acting on decisions is a useful fiction or benign illusion created by the brain. Our ordinary intuition that there is a center to conscious experience is a useful abstraction, but not something grounded in scientific fact. I am highly skeptical because consciousness is something that most people affirm to be immaterial. The book, however, cites a lot of neuroscientific experiments attempting to debunk the theory of consciousness. To me, materialism does not debunk immaterialism - it is a philosophical position, not a scientific one. The book sounded clever until the last sentence where you exposed yourself as talking a load of nonsense due to her poor philosophical thesis and evaluation.

Let us first define consciousness: It is commonly agreed that the idea of subjectivity lies at the heart of the problem of consciousness. What it is ‘like’ for a person to have experiences, make plans or perform actions does not seem fathomable with standard rational techniques. My personal experience of the redness of an object might be completely different to your experience of the same object, and though we use the same terminology to describe redness, we can never really be sure that we have the same thing in mind. It deeply offends a certain class of objectively-minded people that something like this could be so fundamental to our being and yet scientifically unexplainable, and they adopt two major strategies for coping. The first soft-naturalistic strategy is to isolate this peculiar phenomenal experience from the physical world and neural processes. It is allowed to ‘emerge’ from the evolved physical brain but has no causal effects and is only describable in ordinary language or special codes such as ‘memes’. The second approach is to marginalize and diffuse the phenomenal experience, treat it as illusory, and hope that scientific advance will eventually do away with it. This latter hard-naturalistic approach is the one that Blackmore and Dennett promote. They say that most of what we do is unconscious, and when we finally succeed in understanding how all our individual mental capacities such as intelligence, perception, thinking or language function, we will understand consciousness.

Blackmore presents a large quantity of scientific evidence from unusual neurological conditions, split-brains, drug-induced hallucinations and altered mental conditions that she says disabuses us of the notion of a conscious self (there are countless of experiments, even famous ones, such as the Libet Experiment which is commonly cited to dismiss free will). She fails to account the other interpretations of such experiments (even if materialism can be tested on the meta-physical). Moreover, there is ample circumstantial evidence from normal human experience that our intuitive ideas about consciousness are indispensable. We assume that it is proper and useful for us to reflect on our own guilt and motivations and to try to understand other people through patient attention to their beliefs and life histories. Blackmore recommends that we set little store by these touchy-feely aspects of consciousness since they are all part of the illusion. Presumably she also dismisses the idea that this activity of reflecting on ourselves or each other has any inherent value. If science is going to reduce all such mental activities to brain functions there will eventually be no questions about value left to ask. The act of dismissing consciousness altogether attacks the fundamental pillars of the philosophy of science.

Despite, my disagreements with the Author, I still found it fruitful to learn about the different scientific experiments and philosophical positions from past psychologists and philosophers on the matter.

The best-known dualist theory about the mind is the one proposed by Rene Descartes, the famous Seventeenth Century French philosopher. According to Descartes, the mind is non-physical and resides in the pineal gland in the centre of the brain. However, the problem of the interaction of the non-physical mind with the physical brain is not so easily solved, therefore most scientists and philosophers prefer a
monistic

explanation – either the mind being fundamental, or the body. Modern science takes the materialistic view that the mind arises from mental processes. But this does not solve the problem of how a physical brain, made purely of material substances, can give rise to conscious experiences which scientists call the ‘qualia’, the indescribable experiences. This is traditionally called the ‘hard problem’ of consciousness, a term coined by the Australian philosopher David Chalmers 1n 1994.

What does being conscious mean? For example, is my computer which takes inputs from me, interacts with me, and provides output in some way conscious? Most of us would instinctively say no: we are conditioned to think only biologically “live” entities as conscious. But then, is a tree conscious? It is born, lives and dies: reaches towards light, and uses its roots to feed itself. Again, most of us would say no – it has no brain. But then, is a bat, which has a brain, conscious in the same way that I am conscious? “What is it like to be a bat?” – This question was made famous by the American philosopher Thomas Nagel 1n 1974. He said that if there is something it is like to be the bat, that is,
if the bat is self-aware of being itself

, then it is conscious: otherwise it is not. Nagel was using this argument to challenge materialism: since consciousness is subjective, we can never know objectively what it is. What we are talking about here is
phenomenal consciousness
, which is where self-awareness comes from – which is to be differentiated from
access consciousness
which we use for thinking, acting and speaking.

Still there must be something like a consciousness to do all this activity. Blackmore does not disagree – we do feel a ‘conscious self’, but in scientific terms, it is an illusion. She presents an extensive list of interesting experiments to prove that perception is largely subliminal. Even if we are not “aware” of what we perceive, the brain functions just the same. The self, instead of an entity, is a ‘bundle of sensations’, to borrow the words of David Hume. This is also very near to the concept of the ‘Anatman’ – the ‘not-self’ – posited by the Buddha.

Finally, a completely different approach is provided by Dennett. Having rejected the Cartesian theatre, he also rejects its audience of one who watches the show. The self, he claims, is something that needs to be explained, but it does not exist in the way that a physical object (or even a brain process) exists. Like a centre of gravity in physics, it is a useful abstraction. Indeed, he calls it a ‘centre of narrative gravity’. Our language spins the story of a self and so we come to believe that there is, in addition to our single body, a single inner self who has consciousness, holds opinions, and makes decisions. Really, there is no inner self but only multiple parallel processes that give rise to a benign user illusion – a useful fiction.

It seems we have some tough choices in thinking about our own precious self. We can hang on to the way it feels and assume that a persisting self or soul or spirit exists, even though it cannot be found and leads to deep philosophical troubles. We can equate it with some kind of brain process and shelve the problem of why this brain process should have conscious experiences at all, or we can reject any persisting entity that corresponds to our feeling of being a self.

I think that intellectually we have to take this last path. The trouble is that it is very hard to accept in one’s own personal life. It means taking a radically different view of every experience. It means accepting that there is no one who is having these experiences. It means accepting that every time I seem to exist, this is just a temporary fiction and not the same ‘me’ who seemed to exist a moment before, or last week, or last year. This is tough, but I think it gets easier with practice.

title: Thinking and Reasoning
author: Jonathan St B.T. Evans; Oxford University Press

text.t: I have recently started reading the Oxford Short Introduction series, which provides succinct information covering a wide scope of each topic. 100 pages long with a summarized academic report on the topic? Count me in. I felt that this book was best appreciated with some pre-requisites in Aristotelian logic and Dual Processing Theories posited in
Thinking Fast and Slow

. It may be too complex as a general introduction which was the main intention of the book. In my opinion, the question that were spammed to highlight human fallacies and biases was a little excessive to me.
Thinking and Reasoning is a good introduction, however, I am pretty familiar with most of the topics covered. For instance, one quarter of the book was a re-hash of Daniel Kahneman’s
Thinking Fast and Slow,
other parts of the book include Bayes Theorem and Aristotle’s logic syllogism which I am already aware about, having read statistical and philosophical books respectively.

The book covers a bunch of questions which highlights the biases and logical fallacies in both statistical and logical methods which is interesting but is just a re-hash of academic research reports. If one were to look for practical tips, this may not be the book for you. The central theme is also to highlight if human’s are even rational to begin with (some believe this as a presupposition to other arguments which could be begging the question). The most interesting part of the book was the history of thinking and reasoning which ranged from philosophy, psychology and the statistical sciences:
Finding out how the mind works; Understanding the History of Psychology:

Aristotle’s Introspection Method (Association) -> Sigmund Freud unconscious, repressed emotions deemed by rationalizations -> Behaviorism (Discards all references to consciousness; focuses on classical conditioning & habit learning: Studying other animals to find out more about humans) -> Cognitive Methods (Theoretical, treating the brain like a computer & finding out the programs)

The book remains to be a good introduction to Dostoevsky’s work since it is the easiest to read and is one of the shortest novels (at about 100 pages). Dostoevsky is one of the greatest of all time in the fields of classic literature, but when compared to his other works philosophically, I did not get much out of this writing. It was a little draggy and boring despite its length which left me in confusion, despite somewhat understanding the contents and deeper meaning of the book.

I found the book somewhat strange. Dostoevsky is known for his peculiar characters, in this book particularly, it is the main character who was never revealed. He is known as “the dreamer.” My interpretation of it was that the man was so ousted from society that he began “dreaming” as a form of escapism which gave him the illusion that he is engaged in reality but ironically, is further away from reality itself. What a weird fellow. Nastenka’s story is more “normal” in the sense that she is similar to the protagonist due to her grandmother’s situation, yet she just seems like a massive red flag towards the end (don’t mind the informal language). The protagonist dodged a bullet indeed. The ending was also somewhat unusual: The whole experience of these nights made him finally engaged in reality which gave him a “moment of bliss,” but now will he go back to dreaming?
Let us all be like the lodger, a huge contrast from both of them, someone who is leading a normal life who is fully engaged with the life’s struggles and in reality.
Chapter Breakdown (Credits: Reddit; U/DrNature96)
Chapter 1

It is spring, and many citizens of Petersburg have gone to their dacha with their families while our protagonist remains in his own home, where he tries to fix something that feels amiss. For some evenings now, our protagonist has been walking about the city in a pensive and miserable mood, looking at familiar things, remembering people he 'knew', 'talking' to houses, or walking obliviously. Outside the city gate, as he walked through the fields and meadows, he was enraptured by the natural scenery and people he saw. He thought of spring like a frail and sickly girl turned beautiful and he wondered, what power gave her strength and animation, and made her come alive and glitter? But our protagonist explained that this feeling is momentary, that after feeling this, you will go back into the same brooding mood, and will feel annoyed at having been carried away, but sad that you had no time to fall in love with the beautiful moment.

On one of these nights, he spotted a young woman on a bridge. Although he failed to approach her initially, an encounter between her and a stalker caused our protagonist to intervene.
Although nervous, he asked for her hand, to keep the stalker away. She gave her hand and they walked on together. While escorting her home, our protagonist told her what he has been feeling and dreaming of. When she asked about his initial approach, he said that he noticed her weeping, but the young woman refused to continue the subject. Near her home, although she was initially reluctant, they arranged to meet the next day. Our protagonist was happy to have someone to talk and listen to, particularly a woman since he had never met any women besides landladies; meanwhile, she has a secret she wants to confide in him; and she revealed that she too has nobody to talk to nor ask for advice. She explained that she was meeting him again only because she 'knew' him, and on one condition: she asked him not to fall in love with her. Our protagonist swore it; he told her how happy she made him, and how she has resolved all his doubts, which he will tell her about. With that, they agreed he would tell his story first, and they parted. Our protagonist walked about all night, unable to bring himself home.
Chapter 2:

It is the next day, the planned meeting between our protagonist and the young woman, whom we now know as Nastenka. As Nastenka decided that she does not actually 'know' our protagonist, she requested to know his life story. Our protagonist began by describing himself as a 'character' or 'type' that is 'eccentric' or 'absurd', and called himself a 'dreamer'. Sadly, however, the end of dinner takes him back to reality; although moments later, he gradually starts daydreaming again, into a 'new enchanting world'. He rhetorically asked Nastenka why he gets a strong physiological and emotional reaction in moments where he feels that his daydreams are reality. He told her about the woman he loves from his daydreams and their 'experiences' together. Finally, he showed his appreciation for Nastenka, but also revealed that he is afraid of being lonely again, supposedly after he and Nastenka part ways. He concluded his story by telling of how affected he is by the people he sees and hears living a real life; that he celebrates the anniversary of the sensations he got from his dreams; that a year ago he was just as sad but without the black thoughts that he had now; that he had not lived his best days; and finally, that his dreams will fade and he will be alone, without any regrets even, because all he had lost were only dreams.
Chapter 3

We're still in the same night, same meeting, but it's Nastenka's turn to tell her story. She started by describing her grandmother and their relationship, then about the new lodger, who was not so young, not so old, but pleasant-looking, qualities which her grandmother criticised. One morning, the lodger saw the pinned dress situation, which greatly embarrassed Nastenka. A fortnight later, the lodger started providing Nastenka with books to read. One day, upon meeting on the staircase, he asked if she wanted to go to the theatre with him. Not wanting to upset her grandmother, Nastenka declined; but later, the lodger spoke to her grandmother, who was keen to go. At the theatre, the lodger was very sweet to Nastenka; she imagined he would be dropping in to see her more often - but this didn't happen. Instead, he visited her only about once a month, to take them to the theatre, and Nastenka saw that he did it only out of pity.

Finally, Nastenka recounted that exactly a year ago in May, the lodger notified them that his business was done and he had to go to Moscow for a year. However, at present, Nastenka was aware that he had returned but had not gone to see her. Our protagonist was eager to help her - he advised to write him a letter. Unexpectedly, she handed our protagonist a letter that she had already prepared. She requested him to give the letter to some friends of hers who will pass it on to the lodger. This reminded our protagonist of Rosina from The Barber of Seville (the play that the lodger took Nastenka and her grandmother to see), who when advised to write a letter had already prepared a letter herself in advance; anc they broke into song with tears and laughter. Hastily, Nastenka said her goodbyes, and left, promising to meet again tomorrow.
Chapter 4

This chapter is told differently. The first two chapters were told as the events were happening.
The third night is told in memory, i.e. the third night (or third meeting) has happened, and our protagonist is telling us what happened.

The weather is 'dreary and rain-sodden', our protagonist is having 'dark sensations' and 'vague questions', without the 'strength to resolve them', unable to make sense of it all. He reflected about how they saw each other, and regrets at mistaking her behaviour for something else. He recounted what happened in their third meeting... Nastenka had arrived before our protagonist did this time; they are both waiting for a letter or for the lodger to appear. Our protagonist had let go of Nastenka's hand and she asked why he did that. She said she wanted to show the lodger their love for each other. This was painful for our protagonist to hear. He hinted to her of a weird feeling he had, which he thought she understood but ignored. She continued to be affectionate with him. In a fit of spite, our protagonist made her listen to the clock that rang eleven o'clock, which he regretted doing, because it greatly upset her. He tried to reassure her that there may be practical reasons why the lodger hadn't responded. She reluctantly agreed with him, and requested that if he heard anything, then he should see her at her address.

Afterwards, she became affectionate with him again, but started crying. She said she was thinking of our protagonist; she compared him with the lodger, and wondered why the lodger was not like him? That he's not as good as our protagonist but she loves the lodger more. She's upset by the thought of people always keeping something back instead of revealing everything on their mind that is worth saying. She suspected that our protagonist was sacrificing something for her sake. She recalled his description of himself (as a dreamer, from the Second Night), and said that she's better than what he described himself to be. She believed that the woman he falls in love with will be happy with him. Several minutes passed, and she decided the lodger wouldn't come, and they should try again the next day. They parted and returned home.

Our protagonist however could not stay at home, so he went out again despite the bad weather.
He walked towards her street, but changed his mind and turned back. Due to the bad weather, he stayed at home, if not he would have walked about more. Finally, he reflected, that although the letter had not come today, Nastenka and the lodger are 'together by now'.

She was rushing him for an answer, whether he had any letter from the lodger, but was shattered when he said there was no letter. Superforecasting

is the super-summary of Tetlock's research and experiments where he ran a large-scale forecasting competition. He first identified a group of “normal” individuals who significantly outperformed expert analysts. I first came across
Superforecasting
from the book,
Range

, where they focused in a lot on how individuals from different fields performed extraordinarily compared to the “experts,” often citing the analogy of Foxes versus Hedgehog. The book is the story behind this result and a subsequent discussion of the characteristics of these "superforecasters". This part is dedicated to the first one-thirds of the books. The other parts talk about the methods and mindsets these “superforecasters” use.
Personally, this is a phenomenal and insightful book. It essentially summarizes, Daniel Kahneman’s
Thinking Fast and Slow
, Nassim Taleb’s
Anti-fragile
and
Black-Swan

in merely a few pages with real, practical applications, together with comprehensive rebuttals. The use of real historical evidence (i.e USA invasion of Iraq, Keynes in 1929 macroeconomic predictions, Bays-of-Pigs invasion, PLO being poisoned by Israel, to name a few) and statistical concepts such as Bayesian statistics, really made the arguments and points a lot more robust and a super interesting read. Super happy to have read this book to start off my 2025! A must-read for those who practice forecasting in their day-to-day lives, which makes up everyone - a value add indeed.
Book Contents:

In a philosophic outlook, we have to be cautious - for nothing is certain, to be humble - for reality is infinitely complex, non-deterministic - for what happens is not meant to be and does not have to happen. In our mindsets, we have to be actively open minded - for beliefs are hypotheses to be tested; not treasures to be protected, intelligent and knowledgeable - where we need to be intellectually curious, reflective - introspective and self-critical and numerate - comfortable with numbers. In our methods, we have to be pragmatic - not wedded to any idea or agenda (using an outside view before an inside view), analytical - capable of stepping back from the WYSIATI and bait-and-switch notions and considering other views, dragonfly-eyed - value diverse views and synthesize them into their own judgement, probabilistic - judge using many grades of maybe and have thoughtful updates - when facts change, they change mindsets. Lastly, have a growth mindset band grit, together with good intuitive psychologist to defend against cognitive and emotional biases. Make an effort to stick to the 10 Commandments of Forecasting for life (can be found in the Appendix of the book):
Triage - choose questions that are forecastable
Break down problems into key drivers
Balance between priors and Bayesian updates
Update your beliefs in light of new information (think carefully about calibration)
Synthesize opposing views into a probability
Be granular about the spectrum of possibilities.
Actively seek to reduce both false positives and false negatives
Understand your biases and track your performance.
Take perspectives from others but don't be completely swayed (without evidence)
Incorporate feedback (from outcomes), but don't overreact.
These commandments are not binding rules. Be nimble, mindful, and ever-rational.
The Value of Forecasting (Rebutted):

Really interesting perspectives when he rebutted the ideology proposed by Nassim Taleb, especially when Taleb has dismissed the whole premise of forecasting altogether because of the limits of predictability in the butterfly dynamics of nonlinear systems of the world. But as Eisenhower said about preparing for battle, “Plans are useless, but planning is indispensable.” Instead of planning for hard-driven outcomes, we should plan for adaptability and resilience, knowing how well we would respond when facing such black-swan events. Nassim Taleb also talks about anti-fragility, essentially using Nietzsche’s “what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger” ideology, saying how we should embrace shocks and be strengthened by them. What Tetlock pointed out instead is that preparing for such surprises like that is costly. Since we have to set priorities, it then puts us in the forecasting business altogether, making it a circular argument (think of Japanese earthquakes and priorities to build defensive mechanisms in wealthier cities more prone to quakes than smaller and poorer countries).

Answers will always hinge on probabilities. If we were to use Taleb’s analogy, the United States which has a policy of maintaining the capacity of fighting two wars simultaneously, but not consider three or four, or even an alien invasion?
The answer always hinges of probability

, where the likelihood of the military fighting two wars simultaneously was high enough to justify the huge expense, but the same was not true of a three-war, four-war and an alien invasion future. It leads us back to forecasting where judgements like these are unavoidable. Thus, there is a need of probabilistic judgements that are explicit and as accurate as they can be. Daniel Kahnmen exaggerates when we take forecasting to an absurd extent (i.e Forecasting 20 years out and bestsellers about the coming century) as well. Even Taleb’s idea of statistical distributions, similar to that of parallel universe when opposing a finely-tuned universe, is also pretty unintuitive. True, fat tails happen but lets not take history as an virtually infinite array of possibilities. Same goes for Daniel Kahneman’s thought experiment of “how would the world turn out differently if Hitler was born in another country” etc. just leads to another complication of hard-determinism versus free-will which is stretching the topic of forecasting a little far.
Franz Kafka’s
The Metamorphosis

explores the degradation and transformative power of alienation. As its protagonist, Gregor Samsa, experiences personal alienation from the people he has cared for and served, he is transformed, losing himself altogether. Simultaneously, in ironic contrast to his experience, his transformation enables those around him to grow. Their lives are renewed at the cost of his own.
Every writer’s works are a reflection of their own lives.
The Metamorphosis
makes more sense after reading about the author’s biography. A short story and one that is easy to read. Nothing too mind-blowing but still a solid classic to recommend!
Book Content from SparkNotes:

In the novella’s inciting incident, Gregor, a traveling salesman, wakes to find himself transformed into an insect. The narrator recounts this bizarre change in a straightforward manner, at once setting the story’s absurdist tone and suggesting a universe that lacks order and justice. Gregor’s imprisoning transformation, symbolic of the conditions of his existence, separates him physically and emotionally from his family, his coworkers, and humanity in general. This theme concerning the effects of alienation is prevalent: Gregor’s metamorphosis into an insect reflects the alienation he experienced in life. Even before his transformation, he had disliked his job and office manager, had few friends, spent evenings alone reading the paper or train schedules, and supported his family in an emotionally detached way.

Gregor struggles to reconcile his growing awareness of his condition with what he had believed his condition to be, forming his internal conflict and the central conflict of the story. Despite his hideous appearance, Gregor retains his inner life and strives to reconcile his humanity with the reality symbolized by his physical state. He does not appear to be fazed by his newfound body; that which is essential about him remains unchanged. Instead, he focuses on day-to-day concerns that define him. He worries about losing his job and about his family’s financial situation. His income supports his parents and sister, Grete, and he works to pay off his unmotivated father’s debts. His father remains unnamed throughout the story, underscoring his estrangement from Gregor, a biographical echo of Kafka’s relationship with his own father.

Events in the rising action emphasize Gregor’s tragic awareness of his alienation, yet they also reveal that his family has begun its own transformation, gaining independence to grow. Once Gregor manages to open the door to his bedroom, his family and the office manager are horrified by his appearance, foreshadowing the fact that Gregor’s isolation will become even more pronounced. However, Grete—the only other named character in the story—engages with him, discovering that he prefers to eat moldy scraps since he has lost his taste for milk.

As events unfold, Kafka emphasizes the growth of the family as Gregor declines. Gregor spends most of his time listening to his family, separated by the door, and discovers that he enjoys climbing around his room. His mother and sister, in response, remove the furniture so he has more physical space, although he remains emotionally disturbed. In a pivotal scene, Gregor clings to a picture of a woman in furs hanging on the wall—he does not want this association with the human world and his past to be removed. Gregor’s mother, seeing him on the wall, faints, and his father, newly clean and healthy since becoming a bank attendant, misunderstands. He acts, throwing fruit at Gregor, treating him like a wild animal, and the apple that lodges in Gregor’s back eventually ends his life. Even Grete’s initial concerns and gestures toward Gregor sour throughout the rising action as he becomes burdensome, suggesting her own growing independence.

At the story’s climax, Gregor’s struggle ends, concluding his tragic life. The life of his family, however, is on its way to renewal. Gregor has become further isolated. His sister’s sympathy for him has waned; she has delegated responsibility for his care to the cleaning lady. The family has relegated Gregor to his cluttered room; for extra money, they have taken in three boarders who value order and cleanliness. Then, in a desperate act to retain his humanity, Gregor creeps out to hear his sister playing the violin. He is spotted by one of the boarders, and they declare that they will move out and refuse to pay rent. Gregor, it is clear, has become a liability. Grete tells her parents that they must stop thinking of the insect as Gregor and find a way to get rid of it. Gregor, his alienation complete, retreats to his room, accepts his condition, metaphorically having disappeared altogether, and dies that night.

Although Gregor’s death represents a tragic failure to end his own alienation, the falling action suggests that the death is transformative and positive. In a set of surreally hopeful events, the family travels into the “warm sunshine” of the countryside, a stark contrast to their cramped apartment. Each member reflects on their respective job prospects, envisioning the move on to better things in a new, smaller, and more affordable home. Their feeling of relief is palpable.

The story concludes with yet another metamorphosis. Grete has transformed into a woman in her parents’ eyes. They ponder finding a husband for her, pointing to the next chapter of her life. In the final scene, she stretches her arms wide, suggesting her emergence from her youthful cocoon.

it. Jordan Peterson is a hit or miss, I really liked when he talks about morality and how one’s consciousness can destroy you when he cites from Raskolnikov in
