Book Summary:

A crisis develops in the Oblonsky household when Dolly finds out about her husband's affair. Stiva's sister, Anna Karenina, arrives to reconcile the couple and dissuades Dolly from getting a divorce. Konstantin Levin, Stiva's friend, arrives in Moscow to propose to the eighteen year old Kitty Shtcherbatsky. She refuses him, for she loves Count Vronsky, a dashing army officer who has no intentions of marrying. Meeting Madame Karenina, Vronsky falls in love and begins to pursue her. He and Anna are so involved with each other at the grand ball that Kitty's hopes for Vronsky are shattered. Anna, followed by Vronsky, returns to her husband and son in St. Petersburg, while the disappointed Levin returns to his country estate. Kitty falls ill after her humiliating rejection by Vronsky. At the German spa where she takes a rest cure she tries to deny her womanly nature by becoming a religious do-gooder. Realizing the hypocrisy of this new calling, Kitty returns to Russia cured of her depression and ready to accept her ultimate wifehood. Consummating her union with Vronsky, Anna steps into a new life with much foreboding for the future. By the time she confesses her adultery to the suspecting Karenin, she is already pregnant with Vronsky's child.

Devoting himself to farming, Levin tries to find life meaningful without marriage. He expends his energies in devising a cooperative landholding system with his peasants to make the best use of the land. Seeing his brother Nicolai hopelessly ill with tuberculosis, he realizes he has been working to avoid facing the problem of death. He also realizes he will always love Kitty. Vronsky's career ambitions rival his love, and as he has not chosen between them, he is still uncommitted to Anna. Having rejected her husband, but still unable to depend on Vronsky, Anna finds her situation desperate. Her life is in a state of suspension.

Kitty and Levin are engaged to marry. Karenin, who has tried to maintain appearances of domestic tranquillity, finally builds up enough anger to hire a divorce lawyer. Anna is confined of a daughter, but dangerously ill from puerperal fever. At her deathbed, Karenin forgives her and feels sanctified by this surge of humanity and Christian charity. At this sudden reversal of their roles Vronsky feels so humiliated he attempts suicide. These incidents form the turning point of the novel. After Anna's recovery, the lovers go abroad and Anna refuses divorce (though Karenin agrees to it) for fear of giving up her son.

Levin and Kitty, after some initial difficulties, adjust to being married. Nicolai's death affects Levin deeply, and he realizes that emotional commitment, not reason, enables one to overcome life's problems. As if to underscore his life-affirmation, they learn Kitty is pregnant. After they honeymoon in Italy, Anna and Vronsky return to Petersburg. Violently affected from seeing her son again, Anna's love for Vronsky becomes more desperate now that she has no one else. Despite his objections, she boldly attends the theater as if to affirm her love before conventional society. Humiliated at the opera, she blames Vronsky for lacking sympathy with her suffering, while he is angry at her indiscretion. This keynotes the decline of their relationship, although it is temporarily restored as they go to live in the country.

Among Levin's summer visitors is a socialite who pays so much attention to Kitty that Levin asks him to leave. Visiting Anna at Vronsky's estate, Dolly finds her own drab life preferable to the formal luxury and decadence of Anna's. Complaining that Vronsky is eager for independence, Anna tells Dolly she must rely on her beauty and her love to keep his interest. Vronsky feels especially burdened by the demands of Anna's love when she calls him home from a refreshing political convention. Kitty gives birth to a son. Karenin, under the influence of his fanatically devout friend, Countess Lydia Ivanovna, becomes religious and uses his hypocritical faith as a crutch to overcome his humiliation and loneliness. Anna, seeing the irreversible decline of her love affair, has no more will to live and commits suicide.

Vronsky volunteers for service in the Russo-Turkish war. Tolstoy uses this part of the novel to express his pacifist principles. Levin discovers salvation" when he resolves to "live for his soul" rather than for selfish goals. He realizes the meaning of life consists in living according to the goodness inherent in every individual. Understanding death as part of a reality-oriented life, Levin is at peace with himself.
The book is a sequent to
The Three-Body Problem
(check out my review for the first book if you have not done so).
The Three-Body Problem
explains the history of how contact was made with the Trisolarians and their intentions.
The Dark Forest

, on the other hand, details how humanity is trying to prepare for an unknowable future and what extent will we go to for survival. The Netflix series ended 100 pages into the book where the main character, Luo Ji was selected to become a Wallfacer in the Wallfacer project, at the same time, the ETO was trying to assassinate him because “
Our Lord is afraid of him.
⚠️ Story (Spoiler Alert!)
The Wallfacer project

- The only way to fight the photons is to give specific people unlimited resources, but they don't have to tell anyone what they are doing with them or their intention. Brilliant strategy, but very questionable in terms of ethics. For instance, the first guy wanted to betray humanity and then bomb the Aliens, the second guy wanted to Kamikaze into the aliens and the third guy created something called the
Mental seal program

which ultilises thought control to eradicate the defeatism mentality (but turned out he was using it for his own agenda). In short, so people will believe humanity can overcome the alien invasion, and life can carry on. Also, a negative mentality can sometimes be the most infectious. Leave my brain alone. In response to this, Trisolar used the ETO and Sophons powers to form a group called the Wallbreakers to “break” and decipher the Wallfacer’s plans.

There is a mix of old and new characters in this installment. Da Shi, a planetary defense officer, was back and still his old reliable self. He is cunning, with street smarts that a lot of the more intellectual characters of course lack. Zhang Beihai, space force officer and former Chinese naval officer, who has an unshakable belief in humanity and his duty to its future. The main character, Luo Ji, is a new character. He is an astronomer and sociologist who is tasked with becoming part of a UN project known as The Wallfacer Project. He is lazy and somewhat self-absorbed, but also brilliant and clever in his own way. His first 5 years of his project of Hedonism was also somewhat very questionable.
I had several WTF moments when certain characters true intentions were exposed or when the ETO’s Wallbreaker used the one-liner “___, I am your Wallbreaker.” Chills down my spine.

Note that there aren’t really any chapters, but merely a few parts, but these are divided between constant switches of POV’s that is able to keep the reader engaged amongst all the areas the novel needs to cover. I really liked the ending and at how it really fitted the title of the novel.
The Negatives:

The side stories at the beginning bored me completely and I couldn't connect or get excited about the plot. The only story that caught my attention was that of the astrophysicist Luo Ji, but that interest was disturbed when they talked about his "girlfriend" and told about his past. It was the strangest thing I have ever read in my life. It is very unusual for an adult to have an imaginary girlfriend and even go out for walks with her. We often think we have strange behaviors, but meeting Luo Ji makes you feel completely normal.

At times, the side stories got a little bit draggy, especially when talking about the generals, the fleets or even the Great Ravine post-hibernation era. It did not strike me as a Sci-Fi book anymore, rather a political or sociological one.

Lastly, the Dark Forest was the only strategy that worked. Ye Wenjie gave Luo Ji a lecture and asked him to pursue Cosmic Sociology. Ye Wenjie knew the answer to stop the Alien invasion the whole time and Luo Ji managed to figure out what the answer was at the end of the book.
Axioms of Cosmic Sociology:
Survival is the primary need of civilisation
Civilisation continuously grows and expands, but the total matter in the universe remains constant
Chains of suspicion: it is impossible to establish common knowledge of mutual goodwill. Even if you think they are benevolent, you don’t know what they think of you.
Technological explosion: because of nonlinear technological progress, even a “young” civilisation poses an existential threat.
In Summary:

The universe is a dark forest. Every civilization is an armed hunter stalking through the trees like a ghost, gently pushing aside branches that block the path and trying to tread without sound. Even breathing is done with care. The hunter has to be careful, because everywhere in the forest are stealthy hunters like him. If he finds other life—another hunter, an angel or a demon, a delicate infant or a tottering old man, a fairy or a demigod—there’s only one thing he can do: open fire and eliminate them. In this forest, hell is other people. An eternal threat that any life that exposes its own existence will be swiftly wiped out. This is the picture of cosmic civilization. It’s the explanation for the Fermi Paradox. But in this dark forest, there’s a stupid child called humanity, who has built a bonfire and is standing beside it shouting, ‘Here I am! Here I am!’
Fascinating and thought-provoking book. Can’t wait to get my hands on
Death’s End
before the trilogy ends.
P.S I am happy to see the Alien pacifist making a cameo when he was communicating with Luo Ji at the end of the book.
I was first introduced to
The Three-Body Problem
through the Netflix Series. The series itself was an exceptional piece of Sci-Fi work which motivated me to read the book (books are always better than the movies!).
⚠️ Story (Spoiler Alert!)
Below contains major plot details that may affect your reading experience. Read at your own discretion!

The Three-Body Problem takes a classic scenario -- contact with alien life -- and cranks up the sinister factor to maximum. The story begins during the Cultural Revolution when young Ye Wenjie watches her scientist father beaten to death by fervent revolutionaries. She is sent off for hard labor at a re-education camp, but by a strange twist of fate gets a chance to work at a top secret government project seeking out extraterrestrial life. Fast forward to the present, when nanotech scientist Wang Miao is snatched up by cops and brought to a secret meeting of military officials who are fighting an unnamed enemy -- some force that is trying to destroy the roots of human science and technology by killing scientists or driving them to suicide.

Wang goes undercover in this strange conspiracy when he started playing a virtual reality game called The Three-Body Problem, which only the most brilliant scientific minds can hope to beat. The game transports the players to the Trisolar Universe, a universe with three suns that really exists. In most respects, Trisolar is behind earth technologically (they are playing out earlier eras in earth history), but in certain respects they are ahead of earth. Trisolar swings between "chaotic eras" and "stable eras". Both of these last for indeterminate time periods. Hundreds of civilizations there are destroyed by extremes of heat and cold produced by configurations of the three suns. Residents of Trisolar dehydrate themselves to survive chaotic eras. The game's purpose is to spread information about Trisolar among persons of high intellectual capacity and high social standing. Even though Trisolar really exists, the game plays out differently for different players.
The premise is fascinating and well-grounded (as far as I can tell) in hard science. The book raises haunting questions: Do we really
want

to contact other civilizations? If you had the chance to pull the plug on the human race, would you do so? Is science truly objective and provable, or is it simply the best we can do given our limited understanding of four dimensions?
Personal Insights:
Some parts are excluded in the Netflix series such as the Sophons testing in Trisolar and the Alien Pacifist’s punishment for sending out “Do not reply!”

Beyond its excellent treatment of scientific principles, The Three-Body Problem raises several important philosophical questions, the deepest of these being: Is humanity worth saving? As Ye Wenjie becomes one of the leading scientists searching for extraterrestrial life, her experiences during the Cultural Revolution have molded her views on the value of humanity.

The book is definitely not for the average Sci-Fi reader as complex physics concepts such as quantum entanglement and light cones should be understood beforehand to gain a full appreciation of the plot.

title: The Hundred Years’ War On Palestine
author: Rashid Khalidi

text.t: There is no good time to start than now. With the war between Israel and Hamas ongoing, many have taken up the social movement #freepalestine due to the “killings of the innocent civilians” which include woman and children that the media has painted. The war has led people to take radically different stance, increasing our confirmation bias on digesting information that we deemed “right,” resulting in greater polarization amongst pro-Zionism and pro-Palestinians.

I found Khalidi’s book cogent and easy to read, a clear summation of his perspective on the last hundred years in the Middle East from the point of view of a Palestinian academic who witnessed and participated in the events he is describing. Drawing from the experiences and memoirs of his own family, Khalidi was able to focus this century-long history on the impacts it had on his own ancestors and relatives, going back to the nineteenth century.
My Personal Opinion

The situation is ridiculously complicated. We cannot just blame one party alone for all the mayhem that is happening. Personally, I believed the external parties such as UK, US and UN did messed up pretty bad in terms of the poor policies and selfish nationalistic interest which enabled Israel’s advantage over Palestine, together with the rise of terrorist groups such as Hamas and Hezbollah. These terrorist groups, coupled with Oslo Accords and Resolution 181, then gives Israel the right to defend its state. Ultimately, we have to ask the fundamental question of “who truly owns this land?” Let us be clear that Palestine was never established as a state (stated by the Balfour Agreement) and even today, UN vetoed power to prevent PA to be recognized. During the 1917 and before, it was just a religious land with a mix of Arabs and Jews. Therefore, the land of the ingenious people does not officially belong to them in a nationalistic way. At the same time, Jews were being persecuted and were finding a place of refuge. We could date back to the book of Exodus where Moses did in fact lead to the Israelites to the land. With such strong Biblical connotations, it is not surprising for Zionism to rise, given the circumstances. However, the innocent lives loss is also not justified. This is such a tough issue to comment on due to the myriad of factors.

One critical aspect of the book is that Khalidi is obviously pro-Palestinian which comes out a lot in his writing. Some parts I am a little skeptical, especially when framing Hamas and Hezbollah in a positive light, but in fact, they are clearly terrorist groups that want absolute control. Khalidi downplays the terrorist tactics regularly implemented by Palestinians throughout his chosen time period without talking about the massacres against the Jewish population. Israel is also surrounded by their enemies, so that is essentially adding fuel to the fire.

I found this book to be super useful, insightful and packed with information. It is also really captivating and easy to read! However, we need to be skeptical of the framing of the pro-Palestinian cause because at some points, it felt like propaganda especially when I was looking for an objective introduction to the subject. We all have all biases. I recommend checking out Ben Shapiro’s debates and videos when taking the pro-Israel stance.
The book itself splits into six declarations of war which sums up the 100 year period:
Summary

The first colonization was by the British who conquered Palestine during World War I from the Ottoman Empire. They had issued the Balfour declaration in 1917, stating their intention to provide a national home for Jewish people in Palestine. Although 94% of the population in Palestine in 1917 was Palestinian, the declaration did not promise them the same political or national right guaranteed the Jews. Britain then embarked on a program granting Jewish immigrants preferred status in their new colony. Britain even armed Jewish immigrants to help suppress the great revolt against the British from 1936-1939. Britain was following an old colonial strategy of divide and rule, setting two groups against each other. It had used this strategy before, in India, Muslim against Hindu and Ireland, Protestant against Catholic. This provided the Zionist movement 2 advantages: they had a nascent military force and it greatly weakened the native population.

The subsequent 1947-48 war between the Palestinians and Jewish settlers saw the Zionists win and steal land and homes from thousands of Palestinians. Israel calls it "settlements." This chapter also details the shifting global power structure in which the old colonial powers were replaced by the US and USSR as the major imperialist forces in the Middle East after WWII. A situation shrewdly foreseen by Israeli leadership. Khalidi emphasizes the internal division, ineffective leadership, and disorganized institutions (the AHC, ANF, Arab Office) on the Palestinian side as contrasted to the organized, sophisticated, well-funded and well connected Jewish para-state throughout the 30s and 40s. The outbreak of violence as Britain ceded control of Mandatory Palestine to the UN in '47 resulted in decisive military victories for the Israelis and, ultimately, the ethnic cleansing of the Palestinians. This also coincided with the UN vote on Resolution 181 in favor of partitioning Mandatory Palestine.

The Third Declaration of War is the 1967 Six Day War and its aftermath due to its hostile Arab neighbors seeking its destruction. The factors leading up to the war included Arab popular distress at Israel's diversion of Jordan River waters to its territory, Fatah harassment (mostly symbolic actions of sabotage), Israeli threats and attacks on Syrian targets, and the needlessly provocative saber rattling of Egypt moving troops into the Sinai ultimately giving Israel the signal to initiate its pre-emptive attack. The main ideas of this chapter revolve around the changing power alignments and evolving terms of the Palestinian debate following the war. While the Truman, Eisenhower, and even Kennedy administrations occasionally pushed back against Israeli overreach (see Eisenhower and the Suez Crisis), the Johnson administration and his pro-Zionist circle of friends and advisors like Fortas, Goldberg, and Clifford proved utterly supportive of Israel in essentially all respects. Furthermore, new militant activism sprung up in the 60s like the Movement of Arab Nationalists, the Marxist PFLP, Fatah, and the PLO which had been originally intended by the Arab League to coopt rejuvenated Palestinian nationalist fervor but soon lost control of the organization after '67. The political alignments of the Arab League itself was also changing as with the Carter Admin's success in prying Egypt away from Palestine and into the Israel/US fold culminating in the bilateral Camp David treaty of '79. The chapter ends on the Lebanese civil war, the PLO's role, and the various motives/interests/players involved.

The 4th Declaration of War is the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon--a country already years into its civil war--aimed at dislodging the PLO from the country. The plan was to knock out PLO operations in Israel's northern neighbor, destroy the Palestinian national movement, and use the opportunity to consolidate control over and eventually annex occupied territory. The upshot of the war, however, was not the annihilation of the Palistinian national movement Israel hoped for but rather an intensification of the civil war, the rise of Hezbollah, and the relocation of the movement back into Palestine itself where it soon developed into the First Intifada.

The Fifth Declaration of War spans the period between the First Intafada in 1987 to the Oslo II accords in ’95. During this period, the Israeli army carried out brutal repressions against the Palestinian uprisings and secured a legal codification of the status quo through the Oslo framework which Khalidi argues was a major defeat for the Palestinian national cause. The authors details how simmering tensions erupted in the largely non-violent wave of uprisings beginning in Dec. 1987, the excessive Israeli response, the global public’s response, and the response of the PLO to the Intifada—which was to renounce terrorism, recognize Israel’s “right to exist” and support of a two-state settlement based on Resolutions 242 and 338 thus marking a major strategic shift toward diplomatic resolution.

The final (sixth) declaration of war consists in the continued colonial occupation of the West Bank and Gaza well after “final status” settlements were supposed to be adopted according to the Oslo accords, including the 3 massive attacks on the Gaza Strip during operations Cast Lead, Pillar of Defense, and Protective Edge. Topics also include the Camp David conference, the rise of Hamas, the politics of the Palestinian Authority, and the failures of the Obama administration to produce any substantive change.

Do we need to be free to be innovative, prosperous, or even happy? The lessons of the last five centuries were unequivocal-without freedom, there could be no prosperity or happiness. However, does this still hold true in the Information Age? Modern technologies are disrupting our societies, altering every facet of our lives, from the nature of work and what we intrinsically value, to how we are informed, entertained, and educated-it promises to be a far deeper disruption than Industrial Revolutions. Humanity is at a major turning point, and how we respond to the merger of technology and financialization will decide our future. Will it be capitalism or communism, feudalism or despotism?  By learning from the past and projecting into the future, global market strategist Viktor Shvets explores the weakening nexus between freedom and prosperity and what that means for the future of humanity. From the birth of our modern world, pivotal events in human history have led to the collapse of non-Western civilizations-Mongol warriors sweeping across Eurasian steppes; the Black Death and a re-awakening of human spirit; Zheng He's voyages and the collapse of Novgorod republic; and finally, the ban on printing in Arabic. What can we learn from these events to better prepare ourselves for the future? As we hurtle toward that uncertain future, we must decide whether our cherished individual freedoms are still necessary for success and prosperity, or if in adapting to new technologies, non-Western civilizations are now better positioned for this new world, creating illiberal orders that might no longer suffer from stagnation of ideas. For the first time in at least five centuries, we have an opportunity and tools to build a different society and economy.

The book offers a mix of technology, societies, and macroeconomics so you might expect some bias in the review, but is nonetheless a bird’s eye view of all the historical implications that took place. Viktor starts by giving you some amazing historical arguments as to why civilizations prospered or failed—he focuses on the Ottomans, the Chinese, and the Russians—, and how they were actually leading the west in terms of their progress. At the same time, he presents three major turning points—the Black Death, the Mongols, and the Renaissance—that made the West the winner of them all. I found the first part of this book fascinating as I finally comprehend the circumstances the three countries faced that made it “slower” when compared to the west.

The second part of the book takes you to the present and explains what changes society will face—the biggest one being the massive unemployment we’re about to experience—and proposes some solutions to the problem. For instance, the book mentions the change in dynamic nature of the industrial revolution and how laissez faire economics -

the practice of allowing people or institutions to act or behave however they want, with little or no interference or regulation - dominated the communism and socialism economic systems. However, Viktor argues that the information age would require a more closed, government-regulated and nationalistic change to avoid the problems of capitalism - mainly technology and financial securitization (for more detailed books illustrating the problems of fiat currency, check out
The Bitcoin Standard

). We are already moving towards a future that was less liberal than what most readers would have imagined possible. The speed of the transformation into an "illiberal world order" may have seemed impossible, yet it is occurring smoothly and broadly without much opposition. Rather than China moving towards liberalism, the world could be moving towards China. Communist utopia might well be the end state but dark times lie ahead in the decades to follow. While the author's own life experience places him in an ideal position to look from great heights at these momentous transformations, it still takes courage to commit to print such bold thesis that seemed at the time so implausible. If anything merits criticism is that this book is actually 3-in-1. But such arguments can only be developed within the realms of 300 pages. The last part felt a little rush which is why I gave it 4.5/5 stars.

In short, this book is a great source of references and touches on the wider arc of history. If you would like to have a crash course of history and the making of the modern world, you will cover ground fast. This book would be a good introductory material for geopolitics for sure and it definitely inspired me to dive deeper into the geopolitical / historical field. Highly recommend!

title: Inside the Black Box: A Simple Guide to Systematic Investing
author: Rishi K. Narang

text.t: I came across this book when I was looking for new books to read about systematic trading, quantitative finance or financial data science. I have been following this guy’s Youtube channel, Coding Jesus, for a while now. Recently, he posted his renewed book recommendations for 2024 for anyone aspiring to break into the quant industry. That was when I came across this book.
The video link:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cXNL4JKBL6w

“Inside the Black Box” was an honest, a random purchase. It striked me as one of those books which gave all the different models available before proceeding to tell me how it works. Not going to lie, I was a bit skeptical but I was confident due to its good reviews.
My verdict:

Man, I wished I read this as my very first textbook. It covered a lot of introductory material and reinforced my concepts in the field of systematic trading. The book gave a bird’s eye view of what a quant does, why choose quant, the idea generation processes before giving a clear and concise breakdown of the individual components. These individual components construct a quant’s workflow from types of models (alpha, transaction, execution), portfolio construction and finally, data and research surrounding the whole process. At the end of the book, it gave an introduction to high frequency trading and the different methods surrounding it which was particularly insightful for me as Michael Lewis’s
“Flash Boys”

was my only resource on the topic. Some parts were skipped because I am pretty familiar with the concepts such as data cleaning, overfitting and some of the portfolio models, but I loved the analogies used to explain.

Turns out that quants are not so mysterious after all! They are pretty similar with their discretionary counterparts, albeit the methods used. I can foresee this book being a classic for introductory quants! Highly recommend :)
Inside the Black Box: Introduction to Systematic Investing

Jim Simins: “The advantage scientists bring into the game is less their mathematical or computational skills than their ability to think scientifically.” Systematic trading is an art. For instance, you cannot tell a computer to find
cheap stocks
because what do you mean by cheap and what stocks?

A quant is someone who systematically applies an alpha-seeking investment strategy that was specified based on exhaustive research. It is rarely the case that quants are different from discretionary traders in what their strategies are doing. Good human judgment is what separates the best quants from the mediocre. When a quant intervenes with the execution of her strategy, it is most commonly to mitigate problems caused by information that drives market behavior but that cannot be processed by the model.
Garbage in, garbage out
- A model will make poor decisions based on bad information.
Quants help to make the markets more efficient:
Providing liquidity when other traders’ needs cause an imbalance in the supply and demand for a security via statistical arbitrage / pair trades
Execution algorithms for speed

Quants do not accept accidental risks, instead they attempt to isolate exactly what his edge is and focus his risk-taking on those areas that isolate this edge. Some risk management includes exposure to the market via net dollar or beta exposure (balancing their long portfolios against their short portfolios).
The Quant Workflow: Starts with Data
=> Alpha Model + Risk Model + Transaction Cost Model
=> Portfolio Construction Model
=> Execution Model
Research Encapsulates all processes
Alpha Models:

All successful alpha models are designed to have some “edge,” which allows them to anticipate the future with enough accuracy that, after allowing for being wrong at least sometimes and for the cost of trading, they can still make money.
Alpha Models: Both start with observations and data
Theory Driven Alpha Models (More Common)
Theoretical scientists try to make sense of the world around them by hypothesizing why it is the way it is (Theories of Aerodynamics to Long-Distance Aeroplanes).

Start with observations of the market, think of a generalized theory that could explain the observed behavior, rigorously test it with market data to see if the theory is shown to be either untrue or supported by the outcome of the test.
Data Driven Alpha Models

Empirical scientists believe that enough observations of the world can allow them to predict future patterns, even if there is no hypothesis to rationalize the behavior in an intuitive way (Human Genome Project / Chat-GPT).

Recognizable patterns in the data that can be detected with careful application of the right techniques. Empiricists are less sensitive to whether human minds can synthesis e a “story” to explain the data even if, in the process, they risk finding relationships or patterns that are entirely spurious.
Trend-Following:
Specify what forms an upward trend (How many days between 2 moving averages crossover)
Specify what forms a significant trend via filtering and conditioning
Mean Reversion:
Specify what is the center of gravity in which the price fluctuate, the upper and lower boundaries that are considered overbought and oversold
The a point of divergence from that equilibrium that warrants a trade
Actions taken if the price moves up abruptly which increases the probability that the price will reverse again due to excessive demand / supply
Identifying longer term trends occurring even as smaller oscillations around these trends occur in the short term

Note: Trend Following and Mean Reversion are theoretically opposite ideas but both seem to work due to different time frames - Trends can happen over longer time horizons, whereas reversions tend to happen over shorter-term time horizons. Thus, mean reversion can or as the longer-term indicator while momentum can be used as a faster indicator.
Technical Sentiment: Prices, Volume, Volatility behaviors
Aside from price levels, one can look at the volume of puts and calls as an indicator of sentiment

Option-based sentiments in equities also include implied volatilities of puts versus calls, downside versus upside volatility via sellers of call options that is far out-of-the-money. Proxies also include credit default swaps as an indicator for investor sentiment
Higher frequency traders may evaluate “shape” of the limit order book to determine near-term sentiment, bids or offers away from the mid-market relative to the size at the best bid-offer
Fundamental Data:

Academic Papers include Fama-French Paper “Cross Section of Expected Stock Returns” - Combining stock’s betas with historical data about the book-to-price ratio and the market capitalization of stocks of future returns.

Value/Yield: P/E Ratios (or more commonly E/P Ratios to get a positive number when earnings per share are zero). The idea behind value investing is that markets tend to overestimate the risk in risky instruments and possibly underestimate the risk in less risky ones. Therefore, it can pay off to own more risky assets and sell the less risky asset. Other metrics also include accounting EBITA, EV or book-to-price.
The argument also include instruments having a higher yield than it is justified by their fundamentals simply because the market is requiring a high yield for that kind of instrument at the moment.

Instruments do not usually become cheap because their prices do not move while their fundamentals improve drastically. Rather, prices are more often the determinant of value than changing fundamentals.

Carry trades are a good example of Value/Yield. Yields and higher risk are more widely understood in fixed income markets such as the juxtaposition of yields on government bonds, corporate bonds and AAA-rated company bonds. In commodities, a cheap/expensive analysis is done via the expected demand and supply rather than yield. They then trade the roll yield (the spread between the prices of commodity in a futures contract versus the spot via contagion or backwardation)
Note that quant equity traders who use value strategies are seeking relative value rather than simply making an assessment of whether the stock is cheap or expensive

Growth/Sentiment: It is better to buy assets that are experiencing rapid economic growth and to sell assets that are experiencing slow or negative growth. Metrics include Price/Earnings-to-Growth (PEG) ratio. Macro and microeconomic factors play a huge part for Quant Long Short (QLS) strategies via sell-side analysts' expectation versus buy-side’s view.
Supply/Demand: Use of alternative data via satellites or auctions for forecasting purposes.
Quality: Leverage, diversity of revenue sources (volatility of revenues), management quality, fraud risk and sentiment investors. Long quality companies and short poor quality companies.
Tactical/Events: One-Off, Tail Risk Events.
Data-Driven Strategies:

Less practiced as it is more difficult to understand and the mathematics is far more complex. Data is quite sparse and the market is always adjusting to you which renders your strategy useless overtime (high signal-to-noise ratio). However, data mining, when done well, is based on the premise that the data tell you what is likely to happen next, based on some patterns that are recognizable using certain analytical techniques.
The researcher has to decide what data to feed the model (via feature selections or feature engineering) with constant adjustment to keep up with the changes going on in markets
Look at current market conditions, search for similar conditions in the historical data and determine the probability that a type of outcome will occur afterwards
Define “current market condition,” the type of search algorithm used and why it is used (Page 50-51)

Understand what the model is actually doing: Understand the relative importance of the features to the resulting decisions. Use models that can make sense to us and give those models more credence that the ones that seem to come out of nowhere, even if the latter have nominally better results

More recent data matter a lot as they are most relevant to the immediate or near future but there is sparse data. However, more data would improve one’s confidence in its statistical conclusions drawn.
Implementation:
Forecast Target
Time Horizon: Short-term strategies (one day to two weeks), medium-term strategies (a few weeks to a few months), long-term strategies (few months to a few years ahead)
Bet Structure (Page 56-57):

Models can make bets on single instruments or instruments that are relative (multi-security bets) to each other. A model can forecast that gold is cheap and its price is likely to rise or that gold is cheap relative to silver, and that gold is therefore likely to outperform silver.

When looking at relative forecasts, one can forecast the behavior of small clusters (pairs) or larger clusters (sectors). Pairs is easy to analyze but very few can actually be compared so precisely and directly with one another (i.e Content-driven business versus search engine revenues despite being an internet company - fundamentally different).

Making bets with large clusters help to isolate and eliminate common effects among the group such as general movement in the sector and focusing on the relative movement within the sector (idiosyncratic behavior). Clusters can be made using statistical techniques (but might make the same mistake as pairs) or using heuristics (fundamentally defined industry groups theoretically but possibly rigid).
Investment Universe: Assets to choose (More liquid instruments to forecast stable transactions costs and predictable by systematic models)
Model Specification: Specifically define every aspect of the strategy before it is usable. This includes conditioning variables and run frequency of the model
Alpha Blending
Multiple types of alpha models are employed with multi-strategies. Alpha blending on linear, nonlinear and machine-learning models are used in combination to best predict the future.
Linear models:
Most common for quants combine alpha factors to construct a composite forecast.
A linear model is a reasonable facsimile for one of the more common ways that humans normally think about cause-and-effect relationships.

In linear models, the inclusion of one factor is independent of the inclusion of other factors, and each factor is expected to be additive, independently of the other factors that might be included or excluded.

Assign a weight to each alpha factor that is typically done using a technique known as multiple regression, which is aimed at finding the combination of alpha factors that explains the maximum amount of the historical behavior of the instruments being traded. The presumption is that, if a model reasonably explains the past, it has a reasonable chance of explaining the future well enough to make a profit. These weights are then applied to the outputs of their respective alpha factors, which are usually a forecast or score of some kind. The weighted sum of these multiple forecasts gives us a combined forecast.
A special case of linear models is the equal-weighted model. Though not highly quantitative, equal-weighting methods abound among quant traders.

The general idea behind equal weighting is that the trader has no confidence in his ability to define more accurate weights and therefore decides to give all the alpha factors equal importance. A variant of this approach gives each factor an "equal risk" weighting, which incorporates the concept that giving a dollar to a highly risky strategy is not the same as giving a dollar to a less risky strategy.
There are many forms of nonlinear models that can be used to combine alpha factors with each other.

In contrast to linear models, nonlinear models are based on the premise that the relationship between the variables used to make forecasts either is not independent (i.e., each variable is not expected to add value independently of the others), or else the relationship changes over time.
The two main types of nonlinear models are conditional models and rotation models.

Conditional models base the weight of one alpha factor on the reading of another factor. A conditional model might indicate that E/P yields should drive forecasts, but only when the price trends are in agreement with the E/P yields. In other words, the highest-yielding stocks would be candidates to be bought only if the price trends of these stocks were also positive. The lowest-yielding stocks would be candidates to be sold short, but only if the price trends of these stocks were also negative. When the agreement condition is met, the yield factor entirely drives the forecast. But if the price trend doesn't confirm the E/P yield signal, the yield signal is ignored entirely.

Rotation approach follows trends in performance of the alpha models. As time passes, the more recent data are used to determine weighting schemes in the hope that the model's weights are more relevant to current market conditions. This method usually results in giving higher weights to the factors that have performed better recently. As such, this is a form of trend following in the timing of alpha factors.

Machine-learning models are also sometimes used by quants to determine the optimal weights of various alpha factors. As in the case of determining optimal parameters, machine-learning techniques applied to the mixing of alpha factors are both more common and more successful than machine-learning approaches used to forecast markets themselves.

These techniques algorithmically determine the mix of alpha factors that best explains the past, with the presumption that a good mix in the past is likely to be a good mix in the future. As in the case of rotational models, many machine-learning approaches to mixing alpha factors periodically update the optimal weights based on the ever-changing dataset.
Note: Machine learning to determine the weights of various alpha forecasts is more common and significantly more successful.
Risk Models:

The key to understanding risk exposures as they relate to quant trading strategies is that risk exposures are those that are not intentionally sought out by the nature of whatever forecast the quant is making in the alpha model. They control the size of desirable exposure or to deal with undesirable types of exposure. Risk models can be used within the alpha model itself - one example is computing the residuals of equity returns to the set of factors in the risk models, and then focusing on trying to predict the future path of those residuals.
The ways risk models work when limiting size:
The manner in which size is limited
Hard Constraint - Drawing a boundary in terms of its risk no matter how strong the signal (more commonly tested via a theory driven approach mentioned above)

Penalty - a function in which the further past the limit level, the more difficult it becomes to increase position size. This is a way in which the model attempts to dress the idea that an opportunity can sometimes be so good as to warrant an “exception” to the rule - making rules to govern exceptions

Some even eliminate the full exposure by balancing their longs and their shorts, creating a neutral portfolio that isolates the outperformance of relative securities. This can be varied by how a want structure his bets (i.e Forecasting stock returns relative to sector returns, not betting on the direction of the sector bets itself)
How risk is measured: Usually volatility / standard deviation or level of similarly

Level of similarity is frequently calculated by taking the cross-sectional standard deviation of all the relevant instruments for a given period. This concept is known as dispersion where it is measured by the correlation or covariance among the instruments in a given universe

Volatility and dispersion as proxies for risk is usually measured via VaR models where they vary the amount of leverage to the amount of risk based on current volatility levels. But given the problems of VaR, more robust alternatives include changing the level of leverage to vary with the overall strength and certainty of the predictions from the alpha model or take a position in the options market if you can forecast the volatility / dispersion
What is having its size limited

Theory driven risk models focus on systematic risk factors which are derived from the theory in which a quant can make an economic, rational argument. These models use a set of predefined systematic risks which enables the quant to measure and calibrate a given portfolio’s exposure. Systematic risks are those which cannot be diversified away - i.e Fixed income market bonds are all subject to interest rate risk regardless of the level of diversification of the actual portfolio.

Empirical risk models are based on the same premise as theory driven ones, but the empirical approach uses historical data to determine what these risks are and how exposed a given portfolio is to them. PCA techniques are often used to discern systematic risks that do not have names but may well correspond to risk factors. However, one problem is that statistical techniques might find a spurious risk factor that is not sustainable for the future - “fooled.” This models are employed due to its benefit of adaptiveness as theory driven models are relatively rigid (risk factors are not altered often). It is especially useful during regime change using intraday data.

Note that a problem is that it will take quite significant data points to identify this pattern of regime change, at the same time, if we used too short of a window, it will not be statistically significant.

Let's consider a metaphor. Suppose that we are observing a forest on a still, peaceful day. The individual leaves on a tree are moving for largely idiosyncratic reasons- a caterpillar munches on this leaf, a bird's wingbeat moves another: Now, let's imagine a Category 5 hurricane comes through the area. Pretty much every leaf, every branch, every trunk will be straining in the same direction. Applying this to our taxonomy of alphas. We put forth that you can have many definitions of the concept of "value," or

"growth," and many ways to implement these signals, for example, in the definition of "relative." In a period where there are no major risks of blowing up, it is like a peaceful day in the forest. Each of these variations will have some diversification benefits, moving idiosyncratically. But the more that major risk factors (including and often exclusively ones that are exogenous to one's risk model) are driving markets, the less these variations matter. In fact, it is in scenarios like this that we should consider that we don't have anywhere near seven independent strategies-even if we are actually doing all seven of those named in Chapter 3. Value tends to behave like mean reversion, when push comes to shove. Growth tends to behave like momen-tum. Supply and demand, quality, technical sentiment strategies, depending on what specific ones we have, might offer some diversification, or might end up correlating to one or another group of strategies. Or, equally pos-sible, such strategies may simply offer no insight into market movements, given whatever risk factors are prevalent. If World War III breaks out, it is pretty unlikely that our technical sentiment or management quality signals have much to do with asset prices.

Three major components:
Commissions and fees: Mainly from banks, brokers and settlement houses
Slippage: The change in the price between the time a trader decides to transact and the time when the order is actually at the exchange for execution
A function of the amount of time that passes between the order being decided and the order reaching the market for execution
A function of the volatility of the instrument being forecast

Market Impact: Measurement of how much a given order “moves” the market by its demand for liquidity. It is defined as the difference between the price at the time a market order enters the exchange and the price at which the trade is actually executed.
Pricing that is affected by the trader’s order
Quantifying it is not straight forward as one does not know how much a particular trade impacts the market until the trade has been completed
Market impact focuses on the size of the order relative to the liquidity present at the time which may be provided by the market maker at a premium

Note: Commissions and fees are usually fixed charges as a baseline while other costs such as slippage and impact are variable and cannot be known precisely until they have been incurred. Slippage is affected by a number of factors such as the volatility of the instrument in question or its prevailing trend. Same for market impact such as size of order being executed, the amount of liquidity ty that happens to be available to absorb the other side of the trade and imbalances between supply and demand for the instrument at the moment.

Total transaction cost is generally accepted to be quadratic when cost of trade (y axis) is against size of trade (x axis) since the cost gets higher more quickly as the size of the trade gets larger based on slippage and market impact.

Overfitting:

The biggest problem in quants: Pick the point with a margin of safety around both sides. Based on the premises of scientific research, all quant trading (and all science) implicitly assumes that the past can have some value in helping us understand the future. But it is a general guide to the future, not an exact copy. Pick the point which has a better chance of being good but not solely as a result of some accident of the sample data used to find it.
Parsimony: Sparingness and Frugality

Models that ultimates as few assumptions and as much simplicity as possible in attempting to explain the future. Models with a large number of parameters or trading signals are generally viewed with more skepticism, given the increased risk of overfitting.

Occam’s Razor
which is:
Entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity

. In science, this has been understood to mean that it is better to use as few assumptions and as simple a theory as possible to explain the observations. Theories are better when they are more easily tested as they contain more empirical value.

In the past, overfitting was the main preoccupation of most researchers as underfitting was also a big risk. For many decades, the supply of alpha, relative to the demand for it, was ample. However, as competition increased and market inefficiencies disappeared, it became harder to make money with broad/universal models and more and more researchers began to push the envelope of fitting risk.

Passive orders are orders that cannot be immediately filled while aggressive orders can be immediately filled. If 2 traders input the same price, the priority would go to the one with a higher price/size ratio which puts large orders at a higher priority than smaller orders at the same price.
To
join

implies that one adds to the size of the best bid (or offer), which is also known as the first level of the order book, or the inside market. These are passive orders and it will always have a lower time-priority.
To
improve
implies that it narrows the bid/offer spread which improves the best offer price. It receives the highest priority even if it is the most recent.

Passive and aggressive orders does not mean providing and taking liquidity respectively as increased volumes do not always imply increased liquidity. Liquidity is the immediate availability of units to be transacted at a fair price. Depending on the scenario, imbalances in the volumes of buys versus sells can lead to liquidity while aggressive buying orders when there are many sellers provide additive liquidity.
A price is fair when:
It is broadly reflective of the fundamentals of the instrument’s underlying economic exposure
It is sensible with regard to other instruments that are similar to it

Michael Lewis, known for his ability to elucidate complex stories about finance and technology, turns his focus to the U.S. government. I have read a couple of Michael Lewis’s books such as “Flash Boys” and “The Big Short,” which are phenomenal. Thus, there were definitely high expectations coming into this.

The whole plot of the book investigates three lesser-known departments: the Department of Energy (DOE), the Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Commerce, revealing what happens when government agencies are entrusted to highly unqualified and sometimes hostile leaders appointed by the Trump administration.

The title of the book, "The Fifth Risk," refers to the concept of 'project management' or the risks that arise from the failure of imagination to foresee what might go wrong. Lewis emphasizes how government manages risks that no one else can or will—risks that can be deeply catastrophic, spanning everything from nuclear weapons management to food safety. He talks a lot about the role of government that provides its citizens with welfare and public goods. The most ironic part is that the public thinks the government is useless in its role of safeguarding its citizens. I feel this sentiment is a very common in Singapore and that it should be changed!

At the same time, Lewis highlights the critical work done by career civil servants, scientists, and experts within federal agencies, showcasing their dedication, depth of knowledge, and the essential nature of their work in keeping the country running safely and efficiently. Most of them are not doing it for the money, rather, they are doing it to serve.

The key problem that arise during the Trump Administration was its inefficient transitionary provide. The book talks about the transition process from the Obama administration to the Trump administration, capturing the chaos and lack of preparedness among the incoming officials. The officials could not be bothered to learn what was going on and to make matters worse, they were profit-driven and could not care less about society. Somehow, these officials shut down potential projects which can save the lives of many. It is because of this that leads to underlying dangers within vital departments that play essential roles in the safety and well-being of US citizens.

Finally, the book gives credit to those who made ground-breaking discovery and saved millions of lives, yet, they are not even famous! One such example is Arthur Art Allen in his drift equations calculations when saving lives at sea. Efforts to bring about meritocracy to such figures are often turn-down by the media. This part really changed my perspective in the people working in key government sectors.

My favorite part of the book was the last chapter on data. Half of the book explains why data is so important for generating insights to prevent natural disasters and solve challenging issues. It talks a lot about the origins and rise in Data Scientists, stemming from technological advances and chaos theory. The book also highlights the data scientist’s workflow. I felt that a lot of this could be linked to the main intention of the book to talk about Trump’s inefficiency rather than the importance of the Department of Commerce.
A chill read that is about 250 pages long which is recommended to anyone who wants to find out more about the key roles and struggles the US government undertakes.

Trading requires skill but luck plays a part too (skewed statistics due to survivorship bias). No matter what style a trader uses, each trading program is essentially one long trade; one is investing in the algorithm for example and not the individual trades it is performing. And an algorithm makes money like a trending security until it doesn’t due to the loss in terms of a trader’s edge.

How do you find dislocations?
How do you profit from those dislocations?

For Alex, the thrust of his investment strategy is not limited to analyzing forces that drive markets, rather understanding the forces that drive successful trades.

Avoid trades that are expected to lose money if held for the long term, no matter how compelling the shorter horizon arguments for those trades are (house versus gambler analogy; Alex has a long term view which takes a few years to play out).
Carry Trend Trades
The trend has to earn your respect via intellectual rigor - don’t trade against the trend in a market that tends to be trending.
Trend does not mean consistent moves, instead it yields historically a positive expectation from betting on the trend to persist. Within a multi-trend, there exists smaller sub-trends.

Just like boom and bust cycles, trends operate like a pendulum (the bottom possesses max momentum while the ends possess max economic gravity acting towards equilibrium). Think of economic policies like currency appreciation and depreciation affecting other parts of the economy like interest rates and exports.

It is tempting to just trade the fair value (the equilibrium), but the momentum created by the past economic gravity and past policy actions is likely to carry the price beyond the fair point. To fight the pendulum forces of cyclical currency trends and the relentless momentum of secular interest rate and equity trends is an undeniable case of stacking the odds against yourself.

A common carry trade is to long the high interest yielding currency and short the low one, but such trades tend to be risky and often viewed as reckless as high interest rate yields tend to be associated with lower economic stability and a higher potential for currency devaluation.
True impact of a position has to be assessed through the total return that includes the impact of the carry, especially for long term horizons.
Wait for blowouts before longing the currency, instead of fighting the carry.

It is a fallacy to look at the world of investments through the lens of asset allocation. 2014 US Treasury Bonds may seem like a bad trade due to low yields, but asking “What happens to my portfolio if the US government defaults” is the same as “what happens to my portfolio in a global nuclear war” - Debt is not absolutely safe but it is the safest way to deposit money and most liquid as far as the market is concerned.

Jesse Livermore - The intrinsic value of a security is the maximum price that an investor would be willing to pay to own the security if she could not ever sell it nor could she lend it and use it as collateral. If the security cannot be transferred to another person, it is useless to them as collateral.
No matter how risk free, if it is not liquid enough, the opportunity cost is too high. Therefore, we should be willing to accept lower yields for liquidity.

Overnight purchase via Fed Funds effective rate or rolling over future contracts with leverage shows safe profit over a 10 year span. For instance, rolling the contract into a cheaper, further forward contract (cheaper due to discount of the carry that could have been earned if invested earlier) is an essential way to collect carry in advance without putting up cash for actual physical securities.

Apart from carry, interest rate futures also have slides as every time you roll, you not only monetise the carry but also switch to a security that is on average 3 months longer in duration. The slide in thus the velocity of the change of yield as the securities become shorter in duration. Slide is akin to carry as it is essentially the profit or loss incurred as the maturity of the transactions in your portfolio slides with time. Just like regular carry, do the no arbitrage principle, a function futures market has to compensate you for the slide with every roll. Cheaper treasury notes or higher yielding indicates a rising market anticipating higher interest rates.
It is not just “interest rates rising” but “interest rates rising relative to the market-anticipated forwards.”

Do not just bet on rising and falling interest rates. The bond futures chart includes carry which accumulates over time, just like the casino. Positive carry is an important characteristic of a future trade and you have to be right on a trade that carries and slides against you. Do not be too sure on that, not too often.
Interests rates have hardly any predictive power (the decade of 30 years of bonds is just an upward trend)
Valuation Pull

Each time the price of any position changes for a noneconomic reason, the value of this position incrementally changes. Such changes in the value proposition are not to be confused with those stemming from new information.
The flaw with behavioral finance theory is the assumption that market participants transact as they choose to.
Ask yourself: If all else being equal, would you choose to trade it (when new information does not affect the company fundamentals -> spurious rise/fall in price levels).
Valuation is the strongest when dealing with fixed income instruments due to the idea of terminal value.
Undervaluations tend to self-correct over the long term, the same cannot be said of overvaluations (they can trend high for long periods of time).
Other instruments like delivery of commodities, IPOs and acquisitions, do not have expiry dates or when the trade is finally over.

Interest rates generally do not have easy to follow cyclical trends like currencies. There is an underlying secular trend, but the severity of corrections precludes pyramiding into it. Therefore, Alex establishes a central terminal value and takes advantage of the dislocation by positioning as it moves against him and reduces it as some gains are realized. He wants to have the maximum position on, where the dislocation against the terminal value is the highest.
He senses the terminal value by focusing on LIBOR yield curve and Treasury bonds as they depend primarily on the projected Federal Reserve policy and on the supply/demand driven risk premiums.

Current news and price action, therefore, may distract you from recognising the slow, but consistent, pull of valuation. Value-orientated strangles are easier to apply to financial products with clear expiration horizons and mechanisms for rectifying dislocations. Even when the terminal value is difficult to establish, “all else being equal” principle may help to identify postivie expectations trades.
Historical Pattern
Look at corporate borrowing rates - when they shift significantly up, reduce your equity exposure. Conversely, when rates fall, load up and stay loaded.

Lower corporate rates -> stock market is likely to be lower as interest rates are more likely to fall in the environment of economic slowdown and poor equity performance. However, lower interest rates are not associated with a higher stock market, rather, lower interest rates indicate a subsequent rally in the market.
The question is therefore:
If interest rates are lower today than they were two years ago, is the stock market likely to be higher two years in the future than it is today?
If the answer is yes, it suggests a trading strategy.

Plot a backward looking US 10 Year Yields and Forward Looking S&P in the same graph -> Notice that upward spike in the backward looking rate would indicate an incline to buy and hold in the stock market.

The benefit of this is that it is not calibrated to fit the past, we are merely using the 10 year treasury note yield as a proxy for corporate interest rates. Therefore, it prevents a biased data selection.
Get a grasp of the debt market to understand every other market.

Short-term interest rates (anchored to expectations about Fed’s actions) and long-term rates (reflect inflation expectations) do not always move in unison due to the negative predictive power of interest rates (9/11 impact for example: Yield curve did not react to Fed’s cutting).

Whenever the Fed is actively changing the rates policy, the market is very reluctant to project moves into the future. The forward expectations will decouple from current policy. Never underestimate the scope of possible shifts in the shape of the yield curve.

When your economic view contradicts with your strategic principles, it is better to stay out. There are better places to commit capital. But if given no choice, trade with the pattern rather than economic intuition.
The ability of our human brains to identify patterns governing financial instruments is a key reason we are not yet fully replaced by algorithmic trading.
