Stopping Out of Success:
Always trading with tight stop losses can be detrimental when you are stopped out of profitable positions due to mismatch between the reasoning behind a trade and the strategy of execution.
Modern information flows are nearly instantaneous and market overshoots frequently, tight stop losses are whipsawed by price action.

2 criterias for a successful trade at inception (the truth of the statements defines the success of the trade idea) - “I am buying X anticipating that it will be higher than it is now in 2 years time.”
Profit target and loss tolerance
Time horizon
A distinction between a trade being successful and a trade being superior:
A successful trade produces a desirable return on capital, regardless of whether luck was a major reason for profit.
A superior trade is a strategically superior way of expressing one’s market view, given the information available at the time of trade initiation.
Do not just hope from price level changes and launch a trade, rather, state your time horizon and what you are planning to do if it moves for or against you.

Easier to play well when you are psychologically comfortable - profitable to keep playing while winning and take a break when encountering a losing streak. But putting yourself in a position of hoping for a sequence of events is inviting the market to torment you (this is hope, not strategy).
Instead of stop losses, play by position size - the initial position should be relatively small compared to the potential full size (anticipating the pendulum economic swings).

If you wait till the trend is established, you would jump in when the move appears to have started and stop out if the trend does not follow through - it only risks small lossess and does not tie up capital prematurely if you do not use stop losses.

Just like our living philosophy, you have to rely on some things (an act of faith). You cannot be a skeptic on everything. You will have a high chance of being correct when your views are properly and clearly expressed.
Unlike high frequency trading, opportunities to capture a massive move of a developed market currency are very rare - you will only have a few of those in your career.

Develop a proposition of an edge and keep repeating it, the risk profile of the average performance will keep improving with more repetitions (think of coin flipping heads versus 3 coin flipping heads - the odds of the latter is more than the former).
However, if you have a super high probability superior coin, it outweighs the diversification effect of 3 less superior coins despite having more than 50% probability.
Be long more than short because in reality the euro will not appreciate 10 times versus the dollar unless the US suffers some sort of collapse.
Know your payoffs: unlimited upside versus unlimited downside -> dealing with emerging carry versus long emerging market currency (negative versus positive carry).
However, if you long an emerging market currency, you may lack the advantage of economic gravity. When a currency gets too expensive, the central bank steps in via QE.
If the government is in a debt downward spiral, the government may lose control as it is burdened by dollar-denominated debt (Asia currency crisis).

More often stopping out in interest markets than other markets as interest rates positions are so sensitive to the economic data and geopolitical risks that they often have no choice but to be flexible and reassess views promptly and aggressively to prevent portfolio drawdown.
Stop out when you know that you are wrong, not when you lose a certain amount of money.
Fear the Visible Forest

See the big picture, do not be like those who say “Surely this position will make money eventually, but at this point it is too volatile and illiquid to enter” - this fear of not having short-term control prevents them from capitalizing on their knowledge.
Smaller size, longer term, bigger move.
Sizing is determined by trial and error when you are a beginner, while experienced traders will already know the size in their heart - “What is it I fear, and what is it I hope for?”

Psychologically neutral position - The size of the trade should gravitate towards over the long horizon while not worrying about the price action at the current stage (if it moves strongly against you, flat, or moves strongly for you).
Slowly transition to your max position which is the most you can hold without the fear of being stopped out by a violent correction (used from your judgment).

Alex never fully exits a position despite violent moves, he believes that exiting a position completely would risk too much of missing a big move (never reduces below 50% of core or 30-40% of maximum).
Make more by adding on dips and reducing overextensions. The latter scenario provides a re-entry opportunity.
Adding Unnecessary Complexity

10 year swaps is the most important benchmark for interest rate derivatives trading which reflects the difference between the 10 year swap yield and the 10 year treasury yield. It can be viewed as reflecting the difference between US Government credit and bank credit, and thus serves as a proxy for overall valuation of credit risk.

An illusion of risk management is to own XYZ but selling something to hedge (LTCM bond trade and Russia default is an example of this) - the idea that treasuries can be used to hedge other instruments is debunked, if you own risky bonds, selling treasuries against them is changing your profile to an entirely different trade, not reducing risk.
Account of the idiot factor - the possibility that you screwed something up in reasoning, calculations or execution.
The funding cost of a 10 year note can be approximated by the Fed Funds Effective Rate, and the Fed Effective is closely linked with LIBOR.
2 issues with options (which expressing your directional views with them like trading with stops) - Essentially paying a certain amount for the “whipsawing” upfront:
Not guaranteed to make money even when the market moves in the desired direction
Option might expire before the move you are hoping for happens
Double Whammy Situation: The premium on the option lost and lost the chance of making on the move down to the strike level

Just like stops, you can dilute the superior risk profile of the fundamental view by being stopped out of a position unlimited number of times, losing premium on options (not risking an instant portfolio meltdown but is exposed to the risk of “death by a thousand cuts”).

Some traders use exotic option structures to avoid the premium paid altogether, but as a gross generalization, they tend to pay for the appearance of saving on premium by being long optionality when the market performs the way they expect and short optionality when the market does something unexpected. Thus, it is really bad if it goes against you (see Page 81).

Be cautious when increasing complexity out of fear of taking simple directional risk. Such complexity almost invariably increases transaction costs and the amount of risk variables. An illusion of risk management benefits might be dispelled when the market shifts out of the “normal” paradigm.
Reduce portfolio complexity and wait for quality of opportunities (assign markets with grades):
A time of unique and unprecedented opportunity (Grade A, rare)
Massive dislocations, resulting a strong and obvious trend (stock market recovery, Grade B)
Time of chaos and crisis, presenting great opportunities (Grade C)
Regular Markets (Grade D)
Hold back capital when in Grade D as there are better options out there if you are a macro trader.
Choose Dominant Trades

Every trade has its own set of assumptions. Mathematicians choose a non-self-contradictory set of exists and use irrefutable logic to build a theory based on it. Choose different axioms and you will get a different theory. Each theory will work perfectly within the world defined by its axioms and the theory which has the best axioms best approximating reality will be most useful for practical applications.
Trade X dominates trade Y, if under reasonable assumptions, X is likely to succeed in a strictly broader range of future scenarios than Y.

Do not just stick on one bet or trade because you will need to have an opinion on it all the time, instead, look at it from a multidimensional space of all interconnected asset classes, the same strategy may be far behind the efficient frontier of trades, trapped in the bowels of investment mediocrity.
Parse the matrix of accepted economic casualties and convert it into a system of concurrent necessities.
Bet on the Necessary, but not on the Sufficient
Every fish is a salmon but not every salmon is a fish
> Salmon implies fish
> A implies B, then A is sufficient, and B is the necessary and B is the dominant trade
Understand that the assumptions in the economy are not permanent, but rather a function of an economic environment.
Do not associate implication with causality: A is sufficient to cause B signifies that A implies B but A is necessary to cause B leads to the opposite of implication.
Concurrency is everything

When we say A causes B, we are not actually divulging much useful information, unless we also give some idea as to when. Proposing that “If A happens, sometime afterwards B will happen,” is not much of a trading strategy. It is like saying after a bull market comes cash, which makes sense but it appears that the crash is a necessity but not a concurrent necessity.

Every trade is a relative value proposition. If I long ABC and short XYZ, I am not just saying that at some point in the future ABC will go up and at some point XYZ will go down. All financial instruments go up and down at the same point.
Taking a relative position means that I think that ABC will outperform XYZ in a concurrent sense.
Taking a single position is also a relative value proposition: I am saying buying ABC stock offers a better risk / reward ratio than the rest of the market.
A implies B has no time in it and it is not good enough to establish B as a dominant trade. We say instead
by the time A happens, B will have already happened
. This is concurrent necessity which might be counterintuitive if we are considering A as a sufficient cause of B, because it places B ahead of A in the timeline (think of the dollar strength
concurrently
or
in anticipation
of higher rates, even though higher rates is the cause and implies a stronger dollar).
When considering a trade A, ask what else has to have happened. by the time A succeeds and if there is a trade B which answers this question, consider A as an inferior trade.
Economic causality chains do not stop with one implication, rather asset classes form interrelated feedback loops.
Chicken and Egg
Here is a causality loop: Higher stocks >> Higher rates >> Lower stocks >> Lower rates >> Higher stocks
So where is the chicken and where is the egg? It is not about the economic meaning of the movements of stocks and bonds, but
how and how fast will.
The chicken can lay a new egg each day, but the egg takes three weeks to hatch: The chicken is the asset class whose movements cause immediate response in other asset classes.
The egg is the asset class that works slowly through the real economic forces and sometimes takes years to complete the feedback loop.

As a consequence, whenever there are chickens, there are eggs, but the eggs might be there even if the chicken is not around. It means that chickens are concurrently sufficient for eggs, but eggs are not concurrently sufficient for chicken.

Note that while it seems that egg is the dominant trade, we must account for another layer of complexity: A negative feedback mechanism where we think of chickens hatching from the eggs being a rebellious generation and rejecting what their parents have stood for. If “higher stocks” are the chickens and “higher rates” are the eggs, then “lower stocks” are the chicks.

When the chickens and chicks go in the opposite direction, we cannot directly compare them in terms of dominance since they are just different generations which represent different points in the business cycle.
It is crucial to understand that the determination of which of the asset classes is the chicken is not invariant and depends on the current market regime.
When, due to inflation fears, rising rates become a concurrent necessity with respect to strong stock market performance, the growth outlook becomes dim.

If the dominant way to express a particular economic view appears to be an inferior trade, the underlying view should be reexamined. Think about the year 2000 where early market jitters did not prevent the Fed from moving forward with its tightening program. Betting on higher stocks would have been an inferior trade, but the trade that dominated it, betting on higher rates, was inferior based on the secular trend.

To construct a negative view of the economy, we can buy puts or short the stock but it gives us unlimited downside. We can instead, based on historical patterns, buy the long end of the interest rate curve. If the Fed raises short-term rates, the longer term bonds will show resilience in anticipation of the inevitable economic slowdown.

Observing price actions provides an empirical way to discover the concurrent necessity. Rather than trying to predict short-term price moves based on technical parameters, Alex looks for shifts in the market regime. Observations alerts us to potential concurrency, but
causality is derived from economic principles

In any financial crash, the stocks are still the chicken, because the interest rates were driven by anticipation of how much the Fed would react to the developing crisis (the egg hatching). Thus, bet on the fall in short-term rates acting as a concurrent necessity and becoming the dominant trade.

In fixed income, the “rates concern” comes into play when the economic recovery is well-established, but the rates are still historically low. Corporate profitability is assured due to the abundance of cheap credit. The only threat is the Fed starting to normalize interest rates. The way to identify such a regime is by observing a perverse stock market reaction to the economic data releases. Stocks rally off mediocre employment numbers, as weaker data implies less risk of an imminent rate hike. The distinguishing feature of this regime is that stocks react to a fall in projected interest rates immediately, as opposed to a gradual economic process of improving profitability. In this case, lower short term rates becomes a chicken trade with respect to the egg of the higher stock market.
This relationship of concurrent necessity does not lead to a dominance, as lower rates and higher equities reflect opposing economic views

High rates -> This egg will eventually hatch into slower economic growth and a lower stock market, eventually looping back into lower rates. Long bonds are then a superior trade and a concurrent necessity with respect to short stocks.
Low rates -> This egg will hatch into better profitability and higher share price. Long stocks is then a superior trade and a concurrent necessity with respect to short bonds.
The “Even If” Principle
Trades that are expected to succeed, even if the view that is driving them proves to be incorrect:
Extreme price dislocations

This could be in the form of bottoming of equities as the Fed cut rates and it is highly unlikely that the Fed will hike their rates extremely fast or metals being historically cheap but the annual surplus kept weighing on the price (demand of technology advances would not increase the demand for palladium but failing that it was not likely to become cheaper).
A chicken and egg mechanism, which has the trade’s success built-in into its failure

Buying 10 year notes in the middle of a hiking cycle and the Fed is projected to keep tightening. The only 2 possibilities are Fed stops earlier than projected and rates fall or Fed continues to hike to the point of recessing and consequently an easing cycle. Rising rates is a self-defeating chicken which lays the eggs of economic slowdown, being opposite to a superior trade. If interest rates are high today, then an economic slowdown is a concurrent necessity with regards to the rates staying high (rates falling may or may not indicate economy slowing down and rates staying high will slow down the economy for certain).

The regime of persistent disinflation likely caused by automatization and globalization. In a disinflationary environment, high nominal interest rates imply high real interest rates. Persistently high interest rates are a drag on the economy and when inflation is not a threat, there is no reason for the Fed to jeopardize the job market by keeping rates high.

So 1998 “Greenspan Put” was the idea that being long stocks was an “even if” trade since it would be great if stocks went up or stocks went down. The latter because Greenspan would cut rates and then stocks would go up.

But it does not apply for the 2008 crisis since leveraged speculators were waiting for the Fed to bail them out and were generally wiped out. This is different as it does not constitute credible inflation threats.
Due for a re-read and review.
The World for Sale: Money, Power, and the Traders Who Barter the Earth's Resources

" illustrates the often opaque world of commodity trading and the traders who shape the global economy. The book provides insights to the high-stakes industry that deals with the trading of oil, metals, and grain, revealing how a handful of individuals have managed to redirect the flow of entire nations' wealth, influence political outcomes, and impact the environment.
Note to the reader:
They are trading the actual commodity. Supply chains, logistics management and relationships are needed to run the company. It is not the Wall Street trading one is thinking of.

The book spans several decades, detailing the rise of key trading firms and the personalities behind them—from Marc Rich's controversial dealings that led to a presidential pardon to the executives at Glencore and Trafigura who operate vast networks that handle a significant portion of the world's oil, metals, and food supplies. Just read, becomes readers will be shocked at how powerful these commodities companies really are.
From the very beginning (1960s), small groups of trading companies and their executives manipulate commodity markets
, control critical supply chains, and amass vast fortunes by acting as middlemen between producers and consumers of raw materials.

The book talks about the formation of important relationships between traders and political regimes. These relationships empower traders to exploit unstable regions, deal with sanctioned states, and sometimes perpetuate corruption and fund conflicts to secure access to valuable resources. Examples include Vitol funding the Libya Rebels, Glencore overpowering the China coal market, Trafigura exploiting the republic of Congo and Glencore taking control of Africa.

The industry can be coined as a “gray” one. The ethical implications of the trading practices and the environmental impact, particularly in terms of resource exploitation and the ecological footprint of mining and drilling operations, can be quite extreme. The companies do have records of bribery, no ethical objectivity and fraud. It has a similar profile to the Netflix show “
Ozark

” where cartels and gang members run the operation, working as a subsidiary or agent for the big firm. People get executed, rural villages get poisoned due to the unethical dumping and the executives are just counting cash.

In terms of learning, I would say that I have gained a good grasp of the history of geopolitical dynamics underlying the commodities market. The book recounts pivotal moments, such as the 1970s oil crisis, Gulf war in Iraq, China’s massive industrialization, post-collapse of the Soviet Union, the bankruptcy of Jamaica, Putin’s annex of Crimea and the more recent global financial crisis of 2008, which shows the power and impact these companies have.

This book is crucial for readers looking to grasp how global markets really work, far beyond the stock exchanges and into the trading pits that quietly but powerfully dictate much of the world’s economic activity. It also includes a nice reflection at the end that talks about the future of commodities trading. I gave it a 4/5 because I did not really know the companies well enough and the geopolitical context they operated in to fully appreciate the events that unfolded. Maybe with more supplementary readings it would then be a 5/5.
The Meaning of Marriage: Facing the Complexities of Commitment with the Wisdom of God
" delves into the theological and practical aspects of marriage, presenting it as a spiritual institution that reflects God's commitment and relationship with humanity.

This book is more of a personal learning growth for me and I classify this book as the most important “self-help” book ever. The book argues against the modern view of marriage as primarily a venue for personal fulfillment (i.e Hook Up Culture and Sex Before Marriage) and instead presents it as a lifelong covenant that offers a unique framework for personal and spiritual growth. The book revolves around
Ephesians 5.

This book remains relevant as it addresses the timeless questions and challenges associated with marriage. In a society where views on marriage are rapidly evolving, Keller’s biblically grounded perspective offers a counter-narrative that emphasizes the sanctity and significance of the marital vow.

Some of it is “common-sense” like other self-help books (so it did not blow me away with a 5/5) with a Biblical twist so I think there is much value in that, especially in today’s culture. You do not need any more self-help books after this, would recommend!
The Meaning of Marriage
You will never marry the right person:
Feelings wane and flee (honeymoon stage), marriage in a Christian sense is a lifelong commitment to another person.
Ephesians 5 - The secret of marriage is about Christ and the church - “Husbands, love your wives just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”

The husband should do for their wives what Jesus did to bring us into union with himself - Jesus gave himself up for us, went to the cross and paid the penalty for our sins so that we could be united with him (Romans 6:5) and take on his nature (2 Peter 1:4).

Current culture notions are for our personal gain (what can you do for me), rather, the Christian value is to serve (Philippians 2) - think of what Jesus did for us, he stood nothing to gain, yet he served us.
Do for your spouse what God did for you in Jesus, when God invented marriage, he already had the saving of Jesus in kind.

Romans 15:1-3 and Galatian 5:13 - Bond servants because Christ humbled himself and became a servant and met our needs even at the cost of his own life - In the chapter of Matthew, Jesus washed the Apostles’ feet. We should do the same by serving others rather than our personal, selfish gain.
The sin of marriage is due to self-centeredness. Marriage is to serve one another.
Psalms 130 - Fear Christ. Fear in the Bible is to be overwhelmed with wonder before the greatness of God and his love - God’s grace and forgiveness liberates us to serve one another.
Purpose of marriage:
To be filled with the Spirit - both need to be secure of their own value and purpose (why they were made by God and who they are in Christ).

Marriage should be with a believer: To know someone fully is to know them fundamentally, to know someone intimately and fully, it is only made possible if he or she is a believer of Christ. If not what happens? The other party will not fully understand us and see it as a waste of them (being deep in Bible studies and helping out at Church for example). It’s that believers must compromise which inevitably drifts from God.

Some people may claim that marriage is just a piece of paper but it does not define one’s love for someone. In a way, it does. It is like saying “I am not ready to serve you fully or committing to you.” What is your definition of love? If it is just great sex, then a piece of paper is useless.
Marriage does not depend on mood but on commitment - it is described as a convenenants (relationship between both God and beings) with duty, passion and promises.
Wedding vows are not a declaration of present love but a mutually binding promise of future love - a public oath to the world.
God made marriage special specifically for a man and a woman (quoted in Genesis 2).
We have free will to make promises and perform our duties, despite our feelings.
Priority of marriage:
Your spouse should be your number one priority in life just like the principle of marriage-as-friendship. It supersedes all other relationships (socially, financially etc.)
The end goal of marriage is to look at one another and to build them towards the image of perfection that was made in Christ. It is to “sanctify” us.
Singleness:

Paul wasn’t married. Even in both marriage or singleness, the number one priority is to have a strong relationship with God. Someone eternal and fully loving that can fill our hearts, rather than the material things in life. Both have the same end goal which is to seek God.
Gender Roles:
Christ specifically made men and women to complement each other. Men are said to be an authoritative servant and women have the resources available to complement the men.
Love language through communication.
Obviously not towards the extreme of rejection of marriage (liberal) and toxicity (overly masculine to the point of verbal abuse).
Sex before Marriage:
Sex should be celebrated - hook up culture totally contradicts that (you feel feelings and unity when you perform an act of love)

Sex and marriage are essentially unity to one another (Ephesians 5 - “where two become one flesh”) where one belongs completely, permanently, exclusive to you (remember marriage is a covenant relationship) - creating a place of security for vulnerability and intimacy.

1 Corinthians 6:17, Paul clearly states why having sex with a prostitute is bad - sex outside of marriage is immoral since sex is destined to be part of making a covenant and experiencing that covenant’s renewal (an emotional “commitment apparatus” of whole life entrustment and self-giving).
Laws are made by God for a reason, it does not make sense for it to be broken so easily to sin and temptation.

Albert Camu, one of the three great Existentialists, wrote his philosophy in this non-fiction book. "The Stranger" is then considered a seminal work of existentialism and an exploration of the absurdity of life. The book is known for its sparse, straightforward prose and its exploration of the emotional disconnection experienced by its protagonist, Meursault. This is a short fiction book that essentially talks about our lives having no meaning and it does not matter what we do.
Albert Camu is known for his captivating starting and ending of his book. This is the introduction of this book, “
Mother died today.
Or maybe it was yesterday, I don't know.”
Okay, now I have got you hooked.

The novel is set in French-colonized Algeria and follows the life of Meursault, a seemingly ordinary clerk who is emotionally detached from the world around him. The story begins with Meursault receiving news of his mother's death, to which he reacts with a disturbing lack of emotion. He attends her funeral but is more concerned with the physical discomforts of the situation than with mourning her death. Following the funeral, Meursault returns to Algiers and resumes his routine life, engaging in a relationship with a former colleague, Marie (which did not matter to him) and befriending his neighbor, Raymond, who is involved in a violent dispute with his mistress (which he honestly could not care). Through Raymond, Meursault becomes embroiled in a conflict with a group of Arabs, one of whom is the brother of Raymond's mistress. The turning point of the novel occurs when Meursault, on a trip to the beach with Marie and Raymond, ends up shooting one of the Arabs in a moment of confusion and sun-dazed tension. He fires once, then, after a pause, fires four more times into the already dead man's body. He then fights it out in court but he does not really care what happens to him and has no remorse for the murder that he did. It becomes evident that he is being judged not only for his crime but also for his character, particularly his lack of grief at his mother's funeral. He is then viewed as a “stranger” from societal expectations of emotional behavior.

The main teaching of this book is that human life is rendered meaningless by the world's indifference to human existence. Meursault embodies this philosophy as he navigates life with a detached and indifferent attitude, refusing to lie about his feelings to satisfy social norms. His honesty and refusal to conform to societal expectations ultimately lead to his condemnation and death sentence.
This book offers a powerful examination of existential nihilism and the absurd, delivered through Camus's stark, unadorned literary style that effectively underscores his philosophical stance.
'The Stranger

' is simultaneously entertaining and captivating, presenting a smooth and accessible narrative. The question then arises: can one truly live according to the principles depicted in the novel? Having read theistic arguments and Paul Kalanithi's '
When Breath Becomes Air
,' I am inclined to believe that life does indeed have inherent meaning.

I have to commend Camus for being intellectually honest and consistent with his atheistic perspective, suggesting that we are merely cosmic accidents. and that concepts such as virtues and love are nothing more than random neuronal firings without intrinsic significance, and ultimately, nothing we do truly matters in the face of our inevitable demise. Yet, personally, I find this viewpoint challenging to accept. It raises fundamental questions about how Camus himself finds meaning in life and why he chooses not to succumb to nihilism.

For those intrigued by these questions, I recommend delving into Camus's 'The Myth of Sisyphus' and 'The Rebel.' In these works, he explores the notion that we can derive meaning from the act of rebellion against life's inherent absurdity. These writings provide a deeper understanding of Camus's philosophical explorations and offer a broader context for interpreting the existential themes presented in 'The Stranger.'"

title: Five Proofs of the Existence of God
author: Edward Feser

text.t: This has to be without a doubt, the best philosophical book I have read about the philosophical problem about the existence of God. If you need all of the arguments for and against the existence of God, all you need is this book!
For those interested you can check out this video on Ben Shapiro’s show:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9FvYwpyFbIQ

Edward Feser's "Five Proofs of the Existence of God" stands as a scholarly examination of the philosophical discourse surrounding the existence of God. This book explores five classical arguments originating from eminent philosophers including Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Aquinas, and Leibniz. Feser's treatment of each argument is both rigorous and accessible, making philosophical concepts understandable through everyday analogies.

The book begins by introducing Aristotle's metaphysical argument concerning the necessity of an 'actual actualizer' to explain the transformation from potentiality to actuality. Feser employs easy analogies and examples, such as a cup of hot or cold coffee, to discuss potential states and their actualization. He then talks about the coffee being held by the table which in turn held by the ground which in turn held by the earth and so forth, thereby illustrating the concepts of linear and hierarchical causality. This segues into a discussion on the need for an overarching actualizer endowed with divine attributes such as omnipotence, omniscience, and immutability, aligning closely with the traditional theological conception of God. The book really shows the thought processes of past philosophers who came up with robust arguments using everyday items.

Following Aristotle, Feser explores Plotinus' arguments on the simplicity of non-composite parts, Augustine's reflections on the reality of eternal truths, Aquinas' synthesis on essence and existence, and finally, Leibniz's formulation on the Principle of Sufficient Reason and the nature of contingency. Each philosophical proof is not only presented in isolation but is also complementary with others to build a comprehensive and convincing meta-argument for theism.

Moreover, the book also engages with modern atheistic arguments put forth by figures such as Lawrence Krauss and Richard Dawkins, as well as historical critiques from philosophers like Immanuel Kant and David Hume. He provides a thoughtful and detailed defense of theistic perspectives against these criticisms, reinforcing the robustness of the arguments he supports.

Each chapter concludes with a formal presentation of the arguments, complete with premises and conclusions—Aristotle's argument alone encompasses forty premises—providing readers with a clear, logical framework of the discussions at hand with a summarized argument.

"Five Proofs of the Existence of God" is not merely a reiteration of classical arguments (an example would be the basic cosmological argument), rather it offers fresh insights and contemporary relevance. Therefore, this is not a beginner friendly book at all. I took 3 library sessions (spend the whole day even writing my own notes) to roughly understand the arguments presented. If the reader is interested and wants an introduction to a similar flavor, I would recommend “
Why Believe
” by Niel Shenvi instead (you can check out my review!).
If you want a short teaser of the book, let me present to you a simplified version of Aristotle’s proof below:
Even if we live in a simulation like the Matrix (Descartes argues), change definitely occurs (change with respect to your thoughts and experience if you think you are dreaming or hallucinating).

Parmenides argued that change is an illusion - if we consider the cup of coffee, which starts out hot and becomes cold after a while, you might say that the coldness of the coffee, which does not exist while the coffee is hot, comes into existence. But if the coldness of the coffee was initially nonexistent, then at that point it was nothing and when it comes into existence, it is then something.

But suppose if you tried to convince someone about an argument, your mind entertains one premise after the other and reaching the conclusion is itself an instance of the change the argument denies. The very act of casting doubt on whether change occurs presupposes that it occurs.

It is a mistake to think that change would have to involve something coming from nothing. It is true that while the coffee is hot, coldness is not actually present, but there is potential in which other qualities are not. The coffee does not have the potential to turn itself into a chicken but it does have the potential to grow cold. There is a limit to potential but it is not exactly nothing, even if it is not yet actual either.

Change is the actualization of potential - the coffee has the potential to become cold and after sitting out for a while that potential is made actual - something cannot come out of nothing as a potential is not nothing. So change occurs.

Change requires a changer - potential coldness cannot do anything, precisely because it is merely potential. Only what is actual can do anything - the potential coldness of the coffee cannot make itself actual.

When something causes a change, that is sometimes because it is undergoing itself and when that is the case that change too requires a changer. The flick of your wrist causes the flyswatter to come down hard and its impact kills the fly, but the flick of your wrist was itself merely potential until the firing of certain motor neurons actualized it which was caused by your annoyance at the fly’s buzzing, and so forth. Note that not everything which causes a change must undergo a change itself. The point is rather that if something which causes a change is undergoing change itself, then that change requires a changer of its own. So, we sometimes have a series of changes and things change.

Suppose the above argument extends on the infinity to the creation of the universe, we might think of it as a linear fashion of changes. Suppose if the universe did not have a beginning, the material then we are supposing, has always been here and always changing.

Even if such a linear series of changes and changes might in theory extend backward to infinity, with no first member, it is then a hierarchical kind which must have a first member. Instead of a linear fashion of changes, think about what might exist at a single moment of time. If we consider the coffee cup sitting there for hours at some particular moment, it is sitting there at that moment only because the desk is holding it up at that moment and the desk is holding it up at that moment only because it is in turn being held up, at that same moment, by the floor. It might be odd to consider this as change but the definition of change is actualizing a potential, therefore, the hierarchical series does exactly that as well - the potential of the cup to be three feet off the ground is actualized by the desk, the potential of the desk to hold the cup aloft is actualized by the floor and so forth. The series is hierarchical, not because it is simultaneous, but there is a certain sort of dependence of the later members on the earlier ones - the cup has no capacity on its own to be three feet of the ground, it will be there only if the desk holds it up, but the desk has no power on its own to hold the cup there unless the floor held it aloft and the floor is held up by the house’s foundations and that by the earth. If the foundations fall, it is like a domino that all the others will also fall. A linear series is not like that, if you turn on the air conditioner, the air conditioner will keep cooling the room even if you left the house - thus members have their own causal power. A linear series does not require a first cause, unlike a hierarchical series.

In a hierarchical series, there needs to be a first member, the claim is not that the series has to be traced back to some beginning point in the past. Something must have the power to hold up the intermediaries such as the desk and the cup which are only derivative power to hold things up, then there must be something from which they derive it, something which does not have to derive it from anything else in turn but just has it “built in.” The first point therefore has to be non-derivative and non-instrumental - the sort of thing that can actualize a potential without itself having to be actualized. Note that a series of causes that is only finitely rather than infinitely long is not essential to the notion of a hierarchical causal series - for an infinitely long brush handle to move, there still has to be something outside it which does have the “built-in” power for it to move. The first cause is not a number of a series, rather, it is the first cause in the sense that it has inherent causal ability while the others have only derived its causal power.

Linear and hierarchical causes can be thought of as a series of causes accidentally versus essentially. To apply hierarchical causes to the passage of time is not relevant, demonstrated by the finite versus infinite example above. Every linear series, thus, presupposes series of the hierarchical sort where it leads to a single first cause.

How so? Go back to the coffee in the cup. To state the obvious, it can only get cold, or be held up by the desk, if it exists - nonexistent coffee cannot do either, or anything else for that matter. Now, what makes it the case that the coffee exists? Obviously someone made it by pouring hot water through coffee grounds, but that's not what Feser is asking about. What makes it true that the coffee exists here and now, and at any particular moment that it exists? What keeps it in existence? For one thing, the coffee will exist only insofar as the water that makes up the bulk of it exists, so to simplify things somewhat let's consider that. What keeps the water in existence at any particular moment? After all, given the chemistry of the water, the matter that makes it up also has the potential to exist instead as distinct quantities of oxygen and hydrogen. But that is not the potential that is being actualized right now; instead, it is that matter's potential to exist as water that is being actualized right now. Why? It is no good to answer that such-and-such a process occurred at some time in the past so as to combine the hydrogen and oxygen in just the right way. That tells us how the water got here, but that is not what we are asking about. It is also no good to point out that nothing has yet come along to separate out the hydrogen and oxygen. That tells us how the water might someday go out of existence, but that isn't what we're asking about either. What we're asking about, again, is what keeps the water in existence at any instant at which it does in fact exist.

You might say that it has to do with chemical bonding between atoms, but that merely rephrases rather than answers the question. For the atoms have the potential to be bonded in other ways, and yet, they are not so bonded. It is their potential to be bonded in such a way that water results that is in fact being actualized. Again, why? Appealing to the structure of the atom won't answer the question either, but merely pushes it back a stage. For why are subatomic particles combined in just the specific way they are, here and now, rather than some other way? What is that they realize that potential rather than another? The very existence of a thing is now at issue rather than its particular location.

So far, we have only explained is the actualization of a thing’s potential for existence, the sort of “first” cause that we talk about is one which can actualize the potential for other things to exist without having to have its own existence actualized by anything - the cause does not have any potential for existence that needs to be actualized in the first place, it is just an unactualized actualizer. Therefore, the reason why it exists at any moment only insofar as it is caused to exist by an unactualized actualizer that actualizer it at that moment.

title: Finding the Right Hills to Die On
author: Gavin Ortlund

text.t: I was really impressed with Gavin’s “
What It Means to be Protestant
” and thought to give this short book a read. “
Finding the Right Hills to Die On”

is aimed at fostering unity and discernment within the Christian community. This work navigates doctrinal disagreements, offering an approach to engaging with theological issues based on their relative importance to the core tenets of the Christian faith.

The central thesis of this book is the concept of "theological triage," a term borrowed from medical triage, which refers to the process of determining the urgency of medical cases to decide the order of treatment. Similarly, theological triage involves categorizing theological issues into levels of priority to determine how they should be handled within the church context. Ortlund argues that not all theological disputes require the same level of division or urgency in response, and that recognizing this can help maintain unity within the Church.
Levels of Doctrinal Importance:
Ortlund outlines a method to categorize doctrines into four ranks based on their importance to Christian identity and practice:
First-rank doctrines
are essential to the gospel itself, such as the Trinity, virgin birth of Marry, the doctrine of justification by faith and Scripture (Sola Fide and Sola Scriptura).
Second-rank doctrines
are urgent for church practice but not core to the gospel, such as the meaning and mode of baptism. It is second rank as it affects the workings of the Church and this is where denominations come in.
Third-rank doctrines
are important but not enough to justify division or separation among Christians, such as eschatological beliefs.
Fourth-rank doctrines
are less clear and less important, often open to wide interpretation among faithful Christians which includes the analysis of Genesis 1 and Revelation (which is difficult to interpret literally).

Ortlund emphasizes the importance of unity in the church and suggests that understanding the different levels of doctrinal importance helps Christians know when to unify and when division might be necessary. His approach advocates for humility and charity in theological discussions, promoting a spirit of grace over contentiousness.

Ortlund supports his arguments by referencing historical church conflicts and resolutions, demonstrating how theological triage has implicitly guided church decisions throughout history. He also grounds his discussion in a robust theological framework, drawing from Scripture and church tradition. He does not give his own personal opinion but he does give objective historic evidence for why certain beliefs are the way it is today.

Really short and sweet book! Would recommend to anyone interested in Protestants or members who are currently residing in the Church. Gave it a 4/5 instead of a 5/5 as I am pretty aware of the issues presented with my upbringing and values imbued in me. Nonetheless, there is something fore everyone to learn :)

title: What It Means to be Protestant
author: Gavin Ortlund

text.t: Gavin Ortlund's book "What It Means to be a Protestant" highlights Protestant historical roots, doctrinal distinctions, and its impact on the landscape of Christian theology.
For those interested, you can check out the following links which encapsulates some of the core concepts talked about in the book:
The 5 Minute Case for Protestanism:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EBAK_Oc6SsI
A Protestant View of the Church:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2AEMGcpf4f8
Is Sola Scriptura True:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kn7qdPSHSJk&t=879s

Ortlund's work serves as an introduction to Protestantism, addressing both those within the Protestant tradition and those outside of it who seek a deeper understanding of its beliefs and practices. The book outlines the core tenets that define Protestantism and distinguishes it from other Christian denominations, particularly focusing on the doctrinal and theological aspects that have historically separated Protestant churches from Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christianities.

Ortlund provides historical insights into the origins of Protestantism, particularly its emergence during the Reformation in the 16th century as figures like Martin Luther, John Calvin, and others challenged the prevailing ecclesiastical structures and theology of their time. It talks about why the reformed even took place.
An easy to read book, packed with full of insights and wisdom. All arguments are substantiated with historical context and Scripture evidence. Learned a lot and would highly recommend!
What It Means To Be Protestant

What is Protestantism? Philip Schaff, historian of the 19th century, says it is best understood as a renewal movement within the one true church. The four principles of Mercersburg Theology highlights how protestantism is well positioned to serve catholicity and renewal in the church:
Protestantism can affirm the good in the good in the pre-reformation church and in the non-protestant traditions

Prior to and outside of the Reformation, Christ was actively building his church. The Reformation would be illegitimate if it did not stand in organic continuity with the early and medieval church and this must be rooted in catholicity. It therefore represented a new movement of life in the church, but on the grounds of retrieval and catholicity.
Protestantism can acknowledge its own eccentricities, errors and sins

Suppose there is a married couple who, after decades of marriage, while the husband and wife get a divorce. In the following years, both sides diminished. The wife’s house starts to fall apart slowly and her finances are in bad shape while the husband becomes socially award, feels lonely and becomes a bad dresser, Recognising that both sides are diminished by the split does not necessarily entail the blame is a 50/50 split (maybe someone was unfaithful). Similarly, a Protestant today can maintain that the Reformation was and is justified while also acknowledging various unfortunate tendencies that have characterized many of Protestantism in its overall development and current state. Thus, a Protestant today can celebrate the doctrinal recoveries that led to separation from Rome while grieving some of the long-term results of this separation and the overall fact of division itself. Furthermore, a Protestant today can work freely and cheerfully toward the renewal within the church - particularly because we are not bound by dogmatic claims that cement boundaries between different Christian traditions.
The glory and strength of Protestantism lies in continual reforming,
semper reformanda
The principles for reformation are
sola fide
and
sola Scriptura
justification by faith alone and Holy Scripture is the only infallible rule for the church’s faith and practice.
Sola fide
is the “what” and
sola Scriptura
is the “how” of the Reformation. The first is an object like a precious jewel and the second is a method that protects this jewel.

Schaff critiques the overemphasis of super meritorious good works that may be deposited into the treasury of merit and deployed by the church to help other Christians or souls is purgatory. It basically removes the laity the assurance and peace the gospel is supposed to provide. Therefore,
sola fide
had the effect of returning to the laity a meaningful experience of their forgiven status and good standing in the sight of heaven.
The One True Church

Outside of Protestantism - Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodoxy, Oriental Orthodoxy, and the Assyrian Church of the East - all claim to be the ‘one true church’ with its own unique hierarchical structure. Protestantism does not entail a denial of the visible church - it is simply a distinction (the church knows the number of baptized Christians but God knows who is truly united to Christ). Protestants distinguish between the visible and invisible church. We deny the claim that this visible church coheres within multiple institutions - we deny the claim that any one institution hierarchy constitutes ‘one true church.’
Eastern Orthodoxy: No salvation outside the church

To be outside of the orthodox church is to be cut off from the grave of the Holy Spirit and therefore cut off from salvation. The basis for this claim is due to the church being ontologically one such that there are no schisms in the church, only schisms from the church (picture Noah’s Ark and being in the Ark).
Roman Catholic: No salvation outside the church, but there can be true Christians outside of the church

Like the Eastern Orthodox imagery of Noah’s Ark, it restricted salvation to those in submission to the pope. Medieval outlook has found its way into magisterial (which is what Catholics deem as infallible) teaching. The unity of the ecclesiastical body is of such importance that only for those who abide in it do the Church’s sacraments contribute to salvation.

However, people will speak of being unknowingly within the church but how can they be drowning in the flood if they are unknowingly on the ark of Noah? If hardly any Catholic held this view prior to the modern era, why should it be allowed as any authentic interpretation of the doctrine “no salvation outside the church,” rather than a change in its meaning. This is a significant problem with the Catholic notion of doctrinal development: its tendency to move the goalposts in order to make the goal.

The above raises a practical concern about the actual value of an allegedly infallible magisterium. For example, we are told that we need an infallible magisterium to interpret the Bible, but much less appreciated are the intractable problems of interpreting the magisterium itself. Is it really the solution for the misunderstandings and confusion for the past 600 years?

The above two contrast the Protestant’s version of a true church where Christ is present in Word and sacrament - and wherever such a church exists, there is the potential for a valid Eucharist. Suppose a group of Muslims saw Jesus in a dream and started to take Holy Communion, repented for their sins and was baptized. Is this a valid church or is this a valid Eucharist? A Protestant would say both since no qualifications, conceptually gymnastics or revisionist readings of historical standards are needed to explain this phenomenon. It is simply Christ the Lord building his empire. Protestants therefore do not just restrict to the ‘one true church’ to a single, visible hierarchy while at the same time, believing there are boundaries to the church where not everyone is in it.
Why did the Church reform?
Indulgences

The Church fathers use the treasury of merit as a motivation to gather funds for the Church. Picture this: Your mum has passed on and you are told that giving money to the church will not only release her from thousands of years in the treasury of merit but will also fund the reconstruction of St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome (1500 AD). Obviously, you would donate but the funds are actually hoping to the bishop to pay off the massive debts he owed for buying his archbishopric.

Subsequently, the funds funded the Crusades led by Pope Urban II (1095 AD). Pope Eugene III offers of indulgence for participation in the second crusades went further, extending indulgences for the remission of temporal punishment not only in this life but also in purgatory.
Different Popes command different things, like moving the goalpost again.
Persecution: Resistance to Reformation

For those who voiced out and were against this, they were slaughtered. It is true Protestants also commanded slaughters. Both sides are wrong, but at the same time, it is also wrong to attempt to equalize the blame on both sides when they are not to scale. There is simply nothing on the Protestant side that compares to the quantity and organization of the late medieval Roman Catholic violence. Medieval persecution resulted from theology promulgated by the highest level of authority within the Catholic church. Reformation was thus good news in 1500-1600 AD.
Hus’s death showed the opposition to the abbvie practice that was persecuted by the highest levels of leadership within the Catholic Church.

The Catholics distinguish between the “temporal sword” - weirded by secular authority and the “spiritual sword” wielded by the church, insisting that the temporal is subjected to the spiritual. Take note that although the church does not hold the temporal sword, the civil authority does so at the church’s discretion. The Bishops then quote Romans 6 in their justification for the brutalities committed on Hus. Hus appealed to Augustine on heretics should be appealed to with Scripture and reason - bless our enemies rather than kill them and that money cannot procure forgiveness.
What Hus (before Luther preached):
Church as all the elect
Ecclesiastical authority must not be followed when they depart from Scripture
This applied to the Pope - all apostles had equal right of binding and loosing and that when the pope departs from the law of Christ, his authority is null and void.
Popes are fallible and thus subordinate to Scripture. Scripture is the highest authority.
Sola Fide

The doctrine does not deny that necessity of good works, rather, good works will issue forth from a genuine faith. Luther insisted that good works contribute nothing to how a sinner is actually made right in the sight of God. Justification, for Luther, was a forensic declaration of our status before God, grounded solely on the imputed righteousness of Christ, received by the empty hands of faith.
We are made right with God simply by repenting and receiving the gospel.
Note the different terminologies Catholics and Protestants use:

Justification to the Catholics means “making righteous” - sanctification. Justification is not only the remission of sins, but also the sanctification and the renewal of the interior man. Catholics also distinguish between initial justification and ongoing justification. Thus, good works are not necessary to come into an initial state of reconciliation with God.

Protestants, on the other hand, justification means “declaring righteousness.” It refers to the forensic act by which we enter into right standing in God’s sight, distinct from our subsequent moral transformation. However, justification and sanctification are inseparable. Through union with Christ, we received both. It is therefore faith alone which justifies, yet the faith which justifies is not alone: just as it is the heat alone of the sun which warms the earth, and yet in the sun it is not alone, because it is constantly conjoined with light.
Both systems speak of an initial change by grace and then a subsequent process requiring works but here are the differences:

Protestants insist that the Aristotelian formal cause of justification is the intrinsic component of our justification that it essentially consists of - must be identified as the imputed righteousness of Christ as opposed to infused or inherent righteousness wrought within us. Our legal standing before God is not ultimately based on anything within us but on the external, alien, perfect righteousness of Jesus.

Such an account is necessitated by Paul’s teaching on justification, particularly in Galatians and Romans (Romans 4:5, 4:23-24). Such a justification is necessary for the assurance of salvation since an infused righteousness within us can never be the basis of our standing.
This is important because it bears upon the question of how we are actually acceptable to God.

Roles of baptism, penance, and indulgences are different with respect to justification. The basis in which we are accepted as righteous in God’s sight after our initial justification. Purgatory in the afterlife are different to name a few.
The Catholic Church believes if you commit a mortal sin before confession, you will go to hell.
Faith,
sola fide

, is different as well - faith does not mean intellectual assent, rather, it is a disposition of trusting assets and consecration and through love (Galatians 5:6). The faith is instrumental means by which we are actually made righteous in God’s sight and holds that good works must follow as the fruit of that faith.
The Case for Sola Scriptura

The core is that Scripture is the church’s only infallible rule. A rule is a standard that governs the church’s faith and practice. Infallible means being incapable of error. So Sola Scriptura is essentially the claim that Scripture is the only authority standing over the church that is incapable of error. The case is broken down into two parts:
Scripture’s unique role among the people of God

Catholics, Protestants and Eastern Orthodox generally agree but the difference is this: Does the church possess any rule other than Scripture that is infallible? Can Popes, councils, and all other postapostolic organs of the church fallible?
All that is infallible is authoritative but not all that is authoritative is infallible, think of the referee at a football game, nearly all authority we encounter in this world are fallible.
Sola Scriptura does not deny works (confessions, council functions), it just maintains that they are not infallible and therefore are placed under Scripture within a hierarchy of authorities.

Scripture is the “word of God,” it originated in God's mind and was communicated from God’s mouth by God’s spirit, for God spoke it (2 Timothy 3:16 - Paul calls it theopneustos - “inspired by God”, Romans 3:2 - “ta logia tou Theou” - oracles of God, God speaking - Mathew 19:4-5, John 10:35 - Scripture cannot be broken).

Despite Roman Catholics and Eastern Orthodox agreeing that Scripture is the inspired words of God, they separate infallibility from inspiration. Those positions have the burden of proof to show why another rule of faith that is not the inspired Word of God should nonetheless be accepted as equal to Scripture with respect to infallibility. Alternative proposals are needed to demonstrate the grounds for their elevation of additional rules of faith up into the realm of infallibility.
Scripture’s unique role among the people of God

In addition to meditation of Scripture for flourishing (Joshua 1:8, Psalms 1:2, 119), the specific position of authority is evident in how other authorities (including those ordained by God) are subordinated to it. Scripture is above tradition (Mathew 15, Mark 7). Even the Pharisees had God-given authority to teach God’s people, not merely humans from the oral law of Moses handed down the Mt. Sinai but oral traditions are not the inspired word of God, Scripture is.

Although the Pharisees did not contradict Scripture, Jesus rejects Pharisees’ inflated view of tradition (Mark 7:13, “many such things you do”) since their entire theory has been falsely claiming divine authority for their traditions.

New Testament apostles measure their teachings against Scripture (Acts 17:11). Further in Galatians 1:8, Paul goes to command that not only apostolic teaching but even angelic teaching must be tested according to the deposit of divine revelation given in the apostolic age.

For Protestants, we agree that Scripture was written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they have God as their author, and were as such committed to the church. The church’s charge extends not only to recognizing the canon but also to protecting the Scriptures during times of persecution and to translating, teaching and proclaiming them. Thus, Protestants have spoken of the church as not only a necessary witness to the Word of God, but also the custodian and herald of the Word of God.
Objection 1: What about the Cannon? (A biblical canon is the collection of books that comprise the sacred scriptures or Bibles of Jews and Christians)
The necessity of the church does not entail her infallibility: It is like comparing John the Baptist having paralleled authority to Christ. Church is a ministerial role of witness or testimony.

“As it is foolish to tell us that the candle receives its light from the candlestick that supports it, so it is ridiculous to ascribe the Scripture’s authority to the church” or “Sir Isaac Newton gave us the force of gravity. Newton did not create gravity, he recognized it.”
Ultimately, the trustworthiness of the canon is rooted in the guidance of the Holy Spirit, as well as the progressive nature of revelation itself.

It is not necessary to be infallible to discern what is infallible - When Moses heard God at the burning bush, he did not need a second voice whispering in his ear that this was indeed God. This is what Protestants intend when they speak of Scripture as self-authenticating. It simply means that the ultimate ground on which we receive the Scripture is inherent in it, rather than external to it. Transmission is through the Holy Spirit, not the result of an infallible statement from the Pope of Rome or an ecumenical council.

If you think you do have to possess infallibility to discern infallibility, you have a continual regress, because now you need infallibility to receive and interpret the infallible teachings of your church.
Objection 2: Doesn’t the New Testament teach us to obey “Traditions”?

Objectors often quote 1 Corinthians 11:2 & 2 Thess. 2:15 but it has nothing to do with sola Scriptura. Despite the church being established before written Scripture, the transmission of oral teachings is fallible and led to immediate disputes amongst the church.

Sola Scriptura in no way designates Scripture as the only authority to be obeyed (as opposed to only infallible rule). Sola Scriptura is a framework for the church as such, not for Christians in the apostolic age sitting under the teaching of living apostles, during the era when Scripture is still being written. Therefore, when passages like 2 Thessalonians 2:15 are set at odds with Scripture, its doctrine is being misunderstood.

Tradition itself is different amongst everyone until the council of Trent was established. There were 8 different definitions of the word tradition. Furthermore, the first 7th (only the 8th is opposed to Sola Scriptura) are in harmony with sola Scriptura.
Objection 3: Sola Scriptura has no precedent in church history

St. Augustine says that Scripture is qualitatively unique, grounds its uniqueness in its infallibility, and this unique infallibility is contrasted with an increasing chain of postbiblical authorities the church, including the highest expression of authority. He talks about how they can be corrected through the unveiling of new information, not from genuine error.

It is possible to hold to both Scripture and a larger cannon since Scripture is about the nature of the books’ authority. It is also perfectly consistent to accept a high view of tradition and the authority of the church while maintaining that only the Scripture is the infallible rule of the church.
The earlier Christians can practice Scripture since sola Scriptura is a conceptual framework for the church and is not refuted by circumstantial variation in practice.
Objection 4: Sola Scriptura depends on private judgment, leading to anarchy

Private judgements are itself not the authority, but note the necessity and dignity of private judgment - we all use private judgment for the most important and poignant decisions of life- this includes whether to be a Christian, which church to join and whether to remain in that church.

Another danger that is worse is erroneous ecclesiastical judgements which is what Scripture seeks to guard against. Those who adhere to Scripture simply seek to follow our conscience. Democracy is clumsy but it is better than tyranny. To submit to a system that requires assent to such beliefs would be dishonest and thus would violate our conscience. For Protestants, it is nothing less than tyranny when churches require belief in indulgences, the assumption of Mary, the veneration of icons or many other points of doctrine that we have no reason to believe are apostolic.

Sola Scriptura, in contrast, involves nothing less than setting the boundaries for what Christianity is and the necessary doctrines a Christian is required to accept. Sola Scriptura, therefore, is to place our ultimate trust in God alone, rather than in fallible, human claims.
History of Papacy
Papacy is an office in the church characterized by succession, infallibility and supremacy.
Succession means the office originates with Peter and succeeds to the Roman bishops
Infallibility means the pope is capable of speaking infallibly under certain conditions
Supremacy means the pope’s leadership is not merely advisory, but rather constitutes an immediate, universal and supreme power of jurisdiction over the whole church
However, both biblical and historical evidence seems overwhelming against the claims that bishops are infallible and a general known fact amongst church history.
Bible Evidence:

The New Testament does not talk about succession and the idea of succession comes after the New Testament. It is difficult to argue about papal succession from the New Testament which is why biblical arguments for papacy focus on Peter. In doing so, they assume succession rather than trying to establish it, but it is problematic as Peter’s office as an apostle was unique. If Jesus and the apostles envisioned an ongoing office in the church characterized by supremacy and infallibility, it is not unreasonable to expect it to come up somewhere in their teaching or writings but not a single verse mentions this.

The idea of a successive office stemming from Peter and imbued with his authority cannot merely be asserted, it has to be demonstrated. Peter certainly has a unique leadership role among the apostles but nonetheless, Peter’s role falls significantly short of the kind of supremacy and unique infallibility envisioned at Vatican I for popes. Furthermore, the other apostles were also the same as Peter , endowed with a like partnership both of honor and power (Galatians 2:9 - James, Peter and John are identified as “pillars.”)

Catholics usually quote Mathew 16:18 - 19 but the responsibilities of binding and loosing given to Peter here are reiterated to all the disciples just two chapters later in Matthew 18:18 - just as, generally throughout the New Testament, the authority to govern the church is entrusted to all the apostles conjointly (John 20:23). When contextualizing Matthew 16:18, Peter is speaking on behalf of the apostles in response to Jesus’s question of “Who do you (plural) say that I am? (Matthew 16:15).”

Rock imagery after which Peter is named has 3 proposals: Christ, Peter himself, or Peter’s confession. The best view is that one that combines all three of these options: The rock is Peter in his confessing Christ. Augustine’s view is that the rock is Christ, and since Peter confesses Christ, Peter is the rock in confessing Christ. Thus, Peter is the rock not as the first holder of an ecclesiastical office, but as a representation of the apostolic confession of Christ (Christ is called the rock on which the church is built - Ephesians 2:20, 1 Corinthians 10:4, Peter 2:8 - with the apostles as group also at times participating in this imagery as well - Galatians 2:9).
Historical Evidence:

Early historical evidence indicates that not only was there not a bishop in Rome who functioned as the head of the church, but there was not a single bishop at all. As church history progresses, though the Church of Rome comes into a kind of primacy, it falls significantly short of infallibility and supremacy throughout the patristic era and even into the medieval era.
Primacy does not necessarily entail supremacy and infallibility.

Papal infallibility is generally seen as explicitly emerging in the 13th century, and even then it remains enormously controversial for several centuries since it was not adopted at the Council of Trent. The doctrine was invented by a few dissident Franciscans because it suited their convenience to invent it,but only after much initial reluctance, it was accepted by the papacy because it suited the convenience of the popes to accept it.
Apostle Succession

Apostolical descent, according to the Catholics, is the ground for ecclesial authority, asserting that through the bishop who ordained them, they received the Holy Spirit, the power to bind and to lose, to administer the Sacraments and to preach. The ceremony of ordination is not idle but actually confers these rights. This exclusivism is the defining characteristic of apostolic succession via valid ordinations and valid Eucharist.
Protestants, on the other hand (except for Anglicans, Moravians, neo-Hussites and some lutherans), reject apostolic succession that the office is divinely commanded or is a result of divine law.

Protestants do not deny the general idea that the apostles’ ministry succeeds to the post-apostolic Christian church - individuals are appointed positions of leadership in the church with the intent that the ministry of the gospel would continue by the apostles. The concern is with the necessity of this specific form of organization, particularly the formal distinction between bishop and presbyter as of apostolic appointment and the resulting denial of valid ministry apart from this system.
Apostolic succession in scholarly appraisal (the stance scholars take): Apostolic succession is not apostolic - due to the indifference between elders and bishops.

There were multiple leaders running the church, not just a single bishop as stated in the New Testament (James 5:14, Acts 14:23, 1 Timothy 5:17, Hebrews 13:7 and 1 Thessalonians 5:12). Jesus’s brother James has a leadership role in the church of Jerusalem, but he is never called a bishop, same with Paul’s associates Titus and Timothy have a kind of itinerant ministry to various churches but also never referred to as bishops. Terms such as episkopos and presbyteros (bishops and elders) are used interchangeably and in 1 Peter 5:1-2, elders are described as “overseeing” the church.

Appointing elders if they are above reproach (free from sinful habits) for a bishop must be above reproach (1 Timothy 3) makes no sense unless the two terms refer to one and the same office. The apostles do not designate two distinct offices. Instead, the New Testament portrays two offices in the church bishop/elders and deacon. This can also be confirmed by first-century literature - Clement’s letter (first Pope of Rome). A clear distinction between the office of bishop and that of presbyter is found in the letter of Ignatius but Ignatius has no conception of apostolic succession as he did not mention bishops as successor of the apostles and instead identifies presbyters as “in the place of assembly of the apostles.” The bishop is therefore not the bearer of tradition, nor a New Testament priest, nor an apostolic succession - he is an office-bearer in a local church and has no authority outside of it (some may say Ignatius emphasized on bishops were due to early, fragile stage of the office such as the rise of heretics and Gnostic claims of private revelation).
The notion that the bishop functions in succession to the apostles itself lacks apostolic authority.

Even if Tertullian and Ienaeus (early Christian literature authors) effect their schemes of successors of the apostles, it would not matter even their doctrine is not apostolic (since it is declared by its own diversity and contrariety that it had for its author neither an apostle nor an apostolic man). They also had lineal succession contradiction between both Clement and Ienaeus.
This resonates with the Protestant instrict to regard succession of office as penultimate and in service of the deeper and ultimate criterion for determining valid ministry: succession of doctrine.

Even St. Jerome famously stated, “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.” This underscores his belief that a deep understanding of the Bible is essential for knowing and following Christ, thus placing Scripture at the heart of Christian life and practice.

Therefore, the recognition that apostolic succession is not of divine constitution but rather represents a gradual development in the early church need not necessarily entail that there is anything particularly wrong with episcopal church government as such, but requiring such a structure - limiting valid ministry to those churches adhering to it - unnecessarily injures and divide the church.
History and Protestantism

Some may argue that history of the church and Protestantism are completely alien to one another. However, the rationale for Protestantism was deep in history - alongside all the good God was doing in the history of the church, various aberrations, declensions, innovations, accretions and errors crept in along the way and the point of Protestantism was to remove these errors.
7 sacraments Catholic believed:
Bishop of Rome has universal and immediate jurisdiction over the church
Mary was bodily assumed to heaven
Kissing and bowing down to icons is necessary
Transubstantiation is the mechanism of real presence in the Eucharist

John Jewel in the Anglican tradition was against the abusive practices of the Eucharist such as withholding the wine to the lait and the denying of the bread and wine ceased to be bread and wine in substance.
Treasury of merit benefits Christians for reduced time in purgatory
Scripture need not to be translated into vernacular languages of the laity
Lord’s Supper need not be taken in both kinds

Calvin claimed that the church fathers were not unanimously in line with either Protestants or Catholics and they are not infallible. Calvin worked on various examples on how the Church of Rome in his day had totally abandoned the early church’s doctrine and being deep in history strengthened the Protestant concerns. Lutherans built a historical case against the violence and tyranny that resulted from a confusion of ecclesiastical and civil power in the church as they saw a departure not merely from Scripture, but from how the early church wielded authority and related to civil power.

When talking about “deep” history, it splits into either ancient or majority depth. Page 149-159 argues that majority depth is a poor representation or criteria of history.
