I was googling “Best Philosophical Books to Read” on Youtube and Reddit. I was presented with answers like “start from the Greeks and work your way up to the Middle Ages, Enlightenment before going onto the Existentialists.” No. Firstly, to do that would mean I am dedicating my whole education to philosophy. Believe me I have tried and had a stroke reading
“Plato’s Dialogues.”
A Reddit comment, however, caught my eye. The Reddit user said that “
Sophie’s World”

was a good introduction book to get a bird’s eye view of the main teaching of the philosophers and a brief timeline of History, plus it is fiction so hopefully I thought it would be an easy read. Thankfully, it did exactly that. At the same time, the fiction part of the book was fantastic mystery.

The story begins with Sophie Amundsen, a fourteen-year-old schoolgirl living in Norway, who begins receiving mysterious letters in her mailbox. These letters contain philosophical lessons addressed to her from a philosopher named Alberto Knox. As Sophie receives these letters, she is introduced to the fundamental questions and big ideas that have shaped human thought throughout history. The journey through philosophy is structured around the historical development of philosophy, starting from the ancient Greeks such as Socrates and Plato, through the Middle Ages, the Renaissance, the Enlightenment, up to the romantic and existential thinkers and beyond.
Metafictional Twist (Spoiler Alert!)

As the story unfolds, Sophie and Alberto discover strange things about their reality, suggesting that their world might not be what it seems. This leads to an exploration of metaphysics and the nature of existence. The novel eventually reveals itself to be a
book within a book

, where Sophie and Alberto are actually characters in a story written by a major in the UN, who is using the story to communicate with his daughter, Hilde. This metafictional twist explores the relationship between creation and existence in a philosophical narrative form.
Why Philosophy

I think this answered why people even learn philosophy in the first place (I mean it was not a very practical subject in today’s day and age). But the book examines the ways in which philosophy can apply to everyday living and encourages readers to question and think critically about their own lives and realities. The themes of curiosity, the pursuit of knowledge, and the questioning of conventional wisdom are central to the novel.

To me, "Sophie's World" is more than just a novel; it is an educational text that offers an impressive overview of the history and development of Western philosophy. In fact, this might have to be the best book I have read this year! 🙂
Sophie’s World
The earliest Greek philosophers are known as the natural philosophers because they were mainly concerned with the natural world and its processes.

The first three philosophers: Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes believed in the existence of a basic substance as the source of all things. But how could one thing transform into something else? They were interested in the problem of change.
Parmenides thought that everything that exist has always existed, nothing can come out of nothing and nothing that exists can become nothing
No such thing as actual change. Nothing could become anything other than it was.

Nature is in a constant change of flux and our senses tell us that things are always changing. However, Parmenides did not trust his empirical senses and believed change was an illusion, our picture does not tally with our reason he claims. The innate thought of human reasoning is known as rationalism where human reason is our primary source of knowledge in the world.
Heraclitus thought that constant change was the most basic characteristic of nature in contrast to Parmenides.
The world is characterized by opposites he claimed.
Both good and bad have their inevitable place in the order of things and without this constant interplay of opposites the world would cease to exist.
Although we humans do not have the ‘same’ degree of reason, there has to be a ‘universal reason’ guiding everything that happens in nature, yet, most people follow their individual reason.
Therefore Permenides says:
Nothing can change
Our sensory perceptions are therefore unreliable
While Heraclitus says:
Everything changes
Our sensory perceptions are therefore reliable

Then Empedocles (490 - 430 BC) came along and said both of them were right in one assertion but wrong in the other. They both assumed that the fundamental substance consists only of one element. Parmenides is right when pure water can only be pure water so nothing changes but at the same time Heraclitus is right when he claims that we should trust our senses. So Empedocles believe that our fundamental substances should be fire, water, air and earth.

Anaxagaros also held the view that there is more than one fundamental substance but these substances consist of an infinite number of molecules that are naked to the eye. Moreover, everything can be divided into smaller parts, but even the minutest part there can be fragments of other things. He constructed the notion that there is ‘something in everything.’
All three philosophers were right in some sense. So Democritus (460-370 BC) came along with the atom theory where he compared legos to objects.

You could use lego blocks to build anything you want. Today we establish that Democritus is more or less correct. The atoms can be broken down to protons, neurons and electrons but physicists agree that somewhere along the line there exists a limit. There has to be a minimal part which nature consists of.

Once again, it is accepted that nothing can change, that nothing can come out of nothing and that nothing is ever lost, then nature must consist of infinitesimal blocks that can join and separate again.

Democritus did not believe in any force or soul that could intervene in natural processes. The only thing that existed were atoms and void. Since he believed in nothing but material things - he is a materialist where there is no ‘conscious’ design in the movement of atoms since everything happens quite mechanically in nature.

Everything that happens has a natural cause and a cause that is inherent in the thing itself. This does not mean that everything happens randomly, for everything obeys the inevitable laws of necessity.

Since Democritus believed that the soul is just made out of atoms, a human’s soul will just be atoms breaking down and ready for a new formation again. This meant that we have no immortal soul and that we cannot have any form of consciousness once the brain disintegrates.
Socrates versus Sophists

Sophists are essentially teachers, however, they doubted traditional mythology but at the same time, doubted fruitless philosophical speculation. Their opinion was that although answers to philosophical questions may exist, man cannot know the truth about the riddles of nature and of the universe - they were skeptics.
Sophists believed that things like modesty and morality are socially induced, not innate.
There were no absolute norms for what is right and wrong.
Socrates, on the other hand, tried to show that such norms are in fact absolute and universally valid.
Socrates believed that the ability to distinguish between right and wrong likes in people’s reason and not in society
The existence of eternal and absolute rules for what was right and wrong and by using our common sense, we can arrive at these immutable norms, since human reason is in fact eternal and immutable.

Socrates thought that no one could possibly be happy if they acted against their better judgment. And he who knows how to achieve happiness will do so. Therefore, he who knows what is right will do right because why would anybody choose to be unhappy?
Plato

Plato attempts to answer the question: Does man have an immortal soul? If man had an immortal soul, one would have to believe that a person consisted for two separate parts: A body that gets worn out after many years and a soul that operates more or less independently of what happens to the body (“
I had always been a young boy at heart

Plato is concerned with the relationship between what is eternal and immutable just like the pre-Socratics. He believed that in the natural world there are fundamental substances. Absolutely everything that belongs to the material world is made of a material that time can erode but everything is made after a timeless ‘mold’ or ‘form’ that is eternal and immutable. He believes the idea of something comes before the reality of that something.

You have a box of legos and you build a lego house. You then take it apart and put the blocks back in the box. You cannot expect to make a new horse just by shaking the box. How could lego blocks of their own accord find each other and become a new horse again? No, you have to rebuild the horse and the reason you do that is that you have a picture in your mind of what the horse looked like. The lego horse is made from a model which remains unchanged from horse to horse just like how a cookie mold makes replicas of other cookies.
This reality, known as the world of ideas, contained eternal and immutable patterns behind various phenomena we come across in nature.

Just like how 6 x 2 = 12, we could say reason is eternal and universal precisely because it only expresses eternal and universal states. Imagine you find a round pinecone and you ‘think’ it looks completely round while your friend thinks it is flat on one side. But you cannot have true knowledge of anything you can perceive with your eyes. On the other hand, you can say with absolute certainty that the sum of angles in a circle is 360 degrees. In this case you would be talking about an ideal circle which might not exist in the physical world but which you can clearly visualize.

In short, we can only have exact conceptions of things we perceive with our senses. But we can have true knowledge of things we understand with our reason. The sum of the angles of things we understand with our reason. The sum of angles in a triangle will remain 180 degrees to the end of time. Similarly, the ‘idea’ horse will walk on four legs even if all the horses in the sensory world break a leg.

Therefore, man is a dual creature. We have a body that is inseparably bound to the world of senses and all of our senses are based in the body and consequently unreliable. But we also have an immortal soul and this soul is the realm of reason.

The soul existed before it inhabited man’s body. We are just discovering various forms of the natural world. When you see a shadow of an animal, you may think it is a horse but you are not sure. So you turn around and see the horse itself which of course is infinitely sharper in outline than the blurred ‘horse-shadows.’ Plato believed similarly that all natural phenomena are merely shadows of eternal forms or ideas.
Aristotle

Aristotle, however, believes exactly the opposite of Plato. He agrees that the actual form of the horse is eternal and immutable. But the ‘idea’ of the horse was simply a concept that we humans had formed after seeing a certain number of horses. The ‘idea’ of a horse thus had no existence of its own. To Aristotle, the ‘idea’ of the horse was made up of the horse’s characteristics which define what we today call the horse species. The mold Plato talked about earlier is irrelevant as the mold exists independently of the particular cookies. The real thing and the ‘idea’ of the thing are just inseparable as the body and soul.
Aristotle claims that the highest degree of reality is what we perceive with our senses while Plato claims that the highest degree of reality is what we think with our reason.

Aristotle believes that things in the human soul were purely reflections of natural objects. Nothing exists in consciousness that has not first been experienced by the senses. All thoughts and ideas have come into consciousness through what we have heard and seen. But we also have an innate power of reason. We have no innate ideas but we have the innate faculty of organizing all sensory impressions into categories and classes.
It is reason that constitutes man's most distinguishing characteristic. But our reason is completely empty until we have sensed something. So man has no innate ideas.
Metaphysics with Aristotle (Aristotle was concerned with the changes in nature):
Potentials and actuals

‘Substance’ always contains the potentiality to realize a specific ‘form’ and ‘substance’ always strives towards achieving an innate potentiality. Every change in nature is a transformation of substance from ‘potential’ to ‘actual.’

The chicken and egg problem: A chicken’s egg has the potentiality to become a chicken. This does not mean that all chicken’s eggs become chickens as they may become other forms such as fried eggs, omelet or scrambled eggs without ever having realized their potentiality. But it is equally obvious that a chicken’s egg cannot become a goose. That potentiality is not within a chicken’s egg. The ‘form’ of a thing then says something about its limitation as well as its potentiality.
The final cause and causality in nature
Aristotle held that there were different types of cause in nature. Altogether he named four different causes, with the ‘final cause’ being the most important.

Peter threw the stone and the stone smashed the window. In the case of window smashing, it is quite reasonable to ask why Peter threw the stone. We are thus asking what his purpose was. There can be no doubt that purpose played a role, also, in the matter of the shoe being made. But Aristotle also took into account a similar 'purpose' when considering the purely lifeless processes in nature. Here's an example: Why does it rain? You have probably learned at school that it rains because the moisture in the clouds cools and condenses into raindrops that are drawn to the earth by the force of gravity. Aristotle would have nodded in agreement. But he would have added that so far you have only mentioned three of the causes. The 'material cause' is that the moisture (the clouds) was there at the precise moment when the air cooled. The efficient cause is that the moisture cools, and the 'formal cause' is that the 'form,' or nature of the water, is to fall to the earth. But if you stopped there, Aristotle would add that it rains because plants and animals need rainwater in order to grow. This he called the 'final cause’ Aristotle assigns the raindrops a life-task, or 'purpose. We would probably turn the whole thing upside down and say that plants grow because they find moisture. You can see the difference, can't you? Aristotle believed that there is a purpose behind everything in nature. It rains so that plants can grow; oranges and grapes grow so that people can eat them.

That is not the nature of scientific reasoning today. We say that food and water are necessary conditions of life for man and beast. Had we not had these conditions we would not have existed. But it is not the purpose of water or oranges to be food for us.

In the question of causality then, we are tempted to say that Aristotle was wrong. But let us not be too hasty. Many people believe that God created the world as it is so that all His creatures could live in it. Viewed in this way, it can naturally be claimed that there is water in the rivers because animals and humans need water to live. But now we are talking about God's purpose. The raindrops and the waters of the river have no interest in our welfare.
Logic
Aristotle also created the concept of logic where it runs with first premise, second premise and conclusion or by asking a bunch of if-else statements to construct your argument.
Nature’s scale

Above we mentioned potentials and actuals. Aristotle made it very clear that nonliving things have no potential for change and nonliving things can only change through external influence. Only living things have the potentiality for change.

Living things are split into two categories: Human and non-humans. We say that all living things have the ability to absorb nourishment, grow and to propagate and all ‘living creatures’ have in addition the ability to perceive the world around us and to move about. All humans have the ability to think or to order their perceptions into various categories and classes.

Therefore, we are made in God’s image and there has to be someone who started all movement in the natural world. Therefore, something must be causing planets to move which is known as the ‘first mover’ or ‘God.’ The ‘first mover’ is itself at rest but it is the formal cause of the movement of nature.
Ethics
Aristotle believed in the golden mean (see Morality document).

Factors that contributes to a person’s philosophy of life:
Upbringing and environment - People living at the time of Plato had a different philosophy of life than many people have today because they lived in a different age and a different environment.
The experience people choose for themselves

But common sense is not determined by the environment, it is by conscience - the ability to respond to right and wrong. My personal opinion is that conscience is innate but just what conscience dictates can vary a lot from one person to the next. The Sophists believe that right and wrong is mainly determined by the environment the individual grows up in while Socrates believed that conscience is the same for everyone. Some say perhaps both views are right. Even if everybody does not feel guilty about showing themselves naked, most people will have a bad conscience if they are really mean to someone.

Timeline Check: After the rise in Cynicism, Stoicism and Neoplatonism, we are now transitioning from BC to AD. This was when Jesus had a large influence, together with Apostle Paul preaching in Greece. Afterwards came the rise of the Dark Ages - a thousand year long period which had settled over Europe between antiquity and the Renaissance.
Middle Ages and Dark Ages

The Middle Ages spanned roughly from the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 AD to the beginning of the Renaissance around the 15th century (approximately 1453 AD when Constantinople fell to the Ottomans).
The term "Dark Ages" is traditionally used to describe the earliest part of the Middle Ages—from the fall of Rome in the 5th century to about the 10th century.

The term was originally intended to denote the perceived cultural and economic deterioration that supposedly occurred in Western Europe following the decline of Rome. The "darkness" implies a lack of written records, cultural achievements, and general backwardness compared to the Roman Empire.
It's typically divided into three phases: the Early Middle Ages (5th to 10th century), the High Middle Ages (11th to 13th century), and the Late Middle Ages (14th to 15th century).

The Dark Ages are part of the Middle Ages. The Dark Ages constitute the initial phase (Early Middle Ages) and are followed by the High Middle Ages and then the Late Middle Ages. The term "Middle Ages" is a more neutral, comprehensive descriptor for the entire medieval period in Europe, whereas "Dark Ages" focuses on the earliest and arguably the least-documented and understood phase.

This period saw the development of feudalism, the rise of the Catholic Church as a dominant institution, the spread of monasticism, and the slow emergence of Europe from societal collapse. It was marked by significant agricultural, social, political, and religious changes.
This period is when Christianity took time to reach the masses with the era and mighty prices, majestic kings, chivalrous knights, friars, crusades and witches.

End of the fourth century, the Bishop of Rome became the supreme head of the Roman Catholic Church and was given the title “Pope” which became Christ’s deputy on earth. Rome was thus the Christian capital throughout most of the medieval period, but as kings and bishops of the new nation-states became increasingly powerful, some of them rebelled against the church.
The Old Roman empire split into three different cultures.
Western Europe had Latinized Christian culture with Rome as its capital
Eastern Europe had a Greek Christian culture with Constantinople as its capital and its called by its Greek name, Byzantium.

North Africa and the Middle East were won over to Islam in 632 after Muhammad conquered them. Shortly after, Spain also became part of the world of Islamic culture which adopted Mecca, Medina, Jerusalem and Baghdad as holy cities.

We could see it as Neoplatonism in the west, Plato in the east and Aristotle to the Arbs in the South but all three teachings converge in Northern Italy which is the beginning of the Renaissance - the ‘rebirth’ of antique culture which survived the Dark Ages.

We are now at the period where society splits into two different groups: Believe in the Christian revelation or approach the Christian truths with the help of reason. Are the Bible and reason compatible or were belief and knowledge compatible. Almost all of medieval philosophy centered on this one question.

This is where St. Augustine (354 - 430 AD) came about and was preoccupied with the ‘problem of evil.’ According to the Stoics, there was no sharp division between good and evil but St. Augustine was largely influenced by Platonic ideas. Much of Greek philosophy was carried over to the Fathers of the Church like St. Augustine.

He pointed out that there are limits to how far reason can get you in religious questions and Christianity is a divine mystery that we can only perceive through faith. Thus, there is a limit to how far philosophy could go.
He believed that God created the world, the ‘ideas’ were in the Divine mind, so he located Platonic ideas in God and in that way preserved the Platonic view of eternal ideas.

He was inclined to Neoplatonism in his view of evil, like Plotinus, evil is the ‘absence of God.’ Evil has no independent existence, it is something that it is not. For God’s creation is in fact only good. Evil comes from mankind’s disobedience. “
The good will is God’s work; the evil will is falling away from God’s work.

Man has a material body which belongs to the physical world but he has a soul which can know God. No man deserves God’s redemption and yet God has chosen some to be saved from damnation, so for him there was nothing secret about who will be saved and who damned. It is preordained and entirely at his mercy.
He believed in determinism but he did not deny free will. But God has ‘foreseen’ how we will live.

At the same time, much of St. Augustine’s work is not influenced by Plato. He was more influenced by the linear view of history in the Old Testament: the idea that God needs all of history in order to realize his Kingdom of God. History is necessary for the enlightenment of man and the destruction of evil.
In 1225 to 1274 AD, the most significant philosopher is known as St. Thomas Aquinas:

So why is there no need for conflict between reason and faith? Faith such as Genesis creation of the world is only accessible through belief and Christian Revelation. But Aquinas believed in ‘natural theological truths.’ Truths that could be reached both though Christian faith and through innate or natural reason.

Aquinas' work was to prove there was only one truth. Aristotle tells us truth is when we describe plants and animal kingdoms but another aspect of truth is revealed to us by God through the Bible. Therefore, it is either through ‘theology of faith’ or ‘natural theology.’

Just like how we can hear the thunder even if we are blind and we can see the lightning even if we are deaf, it is best if we can both see and hear but there is no contradiction between what we see and hear. On the contrary, the two impressions reinforce each other.

God’s Creation and the Bible is like reading the book and finding out about its author. We can get to know the author’s nature through his writing but you cannot expect to get any perAsonal information about him. We can recognise that there is a God just by walking around the natural world (like how he loves animals and plants if not He will not make them), but information about God, the person, is only found in the Bible or God's ‘autobiography.’
The Renaissance Period

Not very long after St. Thomas Aquinas, cracks began to appear in the unifying culture of Christianity. Philosophy and science broke away more and more from the theology of the Church. More people now emphasized that we cannot reach God through rationalism because God is in all ways unknowable. The important thing for a man was not to understand the divine mystery but to submit to God’s will.

This period is when human weapons such as firearms, compass and the printing press were discovered and were preconditions for the Renaissance. Innovation and man were rampant and that forced the Church to relinquish its former position as sole dissemination of knowledge. It brought in a new view of mankind - man is now considered infinitely great and valuable in constant to the sinful nature of a man.

This is where individualism comes in - we are not only human beings, we are unique individuals. Art, science and man were embraced - for instance, sculptures of naked men were created. They embraced culture and the Renaissance humanists saw it as their cultural duty to restore Rome: They began to construct St. Peter’s Church over the grave of Peter the Apostle.

This period also gave rise to the empirical method where every investigation of natural phenomena must be based on observation, experience and experiment and not on figments of the imagination. The scientific method of Copernicus, Galileo, Newton.

This period resulted in a new religiosity where philosophy and science gradually broke from theology. A new Christian piety developed. The individual’s personal relationship to God was now more important than his relationship to the church as the organization. The reformation of the church by Martin Luther posits that people did not need the intercession of the church of priests in order to receive God’s forgiveness. The Scripture alone, he said, is the source of Christianity where he believed in the Bible over the church rituals.
The Baroque Period

This word ‘baroque’ meant irregular shapes. People valued irregularity and abstract art more than the plain and harmonious Renaissance art. Both in art and in real life, there is the rise of flamboyant self-expression. That was when famous Latin expressions such as  “carpe diem - seize the day” and ‘memento mori - remember you must die’ came into being. Theater was highly valued (Shakespeare Hamlet 1600 marked the transition from the Renaissance to Baroque period).

This period was also an age of political conflict - the worst was the Thirty Year War which raged over most of the continent from 1618 to 1648. The French revolution was one of them and wars between Protestants and Catholics were rampant.

The 17th Century gave rise to materialism where all real things are derived from concrete material substances. One famous philosopher is Thomas Hobbes where he believed that all phenomena, including man and animals, consist exclusively of particles of matter. Even human consciousness or the soul derives from the movement of tiny particles in the brain. It is therefore possible in principle to calculate every natural change with mathematical precision since everything was governed by the same unbreakable laws or by the same mechanisms. However, Newton did not see this as a contradiction between the mechanistic world picture and belief in God.

However, this was not the case for all philosophers. Laplace had an extreme mechanistic view where if an intelligence at a given time had known the position of all particles then nothing would be unknown and both future and past would lie open before their eyes. The idea here is that everything that happens will happen - an idea known as determinism. There is no such thing as free will since everything is just a product of mechanical processes.

One can oppose the materialistic argument: Even though an astronaut has been in space many times, he has never seen God or Angels but that is like saying a brain surgeon has operated on many clever brains but has never seen a single thought. Thoughts and consciousness cannot be broken down or reduced to smaller parts. That is the difference between the material and spiritual. The soul therefore, cannot be divided into two.
Modern Philosophy

After the rediscovery of man and the Renaissance period, the need to assemble contemporary thought into one coherent philosophical system again presented itself: The first was Descartes, followed by Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke, Berekeley, Hume and Kant.
Descartes

Descartes' main concern was what we can know, or in other words, certain knowledge. The other great question that preoccupied him was the relationship between body and mind. He was an extreme skeptic. He believes that we should be skeptics because if our foundations give way, the whole house collapses.

In earlier parts of this document, some philosophers did not introduce any radical decision of soul and body as the motions of all material objects - including the body, animal or human - were explained as involving mechanical processes. But man’s soul could not be part of this body machinery, what then is a soul? If I were to lift my arm and my arms lift itself. Or I decide to run for a bus and the next second my legs are moving. There must be some sort of connection between body and consciousness.
Descartes agrees with Plato that mathematics and numerical ratio gives us more certainty than our evidence of senses. If there was anything more we could perceive with the same intrusive certainty.
When we doubted, we had to be thinking and because we are thinking, it had to be certain that we are thinking beings.
“I think, therefore I am.”

Descartes came to the conclusion that in our minds we had a clear and distinct idea of a perfect entity which meant that the idea could not possibly have come from himself. The idea of a perfect entity cannot have originated from one who was imperfect. Therefore, a perfect entity had to come from a perfect entity itself which in other words from God. That God exists was therefore just as self-evident for Descartes as that a thinking being must exist.

We all possess the idea of a perfect entity, and that inherent in that idea that this perfect entity must exist. Because a perfect entity would not be perfect if it did not exist. Neither would we possess the idea of a perfect entity if there were no perfect entity. For we are imperfect, so the idea of perfection cannot come from us. According to Descartes, the idea of God is innate. However, one may say that just because you possess the idea of something, it does not mean that it exists. Descartes' answer to this is that it is not inherent in the concept of something that makes it exist. On the other hand, it is inherent in the concept of a perfect entity that such an entity. It is inherent in the idea of a circle that all points of the circle are equidistant to the center. You cannot have a circle that does not conform to this law, nor can you have a perfect entity that lacks its most important property, mainly existence. Like Plato and Socrates, there is a connection between reason and being.

Quantitative properties are just as clear and distinct to the reason as the fact that you are a thinking being while qualitative properties are linked to our sense perception and as such do not describe outer reality.
To Descartes, there are two different forms of reality: One substance is thought or ‘mind’, the other is extension, or matter.

The mind is purely conscious. It cannot be divided or reduced. Matter can be divided and reduced but it has no consciousness. Therefore, God exists independently of anything else. But although both thought and extension come from God, the two substances have no contact with each other. Thought is quite independent of matter, and conversely, the material process is quite independent of thought.
Man is a dual creature that both thinks and takes up room in space. Man has thus both a mind and an extended body, similar to what Thomas Aquinas and St. Augustine has said.
Spinoza
Spinoza, on the other hand, identities God with nature.

Suppose you had a stomach ache, what is it that feels the pain? It is you. When you later recollect that you once had pain in your stomach, it is you that thinks. So you are a single person that has a stomach ache and is in a thoughtful mood the next.
Spinoza therefore maintained that all material things and things that happen around us are an expression of God or nature. For everything is one.

So who are you? You are an expression of something infinitely bigger. You can say that you are thinking or that you are moving, but could you not also say that it is nature that is thinking your thoughts or that it is nature that is moving through you? Spinoza believed that God is the near cause of everything that happens. God controls the world through natural laws, not a puppeteer who pulls all the strings, controlling everything that happens. This means everything in the material world happens through necessity. Spinoza had a deterministic view of the material or natural world. It is a bit like Stoicism which constituted Spinoza’s ethics.
David Hume

Hume is an empiricist. A complex idea he says consists of two different experiences which are not in fact related, but which nevertheless are associated in man’s imagination. In other words, it is a false idea that must be immediately rejected.
Does it contain any abstract reasoning concerning quantity or number?
(Impression)
By impressions, he means the immediate sensation of external reality.
Does it contain any experimental reasoning concerning matters of fact and existence?
(Ideas)
By ideas, he means the recollection of such impressions.

Hume’s point is that we sometimes form complex ideas for which there is no corresponding object in the physical world. We sense each element and it enters the theater of the mind in the form of a real ‘impression.’ Nothing is ever actually invented by the mind. The mind puts things together and constructs ‘false’ ideas.

Hume says that we imagine God as an ‘infinitely intelligent, wise and good being.’ We thus have a complex idea that consists of something infinitely intelligent, something infinitely wise and something infinitely good. If we had never known intelligence, wisdom and goodness, we would never have such an idea of God.

Therefore, Hume opposed all thoughts and ideas that could not be tracked back to corresponding sense perceptions. How do we explain complex expressions (like ego)? Hume says that the perception of the ego is in reality a long chain of simple impressions that you have never experienced simultaneously. It is ‘nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed one another with an inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual flux and movement.’
Hume was an agnostic - someone who can neither prove nor disprove the existence of God.

According to Hume, he only rejected miracles because he has not experienced any. But he had not experienced that they could not happen either. A miracle is against the laws of nature, but it is meaningless to allege that we have experienced the laws of nature. We experience a stone falling to the ground when we let go of it, and if it did not fall - we experienced that too.

So how are you always so certain that it falls to the ground? Hume says you have experienced a stone falling to the ground many times. But you have never experienced that it will always fall. It is usual to say that the stone falls to the ground because of the law of gravitation. But we have never experienced such a law, we have only experienced that things fall.

Just like how a child will be less shocked than his parents if he sees a man floating, it shows that the child has not yet become a slave of the expectations of habit. The child perceives the world as it is, without putting more into things than he experiences. The laws of nature are not ‘reasonable’ or ‘unreasonable,’ they simply are. We are not born with a set of expectations as to what the world is like or how things behave. The world is like it is and it is something we get to know. Just because you see a whole herd of black horses, does not mean all horses are black. The fact that one thing follows after another thus does not necessarily mean there is a causal link. Correlation does not link to causation. This is what empiricism is.

Hume also rebelled against rationalist thought in the area of ethics where the ability to distinguish between right and wrong is inherent in human reason. It is our sentiments and feelings, not our reasons when we decide to help someone I need. According to Hume, we all have feelings for other people’s welfare.

So why should you not kill a troublesome person? You might say it is because he ought to live. But is that a logical reason? You merely drew a descriptive sentence - “that person wants to live too” - to a normative statement - “therefore, you ought not to kill them.” You might say as well “there are a lot of people who cheat on their taxes, therefore, I ought to cheat on it too.” You can never draw conclusions from
is
sentences to
ought

sentences. More examples include “more people want to travel by air, therefore more airports ought to be built” or “the development of new oil fields will raise the population’s standard of living, therefore we ought to develop new oilfields as quickly as possible.” In both cases, we need to think of the environment, in that sense, we have established that we cannot use reason as a yardstick for how we ought to act. Acting responsibly is not a matter of strengthening our reason but of deepening our feelings for the welfare of others. When the Nazis murdered the Jews, is it because of their reasons or their feelings?
Berkeley (1685 - 1753 AD)

Berkeley felt that current philosophies and science were a threat to the Christian life. As an empiricist, he said the only things that exist are those we perceive. But we do not perceive ‘material’ or ‘matter.’ We do not perceive things as tangible objects. To assume that what we perceive has its own underlying substance is jumping to conclusions. We have absolutely no experience on which to base such a claim.

Suppose you smack the table, you felt the sensation of something hard but you did not feel the actual matter in the table. In the same way, you can dream you are hitting something hard, but there is not anything hard in the dream.
He therefore believed in a spirit where all our ideas have a cause beyond our consciousness, but this cause is not of a material nature. It is spiritual.

Material reality is not the only thing Berkeley questioned, he also questioned whether ‘time’ and ‘space’ had any absolute or independent existence. Our own perception of time and space can also be merely figments of the mind. A week or two for us need not be a week for the Christian God. Immanuel Kant

Kant who is a professor of philosophy who constructs his own philosophy and an expert on the history of philosophy. Like Berkeley, he felt it was essential to preserve the foundations of Christian belief. So far, it is either the world is exactly as we perceive it or it is the way it appears to our reason. Rationalism versus empiricism. Kant agrees with Hume and the empiricist that all our knowledge of the world comes from our sensations, but in our reason, there are also decisive factors that determine how we perceive the world around us. In other words, there are certain conditions in the human mind that contribute to our conception of the world.

Suppose you put on red sunglasses, all you see will be red. This is because the glasses limit the way you perceive reality. Everything you see is part of the world around you, but how you see it is determined by the glasses you are wearing. So you cannot say the world is red even though you conceive it as being so. This is what Kant means when there are certain conditions governing the mind’s operation which influence the way we experience the world.

These conditions are ‘time’ and ‘space’ our two ‘forms of intuition’ which precede every experience. In other words, we can know before we experience things that we will perceive them as phenomena in time and space - we are unable to take off the ‘glasses’ of reason. We may see things differently due to our upbringing but wherever we are, we experience the world as a series of processes in time and space. Time and space, to Kant, are modes of perception and not attributes to the physical world. Just like how water adapts itself to the glass, our perceptions adapt themselves to our ‘forms of intuition.’

Even the law of causality which Hume believed man could not experience belongs to the mind. Hume said that it was only the force of habit that made us see a causal link behind all natural processes, but Kant makes it into an attribute of human reason. The law of causality is eternal and absolute simply because human reason perceives everything that happens as a matter of cause and effect. It is inherent within us. He agrees with Hume that we cannot know with certainty what the world is like ‘in itself.’ We can only know what the world is like ‘for me’ or for everybody. We do not know how things are but how things appear to us. For instance, before you go out, you cannot know what you will see or experience during the day, but you can know that what you see and experience will be perceived as happening in time and space. You can moreover be confident that the law of cause and effect will apply, simply because you carry it with you as part of your consciousness.
Hume says we can neither perceive or prove natural laws but Kant believed he could prove their absolute validity by showing that in reality we are talking about the laws of human cognition.

To sum up: According to Kant, there are two elements that contribute to man’s knowledge of the world. They are external conditions that we cannot know of before we have perceived them through the senses - the material of knowledge. The other is the internal conditions in man himself - such as the perception of events happening in time and space and as processes conforming to unbreakable law of causality - the form of knowledge.

However, Kant believed that there are clear limits to what we can know - ‘the mind’s glasses set this limit.’ As philosophers tried to answer the big questions, Kant believed there was no certain knowledge to be obtained on these questions as reason operates beyond the limits of what we humans comprehend. At the same time, there is in our nature a basic desire to pose these same questions. But when, for example, we ask whether the universe is finite or infinite, we are asking about a totality of which we ourselves are a tiny part. We can therefore never completely know this totality since reasoning had no sensory material to process, no experience to make us of. In short, we have never experienced the whole of the great reality that we are a tiny part of.
In such weighty questions as to the nature of reality, Kant showed that there will always be two contrasting viewpoints that are equally likely or unlikely, depending on what our reason tells us.

For example, it is just as meaningful to say that the world must have had a beginning in time as to say that it had no such beginning. Reason cannot decide between them. We can allege that the world has always existed, but can anything always have existed if there was never any beginning? So now we are forced to adopt the opposite view. Therefore, both views are equally reasonable and unreasonable. Therefore, since human reason is unable to make a certain judgment, we are bound to fail if we attempt to prove the existence of God with the aid of reason. Here, rationalists like Descartes had tried to prove that there must be a God simply because we have the idea of a ‘supreme being.’ Others like Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas, decided that there must be a God because everything must have a first cause. Kant rejected these two proofs of the existence of God. Therefore, since both reason and experience fall short, there occurs a vacuum that can be filled in by faith.

Ethics with Kant: Kant had always felt that the difference between right and wrong was a matter of reason, not sentiment. In this he agreed with the rationalists, who said the ability to distinguish between right and wrong is inherent in human reason. We know objective moral standards because we are born with it and everybody has ‘practical reason,’ that is, the intelligence that gives us the capacity to discern what is right and wrong in every case.
For Kant, the moral law precedes every experience and is not bound to any particular situation of moral choice (objective morality). It says how you are to behave in all situations.

Kant formulates this moral law as a categorical imperative. By this he means that the moral law is ‘categorical,’ or that it applies to all situations. It is, moreover, ‘imperative,’ which means it is commanding and therefore absolutely authoritative.
Act only on that maxim through which you can at the same time that it should become a universal law
. When you do something, make sure you want everyone else to do the same if they are in the same situation.
Act in such a way that you always treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never simply as a means but always at the same time as an end.
It is the same as the golden rule:
Do unto others, what does unto you

The law of morals is just as absolute and just as universal as the law of causality which cannot be proved by reason but it is nevertheless absolute and unalterable. Kent’s law of morals is like describing the human conscience. We cannot prove what our conscience tells us but we know it, nevertheless.

But if you share with others only to be popular, you are not acting out of respect for moral law. You might be acting in accordance with moral law - and that could be fair enough - but if it is to be a moral action, you must have conquered yourself. Only when you do something purely out of duty can it be called a moral action (duty ethics). It is this good will that determines whether or not the action was morally right, not the consequences of the action. Kent’s ethics is also called a good will ethic.

Kant posits we have free will: Kant divides man into two parts in a way not dissimilar to the way Descartes claimed that man was a "dual creature," one with both a body and a mind. As material creatures, we are wholly and fully at the mercy of causality's unbreakable law, says Kant. We do not decide what we perceive-perception comes to us through necessity and influences us whether we like it or not. But we are not only material creatures, we are also creatures of reason.

As material beings we belong wholly to the natural world. We are therefore subject to causal relations. As such, we have no free will. But as rational beings we have a part where the world as it exists in itself, independent of our sensory impressions. Only when we follow our "practical reason" - which enables us to make moral choices - do we exercise our free will, because when we conform to moral law, it is we who make the law we are conforming to. So when you choose not to be mean - even if it is against your own interests you are then acting freely. You're not especially free or independent if you just do whatever you want, in any case.
One can become a slave to all kinds of things. One can even become a slave to one's own egoism. Independence and freedom are exactly what are required to rise above one's desires and vices.

Ending off with one of his most quoted sayings is carved on his gravestone in Königsberg: "Two things fill my mind with ever increasing wonder and awe, the more often and the more intensely the reflection dwells on them: the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me."
Romanticism Period

The Romanticism period was an artistic, literary, and intellectual movement that originated in Europe towards the end of the 18th century and lasted until the mid-19th century. Romanticism emerged as a reaction against the Enlightenment's emphasis on reason, order, and the scientific method, advocating instead for a greater focus on emotion, nature, and individual expression.
Emphasis on Emotion and Individualism:

Romanticism celebrates the individual's emotions and intuition over established norms and conventions. It placed high value on the subjective experience of the individual, often exploring themes of solitary contemplation, melancholy, and personal connection to the natural world.
Nature as a Central Theme:

Nature was a source of inspiration and spirituality for Romantics. They saw it as a direct counterpoint to the industrial revolution and urbanization, which they viewed as corrupting and alienating. Nature was depicted as majestic, beautiful, and a path to spiritual renewal.
Revolt Against the Enlightenment:

Romantics reacted against the Enlightenment focus on rationalism and instead emphasized mysticism, emotion, and the metaphysical. This shift was partially in response to the industrial revolution's perceived mechanical harshness and the cold rationality of enlightenment philosophy.
Innovations in Art and Literature:

In art, Romantic painters like Caspar David Friedrich, J.M.W. Turner, and Eugène Delacroix moved away from precise, classical lines to more expressive, dramatic, and often turbulent portrayals of landscapes and historical scenes.

In literature, Romantic poets and writers such as William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Mary Shelley, Victor Hugo, and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe explored intense personal emotions and complex inner worlds. They also revived interest in folklore, medieval history, and exotic subjects.
Heroism and the Byronic Hero:

Romantic literature often featured protagonists who embodied the Byronic hero—moody, rebellious, and flawed yet charismatic and emotionally complex. This hero typically rejected social norms and struggled against a society they perceived as hypocritical.
Hegel

When Hegel uses the term ‘world spirit,’ he means the sum of human utterances because only man has a spirit. Although Kant denied that man could have any clear cognition of the innermost secrets of nature, Kant admitted there exists a kind of unattainable ‘truth.’ Hegel, on the other hand, said that truth is subjective and thus rejected the existence of any truth above or beyond human reason. All knowledge is human knowledge, Hegel claimed. Hegel’s philosophy is therefore, a method for understanding the progress of history and teaches us nothing about the inner nature of life, but it can teach us to think productively.

All of the previous philosophers had tried to investigate the basis of human cognition and made pronouncements on the timeless factor of human knowledge of the world. Hegel, however, believed that the basis of human cognition changed from one generation to the next. There were therefore no ‘eternal truths,’ no timeless reason. The only fixed point philosophy can hold on to is history itself. Just like how a river is in a constant state of change, it does not mean you cannot talk about the river, but you cannot say t which place in the valley the river is the ‘truest’ river.

History is just like a running river. Every tiny movement in the water at a given spot in the river is determined by the falls and eddies in the water higher upstream, but these movements are determined by the rocks and bends in the river at the point you are observing it. History of thought and reason is like this river where thoughts that are washed along the current of past tradition as well as the material conditions help to determine how you think. You can therefore never claim that any particular thought is correct for ever and ever. But the thought can be correct from where you stand.
Since reason is dynamic, it is a process and ‘truth’ is this same process (there are no criteria beyond the historical process itself that can determine what is the most true or the most reasonable).

Therefore, Hegel claimed that the ‘world spirit’ is developing toward an ever-expanding knowledge of itself and will gradually come to consciousness itself. He claimed it as a historical reality where increasing ‘self-knowledge’ and ‘self-development’ will lead to greater rationality and freedom. As historical development is progressive like a long chain of reflections, history is thus purposeful.

Hegel believes that a new thought is built onto the previous thought but a contradictory thought will oppose the new thought. Then, a third thought accommodates the best of the opposing two thoughts. This is known as a diabetic process. This compromising process (thesis, antithesis and synthesis) is known as the negation of the negation. The synthesis will then be contradicted by a new antithesis and the process repeats itself. This is the progress of the ‘world spirit’ through history.
Kierkegaard

Kierkegaard had a sharp eye for the significance of the individual where he thought that both the idealism of the Romantics and Hegel’s ‘historicism’ had obscured the individual’s responsibility for his own life. To him, religion and knowledge were extreme opposites like fire and water. It was not enough to believe that Christianity is ‘true’ and having a Christian faith meant following a Christian way of life. There is no such thing as ‘to some extent’ religious, either you are very or you are not at all. He is what we know as a ‘existential’ thinker who draws his entire existence into philosophical reflection.

Hegel’s system was being used as a kind of all-purpose explanation for every type of question. Kierkegaard indicated that the sort of ‘objective truths’ that Hegelianism was concerned with were totally irrelevant to the personal life of the individual. Therefore, rather than searching for the Truth with a capital T, it is more important to find the kind of truths that are meaningful to the individual’s life. It is important to find ‘the truth for me.’ He thus sets the individual, or each and every man, up against the ‘system.’ Man’s experience cannot be experienced behind a desk, it can only be experienced when we act and make significant choices that relate to our own existence. Like Buddha, they had both a strong sense of only existing for a brief moment.

Truth is subjective. It does not matter what we think or believe since really important truths are personal. For instance, the question ‘is Christianity true?’ This is not a question one can relate to theoretically or academically. For a person who ‘understands himself in life,’ it is a question of life and death. It is not something you sit and discuss for discussion’s sake. It is something to be approached with greater passion and sincerity. Suppose you fall into the water, you have no theoretical interest in whether or not you will drown, it is just a question of life and death. Such fundamental questions of God’s existence can only be approached through faith as things we can know through reason or knowledge are totally unimportant. Truths like math can be both objective and general but they are nevertheless totally immaterial to each man’s existence. You can never know whether a person forgives you when you wrong them. Therefore, it is existentially important to you. It is a question you are intensely concerned with. Neither can you know whether a person loves you. It is something you just have to believe or hope. But these things are more important to you than the fact that the sum of the angles in a triangle is 180 degrees. You do not think of the laws of cause and effect in the middle of your first kiss. Faith is therefore the most important factor in religious questions.

Many have tried to prove the existence of God within the bounds of rationality but if you intend yourself with some such proof or logical argument, you suffer a loss of faith and religious passion. Because what matters is not whether Christianity is true, but whether it is true for you. Credo quia absurdum - you don’t say - means I believe because it is irrational. If we use reason, it would not be a question of faith. That is what Kierkegaard meant by ‘existential’ and ‘subjective truth’ and his concept of ‘faith.’

3 stages of life where one can live at one of the two lower stages and then suddenly leap to a higher stage (it must come from within your inner need) or maybe stay stagnant at one stage throughout their life:

When Kierkegaard went to Schilling's lectures, he might have sat next to Karl Marx. Karl Marx wrote his PhD thesis on Democritus and Epicurus while Kierkegaard wrote his own PhD art thesis on Socrates. Kierkegaard was what we know of as an existentialist while Marx was a historical materialist. His friend or colleague, Frederich Engels, contributed to what we know of as Marxism with Lenin, Stalin, Mao and others following suit. Unlike philosophical materialists like the atomist antiquity and mechanical materialism, Marx thought to a great extent that it was the material factors in society that determined the way we think. Earlier Hegel claimed that world spirit or world reason was the factor that drove history forward, Marx on the other hand, showed that material changes were the ones that affected history. “Spiritual relations” do not create material change, in fact, it was the other way round, particularly it was the economic forces in society that created change and thus drove history forward.
The way material life of the community was organized, production was mainly based on slave labor, so the citizens had no need to increase production with practical innovations

Marx the material, economic and social relations the basis of society. On the other hand, the way a society thinks, what kind of political institutions there are, which laws it has and, not least, what there is of religion, morals, art, philosophy and science was what Marx called society’s superstructure. Just like the Greek temple, the building needs to have power foundations - the bases - to support the entire construction. Marx believed that material relations support everything in the way of thoughts and ideas in society. Society’s superstructure is then a reflection of the bases of that society. Bases and superstructure had an interactive effect with one another which made him more of a dialectical materialist rather than a mechanical one.
Just like the bases of the Greek temple have three columns to support the roof, the columns represent the three levels in the bases of society.

The most basic level is production - the natural conditions or resources that are available to society. These are the foundation of any society and this foundation clearly determines the type of production in the society, and by the same token, the nature of that society and its culture in general.
The next level is those who own the means of production - the division of labor or the distribution of work and ownership was what Marx coined society’s “production relations.”

The question of what is morally right is a product of the base of society. For example, it is not accidental that in the old peasant society, parents would decide whom their children married. It was a question of who was to inherit the farm. In a modern city, social relations are different.

It is mainly society’s ruling class that sets the norms for morality because the history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles. History is principally a matter of who is to own the means of production. Society’s superstructure could have an interactive effect on the base of society, but Marx denied that society’s superstructure had any independent history of its own. What has driven historical development from the slave society of antiquity to the industrial society today has primarily been determined by changes in the base society.

In all phases of history, there has been a conflict between free citizen and slave. In the feudal society of the Middle Ages, it was feudal lord and serf, later on, between aristocrat and citizen. In Marx’s time, it was the bourgeois or capitalist society, the conflict was between the capitalists and the workers - the conflict stood between those who own the means of production and those who do now. Since the ‘upper classes’ do not voluntarily relinquish their power, change could only come about through a revolution.
Marx’s view on man labor: How we work affects our consciousness but our consciousness also affects the way we work - an interactive relationship between hand and consciousness.

His criticism of the capitalist method of production was because under the capitalist system, the worker labors for someone else. His labor is thus something external to him or something that does not belong to him. The worker becomes alien to his work and also an alien to himself. In a capitalist society, labor is organized in such a way that the worker in fact slaves for another social class. Thus the worker transfers his own labor and with it, the whole of his life to the upper class. The worker is essentially a beast of burden and ethically wrong (i.e Woman had to offer prostitution services to earn extra income). They faced exploitation - if a worker produces a commodity, this commodity has a certain exchange value, deduct this and the workers wages and you get profits. In other words, the capitalist pockets a value that was actually created by the worker. The capitalist would then reinvest his profit in new capital and increase his profits in the future which means the cutting of labor. Therefore, Marx believed capitalism is an economic system that is self-destructive and lacks rational control. If a company is going bankrupt, it would cut its wages and now the workers would be so poor that they are unable to afford basic goods.

The Communist Manifesto in 1848 published by Marx and Engels openly declared that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions and let the ruling class tremble at a communist revolution. Workingmen of all countries unite.

It then split into either social democracy (a gradual peaceful path of socialism) or leninism (to cease the existing old class in society). However, every man became evil as Russia became another oppressed state.
