Suppose that here in the lecture hall and in this audience, whose exemplary stillness and attention one cannot sufficiently commend, there is an individual who is creating a disturbance and by his laughing, talking, distracts one’s attention from one’s task. The lecturer cannot go on with his lecture under these conditions and thereupon several strong men get up and eject the disturbance of the peace for the hall. He is now repressed and the lecturer can continue his lecture. But in order that the disturbance may not be repeated, in the case the man who has just been thrown out attempts to force his way back into the room, the gentlemen who have executed the lecturer take their chairs to the door and establish themselves there as a resistance to keep up the repression. Now, if you transfer this both location to the psyche, calling this consciousness and the outside the unconscious, you have a good illustration of the process of repression.

The disturber of the peace insists on reentering. That is the way it is with repressed thoughts and urges. We live under the constant pressure of repressed thoughts that are trying to fight them all up from the unconscious.

Our unconscious speaks to us through dreams which are wish fulfillment. That is because when we sleep, censorship is at work on what we will permit ourselves and although this censorship or repression mechanism is considerably weaker when we are asleep than when we are awake, it is still strong enough to cause our dreams to distort the wishes we cannot acknowledge. The apparent dream is the actual dream image and the latent dream which has a deeper meaning is hidden from consciousness.

We retain everything we have seen and experienced somewhere deep in our consciousness and all these impressions can be brought to light again through things like memory lapse, sleep of the tongue and suddenly remembering things. We are talking about something which has lain in the unconscious and suddenly slips through the half-open door to consciousness.

Some put it as a Darwinian system where we get inspiration and masses of new ideas via thought-mutants occurring in the consciousness one after the other. Maybe the imagination creates what is new, but the imagination does not make the actual selection. A composition is an interplay between imagination and reason, for there will always be an element of chance in the creative process.
20th Century Philosophy
Existentialism - man’s existential situation - based their ideas not only on Kierkegaard but also on Hegel and Marx.

Another philosopher that had a great influence on the 20th century was Nietzche (1844 - 1900) who reacted against Hegel’s philosophy and German ‘historicism.’ He proposed life itself as a counterweight to the anemic interest in history and what he called the Christian ‘slave morality.’ He sought to effect a ‘revaluation of all values,’ so that the life force of the strongest should not be hampered by the weak. According to Nietzche, both Christianity and traditional philosophy had turned away from the real world and pointed toward ‘heaven’ or ‘a world of ideas.’ But what had hitherto been considered the ‘real’ world was in fact a pseudo world.
Another man who was influenced by both Kierkegaard und Nietzche was German existential philosopher Martin Heidegger.

Another is French existentialist Jean-Paul Sartre who lived from 1905 to 1980 and was a leading light amongst existentialists. He allied himself with the Marxist movement in France. Existentialism is humanism, he said. By that he meant that existing lists start from nothing but humanity itself. In contrast to Kierkegaard who was a Christian philosopher, Sartre was an atheistic existentialist where his philosophy can be seen as a merciless analysis of the human situation when ‘God is dead.’

Existence to Sartre is not being alive - plants and animals are alive and exist, but they do not have to think about what it implies. Man is the only creature that is conscious of its own existence. A material thing is simply ‘in itself,’ but mankind is ‘for itself.’ The being of man is therefore not the same as the being of things. Man’s existence takes priority over whatever he might otherwise be. Existence takes priority over essence. By essence, we near that which something consists of - nature, or being, of something. But according to Sartre, man has no such innate ‘nature.’ Man must therefore create himself and his own nature since it is not fixed in advance.

Throughout the entire history of philosophy, philosophers have sought to discover what man is - or what human nature is but Sartre believed that man has no such eternal ‘nature’ to fall back on. It is therefore useless to search for the meaning of life in general since we are condemned to improvise.

Man feels alien in a world without meaning. Sartre is echoing the central dead of Hegel and Marx - man’s alienation in the world creates a sense of despair. Man’s freedom is a curse (unlike what the Renaissance humanists thought) as man has not created himself and is nevertheless free. Because having once been hurled into the world, he is responsible for everything he does. Nevertheless, we are free individuals and it condemns us to make choices throughout our lives. There are no eternal values or norms we adhere to which makes our choices even more significant because we are totally responsible for everything we do. Man must never disclaim the responsibility of his actions nor can we avoid the responsibility of making our own choices on the grounds that we must live up to the middle class expectations regarding how we should live. On the other hand, our freedom obliges us to make something of ourselves to live authentically.’

In the case of ethical choices, we can never lay the blame on ‘human nature,’ even if we try to blame ‘old Adam.’ But there is no ‘old Adam.’ He is merely a figure we clutch at to avoid taking responsibility for our actions. Although there was no innate meaning to life, he did not mean that nothing mattered. He is a nihilist - a person who thinks nothing means anything and everything is permissible. Life must have meaning and is an imperative but it is we ourselves who must create this meaning in our own lives. To exist is to create your own life. Sartre tried to prove that consciousness in itself is nothing until it has perceived something as consciousness is always conscious of something and this ‘something’ is provided just as such by ourselves as by our surroundings. We are partly instrumental in deciding what we persevere by selecting what is significant to us - for instance, two people can be present in the same room and yet experience it quite differently. A pregnant woman notices only other pregnant women while a convict notices only policemen, it all depends on the lenses you take. Or if you were waiting for your loved one, you ‘might’ hear him or her not calling you amidst the crowd. You may find the crowded unpleasant or aggravating even.

Simon de Beauvoir (Sartre’s wife) fought for feminism as she does not believe in a ‘male nature’ and ‘female nature.’ Existentialism meant that women are exactly as free and independent as they chose to be.

So what is philosophy now? Existentialist philosophy has had radical significance for many people all over the world since Kierkegaard and way back to Socrates. The 20th century has also seen a blossoming and renewing of past philosophies. For instance, neo-Thomism says ideas which belong to the tradition of Thomas Aquinas, analytical philosophy of logical empiricism with roots reaching back to Hume and even to the logic of Aristotle. Neo-Marxism and neo-Darwinism with its significance of psychoanalysis are other examples. Even materialism can be traced back to the efforts of pre-Socrates that explains our current science to provide satisfactory answers to the big questions. Some even make it part of their life philosophy to answer the big questions like ‘what is matter’ because the very questions in pre-Socrates are still being unanswered. Through philosophy and seeking answers to the ultimate questions, we are able to discover clear and final solutions to some problems in the form of science, research and technology. That is how we got to the moon. Now, ecophilosophy and the environment questions the idea of evolution in its assumption that man is at the top - as if we are masters of nature. This could prove to be fatal for our living planet.

title: Behave: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst
author: Robert M. Sapolsky

text.t: Behave: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst

" by Robert M. Sapolsky is an examination of human behavior, exploring the biological underpinnings that shape our actions. It covers neuroscience, genetics, psychology, and evolutionary biology to explain why humans behave the way they do in various situations, from moments of stress and conflict to those of altruism and cooperation.

Let us start with the positives. The book uses an interdisciplinary approach to explore the complex factors that influence human behavior. It is structured to trace the influences on behavior starting from the neurobiological level, going back seconds before an action to the genetic and cultural factors from far in the past. I must say as a student who did not take biology in Junior College, the neuroscience concepts were explained with great ease. I understood it quite well, but Andrew Huberman’s podcast might have helped me too. Just like “
A Brief History of Time
” by Hawking, the theory underpinning the necessary biological concepts such as hormones, genes, and brain chemistry is the best part of the book.

Now, it goes downhill after he started giving his personal opinion, which in my opinion, is fueled with poor evidence and arguments. In addition, the chapter of evolution is totally stolen from Richard Dawkins’ “The Selfish Gene.”

I largely disagree with his point on morality (which he claims to be subjective) and determinism (he claims that we have no free will). I mean just citing the Lembke experiment and saying that free will does not exist is a poor way to structure your arguments. It is like saying “Example A, B, C
is
like
that, therefore it
ought

to be like that.” It is a scientific version of the David Hume’s is ought fallacy. There are many interpretations for the Lembke test and moral responsibility is heavily tied to free will (I mean if he is going to give philosophical claims, I have to challenge it). Furthermore, how can morality be formed from natural selection? Natural selection from the neo-Darwin framework only applies to physical traits. It also does not make too much sense for morality to be subjective because we can’t live that way (so murder, rape and theft can be okay to some?) then what is the point of having laws? Think of these question as starters for further development but I shall stop here since this is just a book review. Instead for additional information, please refer to the links I have put below.
For the free will issue, readers should watch the following video:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ODQRoCOJkag&t=957s
For the subjective morality issue:
https://www.str.org/w/four-problems-with-evolutionary-morality
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vnxGWlciHI4

I bought this book to get a better understanding on the theory of evolution, especially since this is one of the big arguments against God (see my Theology inputs). Richard Dawkins is a well-known Atheist (check out his podcast with Alex O Conor and Jordan Peterson). In this book, Dawkins shared his atheistic view as follows:

Presumably there is indeed no purpose in the ultimate fate of the cosmos, but do any of us really tie our life’s hopes to the ultimate fate of the cosmos anyway? Of course we don’t, not if we are sane. Our lives are ruled by all sorts of closer, warmer, human ambitions and perceptions.

My objective for this book was to see how morality, consciousness and behaviors are formed from his point of view. Overall, Dawkins is a really good teacher (like Stephen Hawking). He explains natural selection at the gene level and different biological processes with such intuitive analogies! This book was an enjoyable and simple read, touching on his theory of the selfish gene and also origins of life. However, one criticism might have to do with the content of the book itself. This book is 300+ pages of reasoning on his theory on “Selfish” genes. Therefore, he essentially uses some concepts and apply it to almost all situations in life, citing main examples from animals. This book felt as if someone told him “I believe we were born altruistic rather than selfish” and he wrote this book to prove him wrong. If you are not into a book of reasoning, maybe it may not be the best book for you.
ANNEX

A central debate within Darwinism concerns the unit that is actually selected: what kind of entity is it that survives or does not survive, as a consequence of natural selection. That unit will become, more or less by definition, “selfish.” Altruism might well be favored at other levels. Does natural selection choose between species? If so, we might expect individual organisms to behave altruistically “for the good of the species.” They might limit their birth rates to avoid overpopulation, or restrain their hunting behavior to conserve the species' future stocks of prey.

What Richard Dawkins posits is that the natural selection process happens at the gene level where individual organisms behave altruistically “for the good of the genes.” (i.e Feeding and protecting kin who are likely to share copies of the same genes). The critical question is: Which level in the hierarchy of life will turn out to be the inevitably “selfish” level, at which natural selection acts? The species, groups, organism or  ecosystem? All of them are wrong - Dawkins will argue why it is at the gene level. But he claims that the selfish gene theory is Darwin’s theory and a logical outgrowth of orthodox neo-Darwinism. “
Rather than focus on the individual organism, it takes a gene’s eye view of nature. It is a different way of seeing, not a different theory
My point is that there are two ways of looking at natural selection, the gene’s angle and that of the individual

There are 2 kinds of units of natural selection and there are no disputes between them. The gene is the unit in the sense of replicator and the organism is the unit in the sense of vehicle. Despite being “selfish”, what Dawkins truly means is that they are cooperative. The book emphatically does not mean that groups of genes prosper at the expense of their members, or at the expense of other groups. Rather, each gene is seen as pursuing its own self-interested agenda against the background of the other genes in the gene pool. Those other genes are part of the environment in which each gene survives, in the same way as the weather, predators and prey, supporting vegetation and soil bacteria are parts of the environment. From the gene’s point of view, the ‘background’ genes are those with which it shares bodies in its journey down the generations. In the short term, that means the other members of the genome. In the long term, it means the other genes in the gene pool of the species. Natural selection therefore sees to it gangs of mutually compatible - which is to say cooperating - genes are favored in the presence of each other. At no time does this concept violate the fundamental principle of the selfish gene.
Dawkins shared his atheistic view as follows:

Presumably there is indeed no purpose in the ultimate fate of the cosmos, but do any of us really tie our life’s hopes to the ultimate fate of the cosmos anyway? Of course we don’t, not if we are sane. Our lives are ruled by all sorts of closer, warmer, human ambitions and perceptions.

Natural selection goes something like this: Within each species some individuals leave more surviving offspring than others, so that the inherently traits (genes) of the reproductively successful become more numerous in the next generation. Natural selection is the non-random differential reproduction of genes.

The argument of the book is that we, all other animals, are machines created by our genes. If we were told that a man had lived a long and prosperous life in the world of Chicago gangsters, we would be entitled to make some guesses as to the sort of man he was. Like successful Chicago gangsters, our genes have survived in a highly competitive world. This entitles us to expect certain qualities in our genes.

The book defines altruistic if it behaves in such a way as to increase another such entity’s welfare at the expense of its own. Selfish behavior has exactly the opposite effect. ‘Welfare’ is defined as ‘chances of survival,’ even if the effect on actual life and death prospects is so small a s to seem negligible.

Dawkins first deals with a particular erroneous explanation for altruism which is based on the misconception that living creatures evolve to do things ‘for the good of the species’ or ‘for the good of the group.’ Much of an animal’s life is devoted to reproduction, and most of the acts of altruistic self-sacrifice that are observed in nature are performed by parents towards their young. ‘Perpetuation of the species’ is a common euphemism for reproduction and it is undeniably a consequence of reproduction. Evolution works by natural selection, and natural selection means the differential survival of the ‘fittest.’ But at what hierarchy (organism, species, races etc.) are we at? It does not matter greatly but when we are talking about altruism it is crucial. If it is species that are competing in Darwinian struggle for existence, the individual seems best regarded as a pawn in the game, to be sacrificed when the greatest interest of the species as a whole requires it. A group, such as a species or a population within a species, whose individual members are prepared to sacrifice themselves for the welfare of the group, may be less likely to go extinct than a rival group whose individual members place their own selfish interests first. Therefore the world becomes populated mainly by groups consisting of self-sacrificing individuals. This theory is known as group selection.

The orthodox alternative is normally called individual selection or what Dawkins prefers to refer to as gene selection. Even in the group of altruists, there will almost certainly be a dissenting minority who refuse to make any sacrifice. If there is just one selfish rebel, prepared to exploit the altruism of the rest, then he by definition, is more likely than they are to survive and have children. Each of his individuals will then inherit his selfish traits. After several generations of this natural selection, the ‘altruistic group’ will be over-run by selfish individuals and will be indistinguishable from the selfish group. Even if we grant the improbable chance of existence initially of pure altruistic groups without any rebels, it is difficult to see what is to stop selfish individuals migrating in from neighboring selfish groups and by inter-marriage, contaminating the purity of the altruistic groups. The individual selection isn’t old to admit that groups do indeed die out, and that whether or not a group goes extinct may be influenced by the behavior of the individuals in that group. He might even admit that if only the individuals in the group had the gift of foresight they could see that in the long run their own best interests lay in restraining their selfish greed, to prevent the destruction of the whole group. Even while the group is going slowly and inexorably downhill, selfish individuals prosper in the short term at the expense of altruists. Evolution is blind to the future.
Replicators

Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection is satisfying because it shows us a way in which simplicity could change into complexity, how unordered atoms could group themselves into ever more complex patterns until they ended up manufacturing people.

Survival of the ‘fittest’ is a special case of a more general law of survival of the stable. The universe is populated by stable things. A stable thing is a collection of atoms that is permanent enough or common enough to deserve a name. For example, sometimes when atoms meet they link up together in chemical reactions to form molecules, which may be more or less stable.

For example, the hemoglobin of our blood is a typical protein molecule which is built up from chains of smaller molecules, amino acids, each containing a few dozen atoms arranged in a precise pattern. In the hemoglobin molecule there are 574 amino acid molecules which are arranged in four chains, which twist around each other to form a globular 3D structure of complexity. A model of hemoglobin molecule looks rather like a dense thorn bush but unlike a real thorn bush, it is not a haphazard approximate pattern but a definite invariant structure, identically repeated, with not a twig nor a twist out of place, over 6 thousand million million million times in an average human body. This structure is stable in the sense that 2 chains consisting of the same sequences of amino acid will tend, like 2 springs, to come to rest in exactly the same 3D coiled pattern. Hemoglobin thorn bushes are springing into their ‘preferred’ shape in your body at four hundred million million per second and others are destroyed at the same rate.

The example above illustrates that if a group of atoms in the presence of energy falls into a stable pattern it will tend to stay that way. The earliest form of natural selection was simply a selection of stable forms and a rejection of unstable ones. It happened by definition.

From this, of course, it does not follow that you can explain the existence of entities as complex as man by exactly the same principles on their own (i.e Shaking the right number of atoms together with some external energy till they happen to fall into the right pattern and a human results). This is where Darwin’s theory comes in.

Since we do not know what chemical raw materials were abundant on earth before the coming of life, some plausible possibilities are water, carbon dioxide, methane and ammonia. Through experiments of laboratory simulations of the chemical conditions of youth earth, we have yielded organic substances called purines and pyrimidines which are building blocks of the generic molecule, DNA itself. Processes analogous to these give rise to the ‘primeval soup’ which biologists and chemists believe constituted the seas some three to four thousand million years ago. The organic substances become locally concentrated and under UV light from the sun, they combine into larger molecules. Nowadays large organic molecules would not last long enough to be noticed as they would be quickly absorbed and broken down by bacteria or other living creatures. However, they are late-comers and in those days large organic molecules could drift unmolested through the thickening broth.

At some point a remarkable molecule was formed by accident: The replicator. It can create copies of itself despite the molecule’s existence being highly improbable (i.e Tail risks events). Since the small building blocks were abundantly available in the soup surrounding the replicator, it will tend to stick to the replicator and be arranged in a sequence that mimics that of the replicator itself to form a stable chain just as in the formation of the original replicator. This process continues as a progressive stacking up, layer upon layer. On the other hand, the two chains might split apart, in which case we have two replicators, each of which can go on to make further copies where some scientists posit for a positive-negative replication.

A new kind of stability thus came into the world. We seem to arrive at a large population of identical replicas (replicators spread their copies throughout seas as soon as it was born until smaller building block molecules became a scarce resource and other larger molecules were formed more rarely), but the copying process is not perfect. But this imperfection gives rise to improvement, and it is essential for the progressive evolution of life. The primeval soup became filled by a population not of identical replicas, but of several varieties of replicating molecules, all ‘descended’ from the same ancestor. Some varieties are more stable, able to have a longer time replicating and thus more numerous than others. However, the more mistakes the replicas make, the population will be less numerous. Thus, a populated stable variety of molecules stem from the stability in longevity or replication speed or replication accuracy.

Although evolution may seem in a. vague sense, a ‘good thing,’ especially since we are the products of it, nothing actually ‘wants’ to evolve. Evolution is something that happens, in spite of all of the efforts of the replicators and genes to prevent it happening. We are just products of our early replicators (founding fathers).

Darwin’s theory also stressed on competition. The primeval soup was not capable of supporting an infinite number of replicator molecules. The earth’s size is finite, but other limiting factors must also have been important. In Dawkin’s picture, replicator acts as a template or mold and is supposed to be bathed in a soup rich in the small building block molecules necessary to make copies. But when replicators became numerous, building blocks must have been used up at such a rate that they became a scarce and precious resource. Different varieties or strains of replicator must have competed for them.

Competition gave rise to a new higher level of stability, or a new way of reducing the stability of rivals, was automatically preserved and multiplied. Ways of increasing stability and decreasing rivals’ stability became more elaborate and more efficient. This may have been how the first living cells appeared. Replicators began not merely to exist, but to construct themselves vehicles for their continued existence where they build survival machines for themselves to live in. But making a living got steadily harder as new rivals arose with better and more effective survival machines. The process gets more cumulative and progressive.
Immortal Coils

Different sorts of survival machines appear very varied on the outside and in their internal organs. Yet in their fundamental chemistry they are rather uniform, and, in particular, the replicators that they bear, the genes, are basically the same kind of molecule in all of us - from bacteria to elephants. We are all survival machines for the same kind of replicator - molecules called DNA - but there are many different ways of making a living in the world, and the replicators have built a vast range of machines to exploit them.

A DNA molecule is a long chain of building blocks, small molecules called nucleotides. Just as protein molecules are chains of amino acids, so DNA molecules are chains of nucleotides. A DNA molecule is too small to be seen, but its exact shape has been ingeniously worked out by indirect means. It consists of a pair of nucleotide chains twisted together in a spiral; the ‘double helix’; the ‘immortal coil.’ The nucleotide building blocks come in only four different kinds, whose names may be shortened to A, T, C and G. What differs is the order in which they are strung together. A G building block from a man is identical in every particular way to a G building block from a snail, but the sequence of building blocks in a man is not only different from that in a snail. Our DNA lives inside our bodies and is not concentrated in a particular part of the body, rather, it is distributed among the cells. Every one of those cells contains a complete copy of that body’s DNA. The DNA can be regarded as a set of instructions for how to make a body, written in the A, T, C, G alphabet of the nucleotides. There is a ‘book-case’ in a cell which contains all the architect’s plans for the entire building. That is the nucleus. The architect’s plans run to 46 volumes in man - the number is different in other species - these ‘volumes’ are called chromosomes. Metaphorically speaking, there is no architect as the DNA instructions have been assembled by natural selection.

The 46 chromosomes (volumes) consist of 23 pairs of chromosomes. We might say that filed away in the nucleus of every cell are two alternative sets of 23 volumes of plans. Call them volume 1a, 2a, 3a, 3b etc., down to volume 23a and volume 23b. We receive each chromosome intact from one of our two parents, in whose testis or ovary it was assembled. It is difficult in practice, but in theory you could look with a microscope at the 46 chromosomes in any one of your cells and pick out the 23 that came from your dad and 23 that came from your mum.
DNA does two important things:

They replicate, that is to say they make copies of themselves which has been ongoing ever since the beginning of life. One cell, endowed with the master copy of the architect’s plans, divided into two where both received its own copy of the plans and continuously divided. At every division, the DNA plans were faithfully copied with scarcely any mistakes.

It indirectly supervises the manufacture of a different kind of molecule known as protein. The hemoglobin mentioned above is just one example of the enormous range of protein molecules. The coded message of the DNA, written in the four-letter nucleotide alphabet, is translated in a simple mechanical way into another alphabet. This is the alphabet of amino acids which spells out protein molecules.

Genes do indirectly control the manufacture of bodies, and the influence is strictly one way: acquired characteristics are not inherited. No matter how much knowledge and wisdom acquired in one’s life, it will not be passed on to one’s children by genetic means. Each new generation starts from scratch. A body is the genes’ way of preserving the genes unaltered. The evolutionary importance of the fact that genes control embryonic development is this:

Genes are at least responsible for their own survival in the future as their survival depends on the efficiency of the bodies in which they live and help to build. Natural selection consisted of the differential survival of replicators floating free in the primeval soup. Now, natural selection favors replicators that are good at building survival machines, genes that are skilled in the art of controlling embryonic development. Genes still have no foreign, but the qualities that determine a gene’s longevity and fecundity are definitely more complex.

The modern replicator is highly gregarious. A survival machine is a vehicle that contains many thousands of genes. The manufacture of a body is so intricate that it is impossible to disentangle the contribution of one gene from that of one another. A given gene will have many different effects on different parts of the body. A given part of the body will be influenced by many genes and the effect of any one gene acts as master genes controlling the operation of clusters of other genes. Some genes act as master genes controlling the operation of a cluster of other genes. In terms of the apology, any given page of the plans makes reference to many different parts of the building; and each page makes sense only in terms of cross-references to numerous other pages. For such a gene complex, Dawkins proposes that it can be divided into discrete replicators or genes where one gene may be regarded as a unit that survives through a large number of successive individual bodies.

In our chromosome example above, we can think of the ‘pairs’ of two alternative pages being identical, but in other cases (i.e Eye color), they might differ. If they make contradictory ‘recommendations’, the answer varies. Sometimes, one reading prevails over the other. In the eye example, the person would maybe have brown eyes: The instructions for making blue eyes would be ignored in the building of the body, though this does not stop them being passed onto future generations. A gene ignored this way is recessive while the opposite of a recessive gene is a dominant gene. The gene for brown eyes is dominant to the gene for blue eyes - a person has blue eyes only if both copies of the relevant page are unanimous in recommending blue eyes. More usually when two alternative genes are not identical, the result in some kind of compromise - the body is built to an intermediate design or something completely different.

Two genes, like the brown and blue eye, are rivals for the same slot on the chromosome, they are called alleles of each other. Imagine the volumes of architects’ plans as being loose leaf binders, whose pages can be detached and interchanged. Every volume 13 must have a page 6, but there are several possible page 6s that can go in the binder between page 5 and 7. One version says blue eyes, another possible one says brown eyes; there may yet be other versions in the gene population which spell out green. But you cannot literally go and choose your genes from the pool of genes available to the whole population since at any given time, all the genes are tied up inside individual survival machines. Our genes are doled out to us at conception and there is nothing we can do about this.

The concept of normal division of a cell into two new cells with each one receiving a complete copy of all 46 chromosomes is known as mitosis (normal cell division). Another kind of cell division is called (meiosis) where it occurs only in the production of sex cells; the sperms or the eggs. Sperm and egg are unique amongst our cells as instead of containing 46 chromosomes, they contain 23 - exactly convenient for fusion to take place. Meiosis takes place only in the testicles and ovaries, in which a cell with the full double set of 46 chromosomes divides to form sex cells with the single set of 23.

During the manufacture of a sperm or egg, bits of each paternal chromosome physically detach themselves and change places with exactly corresponding bits of the maternal chromosome. The process of swapping bits of chromosome (since whole-chromosome distribution does not happen) is called crossing over. Thus, if you took a microscope and looked at the chromosomes in one of your own sperm or egg, you would waste time trying to identify the origins of your chromosomes coming from your father and mother. Thus, any one chromosome in a sperm would be a patchwork, a mosaic of material genes and paternal genes.

The metaphor of the analogies starts to break down as it gets more complex. In a loose-leaf binder a whole page may be inserted, removed or exchanged, but not a fraction of a page. But the gene complex is just a long string of nucleotide letters, not divided into discrete pages in an obvious way at all. There are special symbols for end of protein chain message and start of protein chain message written in the same four-letter alphabet. In between these two punctuation marks are the coded instructions for making one protein. If we wish, we can define a single gene as a sequence of nucleotide letters lying between a start and end symbol and coding for one protein chain. The word
cistron
has been used for a unit defined in this way (some people use it interchangeably with gene). But crossing-over does not respect boundaries between
cistrons

. Splits may occur within cistrons as well as between them. It is as though the architect’s plans were written out, not on discrete pages, but on 46 rolls of ticker tape. Cistrons are not of fixed length and the only way to tell where one cistron ends and the next begins would be to read the symbols on the tape. Look for the end of message and start of message symbols. Crossing-over is represented by taking matching paternal and maternal tapes, and cutting and exchanging matching portions, regardless of what is written on them.

A gene is defined as any portion of chromosomal material that potentially lasts for enough generations to serve as a unit of natural selection. A gene is a replicator with high copying-fidelity - copying-fidelity is another way of saying longevity-in-the-form-of-copies. In any definition, a gene has to be a portion of a chromosome. Any sequence of adjacent code-letters on the ‘tape’ is known as a genetic unit. No matter how long or short this sequence is, it is still a genetic unit - it is just a length of chromosome, not physically differentiated from the rest of the chromosome in any way.

However, the shorter a genetic unit is, the longer - in generations - it is likely to live. In particular, the less likely it is to be split by any one crossing-over. Suppose a whole chromosome is, on average, likely to undergo one crossover every time a sperm or egg is made by meiosis division and this crossover can happen anywhere along its length.

The smaller subunits which make up the genetic unit we are considering may well have existed long before. Our genetic unit was created at a particular arrangement of subunits by which it is defined and did not exist before that moment. The moment of creation may have occurred quite recently, say in one of your grandparents. But if we consider a very small genetic unit, it may have been first assembled in a much more distant ancestor, perhaps an ape-like pre-human ancestor. Moreover, a small genetic unit inside you may go on just as far into the future, passing intact through a long line of your descendants.

An individual’s descendants constitute not a single line but a branching one. Whichever of your ancestors it was who ‘created’ a particular short length of your chromosome 8a, he or she was very likely to have many other descendants besides you. One of your genetic units may also be present in you, in the Prime Minister and your Dog, for we all share ancestors if we go back far enough. That same unit might be assembled several time independently by chance; if the unit is small, the coincidence is not too improbable. But even a close relative is unlikely to share a whole chromosome with you. The smaller a genetic unit is, the more likely it is that another individual shares it - the more likely it is to represent many times over in the world in the form of copies.

This chance of coming together, through coursing-over, of previously existing sub-units is the usual way for a new genetic unit to be formed. Another way, even though it is quite rare, is known as point mutation. A point mutation is an error corresponding to a single misprinted letter in a book. It is rare, but clearly the longer a genetic unit is, the more likely it is altered by a mutation somewhere along its length.

Another rare kind of mutation which has long-term consequences is known as inversion where a piece of chromosome detaches itself at both ends and reattaches itself in the inverted position. In terms of the analogy, it is renumbering of pages. Sometimes, it may join different parts of the chromosome altogether, corresponding to the transfer of a wad of pages from one volume to another. It can disastrously lead to the close linkage of pieces of genetic material which happen to work well together - two cistrons which have a beneficial effect only when they are both present will be brought close to each other by means of inversion -> natural selection will then favor the new ‘genetic unit’ so formed and will spread through the future population. It is possible for gene complexes to have been extensively rearranged or ‘re-edited’ in this kind of way.

Therefore, Dawkins argues that natural selection takes place at the gene level where small genetic units have the properties of surviving in the form of copies for a significant period of evolutionary time, while species, individuals and groups do not possess such properties. What Dawkins has done is to define a gene as a unit which, to a high degree, approaches the ideal of indivisible particulateness. A gene is not indivisible, but it is seldom divided. It is either definitely present or absent in the body of any given individual. A gene travels intact from grandparent to grandchild, passing straight through the intermediate generation without being merged with other genes. If genes continually blended with each other, natural selection would be impossible (which was what Dawkins was wrong about - it was assumed that heredity was a blending process). Genetically speaking, individuals and groups are temporary aggregations or federations as they are not stable through evolutionary time (like clouds in the sky or dust-storms in the desert). They may not even be stable due to evolutionary changes within since they are subjected to a population that is not discrete enough an entity to be a unit of natural selection and unitary enough to be ‘selected’ in preference to another population.

Individuals are fleeting and are not stable. Chromosomes are shuffled into oblivion, like the hands of cards soon after they are dealt. But the cards (genes) themselves survive the shuffling. The genes are not destroyed by crossing-over, they merely change partners and march on - they are replicators while we are survival machines. The defining property of a gene is its potential near-immortality which makes it a good candidate for natural selection.

What makes a gene ‘bad’ and another gene ‘good’? Many qualities are subjective when one considers if it is ‘good’ or ‘bad’ for its survival. However, at a universal and gene level, altruism must be bad and selfishness is good. Genes are competing directly with their alleles for survival and their alleles in the gene pool are rivals for their slot on the chromosomes of future generations. By being selfish, they tend to survive. Therefore, genes are not free and independent agents of control of embryonic development. They collaborate and interact in inextricably complex ways, both with each other, and with their external environment.

As an analogy, think of the influence of a fertilizer, say nitrate, on the growth of wheat. Everybody knows that wheat plants grow bigger in the presence of nitrate than in its absence. But nobody would be so foolish as to claim that, on its own, nitrate can make a wheat plant. Seed, soil, sun, water, and various minerals are obviously all necessary as well. But if all these other factors are held constant, and even if they are allowed to vary within limits, the addition of nitrate will make the wheat plants grow big-ger. So it is with single genes in the development of an embryo. Embryonic development is controlled by an interlocking web of relationships so complex that we had best not contemplate it. No one factor, genetic or environmental, can be considered as the single 'cause' of any part of a baby. All parts of a baby have a near infinite number of antecedent causes. But a difference between one baby and another, for example a difference in length of leg, might easily be traced to one or a few simple antecedent differences, either in environment or in genes. It is differences that matter in the competitive struggle to survive; and it is genetically-controlled differences that matter in evolution. As far as a gene is concerned, its alleles are its deadly rivals, but other genes are just a part of its environment, comparable to temperature, food, predators, or companions. The effect of the gene depends on its environment, and this includes other genes. Sometimes a gene has one effect in the presence of a particular other gene, and a completely different effect in the presence of another set of companion genes. The whole set of genes in a body constitutes a kind of genetic climate or background, modifying and influencing the effects of any particular gene.

But now we seem to have a paradox. If building a baby is such an intricate cooperative venture, and if every gene needs several thousands of fellow genes to complete its task, how can we reconcile this with my picture of indivisible genes, springing like immortal chamois from body to body down the ages: the firee, untrammeled, and self-seeking agents of life? Was that all nonsense? Not at all. We can explain this by means of another analogy. One oarsman on his own cannot win the Oxford and Cambridge boat race. He needs eight colleagues. Each one is a specialist who always sits in a particular part of the boat— bow or stroke or cox, etc. Rowing the boat is a cooperative venture, but some men are nevertheless better at it than others. Suppose a coach has to choose his ideal crew from a pool of candidates, some specializing in the bow position, others specializing as cox, and so on. Suppose that he makes his selection as follows. Every day he puts together three new trial crews, by random shuffling of the candidates for each position, and he makes the three crews race against each other. After some weeks of this it will start to emerge that the winning boat often tends to contain the same individual men. These are marked up as good oarsmen. Other individuals seem consistently to be found in slower crews, and these are eventually rejected. But even an outstandingly good oarsman might sometimes be a member of a slow crew, either because of the inferiority of the other members, or because of bad luck-say a strong adverse wind. It is only on average that the best men. tend to be in the winning boat. The oarsmen are genes. The rivals for each seat in the boat are alleles potentially capable of occupying the same slot along the length of a chromosome. Rowing fast corresponds to building a body which is successful at surviving. The wind is the external environment. The pool of alternative candidates is the gene pool.

As far as the survival of any one body is concerned, all its genes are in the same boat. Many a good gene gets into bad company, and finds itself sharing a body with a lethal gene, which kills the body off in childhood. Then the good gene is destroyed along with the rest. But this is only one body, and replicas of the same good gene live on in other bodies which lack the lethal gene.
Many copies of good genes are dragged under because they happen to share a body with bad genes, and many perish through other forms of ill luck, say when their body is struck by lightning.

But by definition luck, good and bad, strikes at random, and a gene that is consistently on the losing side is not unlucky; it is a bad gene. One of the qualities of a good oarsman is teamwork, the ability to fit in and cooperate with the rest of a crew. This may be just as important as strong muscles. As we saw in the case of the butterflies, natural selection may unconsciously 'edit' a gene complex by means of inversions and other gross movements of bits of chromosome, thereby bringing genes that cooperate well together into closely linked groups. But there is also a sense in which genes which are in no way linked to each other physically can be selected for their mutual compatibility. A gene that cooperates well with most of the other genes that it is likely to meet in successive bodies, i.e. the genes in the whole of the rest of the gene pool, will tend to have an advantage.
The Question on Reproduction

So why do we reproduce? From the selfish gene’s point of view, a gene ‘for’ sexuality manipulates all the other genes for its own selfish ends. So does a gene for crossing-over. Some genes - mutators - manipulate the rates of copying errors in other genes. By definition, a copying error is to the disadvantage of the gene which is miscopied. But if it is to the advantage of the selfish mutator gene that induces it, the mutator can spread through the gene pool. Similarly, if crossing-over benefits a gene for crossing-over and if it is sexual, as opposed to non-sexual, reproduction benefits a gene for sexual reproduction. That is a sufficient explanation for the existence of sexual reproduction. Whether or not it benefits all the rest of an individual’s genes is comparatively irrelevant. However, it comes to a circular argument, since the existence of sexuality is a precondition for the whole chain of reasoning that leads to the gene. being regarded as the unit of selection. It is a consequence of sex and crossing-over that the small genetic unit or gene can be regarded as the nearest thing we have to a fundamental, independent agent of evolution.
The Paradox of DNA

It appears that the amount of DNA in organisms is more than is strictly necessary for building them: A large fraction of the DNA is never translated into protein. From the point of view of the individual organism this seems paradoxical. If the ‘purpose’ of DNA is to supervise the building of bodies, it is surprising to find a large quantity of DNA which does no such thing. So what is the surplus of DNA doing? From the point of view of selfish genes, the true ‘purpose’ of DNA is to survive, no more and no less. The simplest way to explain the surplus DNA is to suppose that it is a parasite, or at best a harmless but useless passenger, hitching a ride in the survival created by other DNA.
What We have Covered so Far

The long-term consequences of non-random individual death and reproductive success are manifested in the form of changing gene frequencies in the gene pool. With reservations, the gene pool plays the same role for the modern replicators as the primeval soup did for the original ones. Sex and chromosomal crossing-over have the effect of preserving the liquidity of the modern equivalent in the soup. Because of sex and crossing-over the gene pool is well-stirred, and the genes partially shuffled. Evolution is the process by which some genes become more numerous and others less numerous in the gene pool. As far as genes are concerned, the gene pool is building one mortal survival machine after another. It is to survival machines themselves, and the sense in which genes may be said to control their behavior.
The Gene Machine

Survival machines began as passive receptacles for the genes, providing little more than walls to protect them from the chemical warfare of their rivals and the ravages of accidental molecular bombardment. During earth’s origins, they ‘fed’ on organic molecules freely available in the soup. It came to an end when the organic food in the soup, which had been slowly built up under the energetic influence of centuries of sunlight, was all used up. A major branch of survival machines, now called plants, started to use sunlight directly themselves to build up complex molecules from simple ones, re-enacting at much higher speed the synthetic processes of the original soup. Another branch, now known as animals, ‘discovered’ how to exploit the chemical labors of the plants, either by eating them or eating other animals. Both main branches of survival machines evolved more and more ingenious tricks to increase their efficiency in their various ways of life, and new ways of life were continually being opened up. Sub-branches and sub-sub-branches evolved, each one excelling in a particular specialized way of making a living. This sub-branching has given rise to the immense diversity of animals and plants.

Colonies of genes, in their behavior, bodies have undeniably acquired an individuality of their own. An animal moves as a coordinated whole, as a unit. Selection has favored genes that cooperate with others. In the fierce competition for scarce resources, in the relentless struggle to eat other survival machines and to avoid being eaten, there must have been a premium on central coordination rather than anarchy within the communal body.

The gadget that animals evolved to achieve rapid movement was the muscle. Muscles are engines which, like the steam engine and the internal combustion engine, use energy stored in chemical fuel to generate mechanical movement. The difference is that the immediate mechanical force of a muscle is generated in the form of tension, rather than gas pressure as in the case of the steam and internal combustion engines. Muscles are engines in that they often exert their force on cords and levers with hinges. In us, the levers are bones, cords as tendons and hinges as joints. However, the most interesting is how muscle contractions are timed.

The main way in which brains actually contribute to the success of survival machines is by controlling and coordinating the contractions of muscles. To do this they need cables leading to the muscles - motor nerves. This leads to efficient perseveration of genes only if the timing of muscle contractions bears some relation to the outside world.

It is important to contract the jaw muscles only when the jaws contain something worth biting and to contract the leg muscles in running patterns only when there is something worth running towards or away from. For this reason, natural selection favors animals that become equipped with sense organs, devices which translate patterns of physical events in the outside world in the pulse code of the neurons. The brain is connected to the sense organs by means of cables called sensory nerves.
Dawkins on Consciousness

One of the most striking properties of survival-machine behavior is its apparent purposiveness. When we watch an animal ‘searching’ for food, or for a mate, or for a lost child, we can hardly help imputing to it some of the subjective feelings we ourselves experience when we search. This has created a property known as ‘consciousness.’ Now Dawkins posits why consciousness may not be a real thing.

Negative feedback: The ‘purpose machine’ is equipped with some kind of measuring device which measures the discrepancy between the current state of things and the ‘desired’ state. It is built in such a way that the larger this discrepancy is, the harder the machine works. He cites the example of the Watt Governor where it will end up at an equilibrium state where the machine will adjust its engine if it is moving too fast or slow.

An interesting example Dawkins cited was computers playing chess. He disagrees with the argument that since a human (who perhaps has a conscious mind) programs the computer, the computer has consciousness. He talks about how the computer is on its own, making its own decisions (
Jonathan’s thoughts: but is that not consciousness in itself?
) where it tries to predict beforehand every possible move (not concurrently thinking of it, but being able to have a prior prediction involved like a guiding missile for example).

Like genes, it works on a time-scale of generations while behaviors works in a fraction of a second. There is thus a need for genes to advance by building a fast computer for themselves and programming it in advance with rules and ‘advice’ to cope with as many eventualities as they can ‘anticipate.’ But life, like the game of chess, offers too many different eventualities for all of them to be anticipated. They thus have to ‘instruct’ their survival machines not in specifics, but in general strategies and tricks of the living trade. For example, some predictions for Polar Bear genes can be made. They can safely predict that the future of their unborn survival machine is going to be a cold one. They do not think of it as a prophecy: they just build a thick coat of hair as that is what was done in previous bodies and that is why they still exist in the gene pool. They also predict that the ground is going to be snowy and their prediction takes the form of making the coat of hair white and therefore camouflaged. If the climate of the Arctic changed so rapidly that the baby bear found itself born into a tropical desert, the predictions of the genes would be wrong and they would pay the penalty - The young bear would die and they inside it.

Every decision that a survival machine makes is a gamble, and it is the business of genes to program brains in advance so that on average, they take decisions that pay off. The currency used in the casino of evolution is survival, strictly gene survival, but for many purposes individual survival is a reasonable approxima-tion. If you go down to the water-hole to drink, you increase your risk of being eaten by predators who make their living lurking for prey by water-holes. If you do not go down to the water-hole you will eventually die of thirst. There are risks whichever way you turn, and you must take the decision that maximizes the long-term survival chances of your genes. Perhaps the best policy is to postpone drinking until you are very thirsty, then go and have one good long drink to last you a long time. That way you reduce the number of separate visits to the water-hole, but you have to spend a long time with your head down when you finally do drink. Alternatively the best gamble might be to drink little and often, snatching quick gulps of water while running past the water-hole.
How do the genes make predictions? They build a capacity for learning. Surprisingly, it is the
exact

same concept in reinforcement learning (rewards, penalties etc.). Another way is to do simulations within the mind which is safer and faster than actually doing it for real. Dawkins claims that perhaps consciousness arises when the brain’s simulation of the world becomes so complete that it must include a model of itself.
The Link to Selfishness and Altruism

By dictating the way survival machines and nervous systems are built, genes exert ultimate power over behavior. But the moment-to-moment decisions about what to do next are taken by the nervous system. Genes are the primary policy-makers, the brain is the executive, but as the brain becomes more highly developed, they take over more and more of the actual policy decisions, using tricks like learning and simulation in doing so.

Dawkins cites the examples of bees (Page 79) to show how different genes lead to different results. One set of genes can be ‘working’ together with another set of genes but more in a conditional format (i.e Gene B only works if Gene A is present). However, both genes have their own ‘selfish’ intentions, acting independently with the goal of survival.

A hypothetical gene 'for saving companions from drowning', and you find such a concept incredible, remember the story of the hygienic bees. Recall that we are not talking about the gene as the sole antecedent cause, of all the complex muscular contractions, sensory integrations, and even conscious decisions that are involved in saving somebody from drowning. Dawkins is saying nothing about the question of whether learning, experience, or environmental influences enter into the development of the behavior. All you have to concede is that it is possible for a single gene, other things being equal and lots of otter essential genes and environmental factors being present, to make a body more likely to save somebody from drowning than a rival gene would. The difference between the two genes may turn out at bottom to be a slight difference in some simple quantitative variable.

Genes’ first priority is to survive and to reproduce which is why animals behave the way they do. This behavior is known as communication. A great number of survival machine actions promote their genes’ welfare by influencing the behavior of other survival machines. Animals go great lengths to make this communication effective (songs of birds enchant, songs of humpback whales, crickets amplify their songs etc.).
Aggression and Stability Machines
Why is it that animals do not go all out to kill their rival members of their species at every other opportunity?

A simple hypothetical example is that there is no obvious merit in indiscriminately trying to kill rivals. In a large and complex system of rivalries, removing one rival from the scene does not necessarily do any good: other rivals may be more likely to benefit from his death than oneself. This is the kind of hard lesson that has been learned by pest-control officers. You have a serious agricultural pest, you discover a good way to exterminate it and you gleefully do so, only to find that another pest benefits from the extermination even more than human agriculture does, and you end up worse off than you were before.

On the other hand, it might seem a good plan to kill, or at least fight with, certain particular rivals in a discriminating way. If B is an elephant seal in possession of a large harem full of females, and if 1, another elephant seal, can acquire his harem by killing him, I might be well advised to attempt to do so. But there are costs and risks even in selectivity pugnacity. It is to B's advantage to fight back, to defend his valuable property. If I start a fight, I am just as likely to end up dead as he is. Perhaps even more so.
He holds a valuable resource, that is why I want to fight him.

But why does he hold it? Perhaps he won it in combat. He has probably beaten off other challengers before me. He is probably a good fighter. Even if I win the fight and gain the harem, I may be so badly mauled in the process that I cannot enjoy the bene-fits. Also, fighting uses up time and energy. These might be better conserved for the time being. If I concentrate on feeding and on keeping out of trouble for a time, I shall grow bigger and stronger. I'll fight him for the harem in the end, but I may have a better chance of winning eventually if I wait, rather than rush in now.

This subjective soliloquy is just a way of pointing out that the decision whether or not to fight should ideally be preceded by a complex, if unconscious, 'cost-benefit' calculation.The general answer is because there are costs and benefits resulting from the outright pugnacity, and not only the obvious costs in time and energy. For instance, suppose B and C are my rivals, and I happen to meet B. It may seem sensible as a selfish individual to kill him. However, C is also my rival and C is also B’s rival. By killing B, I am potentially doing good for C by removing its rivals. I might be better off to let B live, because he might then might compete and fight with C, therefore benefiting me indirectly. The moral of this simple hypothetical example is that there is no obvious merit in indiscriminately trying to kill rivals. In a large and complex system of rivalries, removing one rival from the scene does not necessarily do any good: other rivals may be more likely to benefit from his death than oneself. Dawkins claims that genes follow a
“Evolutionary Stable Strategy

,” where it follows exactly like Game Theory. He believes that genes follow a set of instructions to maximize their payoff which is their survival in the gene pool. Organisms containing an ESS will likely evolve more than those that do not.

Once again, by using words, we have talked ourselves into picturing an oscillation in a population. Once again, mathematical analysis shows that this is not correct. There is an evolutionarily stable strategy, which can be expressed as a mathematical for-mula, but in words what it amounts to is this. Each individual goes on for an unpredictable time. Unpredictable on any particular occasion, that is, but averaging the true value of the resource. For example, suppose the resource is really worth five minutes of dis-play. At the ESS, any particular individual may go on for more than five minutes or he may go on for less than five minutes, or he may even go on for exactly five minutes. The important thing is that his opponent has no way of knowing how long he is prepared to persist on this particular occasion.

Obviously, it is vitally important in the war of attrition that individuals should give no inkling of when they are going to give up. Anybody who betrayed, by the merest flicker of a whisker, that he was beginning to think of throwing in the sponge, would be at an instant disadvantage. If, say, whisker-flickering happened to be a reliable sign that retreat would follow within one minute, there would be a very simple winning strategy: If your opponent's whiskers flicker, wait one more minute, regardless of what your own previous plans for giving up might have been. If your opponent's whiskers have not yet flickered, and you are within one minute of the time when you intend to give up anyway, give up immediately and don't waste any more time. Never flicker your own whiskers? So natural selection would quickly penalize whisker-flickering and any analogous betrayals of future behav-iour. The poker face would evolve.

Why the poker face rather than out-and-out lies? Once again, because lying is not stable. Suppose it happened to be the case that the majority of individuals raised their hackles only when they were truly intending to go on for a very long time in the war of attrition. The obvious counterplay would evolve: individuals would give up immediately when an opponent raised his hack-les. But now, liars might start to evolve. Individuals who really had no intention of going on for a long time would raise their hackles on every occasion, and reap the benefits of easy and quick victory. So liar genes would spread. When liars became the majority, selection would now favor individuals who called their bluff. Therefore liars would decrease in numbers again. In the war of attrition, telling lies is no more evolutionarily stable than telling the truth. The poker face is evolutionarily stable. Surrender, when it finally comes, will be sudden and
unpredictable.

So far we only have been dealing with ‘symmetric’ contests where the contestants are identical in all respects except their fighting strategy. However, in the real world, there are ‘asymmetrical’ contests. For instance:
Individuals with different size or fighting equipment
Individuals with different gain for winning
The duration in which a contest is settled
Individuals have retained memories of past encounters and fights
Territorial defense may simply be an ESS which arises because of the asymmetry in time of arrival that usually characterizes the relationship between two individuals and a patch of ground.
If the gene is truly selfish for its survival, why does cannibalism not occur?
The reason lions do not hunt lions is that it would not be an ESS for them to do so. A cannibal strategy would be unstable for the same reason as the hawk strategy in the earlier example.

There is too much danger of retaliation. This is less likely to be true in contests between members of different species, which is why so many prey animals run away instead of retaliating. It probably stems originally from the fact that in an interaction between two animals of different species there is a built-in asymmetry which is greater than that between members of the same species. Whenever there is strong asymmetry in a contest, ESSs are likely to be conditional strategies dependent on the asymme-try. Strategies analogous to 'if smaller, run away; if larger, attack' are very likely to evolve in contests between members of different species because there are so many available asymmetries.

Lions and antelopes have reached a kind of stability by evolutionary divergence, which has accentuated the original asymmetry of the contest in an ever-increasing fashion. They have become highly proficient in the arts of, respectively, chasing, and running away. A mutant antelope that adopted a 'stand and fight' strategy against lions would be less successful than rival antelopes disappearing over the horizon.

The same logic can also be applied to the analogy of oarsmen mentioned above where there is a need for good team spirit. Genes are selected, not as ‘good’ in isolation, but as good at working against the background of other genes in the gene pool. A good gene must be compatible with, and complementary to, the other genes with whom it has to share a long succession of bodies. A gene for plant-grinding teeth is a good gene in the gene pool of a herbivorous species, but a bad gene in the gene pool of a carnivorous species.
Think of the environment and unit gene, not only the individual gene

It is possible to imagine a compatible combination of genes as being selected together as a unit. Suppose it is important in a really successful crew that the rowers should coordinate their activities by means of speech. SUppose further that, in the pool of oarsmen at the coach’s disposal, some speak only English and some speak only German. The English are not consistently better or worse rowers than the Germans. But because of the importance of communication, a mixed crew will tend to win fewer races than either a pure English crew or a pure German crew. The coach does not realize this. All he does is shuffle his men around, giving credit points to individuals in winning boats, marking down individuals in losing boats. Now if the pool available to him just happens to be dominated by Englishmen it follows that any German who gets into a boat is likely to cause it to lose, because communications break down. Conversely, if the pool happened to be dominated by Germans, an Englishman would tend to cause any boat in which he found himself to lose. What will emerge as the overall best crew will be one of the two stable states pure English or pure German, but not mixed. Superficially it looks as though the coach is selecting whole language groups as units. This is not what he is doing. He is selecting individual oarsmen for their apparent ability to win races. It so happens that the tendency for an individual to win races depends on which other individuals are present in the pool of candidates. Minority candidates are automatically penalized, not because they are bad rowers, but simply because they are minority candi-dates. Similarly, the fact that genes are selected for mutual compatibility does not necessarily mean we have to think of groups of genes as being selected as units, as they were in the case of the butterflies. Selection at the low level of the single gene can give the impression of selection at some higher level.

In this example, selection favors simple conformity. More interestingly, genes may be selected because they complement each other. In terms of the analogy, suppose an ideally balanced crew would consist of four right-handers and four left-handers.

Once again assume that the coach, unaware of this fact, selects blindly on 'merit'. Now if the pool of candidates happens to be dominated by right-handers, any individual left handed would have to be at an advantage: he is likely to cause any boat in which he finds himself to win, and he will therefore appear to be a good oarsman. Conversely, in a pool dominated by left-handers, a right-hander would have an advantage. This is similar to the case of a hawk doing well in a population of doves, and a dove doing well in a population of hawks. The difference is that there we were talking about interactions between individual bodies- selfish machines-whereas here we are talking, by analogy, about interactions between genes within bodies. The coach's blind selection of 'good' oarsmen will lead in the end to an ideal crew consisting of four left-handers and four right-handers. It will look as though he selected them all together as a complete, balanced unit. I find it more parsimonious to think of him as selecting at a lower level, the level of the independent candidates. The evolutionarily stable state ('strategy' is misleading in this context) of four left-handers and four right-handers will emerge simply as a consequence of low-level selection on the basis of apparent merit.

Thus, The gene pool is the long-term environment of the gene. 'Good' genes are blindly selected as those that survive in the gene pool. This is not a theory; it is not even an observed fact: it is a tautology. The interesting question is: What makes a gene good?

As a first approximation Dawkins said that what makes a gene good is the ability to build efficient survival machines - bodies. We must amend that statement. The gene pool will become an evolutionary stable set of genes, defined as a gene pool that cannot be invaded by any new gene. Most new genes that arise, either by mutation or reassortment or immigration, are quickly penalized by natural selection: The evolutionary stable set is restored..
Genemanship

This chapter gives a hypothesis on why we still act altruistic despite having “selfish genes.” Dawkins posits that organisms do some sort of calculation to get their relatedness and generation gap. Essentially, what organisms want to make sure their genes have a high survivability rate and are passed down (i.e If sacrificing yourself to save 10 others increases your gene pool, then the organism goes forth with that action). By some calculations, it benefits more to be altruistic than to be selfish. Besides generation gap and gene retention calculations, Dawkins also includes a “certainty” calculation.

If an organism is your identical twin, then should you care for him twice as much as you care for any of your children; indeed theoretically you should value his life no less than your own (based on the gene calculation). However, you cannot be 100% sure he is your identical twin just based on facial features (assuming you are an animal in the wild) as you both might happen to share the same facial gene features. You will not give up your life for him because although it is possible that he bears 100% of your genes, you absolutely know that you contain 100% of your own genes, so you are more worthy to yourself than he is. The gene for individual selfishness has the enormous advantage of certainty of individual identity. Therefore, we must expected individual selfishness in nature, to an extent greater than would be predicted by considerations of genetic relatedness alone. This fact is probably a key to understanding why parental care is so much more common and more devoted than brother/sister altruism in nature and also why animals may value themselves more highly even than several brothers. In addition to the index of relatedness, we must consider something like an index of ‘certainty.’
Family Planning

Individual parents practice family planning, but in the sense that they optimize their birth rates rather than restrict them for the public good. They try to maximize the number of surviving children that they have, and this means having neither too many babies nor too few. Genes that make an individual have too many babies tend not to persist in the gene pool. because children containing such genes tend not to survive adulthood.
Battle of the Generations

A mother is equally related to all her children, born and to be born. On genetic grounds alone she should have no favorites based on gene relatedness. if she does show favoritism it should be based on differences in expectation of life, depending on age and other things. The mother, like any individual, is twice as closely ‘related’ to herself as she is to any of her children. Other things being equal, this means that she should invest most of her resources selfishly in herself, but other things are not equal. She can do her genes more good by investing a fair proportion of her resources in her children. This is because they are younger and more helpless than she is, and they can therefore benefit more from each unit of investment than she can herself. Genes for investing in more helpless individuals in preference to oneself can prevail in the gene pool, even though the beneficiaries may share only a proportion of one's genes. This is why animals show parental altruism, and indeed why they show any kind of kin-selected altruism.
You Scratch my Back and I’ll Ride Yours

Within each one of our cells, there are numerous tiny bodies called mitochondria. The mitochondria are chemical factories. They are responsible for providing most of the energy we need. If we lost our mitochondria we would be dead within seconds. Recently it has been plausibly argued that mitochondria are, in origin, symbiotic bacteria who joined forces with our type of cell very early in evolution. Similar suggestions have been made for other small bodies within our cells. This is one of those revolutionary ideas which it takes time to get used to, but it is an idea whose time has come. Dawkins speculates that we shall come to accept the more radical idea that each one of our genes is a symbiotic unit. We are gigantic colonies of symbiotic genes. One cannot really speak of evidence for this idea, but, as Dawkins tried to suggest in earlier chapters, it is really inherent in the very way we think about how genes work in sexual species. The other side of this coin is that viruses may be genes who have broken loose from colonies' such as ourselves. Viruses consist of pure DNA (or a related self-replicating molecule) surrounded by a protein jacket. They are all parasitic. The suggestion is that they have evolved from 'rebel' genes who escaped, and now travel from body to body directly through the air, rather than via the more conventional vehicles - sperms and eggs. If this is true, we might just as well regard ourselves as colonies of viruses! Some of them cooperate symbiotically, and travel from body to body in sperms and eggs. These are the conventional genes. Others live parasitically, and travel by whatever means they can. If the parasitic DNA travels in sperms and eggs, it perhaps forms the 'paradoxical' surplus of DNA which Dawkins mentioned in Chapter 3. If it travels through the air, or by other direct means, it is called 'virus' in the usual sense.
A Summarized Version of “
The Selfish Gene”

Let me end with a brief manifesto, a summary of the entire selfish gene/extended phenotype view of life. It is a view, I maintain, that applies to living things everywhere in the universe. The fundamental unit, the prime mover of all life, is the replicator. A replicator is anything in the universe of which copies are made. Replicators come into existence, in the first place, by chance, by the random jostling of smaller particles. Once a replicator has come into existence it is capable of generating an indefinitely large set of copies of itself. No copying process is perfect, however, and the population of replicators comes to include varieties that differ from one another. Some of these varieties turn out to have lost the power of self-replication, and their kind ceases to exist when they themselves cease to exist. Others can still replicate, but less effectively. Yet other varieties happen to find themselves in possession of new tricks: they turn out to be even better self-replicators than their predecessors and contemporaries. It is their descendants that come to dominate the population. As time goes by, the world becomes filled with the most powerful and ingenious replicators. Gradually, more and more elaborate ways of being a good replicator are discovered. Replicators survive, not only by virtue of their own intrinsic properties, but by virtue of their consequences on the world. These consequences can be quite indirect. All that is necessary is that eventually the consequences, however tortuous and indirect, affect the success of the replicator at getting itself copied.

The success that a replicator has in the world will depend on what kind of a world it is- the pre-existing conditions. Among the most important of these conditions will be other replicators and their consequences. Like the English and German rowers, replicators that are mutually beneficial will come to predominate in each other's presence. At some point in the evolution of life on our earth, this ganging up of mutually compatible replicators began to be formalized in the creation of discrete vehicle cells and, later, many-celled bodies. Vehicles that evolved a bottlenecked life cycle prospered, and became more discrete and vehicle-like.
