This packaging of living material into discrete vehicles became such a salient and dominant feature that, when biologists arrived on the scene and started asking questions about life, their questions were mostly about vehicles-individual organisms. The individual organism came first in the biologist's consciousness, while the replicators now known as genes— were seen as part of the machinery used by individual organisms. It requires a deliberate mental effort to turn biology the right way up again, and remind ourselves that the replicators come first, in importance as well as in history.

One way to remind ourselves is to reflect that, even today, not all the phenotypic effects of a gene are bound up in the individual body in which it sits. Certainly in principle, and also in fact, the gene reaches out through the individual body wall and manipulates objects in the world outside, some of them inanimate, some of them other living beings, some of them a long way away. With only a little imagination we can see the gene as sitting at the center of a radiating web of extended phenotypic power. And an object in the world is the center of a converging web of influences from many genes sitting in many organisms. The long reach of the gene knows no obvious boundaries. The whole world is criss-crossed with causal arrows joining genes to phenotypic effects, far and near.

It is an additional fact, too important in practice to be called incidental but not necessary enough in theory to be called inevitable, that these causal arrows have become bundled up. Replicators are no longer peppered freely through the sea; they are packaged in huge colonies—individual bodies. And phenotypic consequences, instead of being evenly distributed throughout the world, have in many cases congealed into those same bodies. But the individual body, so familiar to us on our planet, did not have to exist. The only kind of entity that has to exist in order for life to arise, anywhere in the universe, is the immortal replicator.
Man’s Search for Meaning

was recommended to me during my secondary school days as it act as both an educational and inspirational book. The book’s underlying goal is to explore human resilience and purpose in human life. The book is divided into two parts: Frankl’s experiences as a Holocaust survivor and his development of logotherapy which is a form of existential analysis.

In the first part, Frankl recounts his harrowing experiences in Nazi concentration camps, detailing the physical and psychological suffering endured by prisoners. He emphasizes that despite the extreme adversity, individuals could find meaning in their suffering through their attitude and personal choices. I gained loads of insights in the daily operations of the concentration camp, together with the brutal treatment that followed (i.e 6 Oz of stale cold bread for 5 days, 24-7 in the winters mining and the SS executing those who are too ill or not fit to work). The main takeaway that is repeated many times in the first part is as follows:
Those who have a why to live can bear almost any how.”
The book is essentially Friedrich Nietzsche’s philosophical ideas captured in simple terms.

The second part introduces logotherapy, Frankl’s psychotherapeutic approach centered on finding life’s meaning. Frankl argues that the primary drive in human beings is not pleasure or power, but the pursuit of meaning. He explores how this pursuit can lead to personal fulfillment, even in the face of unavoidable suffering. He provides guiding questions, however, this part of the book was slightly boring for me. Despite that, the first part alone was valuable enough to give this book a 4/5 rating. For those interested in psychology, philosophy, and personal development, I would recommend this book.
"The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking"

by Saifedean Ammous offers a comprehensive exploration of Bitcoin as a revolutionary monetary system. The book explores the historical evolution of money, tracing the transition from barter systems to commodity money like gold, which became universally accepted due to its intrinsic value.

I would say that half of the book argues that traditional fiat currencies, which are not backed by physical commodities but rely on trust and government authority, lead to economic instability through inflation and manipulation. Central banking is critiqued
extensively

in the book, with Ammous detailing how central banks influence economies through monetary policy, interest rates, and inflation. He argues that central banking often results in economic distortions, inequality, and financial crises. In contrast, Bitcoin is presented as a viable alternative, offering a system free from political influence and monetary manipulation.
That is the reason why I had to lower the ratings was because of this part. Although I understand why price mechanisms and
Laissez-Faire

economics has its merits, I felt that the author was basically ranting to me his points. Yes, I get it: Government intervention sucks for you but he went on for about 100 pages. In that sense, I felt that Bitcoin’s operations should be expanded more in those 100 pages. Having said that, the book had a good flow of ideas before talking about Bitcoin’s operations.

In introducing Bitcoin, Ammous presents it as a groundbreaking alternative to fiat currencies and central banking systems. He explains the creation of Bitcoin, its underlying technology, and its economic principles. The book highlights Bitcoin’s features, including its decentralization, security, and fixed supply of 21 million coins, contrasting these with the inflationary nature of fiat currencies.

Ammous applies economic theories to Bitcoin to argue that it could serve as a new standard for money. He discusses how Bitcoin’s scarcity and decentralized nature address many issues inherent in fiat currencies and central banking. The potential adoption of Bitcoin as a global standard is explored, suggesting that it could lead to greater economic stability and individual freedom by eliminating the need for central banks and reducing the risk of currency devaluation.

The book also addresses Bitcoin’s potential and the challenges it faces. Ammous discusses Bitcoin’s role as a store of value, medium of exchange, and unit of account, while acknowledging issues such as regulatory hurdles, scalability, and public perception. He responds to criticisms of Bitcoin, including concerns about its energy consumption and volatility, arguing that these challenges can be addressed and do not diminish Bitcoin’s value proposition.

Looking to the future, Ammous is optimistic about Bitcoin’s potential to reshape the financial system. He envisions a world where Bitcoin’s fixed supply and decentralized nature contribute to a more stable and equitable financial environment, potentially replacing fiat currencies and central banking.

I was a little hesitant to read this at the start - the title does not do it much justice, other than positing a “get rich quick” or “one-size-fits-all” idea. However, in terms of practicality, this book is a must-have and might even become a classic in the future. The book does not provide you with trading strategies, rather, it provides you with a framework of thinking to execute both qualitative and quantitative workings coherently.
"The Laws of Trading: A Trader's Guide to Better Decision-Making"
emphasizes the importance of understanding trading psychology, risk management, and the creation of effective trading systems.

Lebron starts by exploring the psychological aspects of trading, explaining how emotions and cognitive biases can impact decision-making. He highlights common pitfalls, such as overconfidence and loss aversion, and provides strategies to mitigate these issues. The author stresses that
self-awareness and discipline
are crucial for maintaining a rational approach to trading, particularly during periods of high volatility or stress - Chapter 1 on “Purpose.”

The book then shifts focus to risk management, outlining techniques to protect capital and manage exposure. He argues that a solid risk management strategy is essential for long-term trading success, helping traders avoid catastrophic losses and maintain consistency (Chapter 2: “Asymmetry” and Chapter 3: “Risks”).
The most important part of the book for me is Chapter 4 and 5 - “Edge” and “Models”:

In the “Edge” chapter, Lebron addresses what it means to have a trading edge, which is essentially a sustainable advantage that allows traders to outperform the market over time. He defines an edge as any strategy or insight that gives a trader a better probability of success than random chance.

Lebron emphasizes that an edge is not just about having superior information or tools; it’s about having a systematic approach that consistently leads to better outcomes. This could be due to a unique trading strategy, a specialized knowledge of a market, or a disciplined approach to risk management. The chapter covers several key points:

Identification of Edge: Lebron discusses how traders can identify and develop their edge by analyzing their trading strategies and performance. He advises traders to critically assess what makes their approach effective and to continuously refine their methods to maintain their advantage.

Testing and Validation: The chapter stresses the importance of backtesting and validating trading strategies. Traders must ensure that their edge is not based on anecdotal evidence but is supported by rigorous testing and historical performance data.

Maintaining Edge: Once an edge is identified, maintaining it requires vigilance and adaptability. Lebron notes that markets are dynamic, and what works well today might not be effective tomorrow. Traders need to stay updated on market changes and be ready to adjust their strategies as needed.

The “Models” chapter delves into the development and use of trading models. Lebron argues that having a well-structured model is crucial for systematic trading and decision-making. He outlines several important aspects of building and using trading models:

Model Development: Lebron describes the process of creating a trading model, which includes defining objectives, setting rules for trade entry and exit, and incorporating risk management techniques. He emphasizes that models should be built on clear, logical principles and should be adaptable to different market conditions.

Quantitative vs. Qualitative Models: The chapter contrasts quantitative models, which rely on numerical data and statistical analysis, with qualitative models, which use subjective judgment and experience. Lebron highlights the strengths and limitations of each approach, suggesting that a combination of both can often be beneficial.

Model Evaluation: Evaluating a trading model involves assessing its performance through backtesting and real-world application. Lebron discusses key metrics for evaluation, such as profitability, drawdowns, and risk-adjusted returns. He stresses the importance of ongoing evaluation to ensure that the model continues to perform well and meets the trader’s objectives.

Model Adaptation: Markets evolve, and so should trading models. Lebron advises traders to regularly review and update their models based on new data and changing market conditions. Flexibility and adaptability are crucial for maintaining a model’s relevance and effectiveness.
The last chapter “Adaptation”  is also a really good chapter that touches on evolution and how it relates to trading.

In summary, “The Laws of Trading” by Agustin Lebron provides a thorough exploration of the key principles and practices that contribute to successful trading. By addressing psychological factors, risk management, costs, capacity and the development of trading systems, Lebron offers valuable insights and actionable strategies for traders seeking to enhance their decision-making processes and achieve better trading outcomes.

"Algorithms to Live by" posits that we are able to use computer science algorithms to apply to our problems that we face in our lives. Life's greatest problems like "when should we get married", "how should you sort the files in your room", "should we enjoy the things we have at the moment or keep searching", just to name a few, are answered thoroughly throughout the book. Note that a decent grasp of the computer science syllabus (i.e Bayesian statistics, game theory, algorithms, caching, simulations, optimization and overfitting) is required to fully appreciate the concepts underlying the contents of the book. While I do find this book an interesting read, especially talking about familiar problems such as rationality, travelling salesman problem and many more, I do find the working methods rather difficult to apply in our lives. For instance, the chapter on Bayesian Thinking highlights the type of priors distributions and the follow-up methods that can be applied to life's problems. Although this concept sounds intuitive and logical, it is difficult to quantify what kind of prior distribution we are facing as it is ever-changing and dynamic in nature (now imagine applying rationality and game theory). Nonetheless, I enjoyed reading this book and found some interesting take on certain problems. However, readers expecting to get a "self-help, advice" kind of book may feel disappointed. Readers should read this book as a refresher for some of the computer science theories or as an interesting approach to solve life's problems.
Algorithms to Live By
Chapter 1: Optimal Stopping Problem
There are different approaches to the optimal stopping problem. The book uses the interview problem as an example. It advocates the “
Look, Then Leap Rule”

which essentially starts searching to get enough of the necessary data before making an informed decision. It converges to approximately 37% as you increase the number of samples in the pool. A big assumption is that the interviewees will definitely accept the offer should you decide to choose them.

Other variations include those of a full-information game. If the goal is to get the single best person for the job, one would need to weigh the likelihood there is a stronger applicant out there. Having full information enables one to calculate the odds directly which indicates you do not need to look back before leaping. This means that the decision of whether to stop comes down entirely to how many applicants there are left in the pool to see. It recommends the “
Threshold Rule”

where one immediately accepts an applicant if they are above a certain percentile - it does not require to “look” at an initial group of candidates to set this threshold, but one needs to be keenly aware of how much looking remains available.

The math shows that when there are a lot of applicants left in the pool, you should pass up even a very good applicant in the hopes of finding one still better than that but as your options dwindle, you should be prepared to hire anyone who’s simply better than average. In the face of slim pickings, lower your standards. It also makes clear the converse: with more fish in the sea, raise them.

No matter what, never hire someone who is below average unless you’re totally out of options (And since you are still interested only in finding the very best person in the applicant pool, never hire someone who is not the best you have seen so far.
In buying a house, the critical thing to note is that the problem is that our threshold is dependent only on the cost of search.
Even if that offer is guaranteed to still be on the table, you should nonetheless never do so. If it wasn’t above your threshold then, it won’t be above your threshold now
What you’ve paid to keep searching is a sunk cost. Don’t compromise, don’t second-guess and don’t look back.
It is important to know when to optimally stop (see Page 28 on “Skilled Robber Game”) but some problems have an infinite stopping time (“
Triple or nothing”

). If you were to calculate using expected values, the math says that you should always keep playing but if you follow that strategy, you will lose everything. Some problems are better avoided than solve.

Essentially, all of these problems do not take into account emotional effects (perhaps impatience in the secretary problem) and more importantly, the role of time (opportunity cost). There is always a time cost in our lives, it does not come from the design of experiments, but rather, it comes from people’s lives. The theory of optimal stopping is concerned with the problem of choosing a time to take a given action - it is all about timing to do a particular thing.
Chapter 2: Explore / Exploit Tradeoff
This chapter highlights when we should “explore” and when we should “exploit”. The main factor is our time horizon.
Exploration: Gathering information
Exploitation: Using the information you have to get a known good result

Understanding this tradeoff provides fundamental insights into how our goals should change as we age, and why the most rational course of action isn’t always to choose the best. People tend to treat decisions in isolation, to focus on finding each time the outcome with the highest expected value. But decisions are almost never isolated, and expected value is not the end of the story. If you are thinking not just about the next decision, but all about the decisions you are going to make about the same options in the future. More generally, our intuitions about rationality are too often informed by exploitation rather than exploration. When we talk about decision-making, we focus on the immediate payoff of a single decision and if you treat every decision as if it was your last, then indeed only exploitation makes sense. But over a lifetime, you’re going to make a lot of decisions.
The strategy: Explore when you have the time to use the resulting knowledge, exploit when you are ready to cash in.
The book highlights the following algorithms:
Win-Stay, Lose-Shift Algorithm

Gittins Index Algorithm (basically time value of money, future rewards are decreased geometrically) -> Provides a format, rigorous justification for preferring the unknown, provided we have some opportunity to exploit the results of what we learn from exploring -> The unknown has a chance of being better, even if we expect it to be no different or if it’s just as likely to be worse (i.e The untested rookie is worth more than the veteran of seemingly equal ability precisely because we know less about him)
Regret minimization framework:

Bezos, when leaving D.E Shaw to Amazon, “I knew when I was 80 I was not going to regret having tried this. I knew if I failed I would not regret that, but I knew the one thing I might regret is not ever having tried. I know that would haunt me everyday or so, but when I thought about it that way, it was an incredibly easy decision.”

Regret is measured by the difference between the total payoff obtained by following a particular strategy and the total payoff that theoretically could have been obtained by just pulling the best arm every single time.
Algorithm for Regret:

Upper Confidence Bound Algorithm - Using error bars about a data point simulating a confidence interval -> Pick the option for which the top of the confidence interval is the highest -> “Optimism in the face of uncertainty” -> By focusing on the best that an option could be, given the evidence obtained so far, it naturally inject a dose of exploration into the decision-making process, leaping at new options with enthusiasm because any one of them could be the next big thing
Chapter 3: Sorting
This chapter provides an overview on different sorting algorithms, together with their time complexity. The following algorithms were mentioned when sorting a bookshelf in alphabetical order:
Bubble Sort
Insertion Sort
Merge Sort
It then goes about explaining how Olympic games, NBA and other popular sporting events can be sort via the following algorithms:
Single Elimination Algorithms
Round-Robin Algorithms
Ladder Algorithms
Chapter 4: Caching

The goal of cache management is to minimize the number of times you cannot find what you are looking for in the cache and must go to the slower main memory to find it.  The optimal cache eviction policy is when the cache is full, evict whichever item you will need again the longest from now. This is known as the
Belady’s Algorithm

which is a “clairvoyant” algorithm - one that is informed by data from the future. The challenge is to find an algorithm that comes as close to clairvoyance as we can get, for all those times when we are stuck firmly in the present and can only guess at what lies ahead.
Other algorithms include:
Random Eviction (add new data to the cache and overwriting old data at random)
First-In, First-Out (FIFO)
Least Recently Used (LRU)

The LRU principle is effective as problem solving uses the property of “temporal locality”: if a program has called for a particular piece of information once, it is likely to do so again in the near future.
Our best guide to the future is a mirror image of the past. The nearest thing is clairvoyance is to assume that history repeats itself - backwards.

Certain types of computer memory have faster performance but cost more per unit of storage, leading to a “memory hierarchy” that tries to get the best of both. But it is not actually necessary to have memory made of different materials for aching to make sense. Caching is just as useful when it’s proximity, rather than performance, that’s the scarce resource.

In essence, when you are deciding what to keep and what to throw away, LRU is potentially a good principle to use, much better than FIFO. Remember to also exploit geography by making sure things are in whatever cache is closest to the place where they are typically used.

Adderson’s approach to human memory with aging is that the mind has essentially unlimited capacity for memories, but we only have a finite amount of time in which to search for them. The key to good memory then becomes the same as the key to a good computer cache: predicting items are most likely to be wanted in the future. The old basically have more of such “brain farts” and “cache miss” which represents the disproportionate occasional lags in information retrieval. One way to look at it is that the length of decay is partly an indicator of the extent of your experience and the effort of retrieval is a testament to how much you know. And the rarity of those lags is a testament to how well you have arranged it by keeping the most important things close to mind.
Chapter 5: Scheduling

This chapter illustrates the order in which we set out to do our tasks. Do the ones with sharp deadlines? Do the ones that are the easiest? Or do we begin with the most difficult task first before moving on to easier ones?
The author suggests the following algorithms:
Earliest Due Date
Moore’s Algorithm (Earliest Due Date but minimize the number of tasks that are not feasible to do)
Shorting Processing Time (Always do the quickest task you can to reduce the sum of completion time)
Chapter 6: Bayes’ Rule

This might have to be the best chapter in the whole book in terms of the way it was written and the immediate application to our lives. An understanding of Bayes’ Rule would include the likelihood, the prior and the posterior. Would recommend reading this whole chapter as every page is equally important (from history to application).
The chapter essentially summarizes the different kind of prior distributions and their prediction rules which can be summarized as:
Power-law prior -> Use multiplicative rule
Normal prior -> Use average rule
Erlang Prior -> Use addictive rule

The essence of Bayes’ Rule is also to cope with small data points as it captures the intuition of people making decisions for quantities that follow different distributions. Some of these predictions happen both unconsciously and consciously. The reason we can often make good predictions from a small number of observations is that our priors are so rich. Whether we know it or not, we appear to carry around in our heads surprisingly accurate priors based on our experiences. My personal input also suggests that our priors may be subjectively different, leading to different biases due to our different environmental upbringing. Our judgements thus betray our expectations, and our expectations betray our experience. What we project about the future reveals a lot about the world we live in and about our own past.

In today's world where increasing social media presence is a real phenomenon, it is difficult to distinguish noise and exaggeration. People talk about what interests them and offer stories they think their listeners will find interesting, skewing the statistics of our experience. Thus, to be a good intuitive Bayesian, making naturally good predictions requires one to protect one’s own priors.
Chapter 7: Overfitting
Overfitting is prevalent in majority Machine Learning algorithms. It is always a complexity versus overfitting trade off when trying to capture more data. This chapter highlights the idea that “
less is more”

and provides techniques to minimize the problem of overfitting. The author argues that we see overfitting everywhere in our daily lives due to the change in diets, sports, school tests and business which differs from its original purpose of survival in our early human days. The author also argues that us, humans, are shaped not only by our present environment but also by our history. The concept of overfitting gives us a way of seeing virtue in evolutionary baggage. We do not necessarily want evolution to fully optimize an organism to every shift in its environment as it will become very sensitive to environmental changes. As a species, being constrained by the past makes us less perfectly adjusted to the present we know but helps keep us robust for the future we don’t.
The book offers the following techniques which can be applied to our daily lives:
Cross Validation
Regularization
Early Stopping

When to early stop depends on the gap between what you can measure and what really matters. If you have all the facts, they are free of all error and uncertainty, and you can directly assess whatever is important to you, then do not stop early. But that is almost never the case. If you have high uncertainty and limited data then do stop early by all means. The greater the uncertainty, the bigger the gap between what you can measure and what matters, the more you should watch out for overfitting.
Chapter 8: Relaxation

This chapter talks about constrained optimization problems and its difficulty. Constrained optimization problems may not even have a solution (i.e Traveling Salesman Problem). By learning to “relax”, means to reduce some of the constraints to at least have somewhere to start. From there, there might be other alternatives which can “open more doors” to solutions. Just do. Some problems may be factorial time complexity and unless we are willing to spend eons striving for perfection every time we encounter a hitch, hard problems demand that instead of spinning our tires we imagine easier versions and tackle those first. It is one of the best ways of making progress.
The book offers the following methods:
Constraint Relaxation (Simply removing the constraint altogether and makes progress on a looser form of the problem before coming back to reality)
Continuous Relaxation (Turns discrete or binary choices into continuous problems - when deciding between iced tea and lemonade, first imagine a 50 - 50 blend and then round it up or down)
Lagrangian Relaxation (Turns impossibilities into mere penalties, teaching the art of bending the rules (or breaking them and accepting the consequences)
Chapter 9: Randomness

Randomness shows us that making use of chance can be a deliberate and effective part of approaching the hardest sets of problems. The earlier chapter, “Relaxation”, gives a brief highlight that some constrained optimization problems are intractable (efficient algorithms can be used to solve). However, by using the following methods of sampling, we are able to form approximations, distributions and insights which are decent enough to be compared to the real solutions.
The algorithms:
Monte Carlo Simulations
Randomized Algorithms

The chapter then goes on to talk about how randomness can be used to get out of local minima and maximas. The example used: Planning an itinerary of travel around different states with the objective of lowering costs. The first attempt might be taking the cheapest flight first, then taking the cheapest flight to any remaining city and back again. This would be a “
greedy algorithm
” where it is myopic. It takes the best thing available every step of the way without looking or planning beyond. A good baseline but not optimal.
An alternative would be to test alternatives by making slight perturbations to the city's sequences and seeing if it makes an improvement. This algorithm is known as “
Hill Climbing”
. Eventually, you will end up with a solution that is better than all of its permutations but you may be trapped in a global maxima or minima.
The book then offers randomizations such as “
Jitters
” to prevent being trapped. Such algorithms include:
Random-Restart Hill Climbing
Metropolis Algorithm
Simulated Annealing
Chapter 11: Game Theory

Game Theory is simply an act of recursion with different levels - can you anticipate the anticipation of others? Highlighted by John Maynard Keynes, he believes valuation is like a beauty contest where the value of a stock is not what people think it is worth but what people think people think it’s worth. In poker, it is theoretically an infinite recursion. There is your own hand and the hand you believe your opponent to have; then the hand you believe you to believe he has and on it goes. To beat recursion, you have to come up with reasons to make exploitive leveling plays, but a lot of the time you are just making inferior plays for reasons that are really just noise.
Nash argues that by reaching
Nash’s Equilibrium

it will be an optimal solution to any game as it is stable - no amount of further reflection by either player will bring them to different choices. For instance, in rock paper scissors, the equilibrium tells us that if we tried playing more rock, our opponent would quickly notice and start playing more paper, which would make us play more scissors, and so forth until it is settled into the one-third probability equilibrium.
However, computer scientists proved that simply finding
Nash’s Equilibrium

is an intractable problem. Simple games like rock paper scissors have equilibra visible at a glance, but in games of real world complexity, it is now clear we cannot take for granted that the participants will be able to discover or reach the game’s equilibrium.
The flaw of Game Theory comes with the concept of dominant strategy (see
Prisoner’s Dilemma

). Essentially, no matter what your accomplice does, it’s always better for you to rat the other out. It is now a paradox. If everyone does the rational strategy and follows the dominant strategy, then the story ends with a dramatically worse outcome for everyone involved. Computer scientists offer an alternative to algorithmic game theory using “
the price of anarchy
” - this measures the gap between cooperation and competition. In a game like
Prisoner’s Dilemma

, this price is infinite: increasing the amount of cash at skate and lengthening the jail sentences can make the gap between possible outcomes arbitrarily wide, even as the dominant strategy stays the same. There is no limit to how painful things can get for the players if they do not coordinate.

Quantifying this price of anarchy has given the field a concrete and rigorous way to assess the pros and cons of decentralized systems. A low price of anarchy indicates that the system, for better or worse, about as good on its own as it would be if it were carefully managed while a high price of anarchy indicates that things have the potential to turn out fine if they are carefully coordinated but that without some form of intervention, we are courting disaster (usually the most critical games of the world).
Tragedy of the Commons

highlights the concept of “every man for himself”. The world limits the number of people polluting the environment, but who has the right to do so? If burning of fossil fuels provides economic growth, then everyone would have the same mindset to do it, betting on the fact that they are the ones part of the limitation. It is another
Prisoner's Dilemma problem.
A solution to the
Tragedy of the Commons

is to change the game via mechanism design. If the rules of the game force a bad strategy, maybe we should not try to change the strategies, maybe we should try to change the game. While game theory asks what behavior will emerge given a set of rules, mechanism design works in the other direction asking what rules will give us the behavior we want to see (Page 240 - 247).
Lastly, the concept of
Information Cascades

talks about the formation of bubbles. Part of the reason why it is a good idea to pay attention to the behavior of others is that in doing so, you get to add their information about the world to your own (i.e A popular restaurant is good, a half-empty concert is a bad sign etc.) On the other hand, learning from others does not always seem particularly rational.
Information Cascades

offer a rational theory not only of bubbles, but also of fads and herd behavior more generally where they offer an account of how it’s easily possible for any market to spike and collapse, even in the absence of rationality.
Information Cascades
offers the following lessons:
Be wary of cases where public information seem to exceed private information
Remember that actions are not beliefs; cascades get caused in part when we misinterpret what others think based on what they do
Sometimes a game can have irredeemably lousy rules - there is nothing we can do once we are in it but the theory of information cascades may help us to avoid such a game in the first place

What we see in this chapter is that interacting with others doesn’t have to be a nightmare - although in the wrong game it sure can. As Keynes observed, popularity is complicated, intractable, a recursive hall of mirrors; but beauty, in the eye of the beholder, is not. Adopting a strategy that doesn’t require anticipating, predicting, reading into or changing the course because of the tactics of others is one way to cut the Gordian knot of recursion. And sometimes that strategy is not just easy - it is optimal. If changing strategies does not help, you can try to change the game. If that is not possible, you can at least exercise some control about which games you choose to play. The road to hell is paved with intractable recursions, bad equilibra and information cascades. Seek out games where honesty is the dominant strategy, then just be yourself.
After reading “
When Breathe Becomes Air”

, I was inspired to read new neuroscience-related books. Whilst researching on my next read, I was listening to Andrew Huberman’s podcast on Dopamine and was particularly interested. At the end of his podcasts, he recommend “
Dopamine Nation.”

I was quite surprised when I flipped opened the first page. I was expecting a research-heavy book that is filled with clinical experiments from start to finish. Rather, this book was filled with Dr. Anna’s patients experiences which illustrated her workings on the brain. I was glad it was not going to be a dry, research-based book as reading those can be mentally draining and boring (my thoughts on
Thinking Fast and Slow
). This book also draws some parallels to
Atomic Habits
and
Thinking Fast and Slow
in terms of concepts and examples used.

The book starts by explaining how dopamine drives behavior by creating sensations of pleasure and reward. In the digital age, where instant gratification is more accessible than ever—through social media, online shopping, gaming, and other digital stimuli—people are constantly seeking pleasure and avoiding discomfort. This constant overstimulation, Dr. Lembke argues, leads to what she calls “dopamine burnout,” where the brain’s reward system becomes desensitized. As a result, individuals may need ever-increasing amounts of stimulation to achieve the same level of satisfaction, leading to cycles of addiction and dissatisfaction.

What I particularly like was her simple analogy on how the brain’s pleasure and pain system operated like a see-saw. Dopamine is a neurotransmitter that plays a key role in the brain’s reward system. It is released in response to pleasurable activities, reinforcing behaviour that lead to rewards. When people engage in activities that stimulate dopamine release—such as using drugs, eating high-sugar foods, or engaging in excessive social media use—they experience pleasure. This pleasure is often immediate and intense.

Homeostasis and the Pain-Pleasure Balance:
•	The brain strives to maintain a state of homeostasis, or balance, between pleasure and pain. When dopamine levels are elevated due to pleasurable activities, the brain compensates by increasing its sensitivity to discomfort or pain.
•	This means that after a period of intense pleasure, there is often a corresponding increase in feelings of discomfort or pain. This is because the brain adjusts its reward system to counteract the overstimulation.

The “Hedonic Treadmill”:
•	The concept of the “hedonic treadmill” refers to the phenomenon where people need increasingly greater amounts of stimulation or pleasure to achieve the same level of satisfaction over time. This occurs because the brain’s pleasure-pain balance shifts: what once provided a high level of pleasure becomes less satisfying, requiring more stimulation to achieve the same effect.
•	As people continuously seek more pleasure, they may inadvertently exacerbate their discomfort or dissatisfaction, leading to a cycle of addiction and reliance on external stimuli for gratification.

Dopamine Detox:
•	To address the imbalance between pleasure and pain, Dr. Lembke suggests a strategy known as “dopamine detox.” This involves reducing exposure to high-stimulation activities and substances to help the brain reset its reward system.
•	By taking a break from excessive pleasure-seeking behaviors, individuals can allow their brain to recalibrate, making it easier to find satisfaction in less stimulating activities and improving overall mental well-being.

Long-Term Balance:
•	Achieving long-term balance involves engaging in activities that provide sustainable, meaningful rewards rather than immediate gratification. This might include practices such as mindfulness, establishing healthy routines, and focusing on long-term goals and personal growth.
•	Dr. Lembke emphasizes that finding this balance is essential for maintaining mental health and avoiding the negative consequences of chronic overstimulation and addiction.

Dr. Lembke combines scientific research with real-world case studies to illustrate how this overstimulation contributes to mental health issues such as addiction, anxiety, and depression. She discusses various substances and behaviors that activate the dopamine system, including drugs, alcohol, food, and even digital media. By examining these case studies, she highlights the complexities of addiction and how modern society’s easy access to these dopamine-inducing stimuli exacerbates the problem.

Dr. Lembke also explores the societal and cultural factors that contribute to our dopamine-driven behaviors. She argues that while technological advancements and the proliferation of instant gratification are not inherently negative, their misuse can lead to significant psychological and social problems. The book even argues why modern day solutions such as drugs does not contribute much help for true recovery.

In summary, “Dopamine Nation” offers a comprehensive look at the effects of dopamine on modern life, providing readers with practical strategies to achieve a healthier balance between pleasure and well-being. Dr. Lembke’s insights aim to help individuals recognize and address the impacts of their dopamine-driven behaviors, ultimately leading to more sustainable and fulfilling lives.
Steve Jobs

by Walter Isaacson is a comprehensive biography that chronicles the life of one of the most influential figures in technology and business. The book spans Jobs's early life, his work at Apple Inc., his ventures outside of Apple, and his return to lead the company to unprecedented success.
Early Life and Apple’s Founding

The biography starts with Jobs’s childhood in Cupertino, California. Born in 1955, he was adopted by Paul and Clara Jobs. From an early age, he exhibited an interest in electronics and a knack for working with his hands. Jobs’s curiosity led him to explore the emerging world of technology and, together with Steve Wozniak, he founded Apple Computer in 1976. Their first major product, the Apple I, marked the beginning of a revolutionary approach to personal computing. The introduction of the Apple II solidified Apple’s place in the tech industry, but Jobs’s demanding nature and visionary ideas also led to internal conflicts.
Steve’s Personality
Not going to lie, this is what made the book so entertaining. Many who worked with Steve admit that his approach was something like a “
Reality Distortion Field.

” It refers to his ability to convince himself and others to believe in almost anything he set his mind to but in a manipulative manner. He would often bend reality to his will, persuading his team that they could achieve seemingly unattainable goals. Jobs’s RDF was fueled by his deep belief in his vision and his persuasive skills. He frequently set aggressive deadlines and demanded perfection, often pushing his team beyond their perceived limits.

Jobs was known for his relentless pursuit of perfection. He was deeply involved in every aspect of product development, from design to user experience. His perfectionism drove Apple’s innovative designs but also led to intense scrutiny and frequent revisions.
Jobs’s leadership style was often described as autocratic. He had a strong vision for Apple and was known for making unilateral decisions. His management style involved high levels of control and micromanagement, which could be both motivating and stifling for employees.
Jobs could be both inspiring and abrasive. He was known for his demanding nature and, at times, his harsh criticism of others. His feedback could be blunt, and he didn’t hesitate to express his dissatisfaction openly. Despite this, he also had a charismatic and visionary side that could rally people to his cause.
Jobs’s spiritual and philosophical beliefs were also unconventional. He was known to explore various spiritual practices, including meditation and Eastern philosophies, which influenced his approach to business and design. His quest for meaning and simplicity in design reflected his broader existential outlook
Growth and Challenges

The biography delves into Jobs’s role in developing the Macintosh, which was pivotal in popularizing the graphical user interface and shaping modern computing. However, Jobs’s autocratic management style led to tensions within Apple, resulting in his ouster from the company in 1985. The book describes Jobs’s subsequent ventures, including the creation of NeXT, a computer platform aimed at higher education and business markets, and his acquisition of Pixar Animation Studios. At Pixar, Jobs played a crucial role in its growth and success, leading to a series of blockbuster films and eventually a lucrative acquisition by Disney.
Return to Apple and Innovation

Jobs’s return to Apple in 1997 marked a turning point for the company. The biography explores how Jobs redefined Apple’s product strategy, focusing on simplicity, design, and user experience. His leadership led to the development of revolutionary products such as the iPod, iPhone, and iPad. These innovations not only transformed Apple but also had a profound impact on technology and media industries globally. Jobs’s relentless pursuit of perfection and his ability to foresee market trends were instrumental in Apple’s resurgence and growth.
Personal Life and Legacy

Isaacson’s book also offers a glimpse into Jobs’s personal life, including his relationships with family, his battle with cancer, and his philosophical and spiritual beliefs. Despite his professional achievements, Jobs’s personal relationships were often strained by his intense focus on work and his demanding nature.
The biography concludes with Jobs’s legacy, highlighting how his vision and leadership reshaped the technology landscape and influenced various aspects of modern life.
Steve Jobs
portrays him as a complex figure—brilliant yet abrasive, inspiring yet demanding—who left an indelible mark on the world through his work and his vision for technology’s potential.
In Steve Job’s 2005 Stanford Commencement Address:

“Your time is limited, so don’t waste it living someone else’s life. Don’t be trapped by dogma—which is living with the results of other people’s thinking. Don’t let the noise of others’ opinions drown out your own inner voice. And most important, have the courage to follow your heart and intuition. They somehow already know what you truly want to become.”

Nobel prize winner Daniel Kahneman's works compressed into a book. "Thinking fast and slow" has been sitting on my desk for a long time and the inertia to read this has been great - partly because psychology strikes me as a pseudo-science where one idea may be easily replace by another if an alternative experiment confirm different hypothesis. Nonetheless, this was an interesting read though it may be a little draggy due to loads of research explaining three big concepts. The book starts out with the ways in which our brain operates - System 1 and System 2. In essence, System 1 is the "fast moving" component on the brain which operates automatically, intuitively, and quickly, with little or no effort or conscious control. It is responsible for making quick judgments, recognizing familiar patterns, and responding to immediate stimuli. System 1 processes are typically based on heuristics, mental shortcuts, and intuition rather than deliberate reasoning. On the other hand, System 2 is often referred to as "slow thinking." System 2 is more deliberate, analytical, and effortful. It involves conscious reasoning, logical thinking, and mental effort to process complex information, solve problems, and make decisions. System 2 thinking requires cognitive resources and is characterized by careful consideration of facts, weighing of alternatives, and planning for the future. The book proceeds to introduce several concepts of biases and cognitive processes (i.e Heuristics, Herd Behavior etc.) before touching on the flaws of current economic models such as the utility function and provides an alternative solution known as Prospect Theory. Prospect Theory introduces the notion of loss aversion and reference points. The most interesting part of the book to me is the last chapter where it highlights 2 selves - the "remembering self" and the "experiencing self". We often classify our experiences by the peaks of our memories (extreme happiness and sadness) rather than the overall weighted total duration of the experience. Thus, we are prone to the biases of our "remembering self" rather than our "experiencing self" which is more objective. The book is full of information for one to digest, so my advice is: Do not rush it! The reason why I rated it slightly lower is because I find it is a little draggy and mentally draining reading research after research which reinforces the same concept. Indeed, not my cup of tea. After downloading 418 pages of research, I am definitely going to take a break on research-based books.

Theology is something new to me and I never thought of philosophical reasons for my believe in God, yet alone Christianity. It has always been motivated by my personal experience growing up. However, I do think that there is much value learning the philosophical arguments that is often taught in theology to make an objective case for the evidence for and against God’s existence. ‘Why Believe’ to me has to be the best introductory book for anyone who wants to explore the subject matter. Religion is more of a personal subject so I will not comment much. For further exploration on the topic, I recommend podcasts hosted by Trent Horn, William Lane Craig, Alex O Conor, Ben Shapiro, Richard Dawkins and more.
This was my second non-fiction financial storytelling book I’ve read (the first being
The Journey of a Value Investor

), but unfortunately, I had to quit halfway as I did not understand much. A year later, with a more knowledgeable perspective, I finally understand what high-frequency trading is all about and have gained a greater appreciation for it. The premise of this book exposes high-frequency traders exploiting investors in banks' dark pools. Dark pools are essentially private exchanges within banks that operate as black boxes; we cannot see who the buyers or sellers are or where our orders are going. High-frequency traders use different arbitrage methods to buy and sell the same asset across exchanges and profit from price discrepancies. A group of people, puzzled by why prices move against them, sets out to find the culprits. Spoiler alert: It’s the high-frequency traders. This same group of people plans to expose the high-frequency exploitation and create their own exchange where orders are placed at the same time to prevent any price discrepancy. The book argues that the system is at fault, not the high-frequency traders. The traders are simply being rational in exploiting price discrepancies and earning risk-free profits, but it is the financial system that encourages such behavior. I gained much insight into the realm of high-frequency trading from this book and particularly appreciate Michael Lewis's writing style—taking lesser-known stories and presenting them well (I expect no less from him, given his other books such as
The Big Short
and
Moneyball
). I’m glad I revisited this, but a basic understanding of finance is definitely a prerequisite.
Economyths

explores how mainstream economics is built on several key myths, such as fair competition, rational behavior, stability, and perpetual growth. Paradoxically, these myths often lead to their opposites: inequality, an irrational economy, financial instability, and clashes with nature's limits. Each chapter begins with a historical perspective on why orthodox economics is structured the way it is, tracing back to ancient Greek times.

As someone interested in quantum mechanics, graph theory, and mathematical concepts, I found the book’s approach intriguing. It discusses how mathematicians and physicists apply their rigorous sciences to economics, often overlooking the social aspects that govern economic systems. The book highlights flaws in financial models, such as using Gaussian distributions without accounting for kurtosis and fat tails, and suggests alternatives like power laws and geometric fractals.
However, this book is best complemented by other resources, such as
The Misbehavior of Markets
Models Behaving Badly
, and the final chapter of
Frequently Asked Questions in Quantitative Finance

, to gain a fuller understanding of the 'myths' in orthodox economics. I found the last few chapters less compelling, as the arguments didn’t hold up well against rebuttals. Additionally, some chapters felt disjointed, with the author occasionally straying from the main topic before returning to it. The first half of the book was strong, but the second half was less engaging.

title: The Subtle Art of Not Giving A F*ck
author: Mark Manson

text.t: Cliché, I know. This is a book that everyone in my secondary school read during morning assembly. I was taking a break from all the finance books and thought I would give this book a chance (I heard some bad reviews on it). After completing the whole book, I think it is not a bad read at all (you just have to take what the author says with a pinch of salt). The underlying premise of this book is that our time is limited, and in the short amount of time between here and there, you have a limited amount of f
cks to give (pardon my language, but I do not give a f
ck). Yet most of us struggle throughout our lives by giving too many f
cks in situations where f
cks do not deserve to be given. And if you go around giving a f
ck about everything and everyone without conscious thought or choice—well, then you’re going to get f

cked. This book essentially teaches you how to focus and prioritize your thoughts effectively—how to pick and choose what matters to you and what does not matter to you based on finely honed personal values. A lot of the book content makes sense to me (i.e., why suffering is good, how our problems are upgraded to harder problems, becoming self-aware, and how we are not that important in this world). I can see why some people do not like this book, given the author's tone and the sheer number of hypothetical examples used. However, I found it really entertaining. This book should not be read too critically. I would recommend this for someone who struggles socially or to anyone who wants entertaining content.
ANNEX
What I think of “self-help” books:

It is predicted on peddling highs to people rather than solving legitimate problems. It teaches you new forms of denial and pumps you up to feel good in the short-term, while ignoring the underlying issue. Nobody who is actually happy has to stand in front of a mirror and tell himself that he is happy, unless you are living in denial and having a victim mentality.
The Feedback Loop From Hell:
The desire for a more positive experience is itself a negative experience. And, paradoxically, the acceptance of one’s negative experience is itself a positive experience.
In that sense, “don’t try.”

The idea that the more you pursue feeling better all the time, the less satisfied you become, as pursuing something only reinforces the fact that you lack it in the first place. This is the “backwards law”: not giving a f*ck works in reverse. If pursuing the positive is a negative, then pursuing the negative generates the positive (i.e failures and pain). Everything worthwhile in life is won through surmounting the associated negative. Any attempt to escape the negative, to avoid it or quash it or silence it, only backfires. The avoidance of suffering is a form of suffering.

The moments of non-f*ckery are the moments that most define our lives, yet most of us struggle throughout our lives by giving too many f*cks in situations where f*cks do not deserve to be given. Our time is limited and in the short amount of time between here and there, you have a limited amount of f*cks to give. And if you go around giving a f*ck about everything and everyone without conscious thought or choice- well, then you’re going to get f*ck.

Essentially learn how to focus and prioritize your thoughts effectively - how to pick and choose what matters to you and what does not matter to you based on finely honed personal values. It is incredibly difficult as it takes a lifetime of practice and discipline to achieve. And you will regularly fail. But it is perhaps the most worthy struggle one can undertake in one’s life. It is perhaps the only struggle in one’s life.

Not giving a f*ck does not mean being indifferent (like a psychopath), it means being comfortable with being different. There is not such thing as not giving a f*ck. You must always give a f*ck about something as it is part of our biology to always care about something and therefore to always give a f*ck. The question is what do we give a f*ck about. What are we choosing to give a f*ck about. And how can we not give a f*ck about what ultimately does matter.
We do not care about adversity in the face of our goals, we do not care about pissing some people off to do what we feel is right or important or noble. Say
f*ck it
to everything unimportant in your life.
Reserve for the
f*cks
that truly matter.

If you find yourself consistently giving too many f*cks about trivial shit that bothers you, chances are you do not have much going on in your life to give a legitimate f*ck about. And that is your real problem. If you do not find the purpose and importance of your life, your f*cks will be given to meaningless and frivolous causes.

All of us suffer from life. Not all suffering is equal but we all suffer nonetheless. The premise that underlies a lot of our assumptions and beliefs is that happiness is algorithmic, that it can be worked for and earned and achieved. The premise is a problem. Happiness is not a solvable equation. Dissatisfaction and unease are inherent parts of human nature and necessary components to creating consistent happiness. We suffer for the simple reason that suffering is biologically useful. It is nature’s preferred agent for inspiring change. Grass is greener on the other side basically - a feature of human evolution because to us, suffering sucks. Pain is our body’s most effective means of spurring action. Physical pain is a product of our nervous system, a feedback mechanism to give us a sense of our own physical proportions. When we exceed those limits, our nervous system duly punishes us to make sure that we pay attention and never do it again (illustrated in
Atomic Habits

as well!). The concept applies for emotional and psychological pain as well. What is dangerous about our society now is that society coddles itself more and more from the inevitable discomforts of life (an argument for snowflake generation).
Do not hope for a life without problems, instead, hope for a life full of good problems.

Emotions evolved to help us live and reproduce a little bit better. They’re feedback mechanisms telling us that something is either likely right or likely wrong for us - nothing more, nothing less. They are simply biological signals designed to nudge you in the direction of beneficial change (i.e the pain example used above). Emotions are part of the equation of our lives, but not the entire equation. Emotions are merely signposts, suggestions that our neurobiology gives us, not commandments. Therefore, we should not always trust our own emotions. Question them. What feels good may not be good for you, vice versa. Decisions making based on emotional intuition, without rationality, pretty much always suck (behavioral finance confirms this). Everything comes with an inherent sacrifice - whatever that makes us feel good will also inevitably make us feel bad. A bit like hedging, offsetting the risk with a new set of risk that you are willing to accept.
What pain do you want in your life? What are you willing to struggle for?

Because that seems to be a greater determinant of how our lives turn out. Everyone wants the high-lifestyle but can you bear the burdens of it? The solution lies in the acceptance and active engagement of that negative experience - not the avoidance of it, not the salvation from it.
Be in love with the process, not the result.
Who you are is defined by what you’re willing to struggle for.

It is not always about willpower or grit (no pain, no gain), rather, our struggles determine our successors. Our problems birth our happiness, along with slightly better and upgraded problems. It is a never ending upwards spiral. If you think there is any point where you can stop climbing is not the point, rather the joy is in the climb itself.

When real traumatic shit happens in our lives, we begin to unconsciously feel as though we have problems we are incapable of solving. And this assured inability to solve our problems causes us to feel miserable and helpless. Our unconscious figures will make us think that we are uniquely special or defective in some way. That we are somehow unlike everyone else and that the rules must be different. It makes us entitled either by the victim treatment or the overconfidence / arrogant approach. Opposite mindset on the outside, but the same selfish core in the middle. It takes as much delusional self-aggrandizement to maintain the belief that one has insurmountable problems as that one has no problems at all. But you’re not special. Chances are if you have a problem, millions of other people have had it in the past, present and future. It is made worse today. We are all, for the most part, pretty average. But it is the extremes that get the attention. We can say it is statistically improbable that any single person will be an extraordinary performer in all areas of life or even many areas of their life. The ones that catch our attention are those in the 99.99 percentile and we are flooded with the extreme two ends of information. It has conditioned us to believe that exceptionalism is the new normal and it drives us to feel insecure and desperate. This results in the overcompensation through entitlement and addiction. It is linked to mass media driven exceptionalism and it is screwing up a lot of people’s expectations for themselves. The notion of fitting is linked to extremism, radicalized self-assurance.

The self-awareness onion teaches us to question our emotions but at a deeper level, question our values that determine the nature of the problem which in turn determines the quality of our lives. Most self-help gurus ignore this deeper level of self awareness. They take people who are miserable because they want to be rich and then give them all sorts of advice on how to make money, all the while ignoring important value-based questions:
Why do they feel such a need to be rich in the first place? Is it not perhaps some particular value that’s the root cause of their unhappiness?
Much of the advice out there operates at a shallow level of simply trying to make people feel good in the short term, while the real long-term problems never get solved.
People’s perceptions and feelings may change, but the underlying values, and the metrics by which those values are assessed, stay the same

. For example, I am angry that my girlfriend did not reply to my text. My value: My girlfriend is supposed to have a good relationship with me. My metric: Being in contact by phone is how I measure my success as a boyfriend. You need both metric and underlying value to be sensible. From the girlfriend example above, perhaps there just needs to be some sought of mutual trust which would be a better assessment of a relationship than how many text messages both parties exchange. We get to control what our problems mean based on how we choose to think about them, the standard by which we choose to measure them.

We are always choosing, whether we are conscious of it or not. There is a difference between faults and responsibility. It is not your fault that your circumstances happen to you but it is your choices that define your approach to your circumstances. Change your priorities, change your metrics and stop behaving the same way if you feel like a failure. Many of the relationships in your life were built around the values you’ve been keeping. There are necessary, though painful, side effects of choosing to place you f*cks somewhere else, in a place for more important and more worthy of your energies. More than anything, you will feel uncertain when you are met with internal and external resistance along the way and that is a good thing.

Improvement at anything is based on thousands of tiny failures and the magnitude of your success is based on how many times you’ve failed at something. If someone is better than you at something, then it’s likely because she has failed at it more than you have. If someone is worse than you, it’s likely because he hasn’t been through all of the painful learning experiences you have. We can only be truly successful only at something we’re willing to fail at. If we’re unwilling to fail, then we’re unwilling to succeed. A lot of a fear of failure comes from having chosen shitty values (i.e Make everyone like me). Failure is 100% defined by the actions of others, not by my own actions - you are not in control, thus your self-worth is at the mercy of judgements by others. Shitty values involve tangible external goals outside of one’s control. The pursuit of these goals causes great anxiety and even if we manage to achieve them, we will feel empty and lifeless as once they’re achieved there are no problems to solve. Remember: Life is full of problems, solving one’s problems upgrades your problems and solving problems gives you happiness. Better values are process-oriented and must constantly be re-engaged.

Our most radical changes in perspective often happen at the tail end of our worst moments. It’s only when we feel intense pain that we’re willing to look at our values and question why they seem to be failing us. We need some sort of existential crisis to take an objective look at how we’ve been deriving meaning in our life and then consider changing course. To deny pain is to deny our potential.

Rejection makes your life better. We all must give a f*ck about something, in order for us to value that something. To value that something, we must reject what is not that something. To value X, we must reject non-X. It is an inherent and necessary part of maintaining our values, and therefore our identity. We are defined by what we choose to reject. And if we reject nothing, we essentially have no identity at all.

There is a freedom and liberation in commitment. Commitment gives you freedom because you’re no longer distracted by the unimportant and frivolous. Commitment gives you freedom because it hones your attention and focus. Directing them toward what is efficient at making you healthy and happy. Commitment makes decision-making easier and removes any fear of missing out; knowing that what you already have is good enough, why would you stress about chasing more, more and more again? Commitment allows you to focus intently on a few highly important goals and achieve a greater degree of success than you otherwise would. In this way, rejection of alternatives liberates us - rejection of what does not align with our most important values, our chosen metrics, rejection of the constant pursuit of breadth without depth. Yes, breadth of experience is likely necessary and desirable when you’re young - you have to go out there and discover what seems worth investing but depth is where the gold is buried. You have to stay committed to something and go deep to dig it up. This is applicable in everything that you do.
"When Breath Becomes Air"

has always been on my mind. It was the book everyone held during morning assembly when I was in secondary school (high school for you Americans). Taking a break from all the finance, I finally decided to pick this up. The first half of the book details Paul's journey in becoming a neurosurgeon. With a master’s in literature and a degree in biology, Paul ultimately chose to pursue medical school at Stanford to answer the ultimate question he had been pondering: "What is the meaning of life?" The book highlights Paul's journey as a neurosurgeon, discussing the ethics (e.g., is it moral to put someone down?) and the challenges a doctor in primary care faces (such as long working hours and making crucial decisions under pressure). Sadly, Paul was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer and takes the reader through his experience as a patient. It is a sad story, but also an inspiring one. Our First Pillar
Is it Possible to Predict Policies?

Imagine a giant holding a large mug of ale over a hill and the giant tips the mug over. The beer gushes down the decline. If I know the hill, I can predict the ale’s course: it will follow the path of least resistance because it is influenced by the material reality of the hill’s terrain. The forecast must start with its course, rather than the policymaker’s reaction to it. The reaction is a derivative of the flood and the only way to know the flood is to know the terrain. Just like Marx’s book
Capital

, he breaks down the concept of capitalism into the most basic components and using this materialist approach, he rarely delves into the qualitative world of ideas. He focuses on the material realities that underpin capitalism: price, money, labor and means of production. After exposing the system’s inconsistencies, Marx concludes with the forecast that a crisis is coming. Although he was wrong about capitalism collapsing, his theory of capitalism  and materialist dialectic still enabled him to predict a conflict of economic systems. His constraint framework “dialectical materialism” enables him to power these conclusions. It is in opposition to the Hegelian dialectic - “thesis, antithesis, synthesis”. For Hegel, the starting point of the search for “truth” is human thought: ideas. Hegel sees the human actor as possessing agency and the ideological preferences of both the powerful few and the masses influence history. However, the innovation of Marx’s
Capital
is that it rejects the notion that ideas dictate human history, it must not be the starting point of analysis.
What makes the materialist dialectic the
dialectic?
In Marxist thought, the material world - the society’s modes of production - is the concrete foundation upon which all thought, norms, values and institutions ultimately rest.
Idea serves materials
. If Hegel’s theory says the idea egg came before the chicken, Marx’s counters that it was the material chicken that got the idea egg rolling.
The framework’s starting point of analysis is the
material world, not the world of ideas

. Material conditions create human reality. Thought systems develop around this material condition and are therefore a derivative of it. People cannot “think” or “prefer” their way out of material constraints.
Our Second Pillar
Diagnosticity of Constraints

Constraints are observable and therefore empirical. Not all observable data is created equal, and more information often does not produce superior forecasting results. The quality of data matters more than its quantity, especially in circumstances where a complete data set is impossible to obtain.

Judgment is what analysts use to fill gaps in their knowledge. It entails going beyond the available information and is the principal means of coping with uncertainty. While the optimal goal of intelligence collection is complete knowledge, this goal is seldom reached in practice. Thrive on uncertain, paucity of high quality information and concept driven, rather than data-driven, analysis.

The quality of data is what matters and the key determinant of quality is diagnosticity. It is the extent to which any item of evidence helps the analyst determine the relative likelihood of alternative hypotheses.
Imagine a patient with a 38 degree celsius fever. As the body temperature in excess of 38 is consistent with so many reasons to be ill, it has limited diagnostic value.

Diagnosticity helps analysts eliminate unlikely, or competing hypotheses. A nondiagnostic variable is one that does not help eliminate any of the hypotheses. Preferences are not diagnostic variables as they are optional; policymakers choose whether to act on them. Such variables are nondiagnostic as it is impossible to eliminate hypotheses based on a variable that may not affect the outcome at all. In contrast, constraints are the gatekeepers that determine whether preferences affect the outcome. Constraints have high diagnosticity because preference-based outcomes are subject to them.
Our Third Pillar
Fundamental Attribution Error

The person versus the situation (pg 34) experiment on good samaritans versus time constraints. A mistake analysts make when they attribute real-world outcomes to characteristics, personality, and moods of individual actors is known as the fundamental attribution error. The individual’s psychological profile is given primacy over the external context; the person takes precedence over the situation.

The news media is partly to blame because it personalizes events and tells human rather than situational stories (stories do not sell well without individual actors in them, journalists are giving their readers what they want which reaffirms that people matter and that human agency can triumph over the determinism of the situation).
Summary

The starting point for geopolitical analysis must always be rooted in the material world. Investors should always seek the immutable reality - the constraints - in a situation. Given paucity of information and poor data quality, investors must focus on the data that is concrete and iterative, rather than ephemeral data locked away in someone’s brain. Focus on a high level of diagnosticity - policy makers' preferences are not diagnostic, constraints are. Social psychology makes a strong case that the context and the situation, not the person, drive human behavior.

Politics is the study of power: a force that compels others to do something they would prefer not to do. The Soviet Union did not need wealth to threaten the US with nuclear annihilation. Power, or political capital, is not just about economics. It dominates the individual policy maker preferences, particularly as they cannot pursue their intentions without political capital.

Policymakers with ample political capital can expend it on unpopular policies such as structural reforms (i.e China one-party system). A currency trader in emerging markets needs to be sensitive to such power flexes as one of few indicators of long term currency performance is comparative productivity levels. A key factor influencing those levels is whether policymakers pursue productivity-enhancing policies. It helps to think of structural reforms or any controversial policy in terms of a “J curve” - whenever politicians pursue such policies, they drain their political capital, writ large. In doing so they enter the “danger zone”: a moment of truth when the populace may reject the policy - Argentinian election, President Marci failed to get re-elected as he did not have enough political capital to pursue painful reforms. Factors to gauge political capital include: popularity, time in power (risk averse due to elections nearing etc.), legislative math, economic context, special interest group support (to defeat them when creating difficult reforms or policy) and global momentum (regional contingency factors).
How Politicians Aim to Win?
The Median Voter Theorem
Voter’s preferences are “single-peaked”, meaning voters prefer one policy outcome over all other potential outcomes.

Preferences are considered over a single policy dimension. For instance, a voter either supports gun legislation or not, or wants a greater or smaller role for the state in the economy. And in each election, the median voter makes a decision on this single policy dimension.
Politicians want to attain, or retin, political capital above everything else, including consistent policy and positive societal outcomes

As with any theory, the danger with this lies in how its application may simplify reality beyond recognition. It posits that, to win and maintain power, policymakers should follow a three-step process:
Identify the central issue of the day
Ascertain the median’s voter position on that issue
Asymptotically approach the median voter’s position, outflanking opponents in the process

President Trump successfully identified the central issue of the 2016 election: Globalization versus economic nationalism. He next ascertained where the American voter stood between those extremes. To the shock of most pundits, the American median voter was far less supportive of globalization than assumed.

The Median Voter Theory is a powerful tool in predicting outcomes as it forces all policy makers to shift to the median position, lest they become irrelevant political outliers. We must look at it in terms of context and shifts in the skewness of left-right economic dimension (median voter will also be skewed) - pg 85

In the short-term, confounding policy variables obscure voter median preferences - Governing coalitions, gerrymandered electoral results and policy prerogatives of individual parties all mask the long-term influence of the median voter. This illustrates how the Median Voter Theorem allows for policy to deviate from the median voter in the short term, but not in the long term.
In summary, the median voter is the price maker in the political marketplace; in the long term, politicians are mere price takers.

The Economy and the Market
The two constraints: macroeconomics and finance, or the market exist in what Soros calls a reflexive relationship, where investor perceptions can alter the economic fundamentals.

To identify macroeconomic constraints, I rely on economic fundamentals: What are the main drivers of growth? Is productivity high, or is most growth a function of labor force growth? Are there structural imbalances in the economy - long term unemployment and underemployment, over-regulation, protectionism of domestic industries, wealth inequality? Is the current account balanced or unbalanced? If the latter, does the imbalance stem from export dependency or too much imported  goods and capital? To what extent does domestic macroeconomic policy encourage creative destruction and competition? I use macroeconomic fundamentals like a doctor uses the indicators of health. A single red flag - like high cholesterol - is easy enough to deal with in isolation. Like the doctor, if I find enough surprising answers to diagnostic questions, I investigate more thoroughly to find the root cause.

Finance Constraints: A country can have poor macro fundamentals for a very long time, but investor enthusiasm can keep the economy going. While they are in place, investor inflows mask the underlying imbalances - like ibuprofen masking a fever. Investor enthusiasm enables policy makers to grow complacent. The role of a functional market is therefore to discipline and constrain policymakers, but investors do not always foster such an environment. Markets are also not rational but rather driven by their narratives. These narratives can make a downturn worse by exacerbating a panic, but they can also amplify a mania.

The economy is a direct constraint to policy makers. Forecasters need to look beyond the direct causal links and consider the subtler implications. If not, there will be a misunderstanding of the power dynamics between countries.

There is a growing consensus that China and the US are destined to replicate the Cold War.
