The author provides a concise summary of the book’s core premise: "More Than You Know's core premise is simple to explain but devilishly difficult to live: you will be a better investor, executive, parent, friend — essentially a better person — if you approach problems from a multidisciplinary perspective." This foundational idea suggests that broadening one's approach beyond a single field or discipline can lead to improved decision-making and problem-solving.

The book is organized into four primary sections: investment philosophy, psychology of investing, innovation and competitive strategy, and science and complexity theory. Each section functions as a distinct toolbox, offering insights and methods to address different aspects of investing and life. This structure allows readers to explore a variety of topics and see how they interconnect.

The author uses a range of abstract examples to illustrate complex concepts in behavioral economics. For instance, the analogy of "blind ants following the blind" serves to explain how group behavior can lead to unexpected outcomes, while examples from evolution and the "hot hand fallacy" in basketball highlight the often irrational nature of human behavior and decision-making.

Despite the book being packed with information and presenting independent essays on various subjects, it can be quite dense. The theoretical nature of the content may make it challenging to directly apply some of the concepts in practical scenarios. However, the depth of the analysis provides a rich, thought-provoking read that encourages readers to think critically about behavioral economics and its implications.

For those interested in exploring these ideas further, additional insights and notes can be found in my personal notetaking document. Overall, "More Than You Know" offers a unique and valuable perspective on behavioral economics, even if its practical applications might not always be immediately clear.
ANNEX
Be The House: Process and Outcome in Investing

The goal of an investment process is unambiguous: to identify gaps between a company’s stock price and its expected value (derived by the weighted average value for a distribution of possible outcomes). Over the long haul (just like the casino), process dominates outcome which is why the house always makes money over time.

The single greatest error in the investment business is a failure to distinguish between the knowledge of a company’s fundamentals and the expectations implied by the market. The issue is not which horse in the race is the most likely winner, but which horse or horses are offering odds that exceed their actual chance of victory. There is no such thing as “liking” a horse to win a race, only an attractive discrepancy between his chances and his price.

With both uncertainty and risk, both outcomes are unknown. But with uncertainty, the underlying distribution of outcomes is undefined, while with risk we know what that distribution looks like. Corporate undulation is uncertain; roulette is risky. Uncertainty links to the behavioral finance issue of overconfidence.

Decisions are a matter of weighing probabilities but probabilities alone are insufficient when payoffs are skewed. Loss aversion - a loss has 2.5 times the impact of a gain of the same size. A focus on probability is sound when outcomes are symmetrical, but completely inappropriate when payoffs are skewed (look at a call option). Always look at the expected value, not the probability alone.
The Babe Ruth Effect: The frequency of correctness does not matter, it is the magnitude of correctness that matter

Even though Ruth struck out a lot, he was one of baseball’s greatest hitters. A behavioral fact is that people are a lot happier when they are right frequency, but being right frequently is not necessarily consistent with an investment portfolio that outperforms its benchmark. The percentage of stocks that go up in a portfolio does not determine its performance, it is the dollar change in the portfolio. A few stocks going up or down dramatically will often have a much greater impact on portfolio performance than the batting average.

Again, investors must look at past frequencies and consider expected value. The best investors think in all probabilistic fields, yet in many ways, it is unnatural. Investors want their stock to go up, not down - prospect theory states that investors sell their winners too early (satisfying the desire to be right) and hold their losers too long (in hopes that they don’t have to take a loss).
Sound Theory for the Attribute Weary: The Importance of Circumstance-Based Categorization

Slime mold cells operate as independent single-celled units. They move around, eat bacteria and divide to reproduce. When food is in short supply, however, the slime-mold cells converge and form a cluster of tens of thousands of cells. The cells literally stop acting as individuals and start acting like a collective. That is why slime mold is so hard to categorize: it is an “it” or “they” depending on the circumstances.

Similarly, investment approaches based solely on attributes, without considering the circumstances, also do not make sense. Sometimes a stock that looks expensive is cheap, and what looks cheap is expensive. It is context dependent.

Yet, most investments are attribute based: Growth inventors strive to beat the market by filling their portfolios with companies that are rapidly increasing sales and earnings, without too much concern about valuation. Value investors load up on cheap stocks with a decent yield and consider corporate growth gravy. These approaches are grounded in theory: a belief that investor actions will lead to satisfactory outcomes.

The flaw with theory is that it is impractical. But if you define theory as a contingent explanation of cause and effect, it is eminently practical. A sound theory helps to predict how actions or events lead to specific outcomes across a broad range of circumstances. However, investment theory is unsound as it is based on poor categorization (investors generally dwell on attribute-based categorization versus circumstantial based categorizations).

A theory works by predicting what we see based on various circumstances. In doing so, we bump into anomalies which forces researchers to revisit the description and categorization stage. The goal is to explain the phenomenon in question more accurately and thoroughly than in the prior theory. Proper theory building requires researchers to cycle through the stages in search of greater predictive power. It is a virtuous cycle.

However, a theory that must be falsifiable is a challenge of economists as the number of economic constructs assume an answer in their definitions. Take utility maximization for instance. We can define utility in any way that is consistent with the outcome, we cannot falsify the construct. To me, it is reverse engineering the process for consistency, given that we know the outcome. They are “constructs”, rather than “theories”.
Risky Business: Risk, Uncertainty, and Prediction in Investing

How should we think about risk and uncertainty? Risk has an unknown outcome but we know what the underlying outcome distribution looks like. Uncertainty also implies an unknown outcome, but we do not know what the underlying distribution looks like. Roulette or Blackjack (a game of chance) is risky while the outcome of a war is uncertain. According to definitions, risk always includes the notion of loss while something can be uncertain but might not include the chance of loss.

This is important as investment opportunities are fundamentally an exercise in probability. We need to think about how we come up with probabilities for various situations and where potential pitfalls lie.
There are different forms of probabilities:

Degrees of Belief: Subjective probabilities and are the most liberal means to translate uncertainty (like one time off events) into probability. Investors can also frequency update probabilities based on degrees of belief when new, relevant information becomes available.

Propensities: Reflects the properties of the object or system. Like in the book “Range”, risk was derived on individual parts of the rocket, not as a whole. This method of probability assessment does not always consider all the factors that may shape an outcome (i.e human errors when constructing the parts together).

Frequencies: Probability is based on a large number of observations in an appropriate reference class. Frequency users do not care what someone believes an outcome of a die roll will be nor would they care about the design. They would focus only on the yield of repeated die rolls.

Long term stock market returns are based on degrees of belief, with the resulting probabilities heavily colored by recent experience. It is known to have a substantial emotional component. Future results based on historic values is a frequency approach, where we can make statements about possible future results. Academic finance is based on this. Most of the models assume a normal distribution of price change (quantitative finance) which is obviously wrong in extreme scenerios.

The most important point about markets is that acting on a prediction can change the prediction’s outcome. A fair roulette game prediction outcome is independent of the prediction itself. Contrast that with a prediction at the racetrack. If you believe a particular horse is likely to do better than the odds suggest, you will bet on the horse. But your bet will help to shape the odds (demand and supply analysis) which is the same as the marketplace. This point underscores the importance of expected value. As investors, the challenge is to translate those uncertainties into probabilities and payoffs in search for attractive securities.
Are You an Expert? Experts and Markets

This chapter provided me with a good summary of another book called “Range”, where the main concept is that experts will only do well in “kind” domains - one that is familiar and repeatable but will perform poorly in “wicked” domains - one that is uncertain (majority of life’s domains is in this category).

One way to look at expert effectiveness is based on the nature of the problem they address. Experts do well in straightforward problems inherent to static, linear and discrete systems. The opposite side reflects dynamic, non-linear and continuous problems. While experts tend to internalize many of their domain’s features, this practice can also lead to reduced cognitive flexibility. Reduced cognitive flexibility leads to deteriorating expert performance as problems go from the simple to the complex. First is what psychologists call functional fixedness - the idea that when we use or think about something in a particular way we have great difficulty in thinking about it in new ways. We have a tendency to stick to our established perspective and are very slow to consider alternative perspectives. The second idea, reductive bias, says taht we tend to treat non-linear, complex systems as if they are linear, simple systems. An example is evaluating a system solely on attributes, rather than circumstances - focusing on statistically cheap stocks and failing to consider whether or not the valuation indicates value. Expert performance is largely a function of the type of problem the expert addresses.

In the argument of humans vs AI, rules based systems with limited degrees of freedom, computers consistently outperform individual humans due to psychological reasons as documented above. A probabilistic domain with high degrees of freedom (like the stock market), experts can and often do, hold diametrically opposite views on the same issue. The flaw is that we often rely on experts, yet we are faced with unimpressive results. Tetlock uses the analogy of foxes (generalists) who know many small things and exercises cognitive flexibility rather than hedgehogs who only have one powerful tool.
The Hot Hand in Investing: What Streaks tell Us About Perception, Probability and Skill

Basketball - if a player makes a few baskets in a row is considered to have a hot hand which implies that he has a higher than normal chance of sinking his next shot - this is known as the hot hand phenomenon. The hot hand, however, does not exist. Streaks and slumps lie within the domain of chance. We see patterns when none exist because we are wired to expect that the characteristics of chance show up not just in a total sequence but also in small parts of the sequence. Daniel Kahneman calls this “the belief in the law of small numbers” as even a short sequence of repeated heads in a coin flip is enough to convince most people (falsely) that the longer sequence is not random. That is the reason we believe in hot hands. This is what streaks inform us about probabilities - in human endeavors, unlike a fair coin toss, the probabilities of success or failure are not the same for each individual. Long success streaks happen to the most skilful in a field precisely because their general chance of success is higher than average. The problem in finance is that not all fund managers are of equal skill so attributing any fund streak to chance misses the point that skilled participants are the most likely to post a streak.

A fund manager that beats the market amongst all funds where there is an equal probability of beating or not beating the market (just like a fair coin flip), may result in an illusion of “impressive performance”. The problem with this is that outperforming the market is not a 50 / 50 % chance. Thus, in money management, the magnitude of market outperformance (adjusted for risk) is the true bottom line, but streaks are intriguing as they allow for no bad years. Further, as streak lengthens, pressure and tension mount. Luck plays a part but long streaks are extraordinary luck imposed on great skill. Streak does display some important findings.
Time Is on My Side: Myopic Loss Aversion and Portfolio Turnover

Equity-Risk Premium is based on “myopic loss aversion”. Loss aversion indicates that we treat losses with greater weights compared to wins. Naturally, the longer the holding period in a financial market the higher the probability of a positive return. Myopia considers the frequency of evaluating portfolios. The more frequency one evaluates portfolios, the more likely one will see the losses and hence suffer from loss aversion (vice versa).

The most important point is that valuation depends on your time horizon. This is why long term investors say they do not care about volatility/ Immune to short-term squiggles, these investors hold stocks long enough to get an attractive probability of a return and hence, a positive utility. Portfolio turnover is a reasonable proxy for the evaluation period - portfolio turnover being high indicates fund managers seeking gains to short time frames (vice versa). This comes down to policy choices. Even though value investing does have performance benefits, there still exists a high portfolio turnover rate in most funds. This is because an efficient stock market requires investor diversity - across styles and a long-term investor. If everyone were to have a long term horizon, the equity-risk premium will dissipate and the market will enjoy a one time rise.
Changing the nature of the investors changes the nature of the market

. The nature of fund managers is that they focus on the outcome compared to the process since those that underperform risk losing assets and ultimately their jobs. You cannot survive the long run if you cannot survive the short run. Myopic loss aversion, resulting in overreaction, is one of the sources of market inefficiency.
Psychology of Investing
Psychologists discovered that after bettors at a racetrack put down their money, they are more confident in the prospects of their horses winning than immediately before they placed their bets.
After making a decision, we feel both internal and external pressure to remain consistent to that view, even if subsequent evidence questions the validity of the initial decision

. The confirmation bias trap: postdecision openness to confirming data couples with disavowal or denial of disconfirming data. A useful technique to mitigate consistency is to think about the world in ranges of values with associated probabilities instead of as a series of single points. Acknowledging multiple scenarios provides psychological shelter to change views when appropriate. Investors in particular seek informational scarcity. The challenge is to distinguish what is truly scarce information and what is not. One means to do this is to reverse engineer market expectations - in other words, figure out what the market already thinks.
All Systems Go
The unconscious knew what was going on before the conscious did. Even the subjects who never articulated what was going on had unconscious physical reactions that guided their decisions.
Thinking fast, thinking slow: System 1 - fast, automatic, effortless, associative and difficult to modify and System 2 - slower, serial, effortful and deliberately controlled.

System 1 uses perception and intuition to get impressions of objects. These impressions are involuntary and an individual may not be able to verbalize them. Daniel Kahnemen argues that system 2 is involved in all judgements, whether or not the individual is making decisions overtly. Intuition is a judgment that reflects an impression. System 1 needs to operate normally in order for you to make good judgements. The goal of an investor is to buy an asset below expected value. When the outcomes of an opportunity do not have strong affective meaning (affect is the “goodness” or “badness” we feel based on a stimulus), we tend to overweight probabilities. When the outcome does have strong affective meaning, we tend to overweight the outcome. Investors feel good about an investment idea, they deem the risks low and the returns high irrespective of a more objective probability. And when they dislike an idea, the inverse is true - risk is high and reward is low. Great investors are not too swayed by affect, it is a result of how their System 1s are wired.

Experimental systems fail when outside forces manipulate it and fail in nonlinear systems. In nonlinear systems, cause and effect are not neatly linked. The underlying statistical properties change over time which means that the past may not be a good predictor of the future.

One should be careful about extrapolating the implications of affect to suggest that markets are inefficient. We all have our individual hard wiring and experiences and hence we are all going to feel affect in different ways. As markets are an aggregation of individual views, they can be efficient, provided that affect-driven biases are uncorrelated.
Guppy Love: The Role of Imitation in Markets

This chapter (page 89) mainly highlights herd behavior, using analogies of Guppies and Ants in biological situations. It highlights feedback (both positive and negative) that can be used to your advantage but it is also the main reason for boom and bust sequences which is similar to Soros’ concept of reflexivity.
In markets, a symbiotic relationship between positive and negative feedback generally prevails.
Beware of Behavioral Finance:

Humans are irrational, markets are made up of humans and thus, markets are irrational. The aggregation of irrational individuals must lead to an irrational market. This is somewhat true and false. There are two cases: collective and individual. Individual behavior dwells on the fact that we all consistently fall into psychological traps. However, markets can still be rational when investors are individually irrational. Sufficient investor diversity is the essential feature in efficient price formulation. Provided the decision rules of investors are diverse - even if they are suboptimal - errors tend to cancel out and markets arrive at appropriate prices. Similarly, if these decision rules lose diversity, markets become fragile and susceptible to inefficiency. So the issue is not whether individuals are irrational (they are) but whether they are irrational in the same way at the same time. Behavioral finance enthusiasts fail to distinguish between the individual and the collective.

The efficient market hypothesis does not live or die by investor rationality. In many scenarios where some investors are not fully rational, markets are still predicted to be efficient. In one commonly discussed case, the irrational investors in the market trade randomly. When there are a large number of such investors, and when their trading strategies are uncorrelated, their trades are likely to cancel each other out. In such a market, prices are close to fundamental values. We just tend to see a lack of correlation in strategies of the irrational investors, and, for that reason, is quite limited. Since investors are irrational and their strategies are rarely uncorrelated, markets are inefficient. We need sufficiently diverse investors to generate efficiency. But diversification fails in examples such as herding - when one sediment becomes dominant.
Raising Keynes

Two facets of how we form our expectation - deductive process and inductive process. Deductive processes move from general premises to specific conclusions; inductive processes go from specific facts to general principles. Deductive rationality, a building block of neoclassical economics, breaks down in the real world because human logical reasoning can’t handle situations that are too complicated (i.e we have bounded rationality), and any action that deviates from rationality in human interactions ignites speculation on how others would behave. In other words, if no one is rational, it does not pay for you to be. Inductive processes link to hindsight bias, where we tend to overestimate our pre-event knowledge of an outcome.

Keynes believed that you can forecast with varying degrees of confidence, which includes the magnitude and type of investment, as well as demand fluctuations. In forming forecasts, most people fall back on what Keynes calls a “convention” - they start with the current situation and modify it when they have definite reasons to expect a change. He notes the magnitude of actual market observations and business psychology. But there is no way to anticipate what the state of confidence will be because it relies on feedback. Market affects psychology and psychology affects markets. Convention is unreliable as many investors focus not on enterprise - forecasting long term return on investments - but rather on speculation - forecasting the market’s psychology. Markets as a beauty contest - the goal is not to identify the person you find the most beautiful, or even the person you think the average beholder finds the most beautiful. You soon find yourself trying to decipher what the average opinion thinks the average opinion is. Through this, deductive approaches to economics and markets are therefore limited. We are merely reminding ourselves that human decisions affecting the future, whether personal orm political or economic, cannot depend on strict mathematical expectations, since the basis for making such calculations does not exist.
Speculators may do no harm as bubbles on a steady stream of enterprise. But the position is serious when enterprise becomes a bubble on a whirlpool of speculation.
We are inductive machines and deductive approaches can only be useful in easy problems.

We can think of an experiment. Let's say we see the crowd tracker of a gym. If it exceeds a certain threshold, I would not go (vice versa). This problem is too complicated for a deductive solution. As individuals only look at the tracker, there are a large number of legitimate expectation models. The tracker uses an inductive approach. The common expectations backfire as well. If all believe most will go, nobody will go. And if all believe nobody will go, all one will go. Like Keynes’ beauty contest, the issue is not just what you believe but rather what you believe others to believe.
Right from the Gut

The rational classical models used in economics are not realistic. The theory’s informational requirements vastly exceed human cognitive capacity. Human rationality is bounded. As a result people do not make decisions based on optimal outcomes; they make choices based on what’s good enough. People do not maximize; they “satisfy”.
Weighted Watcher

Not all bits of information are created equal. Saying “I do” in a wedding carries a greater significance than reply “I do” when your hosts asks you a question about food. Analysts have not given up their search for proprietary information to achieve an information edge despite its increasing difficulty. Our degree of belief in a particular hypothesis typically integrates two kinds of evidence: the strength, or extremeness, of the evidence and the weight, or predictive validity. For instance, if you want to test the hypothesis that a coin is biased in favor of heads, the proportion of heads in the sample reflects strength while the sample size determines the weight. Probability theory states that we combine strength and weight correctly, but in reality, the strength of evidence tends to dominate the weight of evidence in people’s minds. This bias leads to over and underconfidence. The winner's curse is one such example of the risk of weighting information incorrectly. Information weighting underscores that not all information is of equal value and relevance.

The overconfidence that comes from strong evidence, yet weak predictive validity, seems very prominent in today’s markets. Investors appear satisfied using two or three data points to guide the next trade. This is a very difficult way to make a living. It leads to the following. Evidence shows that the market does adjust to new information rapidly, thus it is most likely to be efficiently priced into stocks, but evidence also suggests that the market is short sighted with regard to long-term information. There is also a substantial difference between understanding the fundamentals of an industry or company and a grasp of the expectations built into the current stock price. Prices reflect collective expectations and generally incorporate more information than any one individual can claim. We must ask ourselves whether or not information that is new to you is also new to the market.

Part 2: Investment Psychology is definitely an interesting read. It highlights psychological evidence in the market place and how it can be used to your own advantage. The author, Micheal, cites analogies which makes behavioral finance a lot more intuitive and easy to read.
Science and Complexity Theory
Complex adaptive systems - generically, a system that emerges from the interaction of lots of heterogeneous agents - is the stock market.

Humans have a deep-seated desire to link cause and effect. Unfortunately, markets do not easily satisfy this desire. We comprehend many systems but remain vexed by complex adaptive systems. We can’t understand the global properties and characteristics of a complex adaptive system by analyzing the underlying heterogeneous individuals as these systems are not linear or additive; the whole does not equal the sum of the parts. As a result, cause and effect defies any simple explanation. Unlike a mechanical system, you can’t understand markets by looking at the parts. Reductionism doesn’t work. Yet we often turn to individuals to explain the workings of the market. Just as an ant relying on local information and local interaction has no clue what’s going on at the colony level, explaining all but the most mundane market moves is beyond the ability of market mavens.
The magnitude of an outcome is not necessarily proportionate to the size of the perturbation. Sometimes small perturbations lead to large changes and vice versa.
Diversify Your Mind: Thoughts on Organizing for Investing Success

This chapter draws parallels to the book “Range”, discussing how diverse groups of “average” people, acting together, solve problems better than experts do. Diverse information and perspectives can help improve investment performance.

Each individual search is random, a collection of individuals reflects diverse experience, preferences and performance. So the collective is really just a normal individual with super information and because of this diverse information, the collective solution is vastly more robust than the average individual solution. The example is analogous to ants: Foraging ants depart the nest with its sole purpose to find and retrieve food. They also have the ability to leave and follow chemical trails. At first, they disperse randomly and when the ants that find food come back to the nest, they leave a chemical trail that their sisters can follow. A couple of ants attract other ants due to the chemical trail, triggering a positive feedback loop. After some time, the ants will periodically break from the main path and begin a random search process again. The ants are “programmed” to strike a balance between exploiting a known food source and exploring for the next food source - a “wild hair” alternative. The ants are hard-wired to seek diversity.

In well-defined systems, experts are useful because they can provide rule-based solutions. But when a system becomes complex, a collection of individuals often solves a problem better than an individual - even an expert. This means that the stock market is likely to be smarter than most people most of the time, a point the empirical facts bear out. To be an expert at a complex system like the stock market, we require the ability to create a “simulation” in your head, allowing you to conceive and select strategies. In addition, you must populate your mental system with information from diverse sources. This is “blind variation and selective retention”. In other words, creative thinkers seek a variety of ideas but only choose those that are useful given their current goals. Idea diversity allows you to find “weak signals”. A weak signal may be the start of a trend away from the dominant path (just like the ants) or the right piece of information at the right time from an unexpected source. Diverse information sources can improve the likelihood of finding a useful idea.
From Honey to Money: The Wisdom and Whims of the Collective

“The most thought-provoking feature of a honey bee colony is its ability to achieve coordinated activity among tens of thousands of bees without central authority. Coherence in honey bee colonies depends upon mechanisms of decentralized control which give rise to natural selection processes analogous to those that create order in the natural world and in the competitive market economies of humans.” - Thomas D. Seeley, The Wisdom of the Hive
Collective behaviors amongst biological animals:

Returning honey bee foragers do a little dance to tell their colony mates where the food is. But what’s remarkable is that the duration of the dance reflects not only the richness of the foraging site the bees are advertising but also the colony’s need for the commodity in question. Each bee’s communication dance considers both the colony’s opportunities and its needs. Thus, a bee colony’s overall allocation pattern is appropriate even though no one bee is in control.

Ants also has no central authority, no one is directing the traffic. Yet, the aggregation of simple individuals generates complex, adaptive and robust results. These decentralized individuals collectively solve very hard problems, and they do it in a way that is very counterintuitive to the human predilection to command and control systems.
The ant algorithm is superior to standard approaches when tackling the traveling salesman problem.

While we may be tempted to lump together all decentralized problem-solving systems, important distinctions exist which shape system performance (stock prices tend to be efficient when investors are heterogenous). But when heterogeneity does not prevail and investor errors become independent, markets become subject to excess. Colonies are not as susceptible to the positive feedback that creates market fragility (investors aim to maximize their own utility while insects aim to maximize the well-being of the colony, not the individual).

Stock market is different from the markets I’ve described because there is no answer - stocks have no specified time horizon or value. As a result, stock investors are susceptible to imitation as they can earn excess profits by selling to someone else willing to pay a higher price.
A Tail of Two Worlds

This chapter highlights the flaws of standard financial theory, mainly about kurtosis and risk management which I am quite familiar with. However, there are some points which I found interesting about Micheal’s perspective - markets tend to become fragile when the diversity breaks down and investors act in a similar way.

Cause and effect thinking: The essential feature of self-organized critical systems is that the size of the perturbation and that of the resulting event may not be linearly linked. Sometimes small-scale inputs can lead to large-scale events. This dashes the hope of finding causes for all effects.
Risk and Reward: Nonlinearity is endogenous to self-organized critical systems like the stock market. Financial theory stylized real world data.

We should measure the current expectations underlying an asset price and then contemplate various ranges of value outcomes and their associated probabilities. This process allows investors to give some weight to potential fat-tail events.
Integrating the Outliers

This chapter draws parallels to the book “Misbehavior of Markets”, discussing how normal distribution fails, drawing examples from Bernoulli's St. Petersburg Paradox - the amount you would be willing to pay is a function of your resources. Micheal highlights that financial systems are fractal and tail risks (fractal systems)  follow the power law.

Are stock market returns fractal? Benoit Mandelbrot shows that by lengthening or shortening the horizontal axis of a price series - effectively speeding up or slowing down time - price series are indeed fractal. Not only are rare large changes interspersed with lots of smaller ones, the price changes look similar at various scales. Simulating a normal coin toss game many times and you will get a normal distribution. Simulate the St. Petersburg game many times and you will get an outcome of a power lower despite the process being stochastic.
The greatest insight we can draw from this is the challenge of valuing the low probability of significant value.
The Janitor’s Dream

We can’t explain the origin of consciousness. We can approach the problem in various ways but that key to understanding consciousness certainly is not in the basement of neural chemistry or the sub basement of quantum mechanics. THere are too many layers of interaction in the brain. The parts don’t explain the whole (which is why reductionism fails as it can only be used in the “Newtonian world” where a system has low complexity and we can define interactions linearly). Complex adaptive system consists of aggregation, adaptive decision rules, nonlinearity and feedback loops. An agent-based approach to understanding markets is gaining broader acceptance but this better descriptive framework does not offer the neat solutions that the current economic models do. We face two cognitive traps: the constant search for a cause for all effects and dwelling on the input of any individual at the expense of understanding the market itself (each individual operates with his or her own decision rules while the market represents the aggregation of these rules).
Chasing Laplace Demon

The concept of cause and effect is a fundamental driver of human evolution as it is evolutionarily advantageous to understand the potential effects of a cause and the causes of an effect. A combination of the concept of cause, language and social interaction drive the increase in size and complexity of the brain, so we humans are wired to make links between causes and effects. Yet, as mentioned above, complex adaptive systems are not linear or additive.

Determinism ruled science. Simon Laplace believed that if we knew all of the forces that animate Nature and the mutual positions of the beings that comprise it at any given moment, we can condense it into a single formula that explains the movement of the greater bodies of the universe and that of the lightest atom. The notion that we can work out the past, present and future through detailed calculations is a very alluring concept because it plays to our cause and effect biases. But complex adaptive systems do not accommodate such simple calculations. We can describe many complex systems as being in the state of self-organized criticality, meaning there is no leader - the system arises from the interaction of many underlying individuals. It also suggests nonlinearity. More specifically, the magnitude of a perturbation within the system (cause) is not always proportionate to its effect. A sand-pile metaphor conveys this idea. Imagine sprinkling sand onto a flat surface. At first, not much happens and the sand grains obey the law of physics. But once the sand pile builds to certain heights and slopes, it enters into a self-organized, critical state. A few additional grains sprinkled on the pile may lead to an avalanche. The size of the avalanche need not match the amount of sand a researcher sprinkles. Replace sand with information. Sometimes a piece of information barely moves the market and at other times, seemingly similar information causes a big move. Humans desire to close the cause-and-effect loop which may lead to some simple explanation that illustrates some silly-after-the-fact narrative. It is wise to filter out useful information amidst the noise. Read the morning paper explaining yesterday’s action for entertainment, not education. In other words, take it with a pinch of salt.
More Power to You:

Why should investors care about power laws? First, the existence of power law distributions can help reorient our understanding about risk as most financial assumptions are false. A power law distribution suggests periodic, albeit infrequent price movements that are much larger than the theory predicts. This fat-tail phenomenon is important for portfolio construction and leverage. Second, the existence of power laws suggests some underlying order in self-organizing systems. Even though scientists haven’t fully explained the mechanisms that lead to power laws in social systems, we have enough evidence that power laws exist to make some structural predictions about what certain systems will look like in the future. Finally, standard economic theory does not easily explain these power laws. For example, neoclassical economics focuses on equilibrium outcomes and assumes that individuals are fully informed, rational and that they interact with one another indirectly (through markets). In the real world, people are adaptive, are not fully informed and deal directly with one another.

A model that generates power laws is “self-organized criticality” - it is the same example of sand piles used in Chapter “Chasing Laplace Demon” and it is useful when thinking about social systems. Economic systems are clearly self-organizing. That is, most companies, cities are countries as a result of interactions among individuals, not of central planning. Also, there is a sense of a critical state. In a physical system, a critical point is one where a small change produces a phase transition. Economists do not define critical points as clearly for economic systems, but we do know that individuals neither stay at the same company forever (steady state) nor haphazardly jump from company to company (randomness).
The Pyramid of Numbers

On the surface the size and frequency distribution for species, cities and company sizes may not seem like they would have a lot in common. Yet each follows a power law, which looks like a straight line when plotted on a log-log scale (it indicates that there are many small occurrences and rare large ones). In nature, there are a lot of ants - the combined weight of ants is larger than the combined weight of humans - but very few elephants.

Take species for example. Why are large carnivorous animals, like tigers, relatively rare, while small animals, like termites, are so abundant? Ecologists answer by pointing out that all animals have a niche - not just physical location but a real place in the grand scheme of things. A species not only must survive in its home but also successfully interact with other plants and animal species that don’t share that home. Thus, with every increment in body size, there should be an associated loss in numbers. The species power law distribution is a natural outcome of interacting animals constrained by the laws of physics. This is known as the “pyramid of numbers”.

The link to stock market: Companies, like species, fit into niches and variance of growth rates is smaller for large firms than for small firms. Furthermore, growth for large companies often stalls, leading to market share-price underperformance as investors recalibrate their expectations. The idea that companies find niches is not new and game theory in particular, addresses how and why companies should seek profitable niches. The main message here is that environments, and hence niches, change over time as the result of technological developments, regulatory shifts and industry entry and exit. New niches open and new companies exploit them. A company’s ability to adapt to a changing environment is critical - and the number of companies that can do so is small. As a result, optimal firm size may not be fixed for a particular industry, and comparing the valuations of companies with different economic models does not make sense. Thus, the growth for large companies often stalls. Investors should temper their growth expectations as companies get larger. But the reality is that investors tend to extrapolate from the recent past and hence miss declining growth rates. Market valuation ratios have little ability to sort out firms with high future growth from firms with low growth. Instead, in line with the extrapolative expectations hypothesis, investors tend to key on past growth. Firms that have achieved high growth in the past tend to key on past growth. Firms that have achieved high growth in the past fetch high valuation, while firms with low past growth are penalized with poor valuations.
Turn Tale: Exploring the Market’s Mood Swings

Sentiment is a critical determinant of performance. Broadscale sentiment shifts like how flu spreads. The first is the degree of contagiousness - how easily an idea spreads. The second is the degree of interactions - how much people bump into one another. If the flu is very contagious but carriers don’t interact with others, it will not take off. If there’s a lot of interaction but the flu strand is not contagious, it will not take off. But combine both and you got an epidemic. Ben Graham said, “value standards don’t determine price; prices determine value standards.” Individuals do not construct value standards based on intrinsic principles but rather are influenced by what other people do (herding etc.). Stock prices reflect the collective actions of others but we all do not have equal potential to be influenced, instead, we have an adaptive threshold which is defined by how many other people must engage in an activity before we join in. Market extremes push the sentiment beyond the adoption threshold of nearly all investors and it can create the conditions for a sentiment reversal. In network theory, ideas can cascade through social clusters (degree of connectedness with one node to another) faster than ever - mass media reinforces our interconnectedness. Warren Buffet states that price and value may diverge from one another, but investors who focus too much on price may have an emotionally difficult time distinguishing between the two.

The lesson to take away is that investors should try their best to maintain perspective and avoid groupthink. In particular, reflecting on history and carefully considering multiple scenarios can be helpful to provide necessary calibration. Buffet, with an emphasis on how easy it is to get swept up in emotion and a dismissal of overly quantitative approaches, comments that good business judgment with an ability to insulate thoughts and behavior from the super contagious emotions that swirl around in the marketplace will make a good investor.
Innovation and Competitive Strategy:

Innovation is inevitable, it is the primary mechanism shaping which companies will win and lose. We need to think about innovation’s cumulative effects, if not, the small changes will escape one’s detection and one will end up with yesterday’s favorites.
Pruned for Performance: WHat Brain Development Teaches Us About Innovation:

The science behind children learning things faster than adults: From a child’s birth to the age of three, there is a huge increase in the number of synapses - connections between neurons - in the brain. In fact, the toddler has roughly 1 quadrillion synaptic connections, twice as many as an adult. Children have brains that are more active, connected and flexible than those of grownups. But following this synaptic proliferation is a significant pruning process. Through experience, these synaptic connections are strengthened, and those that aren’t used get pruned (known as a Hebbian process). This process finetunes the brain to survive in its particular environment. By the time we are adults, synaptic selection has shaped our brains to succeed. It sounds ironic (like why do we prune) but this is actually more efficient. Take neural networks in computer science for example, overproduction and pruning approaches are flexible and more reliable at preserving information than a feed-forward network. Starting with lots of alternatives and winnowing down to the most useful ones proves to be a robust process, even though it appears quite inefficient. This draws parallels to what happens when a new industry emergers: A model of innovation, a basis for understanding bubbles and innovation processes leading to investment opportunities. It is analogous to the transition from infants to adults where we trade vast mental flexibility for capabilities tailored to our environment. Skill and competence improve even as the number of synaptic connections declines. Same for the business world, an industry continues to grow even as the number of competitors shrink as forces select a dominant design, process or both.

How this forms bubbles: Imagine a baby’s brain as a market, with each synapse representing a company or entrant. When the baby is born, the market is buzzing as the brain is creating a lot of synapses and some will be wildly successful. Enthusiasm reigns, introduces prices and you have a foundation for a mania. Investors use prices as an important cue towards a business’ potential success, As the price is bid up, humans naturally want to participate. A positive feedback loop kicks in which bootstraps a bubble. The path to innovation is paved with failure and waste (pruned). We should look around for survivors at the end of the pruning process as a portfolio of surviving companies often presents an opportunity for attractive shareholder returns. The greatest insight is highlighted via the similarity between brain development and industry innovation.
Staying Ahead of the Curve:

Investors cannot just consider innovation, they must assess how the markets will consider innovation. Innovation perceived by the market follows an S-Curve growth. Growth starts slowly, then increases at an increasing pace and finally flattens out (useful when thinking about shifting expectations). Investors often think linearly. So the first and last points happen when investors do not fully anticipate the growth and economic returns from an industry, investors reigning in expectations and adjust prices for more realistic outlook at the last moment. We want to buy at the start and sell before hitting the last stage. We need to recognize the inflection points. Accelerating innovations assures that industry and product life cycles are shortening as waves of innovation are coming faster and faster, there will be more first stage to second stage opportunities and investors must be more nimble to anticipate the expected revisions. Humans often fall into automatic action when an experience imprints on them. Stocks that performed well in the recent past leave an imprint on the minds (we want to avoid those). In a fast changing world, you’re almost better off betting on the new guard than the old as you may not know which new company will generate the excess returns. But you can be almost assured that the older company will not,
All the Right Moves: How to Balance the Long Term with the Short Term

Strike a balance between the short and long term. It is like speeding down the highway in a car. If you focus just beyond the hood, you’re going to have a hard time anticipating what’s coming. Look too far ahead and you’ll lose perspective on the actions that you need to take to navigate safely. There is a tradeoff between short and long term and the appropriate focal point shifts as conditions warrant. The notion that we should only focus on the long term is nonsense. Have you heard of a company that blew twenty straight quarters but had a great five years? It does not happen; the long term, by definition, an aggregation of short terms.

To strike a balance, do not look too far ahead as the information is uncertain. We need to develop options and continuously revise them based on the changing conditions (reinforcement learning for example). Great players consider their next move without playing it. You should never play the first good move that comes into your head. Put that move on your list and then ask yourself if there’s an even better move. If you see a good idea, look for a better one. Good thinking is a matter of making comparisons. Seek small advantages - it is cumulative.
Survival of The Fittest: Fitness Landscapes and Competitive Advanatage

Charles Dawin states that it is not the strongest that thrives, but the most adaptable one. Micheal identifies industries / business in different kinds of terrain (rough represents something like a start-up while smooth represents stable companies). For a company to improve, they are likely to downgrade their terrain (essentially short term loss for long term gain). It is important to understand the type of terrain businesses are in and what course of actions they are taking (adaptability). Different terrains have different organizational structures which require different use of financial tools. Traditional discounted cash flows will only be suitable for stable fitness landscapes where industry activities are often clearly defined (centralized management approach). A course fitness landscape will be more suited using strategic options, a decentralized approach, that has agreed-upon decision rules but lets individuals make decisions at the local level as they see fit.
You’ll Meet a Bad Fate if You Extrapolate: The Folly of Using P / E

It is really hard to manage a system when the underlying data is constantly changing. You cannot draw conclusions from past averages as they do not accurately represent today’s average. It carries directly over to investing - investors blithely applying historic average P / E ratios to value either today’s market of an individual stock. They are only applicable to the degree that they capture current circumstances.

In time series analysis, if the data is always changing then the properties of the data are nonstationary and applying past averages to today’s circumstances can lead to misleading conclusions. While recognition that P / E ratios are likely nonstationary is critical, knowing why they are nonstationary provides more practical insight. The drivers are the role of taxes and inflation; changes in the composition of the economy and shifts in equity risk premium.
When using multiples in general, unpack the embedded assumptions as it reveals how and why circumstances are different today than they were in the past and what that means for the multiple.
Mean Reversion and Turnarounds

What really determines P / E ratio? A company’s value is a function of the market’s expectations for its growth rate and its economic returns. This fundamental concept explains why looking at growth in isolation can be so misleading. Growth can be good (when a company earns returns in excess of the cost of capital), bad (when returns are below the cost of capital), or neutral (when returns equal the cost of capital). You must have a clear sense of whether a company is earning appropriate returns before you can judge the effect of growth. Companies can grow their way into bankruptcy (likewise, some low-growth, high return businesses consistently carry premium valuations). Studying growth in isolation of economic returns is an invitation to failure. A thorough understanding of competitive advantage is needed: Is the company generating returns on investment above cost of capital or is there good reason to believe it will earn attractive returns in the future? If returns do exceed the cost of capital, for how long can the company sustain its excess returns? Once a company’s returns dip below the cost of capital, what is the probability it can stage a sustained recovery to above-required returns?

A microeconomic theory is that a company’s return on investment reverts to the cost of capital over time. Sustaining high returns (evidence shows that it is possible for companies) is a huge potential source of wealth. Given two companies with the same initial returns and future growth rates, the business that can sustain above cost of capital returns longer will be significantly more valuable and hence trade at much higher valuation multiple. A strategic assessment of a business earning high returns should reveal the source of excess spread (consumer or producer advantage) and provide some framework to consider the longevity of that advantage. Stock prices reflect expectations and the key to generating superior long-term returns is to successfully anticipate expectation revisions. Investors need to assess the stocks of all companies versus expectations (not just on high return versus low return). This analysis is particularly important for value investors, who often buy companies that are statistically cheap in the hope that economic returns improve. The classic value trap is buying a cheap company that deserves to be cheap based on poor economic returns but buying a company that is cheap because of a temporary downturn is potentially very attractive if the market does not anticipate the turnaround. Evidence shows that high return persistence does occur and the likelihood that markets misprice this persistence suggests that investors with a strong grasp of competitive dynamics and a sufficient investment horizon have an opportunity to realize superior returns.
Game Theory: Trench Cooperation:

Just like war on the western front (like the movie), during meal times, both parties will cease fire. This chapter highlights prisoner’s dilemma as a rational decision making process in game theory (where not all scenarios lead to a zero sum game). But it shows that a rational solution for a company is not always the solution that is optimal for the industry in total. In business, the interaction is not one time but continual so instead of playing prison’s dilemma once, companies effectively play it on loop. Cooperative behavior would eventually break down, mainly due to the quality of the signals (signals like the ones used during WW1 Western Front to ceasefire). Sometimes these signals are simply too ambiguous or are often misread. It also fails due to the fact that companies do not think over long enough time scales (both past and prospective).

The main message of Game Theory is that competitive markets need not be zero-sum. Under the right conditions, businesses can see their situation as an iterated prisoner’s dilemma and make pricing and capacity decisions that maximize long-term value.
A year after reading my first

book, I felt it was the right time to dive into another installment in the series. With the benefit of additional experience and a deeper understanding of trading, I found that I could appreciate the insights and lessons in this book much more than I did previously. As with the earlier volumes,
Market Wizards
continues to deliver invaluable trading wisdom.
The central thesis of the
Market Wizards

series remains consistent: the key to trading success lies in finding a trading style that aligns with your personal strengths and preferences. The book is replete with interviews and experiences from some of the most successful traders, each sharing their unique approaches and strategies.

In
Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialized World

, David Epstein presents a compelling argument about the limitations of specialization and the advantages of a broader approach. While specialization can be highly effective in fields where problems are well-defined and well-understood, Epstein highlights that it often leads to narrow thinking and a lack of adaptability in more complex, uncertain situations.
The book’s key takeaways include:
Specialists vs. Generalists

: Epstein explains that specialists excel in "kind" environments—those that are predictable and structured. However, as ambiguity and complexity increase, which is common in "wicked" environments, generalists become more adept. Wicked environments are characterized by uncertainty and require a broader range of skills and perspectives to navigate effectively.
Importance of Breadth

: In a world where complex, unpredictable problems are the norm, having a broad set of skills and experiences is increasingly valuable. Generalists, with their diverse backgrounds and varied experiences, are often better equipped to handle these challenges.

Epstein supports his arguments with a range of relevant examples, such as the NASA space shuttle disasters, the performance of DeepBlue AI in Go, and various Harvard business case studies. These examples illustrate how a broad perspective can lead to innovative solutions and better problem-solving in complex situations.

One downside of the book is that it can become somewhat repetitive in certain chapters. Despite this, the overall message is powerful and thought-provoking. Epstein’s exploration of the benefits of generalism over specialization offers valuable insights for anyone navigating complex and uncertain environments. I highly recommend this book for its engaging analysis and practical implications.

When searching for books on rationality and decision-making, I stumbled upon this gem, and as an avid poker player who enjoys games with friends, I couldn't resist diving into it. The book, which explores the intersection of poker and real-life decision-making, exceeded my expectations in remarkable ways.
Core Themes and Insights:
Poker as a Metaphor for Life

: The initial part of the book makes a compelling argument that poker, particularly no-limit Texas Hold’em, closely mirrors real-life situations. It explores how the game’s dynamics and strategies can provide deep insights into decision-making processes and risk management in everyday life.
Risk and Reward

: Typically, players approach poker by calculating risk-reward ratios to maximize their expected returns. Konnikova, with her background in psychology, offers a unique perspective. She delves into the intricate balance between skill and luck, revealing how the game can be a powerful lens through which to understand these concepts.
Skill vs. Luck

: A central theme of the book is the differentiation between skill and luck. Despite making all the theoretically optimal moves, players can still face losses due to the element of chance. Konnikova, who began her journey as a novice poker player, investigates how much of poker’s outcome is influenced by skill and how much by luck. This exploration also sheds light on similar dynamics in real-life scenarios.
Prerequisites

: The book is best appreciated if you have a basic understanding of poker and some familiarity with game theory concepts. These foundations help in grasping the nuanced discussions Konnikova presents about decision-making strategies and their applications beyond the poker table.

Overall, this book is a captivating read for anyone interested in rational decision-making, game theory, or the game of poker itself. Konnikova’s blend of psychological insight and practical analysis makes it a highly recommended addition to your reading list.

Initially, "Chip Wars" didn't immediately grab my attention due to my limited interest in history and politics. However, I’m glad I took the plunge and read it. This book offers profound insights into the semiconductor industry, covering its economic, geopolitical, and technological dimensions, which are increasingly relevant in our interconnected world.
Key Insights from the Book:
Semiconductors as the New Oil

: The book highlights how microchips, often dubbed the "new oil," have become crucial to the global economy. Companies such as NVIDIA and ASML have experienced skyrocketing stock prices, underscoring the critical role of semiconductors in contemporary technology and industry.
Economic and Geopolitical Influence

: Controlling every stage of microchip production—from design to manufacturing—grants significant economic, military, and geopolitical power. Originally developed for military applications, these microchips now power everything from smartphones to vehicles and even influence international political decisions.
Global Competition and Conflicts

: The book sheds light on how the semiconductor industry has fueled global competition and conflicts, such as the ongoing tensions between China and Taiwan, the US trade wars, and broader geopolitical disputes. It explores how the quest for dominance in semiconductor technology has become a pivotal element in international relations.
Production Methods

: "Chip Wars" delves into various production methods in the semiconductor industry, including the Fabless and Foundry models. It traces the origins of these methods back to the Cold War rivalry between the US and the Soviet Union, illustrating how historical conflicts have shaped the industry's evolution.
Accessible Read

: Despite its complex subject matter, the book is presented in an accessible manner, making it a valuable read for anyone interested in understanding the development and impact of the semiconductor industry, from its scientific foundations to its current global significance.

For those who find the geopolitical aspects of "Chip Wars" particularly intriguing and have an interest in finance, I would recommend following up with "Geopolitical Alpha" by Marko Papic. I have always found physics to be a fascinating subject, and my interest particularly in quantum mechanics was sparked by watching films like "Interstellar" and "Oppenheimer." Driven by this growing curiosity, I decided to tackle "A Brief History of Time" by Stephen Hawking.

Hawking's ability to explain complex concepts in quantum physics for the layperson is truly commendable, and his approach makes the material more accessible, though having 'A' Level H2 Physics as a pre-requisite might still be helpful. I enjoyed much of the book, particularly the sections on time dilation and black holes, where Hawking’s clarity shines.

However, I found myself somewhat lost when he delved into the models of the universe's beginning after "The Big Bang." Quantum physics can sometimes feel like a pseudo-science as it ventures into areas with a lot of theoretical assumptions, such as parallel universes and quantum tunneling. The discussions on entropy and the three timelines were particularly challenging for me, leading to moments of confusion and frustration.

Despite these hurdles, I appreciate Hawking’s efforts to simplify these abstract ideas. My fascination with quantum physics has led me to write two articles on the subject, which you can find on Medium. Overall, while the book presents some complex concepts, it is an insightful read for those interested in the fundamental questions of our universe.

I have always been a routine person and have firmly believed in the power of consistency. While I typically don’t delve into self-help books, if you were to choose just one, "Atomic Habits" would be the one I’d recommend. The book’s core premise is straightforward yet profound: consistent actions, no matter how small, will ultimately lead to significant results. By focusing on building positive habits and eliminating negative ones, you set yourself up for success or failure based on the nature of those habits.

"Atomic Habits" dives deep into how habits are formed and maintained, providing a step-by-step guide to creating lasting change. It breaks down the habit formation process into manageable stages and offers practical strategies for each stage. These strategies are grounded in scientific and psychological research, making the advice both credible and actionable.

One of the key insights from the book is the idea of reducing the friction associated with good habits while increasing the friction for bad ones. For example, if you want to develop a habit of exercising regularly, make it as easy as possible to get started, such as by laying out your workout clothes the night before. Conversely, if you want to break a bad habit, make it more difficult to engage in that behavior, such as by removing junk food from your home.

The book emphasizes that achieving our goals isn’t solely about setting them but about creating effective systems that support them. James Clear, the author, argues that we don’t simply reach our goals; instead, we fall to the level of our systems. This means that our daily habits and routines—our systems—ultimately determine our success.

"Atomic Habits" is more than just a guide to forming habits; it’s a framework for understanding how small changes can lead to remarkable transformations over time. Its insights are practical, backed by research, and presented in a way that makes it easy to apply to various aspects of life. If you’re looking for a book that provides actionable strategies for personal growth and improvement, "Atomic Habits" is a compelling choice.

title: Jim Simons: The Man that Revolutionized the Market
author: Gregory Zuckerman

text.t: Where do I start? I wish "The Man Who Solved the Market" had been the first book I read while exploring the quant industry. This biography of Jim Simons, a renowned mathematician with a PhD in Geometry, offers invaluable insights into the world of quantitative trading. Simons, initially an academic professor, found himself disillusioned by the limited financial rewards and sought a more challenging and lucrative path. His solution? Applying his deep mathematical knowledge to the financial markets.

At the time, fundamental analysis was the dominant method in trading, and the idea of using mathematical models and algorithms to predict market movements was revolutionary. However, Simons faced significant hurdles. The computing power and data available during his early attempts were insufficient to support his innovative approach. Despite these obstacles, Simons did not give up. He embarked on a journey filled with challenges, questioning his methods and striving to improve.

Simons' journey was marked by conflicts with co-founders and competition with other systematic trading firms like D.E. Shaw. These experiences were part of his broader struggle to prove that quantitative methods could outperform traditional trading strategies. Through years of perseverance, trial, and error, Simons and his team at Renaissance Technologies began to achieve remarkable success. Their approach revolutionized trading by demonstrating that mathematical models and algorithms could significantly outperform traditional methods.

Simons' story is not just about his professional achievements but also highlights the personal sacrifices and struggles he faced along the way. The founding of Renaissance Technologies and its success in the quant trading industry is an inspiring testament to the power of innovation and resilience.

I highly recommend this book to anyone interested in systematic and quantitative trading. It offers a compelling look at how a groundbreaking idea, combined with relentless determination, can transform an industry. Jim Simons' journey from academic mathematician to pioneer in quantitative finance is both enlightening and motivational, making it a must-read for anyone passionate about the intersection of mathematics and finance.
Due for a re-read and review.

"Misbehavior of Markets" was a book I stumbled upon with no particular expectations, but it turned out to be an exceptional read. The first half of the book provides a critical examination of why the financial theories taught in academia are often inadequate for modeling real-world markets. It delves into the historical development and theoretical foundations of various quantitative finance (QF) concepts, such as the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), Markowitz's mean-variance portfolio optimization, and the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM). This background knowledge was invaluable for me, as it offered a clearer understanding of how financial theories have shaped our current academic syllabus.

The book argues that traditional financial models have significant shortcomings. For instance, it critiques the reliance on Gaussian distributions for market behavior and the instability of EMH as a predictive approach. These critiques resonate with some of the arguments presented in "Economyths," though "Misbehavior of Markets" delivers its insights more concisely. The discussion of these issues highlights how these models can fail to account for extreme market events and volatility.

In the second half of the book, Mandelbrot proposes an alternative approach using fractals to model market behavior. His background in geometry informs this perspective, suggesting that fractals offer a better fit for understanding asset price movements compared to the traditional geometric Brownian motion. While this approach is intriguing, I found it challenging to fully grasp the concept of fractals as an alternative model due to my current level of mathematical proficiency.

Despite this, I believe the core argument of the book is compelling. Financial academic models may perform reasonably well during stable periods but often fall short during times of market extremes and volatility. Mandelbrot's critique and alternative perspective offer valuable insights into the limitations of conventional financial theories and suggest more robust approaches for understanding market behavior.

For those interested in a deeper analysis of financial academic models and their real-world applications, I recommend reading my article on financial academia in today's markets. This book provides a thought-provoking exploration of the limitations of traditional models and offers a fresh perspective on how to better understand market dynamics.
