title: Applied Financial Macroeconomics and Investment Strategy
author: Tomoe Moore

text.t: For anyone with a deep interest in economics, like myself, "Applied Financial Macroeconomics and Investment Strategy" is a highly recommended read, especially for those focused on investment and fundamental trading. The book provides a comprehensive approach to understanding how various stages of the business cycle can influence investment decisions. It emphasizes the importance of recognizing the cyclical nature of markets and understanding how to apply this knowledge strategically.

The core premise of the book is that markets exhibit repetitive cycles with recognizable patterns and occasional deviations. This cyclical behavior means that knowing where we are in the business cycle can significantly inform investment decisions. The book prompts readers to constantly ask themselves, "What’s different this time?"—a crucial question to distinguish between the cyclical patterns and unique, novel market conditions.

The author details how the financial characteristics of asset classes interact with the broader economic backdrop, requiring a nuanced understanding of both the economic outlook and its potential market impact. For example, secular economic trends—those that shift over extended periods—can create either headwinds or tailwinds for various assets. These long-term trends can lead to secular bull and bear markets, driven by significant changes in key macroeconomic variables.

An important distinction made in the book is between "noise" and the true underlying trend. This differentiation is not only vital for investors but also influences the Federal Reserve's decision-making process. The author argues that understanding this difference is crucial for explaining market volatility and making informed investment choices.

The book also covers the principle of "Do not fight the Fed," discussing how macroeconomic policies and indicators affect market dynamics. It provides a thorough analysis of how different economic indicators can be used to a trader’s advantage. The discussion extends to various markets, including equities, credit, and commodities, illustrating how business cycles impact each sector differently.

In summary, "Applied Financial Macroeconomics and Investment Strategy" is an informative and dense book packed with trading wisdom. It is particularly valuable for aspiring market practitioners looking to deepen their understanding of how economic cycles influence investment strategies. The book's detailed examination of macroeconomic trends and their implications for financial markets makes it a highly recommended read for anyone serious about mastering the art of trading.

title: Frequency Asked Questions in Quantitative Finance
author: Paul Wilmott

text.t: "FAQ in Quantitative Finance" is an essential resource for anyone preparing for a quantitative finance (QF) interview. This book serves as a concise summary of crucial concepts in the field, covering a broad range of topics such as econometrics, financial engineering, distribution models, and brain teasers. It is particularly useful for individuals looking to refresh their knowledge or for those embarking on a career in quantitative finance.

One of the key strengths of the book is its structured approach to presenting complex topics. Paul, the author, effectively organizes the content into manageable sections, making it easier to grasp fundamental concepts. The book also includes valuable financial essays that offer insights into the shortcomings of current financial theories and practices. This aspect of the book resonates with the themes discussed in "Economyths," highlighting the disconnect between traditional financial academia and the realities of modern markets.

Interestingly, "FAQ in Quantitative Finance" was my very first purchase when I began exploring the field of quantitative finance. Initially, I made the mistake of using it as a starting point, which proved to be challenging given the complexity of QF concepts. At that time, my understanding was not sufficient to fully appreciate the material, and I found it difficult to absorb the information. Quantitative finance is a sophisticated subject that requires a solid foundation in mathematics and finance, which I lacked at the time.

However, revisiting this book later in my learning journey proved to be incredibly beneficial. It provided me with a clearer roadmap for advancing my skills in quantitative finance. The book's detailed explanations and structured approach helped me to better understand key areas such as econometrics, time series analysis, and financial engineering.

"FAQ in Quantitative Finance" is suitable for readers at all levels of expertise. Each time you revisit the book, you can gain new insights and enhance your understanding of quantitative finance. It is an invaluable guide for anyone looking to deepen their knowledge or prepare for interviews in the field of quantitative finance.

title: Interest Rate Markets: A Practical Approach to Fixed Income
author: Siddhartha Jha

text.t: If you're looking to dive into the world of interest rate instruments—such as bonds, derivatives, and swaps—this book comes highly recommended. It serves as an excellent introduction to the subject, covering a wide range of topics essential for understanding and working with interest rate products.

The book provides a solid foundation in bond and interest rate derivatives valuation. It walks readers through the fundamentals of how these instruments are priced and the various trading strategies that can be employed. For instance, it explains carry trades and relative value trades in a clear and accessible manner, making it easier for readers to grasp these concepts and apply them in practice.

In addition to trading strategies, the book also delves into the basics of hedging. This is crucial for anyone involved in managing interest rate risk, as hedging strategies help mitigate potential losses from adverse movements in interest rates.

One of the standout features of this book is its final section, which covers quantitative methods for valuing interest rate options. It introduces readers to models and techniques commonly found in quantitative finance textbooks, such as binomial trees and geometric Brownian motion. This section provides a deeper understanding of how interest rate options are valued and how quantitative methods are applied in practice.

Overall, the book is a valuable resource for both beginners and those looking to refresh their knowledge of interest rate instruments. It offers a comprehensive overview of the subject, from the basics to more advanced quantitative methods. For those interested in further exploration, key pointers and personal notes can be found in the "notes" section on my website.
Disclaimer: I read only up till Exotic Options before dropping it.

I first encountered this book through recommendations from quants who insisted that it’s a must-read for anyone aspiring to break into the quant industry. Given its reputation, I approached it with high expectations, but I must admit that it proved to be a challenging read for me.

The book is known for its in-depth treatment of various quantitative finance concepts, particularly the use of the Greeks in risk management. Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s exploration of these topics is both detailed and sophisticated. I found his approach to the Greeks—measures used to assess risk in financial derivatives—particularly engaging. His insights into how these measures can be applied to manage risk in trading were thought-provoking and aligned with my interest in understanding financial markets better.

However, the book took a turn into more advanced territory when it delved into shadow Greeks and higher-order mathematical derivatives. At this point, the complexity of the material significantly increased. For someone with an 'A' Level understanding of mathematics, like myself, these concepts proved to be quite dense and difficult to grasp. Taleb’s discussion on shadow Greeks, which are used to measure more nuanced risks beyond the traditional Greeks, and his exploration of exotic options, were particularly challenging. I found myself struggling to keep up, and eventually, I decided to stop at the section on exotic options, as the content had become overwhelming.

This experience highlights that the book is likely best suited for readers with a more advanced background in mathematics, particularly at a graduate level. If you possess a strong foundation in mathematical finance, you may find Taleb’s insights more accessible and beneficial. The book’s rigorous approach to quantifying risk and its detailed analysis of complex financial instruments could be incredibly valuable for those with the requisite mathematical proficiency.

Despite the difficulties I faced, I recognize that the book has substantial merit and offers valuable perspectives on risk management and financial modeling. It’s a resource I plan to revisit in the future once I’ve deepened my understanding of the necessary mathematical concepts. For now, I would recommend this book to those who are well-versed in advanced mathematics and quantitative finance. If you’re just starting out, it might be useful to build a stronger mathematical foundation before tackling this challenging read.

Much like "Neural Networks From Scratch," I approached this book as a supplementary resource to enhance my understanding of machine learning, particularly after taking a machine learning course. In my opinion, this book stands out as one of the best resources for grasping the fundamental concepts behind various machine learning models.

The book provides a thorough exploration of common algorithms used in supervised, unsupervised, and deep learning. It dives deep into each algorithm, explaining their workings and applications in a way that is accessible yet detailed. While I initially focused less on the code (as I was relatively new to the topic), the book’s explanations of the algorithms' underlying principles were invaluable.

In addition to covering algorithms, the book addresses crucial computer science concepts like the bias-variance tradeoff and overfitting. These concepts are fundamental to understanding how machine learning models perform and how to tune them effectively. The book’s detailed treatment of these topics helps in grasping how different factors impact model performance and how to make informed decisions when building and evaluating models.

One of the book's strengths is its density of information—despite being packed with content, it remains clear and structured. This makes it a highly recommended read for anyone seriously interested in the field of machine learning, whether you’re a beginner or looking to deepen your knowledge.
For those just starting or seeking additional resources, you might find my articles on Medium—"Supervised Learning" and "Unsupervised Learning"—useful for a practical introduction to these concepts.

Unlike Taleb's
Dynamic Hedging
, Sheldon’s
Option Volatility
& Pricing

is highly recommended for anyone interested in a comprehensive understanding of options from a quantitative finance perspective. The book is well-structured, making it accessible to readers at various levels of expertise, from beginners to advanced practitioners.

The book starts with the fundamentals, including the basics of puts and calls, and delves into the concept of delta hedging, even demonstrating how to perform these calculations manually. It then progresses to explain the Greeks—important measures for assessing risk in options trading—and explores various trading strategies such as butterflies, straddles, and strangles.

In addition to these foundational topics, the book introduces key quantitative finance valuation methods, including the binomial tree model and the Black-Scholes model. It explains how these models are used for pricing options and discusses their practical applications. The clarity and logical flow of the book make it a valuable resource for understanding the intricacies of options trading and valuation.

However, some prior knowledge in quantitative finance is recommended for fully grasping the content. I found this book challenging when I first read it as a novice, which highlights the importance of having a solid background in the subject for a better understanding.
Overall,
Option Pricing & Volatility
is often considered the "bible" for options traders and is highly recommended for anyone interested in financial engineering or looking to deepen their knowledge of options trading.

I first encountered
Neural Networks from Scratch: Python

during my initial foray into Python programming, which, admittedly, was quite a leap for someone at my level. The rising prominence of neural networks, fueled by advancements like ChatGPT and deep learning, sparked my interest and led me to this book.

The book was instrumental in helping me grasp the foundational principles of neural networks, even though it presented a steep learning curve. The author does a commendable job of explaining core concepts such as nodes, activation functions, regularization, and backpropagation. The explanations are detailed and clear, making complex ideas more accessible.

A key aspect of the book is its approach to teaching through hands-on coding examples. The code examples are provided from scratch, which means you’re essentially developing your own neural network library. This approach is beneficial for understanding the mechanics behind neural networks, although at the time, I was unaware of existing libraries like TensorFlow and Scikit-learn that simplify the implementation process. These libraries make building neural networks much more straightforward and efficient, often requiring just a few lines of code.

The latter part of the book extends into other advanced deep learning concepts, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). These are crucial components in many modern machine learning models.
Overall,
Neural Networks from Scratch: Python

is a valuable resource for anyone beginning their journey into machine learning. It provides a solid foundation in neural network principles while also offering practical coding experience. Despite the initial challenge, it was a rewarding read that I would recommend as a starting point for anyone interested in understanding and working with neural networks.

title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
author: Dale Carnegie

text.t: When my friends saw I was reading this book, they probably thought I was pathetic. In my defense, I was just reading this because Bill Gates and Warren Buffett recommended this book. It was a dry read, but maybe it was also because I was just starting to get into the habit of reading. The book felt like ‘common sense’, be a good listening ear, let people share more about themselves and many more ‘intuitive’ advices. After finishing the book, I dumped it aside in my cupboard. A year later and 36 books later, I bore the fruits of this book. Despite being ‘common sense’, one would be surprised on how much we do not practice these advices. We often get carried away and share more about our experiences than others (this might be a sweeping statement, but it is based on my personal experience). We are more often than not, overconfident due to our cognitive biases (see Thinking Fast, and Slow). As such, we may overestimate our EQ abilities. This book is useful for reinforcing the thoughts you might have and enables you to make more of a conscious effort to reevaluate your communication skills with others. But still, would I read 200+ pages of this? I still find it boring, thus, the rating.

A stereotype for any fin-bro to read "Sun Tzu Art of War", so I joined in. The book focuses on military strategy and tactics, with key concepts like knowing when to fight, how to mislead your opponent, and understanding both yourself and your adversary. These ideas can be applied beyond the battlefield to everyday decision-making.
When I first read it before my national service, I found it a bit dull, similar to
How to Win Friends & Influence People

. However, it offers valuable lessons. For instance, it teaches the importance of information and positioning, which can be applied to various scenarios. In poker, for example, knowing what your opponents have done before your turn is crucial. Similarly,
The Art of War
suggests avoiding conflicts where the odds are against you—don't fight in a situation where you're likely to lose.
The wisdom in
The Art of War
is relevant to many aspects of life and decision-making. It might seem abstract at first, but with experience and a conscious effort, its principles can offer practical insights.
Those familiar with financial history will recognize LTCM and its infamous collapse.
When Genius Failed

explores this hedge fund, which boasted some of the brightest minds in finance, including PhDs and Nobel Prize winners—similar to Renaissance Technologies in that regard. Despite having top talent, LTCM faced a disastrous downfall.

The fund employed an arbitrage strategy involving junior and senior bonds, which they believed was "riskless." However, in reality, no trade is truly risk-free. LTCM was highly leveraged and failed to adequately account for tail risks. The crisis hit when Russia defaulted in 1998, disrupting their expected arbitrage convergence as investors flocked to safer bonds.

This event underscores that even the most intelligent and skilled professionals are not immune to failures. The collapse of LTCM and the subsequent need for a government bailout illustrate the limitations of traditional risk management techniques, such as Value at Risk (VaR), and highlight the interconnectedness of global financial systems. It serves as a crucial lesson in understanding and managing financial risk.

Ever heard of Warren Buffet? If anyone is interested to his approach to investing then this is a must read. Value investing in general, to me, is a fairly simple concept which can be explained quite easily. However, I would say that this book is also generally geared towards the self-help aspect and how value investing can be implemented into your life (I guess it is also because Buffett is not only a value investor but also a philanthropist). "The Education of a Value Investor" by Guy Spier is a fascinating memoir that chronicles the author's journey from a self-centered, greedy investor to a thoughtful, value-driven one. Spier provides an honest and introspective account of his early days as an investor, including the mistakes he made and the lessons he learned along the way. Do not expect anything too technical as that is not the focus of this book, rather, I believe this book aims to focus on the importance of continuous learning, self-reflection and unwavering conviction to one's principles. Just like value investing, life has inherently a long-term horizon. It might get a little dry at the start but it was a satisfying read.
Due for a re-read and review.

You can picture a confused and bored 18 year old, reading about trading strategies and risk management from the Market Wizards. However, the interview style kind of books enabled me to set my foot into the financial pool of knowledge. This was my very first book in finance where i felt so out of this world. I definitely do not remember anything other than "cut your losses, ride your winners" (obviously!). However, it was opened up my mind about the different kinds of trading styles that exists (value, trend-following and contrarian) using systematic, fundamental or technical analysis. Furthermore, all the Market Wizards tend to blow up early in their career which shaped their future trades. I guess you have to know what losing and failing feels like before success. The one key theme from all the "Market Wizards" books is that traders should find their own trading style that suits that personality. In general, good traders tend to have similar characteristics. They are adaptable to new shifts in market regimes, skilled at taking the emotion out of trading and open minded. This book is definitely going to be on my re-read list. A classic must read for anyone interested in trading.

Main Points:
Chapter 1:

Empirical data suggest that more risk does not equal to more return. There is a relationship between maximal returns and volatility, but not expected or average returns and volatility. Examples include lotto tickets where there is an insanely top return with a highly risky bet.
Asset Pricing Theory is not really a theory, but a framework - a set of properties a theory must have but still allow many, possibly infinite expressions.
Risk used to be volatility and covariance with the market, but now it is the covariance against the stochastic discount factor.

Risk is not something that can be directly measured, it is everywhere just like 19th century physics on gravitational and electromagnetic waves (before Einstein’s theory of relativity). Our theory of risk is like the Ptolemaic system where we are overfitting the data and adding more variables to explain the theory, when it is in fact, just plainly wrong as at some point, one would come up with so many auxiliary patches that the theory collapses under its own weight.

Look at expected returns - If a bond has a 15% yield, we might say that there is high default risk being compensated but when looking at expected returns, we must materialise the default risks over the security’s life.

Risk is more subjective than objective. For instance, imagine a beauty contest and the “objectively good features” are volatility and beta to height and facial features. But financial risk features is much harder than a beauty contest (Value companies? Distressed companies?).

Risk has two distinct meanings - In one, it is a measure of variance, or volatility, one can make this as complex a distribution as you desire. If the expectation has a greater-than-zero variance, it is risky. To the extent we are talking about random draws from an opaque urn, investors, and everyone else, seek to minimise it. They also need to estimate it, knowing how bad things can get (Value-at-Risk), or the value of options that are highly nonlinear functions of the payouts and necessitate knowing the state space. The other definition of risk pertains to the specific type of covariance that is priced in asset markets, as say beta represents in the Capital Asset Pricing Model, and this is the risk that is currently a mystery.
An untrue model leads to theories becoming more complex as more data arrive, and the empirical analysis of the data becomes more complex as well.
Chapter 2:
The development of risk from the middle ages:

By showing the world how to understand risk, measure it, and weigh its consequences, they converted risk-taking into one of the
prime catalysts that drives Western society. Like Prometheus, they defied the gods and probed the darkness in search of the light that converted the future from an enemy into an opportunity.
Timeline: Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT) → CAPM → APT → Stochastic Discount Factor (SDF) Models.
Key concepts today: Risk Aversion and Diversification → Systematic covariance is all that matters.
CAPM’s concepts: Diversification & Decreasing Marginal Utility

Standard diminishing marginal returns lead to “risk aversion” which implies that when facing choices with comparable returns, agents tend to choose the risky alternative only if compensated. Dismissing marginal utility of absolute wealth is the sole explanation for risk aversion.

Diversification: The variance of two random variables is less than the sum of their variance. The total volatility of a portfolio declines to a limit equal to the total systematic risk of the portfolio, mathematically, the diversifiable risk cancels out, but the systematic risk stays. As N (no. of assets) becomes large, the risk that remains is the covariance and if the covariances are on average zero, portfolio variance goes to zero.
Covariance is thus all that matters to a large portfolio

An efficient frontier is formed when a set of feasible returns and volatilities from the infinite et of possible portfolios comprised of these securities. That is when the “higher returns could come only via higher volatility” came about. Much of Markowitz work was to calculate the efficient frontier and portfolio weights. It is not really economics but statistical work. It was only of interest because diversification was a free lunch so portfolio volatility should be of interest, not total volatility of an asset in isolation.

Tobin’s Separation Theorem is the next step to CAPM: Any optimal risky portfolio involve two calculations: first, find the optimal risky portfolio on the efficient frontier that contains only risky assets and second, to find the combination of that portfolio, along with the risk-free rate, to reach one’s highest level of utility.
Due to the insane computation, the covariance is ridiculously complex, but given Tobin’s theorem, one could look at an asset’s correlation with the aggregate market, not each individual asset:

Wealthier and risk-averse investors might allocate various amounts to this portfolio of risky assets, but within that risky portfolio, the composition would be exactly the same for all investors, because Tobin’s Separation Theorem implies that regardless of risk preference, every rational person holds the same composition of risky assets, just in different aggregate amounts. Since equities exist in positive supply, in equilibrium, people have to hold
them, and if any rational person holds them, every rational person holds them in the same proportion. Thus, prices must adjust such that everyone holds every asset is exact proportion to its supply in the market. Otherwise,
people would demand more of a stock than exists, or not enough. The argument is an equilibrium result because in equilibrium, supply has to equal demand, so given that everyone holds the same proportion of risky assets, their demand must proportionately match supply, or supply does not equal demand. If the market is the efficient portfolio, it then dictates the equilibrium return for every asset.

Unlike what Knight assumed, not all risk can be diversified away, because in stressed times all assets tend to move downward together (covariances are not all zero). This residual systematic risk, because we are risk averse, is priced in the same way living next to a smelly factory is priced into a house. The risk premium in asset markets is the return of the risky portfolio above the risk free rate: the price of risk. The covariance of an asset with the market, normalised by the variance of the market, is the beta, and represents the amount of risk any asset has. A beta of 1.0, means it is as risky as the market, and so receives the same expected return premium as the market portfolio; a beta of 2.0 has twice the risk, and gets twice the premium. The return to the investor is linear in the amount of risk.
CAPM is thus generated where
Beta

represents “how much” of risk and equal to the covariance of one asset and the market divided by the variance of the market which is basically the same as the coefficient in an OLS regression of asset returns on the stock market proxy. It

Idiosyncratic risk and covariance with assets other than the market portfolio are irrelevant, because presumably only the market represents the non-diversifiable variance that people must hold, yet dislike. E[Rm — Rf], the equity risk premium, compensates you for your pain. This is an equilibrium result.

An equilibrium result in finance can also be presented as an arbitrage result. Linearity in pricing is implicit in that beta, a scalar, is multiplied times the equity risk premium to generate the expected return. Linearity in pricing implies no arbitrage, and vice versa. It’s as if milk costs $2 a gallon, and then every fraction or multiple of a gallon is merely $2 times how many
gallons you bought. An exposure to market risk, as reflected by beta, will give you the same return, regardless of how it’s assembled: by individual stock, portfolio, or risk, such as represented by beta in the CAPM, generates a linear return, aka the equity risk premium.
APT is an extension of CAPM,  made in a multi-factor approach. It explains the difference covariances of each factor to the benchmark.

SDF is a different way to generate the same form as the APT. Some see this as a unified field theory of derivatives, yield curves. equities and so forth as it generalises to macroeconomic models of output and growth.

SDF is often called “inter temporal general equilibrium model.” The basic assumption is that the return of an asset is a function of some risk-free rate, plus a risk premium that is a function of the covariance of the return of that asset with the marginal utility of wealth. Things with high payoffs when the marginal utility of wealth is high, pay off when the level of wealth is low (because marginal utility declines with wealth). The marginal utility of wealth can be proxied by a state
variable representing the state of something that affects utility. As this state changes over time—because of recessions, changes in optimism about the future—this means it is stochastic. As this affects the risk premium, it is
thus a “stochastic discount factor (discount factor being the inverse of the risk premium).” Under some assumptions, this stochastic factor is merely a function of consumption or GDP, which makes it more intuitive (a hedge against recessions).

The basic idea in asset pricing is that the price of a security is worth the discounted value of its payoffs, multiplied by the probability of those payoffs, which is how they are modeled in standard utility functions. Because good times imply we have little need for stuff, and bad times not, this implies we should affect the discount factor for things that pay off in good times versus bad times. It is higher in poor states because in those states of the world, the value of money is higher. Any asset paying off something in the future is merely the sum of the Discount Factors, times their payoffs, times their probabilities.

SDF discount rates relates to the state of the marginal utility and wealth. Essentially the discount factor approach suggests we look for things that are proxies of our marginal valuation of dollars tomorrow. Covariance is then linked the marginal utility tomorrow instead of the market.

The difference between the Discount Factor and APT
approach is merely in the derivation, the philosophy. One is based purely on arbitrage, the idea that whatever risks exist are priced at, they must be priced linearly according to their betas. The other, based on something more fundamental, the marginal utility of investors in various states, but the result
is the same as the APT: we have risk factors (that is, the price of risk) and their betas (that is, the amount of risk).

To include non-linearity to combat the normal distribution: Mandelbrot used some tricky distributions called stable-Paretian and fractals using chaotic systems. His first parameter is alpha, derived from Pareto’s law and defines how fat the tails are, second is the H Coefficient, an exponent that measures the dependence of price changes upon past changes.

The key difference between Keynes and Knight was not their conception of relevant risk, but rather the implication. For Keynes and his followers, the inexactitude of risk, as opposed to probabilities, was key to business cycles. For Knight, the uncertainty of risk was the essence of profitability.
Chapter 3

January Effect: Small stocks outperformed large stocks in the month of January was found to be highly influenced by the error caused by averaging daily returns (Arithmetic versus Geometric Sum). This bias is misleading.
Editors is faced with either publishing noise or missing out on the next big thing.

The bottom line is, there have been many ephemeral results
that are published: the weekend effect, the end-of-month effect, the low-price stock effect (remember low-priced stock funds?). Even today, the very anomalous Internet bubble of the late 1990s was correlated with many things: high growth rates, large R&D. Anything correlated with Internet stocks will, using the past 20 years of data, generate a huge return effect merely because of this huge bubble. One can’t help but be skeptical seeing all these new anomalies, and so be more partial to theory than data. Theory is more convincing than data because data without theory are biased by its peculiarity. Knowing why is much more important than knowing what, because if you have the why correct, you can predict; the what merely describes. Usually data and empirical results alone are just selection biases or just bad data, be more partial towards theory which have some sought of grounding.

In APT, the basic approach has three distinct alternatives:
the macro factor approach (oil, dollar, S&P500), the characteristic approach (size, value), and the latent factor approach (statistical constructs based on factor analysis). Note that the multiplicity of factor models published in literature was inevitable due to no restrictions on what was allowed.

Research for APT seemed promising: The idea that risk factors were statistical constructs, called latent factors because they were statistically implicit, not clearly identifiable by words. These are very statistical constructs that appealed to finance professors familiar with the matrix mathematics of eigenvectors and eigenvalues. If we think about the original mean-variance optimisation objective of investors, the latent factor approach actually makes the most sense. If one
is minimizing portfolio volatility and cross-sectional volatility comes from several factors, all significant factors need to be addressed. One could come up with intuitive factors that span this space, but there are methods that are more powerful than mere intuition. Yet the first factor, which explains about
90 percent of the total factor variance, is about 99 percent correlated with the equal-weighted stock index which alone suggests that latent factors were not a good alternative.
Equal versus Value weighted stock index as a proxy for the market was backed by studies on both ends: Moral of the story is that neither works better than the other, it does not matter.

Most researchers assumed there were around three
to five factors, all declining rapidly in statistical relevance. But while factor 1 looked a lot like the equal-weighted index, the other factors were not intuitive at all. They were not correlated with anything you can put your finger on. Furthermore, many stocks had negative loadings on these secondary factors,
so whereas the loading on the first factor, as in the CAPM, were almost all positive, these other strange factors, with no intuition, had 60 percent with positive loadings, and 40 percent with negative loadings. You could not explain exactly what the factor was, but sometimes it generated a risk
premium, sometimes you were presumably paying for its insurance like properties—even though no one had enough intuition to figure out what this provided insurance against.

Fama and French findings was that market cap explained all of the correlation which essentially just makes CAPM worthless and theory to be rejected. The relation that Beta is linearly and positively related to stock returns is zero. However, their approach was clearly a “mend, do not end” approach to CAPM. They just added what we know of as an a theoretical risk factor identification, an epicycle was added.
Key Takeaways:
Psychological Bias
Confirmation Bias
Availability Bias
Anchoring Bias
Sizing
Position sizing and volatility (“N”)
Risk management isn’t just about what you trade, but
how big
you trade.
The Turtle-style “N” measures average daily volatility, stops set at 1N have ~16% chance of being hit on any given day purely from noise, while 2N stops cut this to ~2%.
Adjusting all positions by volatility normalises risk across trades and makes losses more predictable.
Thematic (discretionary macro) trades
Thematic trades express big macro views (e.g., “short JGBs,” “long gold vs money-printing”) and can be very rewarding, but usually take a long time to play out.
Because they move in big, lumpy steps and can stay “wrong” for years, they should be run in
smaller size
than short-term trades, with a clear idea of downside and maximum pain.
Backtesting & Metrics - Use of VaR
Stress-testing beyond VaR
A simple stress test is to sort the last ~500 days of P&L and look at the average of the worst few days – a more conservative loss estimate than standard VaR.

In low-vol regimes this can still understate risk, so traders should also examine portfolio P&L on famous crisis days (’73 oil shock, ’87 crash, Asian crisis, LTCM, etc.) to reveal tail vulnerabilities that VaR might miss.
Using historical analogs
“Analog” analysis freezes the current price path of an asset (e.g., DXY) and finds past periods with high correlation and similar macro environments.
Studying how the market evolved after that past window gives a scenario map for today
Not a prediction, but a way to frame possible paths and stresses.
Sortino ratio (downside-focused risk-adjusted return)
Sortino replaces total volatility with
downside
volatility, measuring return per unit of bad moves only, which aligns better with capital preservation.
It’s calculated as (excess return over the risk-free rate) divided by downside deviation of returns.
Like Sharpe, it still relies on distributional assumptions and works best over longer horizons.
Build a
scenario set
: strong breakout, failed breakout and mean reversion, or prolonged range.
Risk utilisation and conviction-based sizing
“Risk utilisation” = (Portfolio VaR) / (VaR limit). Running at 5% VaR when your limit is 5% means 100% utilisation; 2.5% VaR is 50%.
Traders shouldn’t always max out their VaR: you go “all-in” only when conviction is very high (the poker analogy: pocket aces vs J-Q offsuit).
Nonlinear / incremental VaR
Risk should scale
nonlinearly
with conviction and performance: after strong gains you may allow a higher VaR limit (e.g., raise from 5% to 6–7%), effectively risking profits rather than original capital.
Equally important is a predefined rule to
cut
VaR after drawdowns (e.g., reduce the limit when the portfolio is down), so the core principle of capital preservation is never compromised.

title: How Countries Go Broke: The Big Cycle
author: Ray Dalio

text.t: Review
Annex & Notes
Chapter 1 — Russia
The flatland problem
Russia spans 11 time zones, the largest country on earth, but its core demographic and industrial heartland sits west of the Urals on the North European Plain.

The plain runs essentially uninterrupted from France through Poland, Belarus, and Ukraine into Russia. There are no mountains, no major rivers running north-south, and no defensive geography between Berlin and Moscow.
Putin praying for mountains in Ukraine. He has none, so he must control the flatland himself.
The plain has been the invasion corridor for Napoleon (1812), the Kaiser (WWI), and Hitler (WWII). Russian strategic memory is built on these traumas.

The plain narrows as it approaches Moscow. At its western (European) end, at the Polish frontier, it is roughly 2,000 miles wide. By the time it reaches Moscow it has narrowed considerably. Holding the frontier far west therefore minimises the defensive line you ultimately have to defend.
The warm-water port obsession
Most of Russia's coastline freezes for part of the year. Vladivostok freezes for around four months, Murmansk is partly accessible thanks to the Gulf Stream but distant from population centres.
Sevastopol in Crimea is the great prize: ice-free, deep, and the home of the Black Sea Fleet since the late 18th century.

Even Sevastopol has a structural flaw. Ships leaving the Black Sea must pass through the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles, both controlled by Turkey, a NATO member. Russian sea power exits the world through someone else's keyhole.
This explains the Russian presence at Tartus on the Syrian coast, its only Mediterranean facility, and a key reason for Russian intervention in Syria in 2015.
Without a functional warm-water port, Russia cannot project naval power year-round. Geography turns it into a mostly land power despite its enormous coastline.
Ukraine as existential
Ukraine sits across the western entry to the North European Plain. Without it, Russia's western frontier extends right up to the Russian heartland.
Ukraine also hosts the Sevastopol naval base under a Russian lease.
A pro-Russian or neutral Ukraine is acceptable to Moscow. A Ukraine moving into the EU and NATO is, in Russian terms, a direct threat.
Marshall reads the annexation of Crimea and the eastern Ukraine destabilisation not as Putin's caprice but as predictable Russian behaviour from any leader holding that map.

Yanukovych's pivot toward the EU trade deal in 2013 was the trigger. Putin began turning the screw with pressure that culminated in Yanukovych's reversal, the Maidan protests, and the annexation of Crimea in March 2014.
The southern soft underbelly
The Caucasus mountains form a natural southern barrier, but they enclose a politically fractured region (Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia, Georgia, Azerbaijan, Armenia).

Beyond the Caucasus lies the Muslim world, including Turkey, Iran, the Central Asian republics. Russian foreign policy in Central Asia (the Eurasian Economic Union, military presence in Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan) is about denying these spaces to rival powers.
The Stans were Soviet republics. Their independence in 1991 represented the largest single geopolitical loss in Russian history, more than offsetting any post-Cold War gain.
The Arctic and the east
The Russian Arctic is enormous and contains substantial untapped hydrocarbons, but climate makes extraction expensive and seasonal.

The Russian Far East is sparsely populated (around 6 million people), bordered by Chinese provinces with around 100 million. Demographic asymmetry is a slow-motion strategic problem Russia has not solved.
The opening miscalculation (24 February 2022)

Almost 200,000 Russian troops were massed on Ukraine's borders. Most observers, including Western governments, thought it was a bluff. They were wrong on the bluff. They were equally wrong on the second assumption: that the Russians would roll over Ukraine in days.

The plan was to reach Kyiv quickly from the north and the Dnieper from the east. Once the land corridor connecting Crimea to the Donbas was secure, Russian forces in the south would turn westwards toward Odesa.

The strategic prize was Odesa. If Ukraine's most important port fell, the country would essentially be landlocked. The drive to the Russian-speaking Moldovan breakaway province of Transnistria would then be easy.

The reality showed the ineptitude and brutality of Russian forces and the resilience of Ukraine. After a fierce fight, a humiliating withdrawal from the Kyiv region followed. When Ukrainians entered Bucha they found bodies of murdered civilians, evidence of torture, and mass graves.
The Bucha discovery shifted Western policy. The Europeans and Americans were shocked into action. Weapons and money slowly began to arrive in Ukraine.
Strategic underestimation of the West

Putin did not realise the invasion was of much greater magnitude, or that it represented such a direct threat to the entire West. He completely underestimated the resolve that the shock would give the Western alliance.

The Russians were in disarray, but sheer weight of numbers meant that by June 2022 they had occupied about 20 per cent of Ukraine. Having failed in the quick war, they settled in for the long haul along a 965-kilometre front line.

The geographic fact that mattered — a flat, open frontier that Russia thought favored an attacker turned out to favor a well-supplied defender once anti-tank weapons (Javelin, NLAW) and drones became universal. The same plain that Russia uses for buffer-zone logic also denies the attacker any cover.
The energy weapon that backfired

Pre-invasion, Russia held a near-monopoly on European heating. Russia remains second only to the USA as the world's biggest supplier of natural gas, and before 2022 had most of Europe over a barrel of crude. On average, more than 25 per cent of Europe's gas and oil came from Russia.
Country-level dependence was extreme. Latvia, Finland and Slovakia were 100 per cent reliant on Russian gas; Bulgaria 90 per cent reliant; Greece 40 per cent; and Germany 50 per cent.

The strategic theory of the case was to weaponise winter. Putin had calculated that European support for Ukraine would collapse under the pressure of keeping factories open and homes heated. It was yet another example of how badly he had gamed out the repercussions of his war of choice.
The substitution happened faster than Moscow expected. Other energy providers increased their supplies to the continent, including Norway via pipeline and the USA via LNG (liquefied natural gas).

The collapse in market share was structural, not cyclical. By 2023, Russia accounted for just eight per cent of pipeline gas entering the EU, and 15 per cent of pipeline gas and LNG combined. Putin's energy bluff was called, the heating stayed on, and support for Ukraine remained.
Naval failure in the Black Sea

The Black Sea Fleet was supposed to be the principal beneficiary of the 2014 Crimea annexation. Under the updated 2011 terms of the lease agreement for Sevastopol, Ukraine had previously had power to block modernisation of the fleet. After 2014 that constraint was gone, and hundreds of millions of roubles were poured into upgrading.
By 2021, refurbished existing vessels, three frigates, four patrol ships and six submarines had reinforced the fleet.
The investment was destroyed by a country with no navy. Between 2022 and 2024, more than two dozen Russian Navy ships were damaged or destroyed, among them the flagship cruiser Moskva.

The wider naval picture is worse than it looks. All four Russian fleets are geographically constrained: the Pacific Fleet faces the Japanese island chain, the Baltic Fleet now faces a NATO lake after Finnish and Swedish accession, the Northern Fleet must transit a long Arctic route under NATO observation, and the Black Sea Fleet has lost two dozen hulls and the leverage to block grain exports.

The Mediterranean foothold was lost too. The Russians had a small naval presence at Tartus on Syria's Mediterranean coast. In early 2025, following the overthrow of the Assad regime, pictures emerged of Russian forces engaged in what appeared to be a withdrawal from the port. This is a direct consequence of the Ukraine war: forces and aircraft that had propped up Assad were redeployed, leaving Damascus exposed when rebel forces moved on it in late 2024.
NATO expansion: the inverse of the war aim
The original Russian justification for the invasion was to prevent NATO encroachment. The result was the largest single NATO expansion in two decades.
Finland's and Sweden's accession doubled the NATO-Russia land border and turned the Baltic into what NATO planners now openly call a NATO sea.

Finland's NATO membership means, if required, that NATO troops can move to within a few hours' drive of the Northern Fleet's headquarters. Severomorsk used to be an Arctic redoubt; it is now a forward exposure.
The geographic point: Russia's western frontier is now harder to defend, not easier, than it was on 23 February 2022. The buffer-zone doctrine produced the opposite of its intent.
Loss of the near abroad
The post-Soviet space Moscow assumed was its sphere of influence has fragmented in plain sight.

None of the Central Asian republics supported the invasion of Ukraine, none recognise the self-proclaimed Donetsk and Luhansk "People's Republics", and all pay at least lip service to the sanctions imposed on Russia.

The trajectory of allegiance is sharply negative. Ten years ago, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Belarus and Armenia could all be placed in the pro-Russian camp. After Ukraine, only Belarus must still pay allegiance to Moscow.

The institutional architecture is hollowing out. The Eurasian Economic Union has not succeeded in becoming a profitable economic alliance and has failed to keep the Central Asian republics in line. The CSTO is the same story. Armenia is fed up with it, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan wonder what the point of it is, and Belarus is in it because Moscow told it to join.
China and Turkey are filling the vacuum. Russia remains the dominant force in Central Asia, but a weakening one.
Economic capture by China
The loss of the European market did not produce diversification, it produced dependence.
The loss of most of the European market forced Moscow to look for other customers. Russia had the hydrocarbons; India and China had the demand and the cash. But it was a buyer's market.
In 2023, half of Russia's oil exports went to China, but at vastly reduced prices, and Chinese exports to Russia rose 50 per cent. Moscow has dug itself into a hole of dependence on Beijing.

The strategic implication is severe. The pre-war Russia was a great power with leverage over Europe. The post-2022 Russia is a junior partner to China, selling discounted hydrocarbons to fund a war it cannot easily exit. The asymmetry is not temporary, it is structural.
Internal cracks

The Wagner mutiny exposed the fragility of the security state. In 2023, frustrated at Russia's progress, Yevgeny Prigozhin, leader of Wagner Group, called on his private army to advance on Moscow. The Kremlin quickly brokered a deal assuring his safety. Two months later, unsurprisingly, he died in a plane crash.
Mobilisation followed the failure of professional forces. By the end of 2022, Putin had annexed parts of the Donbas and ordered the call-up of 300,000 reservists.

Foreign manpower has been brought in to fill gaps. As winter set in for the 2024-25 campaign, the Russian counter-offensive went forward with 50,000 soldiers backed by several thousand North Korean troops. North Korean forces on the European continent in 2024-25 is itself a measure of Russian weakness.

The Ukrainian Kursk incursion broke the taboo on Russian territorial inviolability. In August 2024, with the clock ticking, Ukraine sent several thousand troops into Russia's Kursk region and took 1,300 square kilometres of territory. Kyiv needed a victory narrative and land to swap for a potential peace deal. Russia could not prevent a foreign army from holding sovereign Russian soil for months.
The demographic time bomb in the Far East

The most under-reported strategic failure is the Far East. Fifteen per cent of Russia's population is Muslim, and most live in regions seething with dissent. The Urals and Siberia produce almost all of Russia's oil and gas, much of its metals and a lot of coal. The populations east of the Urals are well aware that they bankroll Moscow but that their regions suffer a lack of development.

The Sino-Russian asymmetry is now extreme. Russia's Manchuria region, with its vast natural resources (water, minerals, iron), has a population of just 4.5 million. Chinese Manchuria has a population of 107 million. That is roughly a 24:1 ratio across a shared border with a partner who has been quietly buying out Russian commercial assets at distressed prices since 2022.

Putin may not have grasped the irony of China potentially recovering lost territory in Russia's Far East by applying his own logic of retaking lost territory in Europe. The same irredentist argument that justifies 2022 also writes a sequel decades later, with Russia on the receiving end.
Plan B and the Trump variable

Once the quick-war strategy failed, Moscow shifted to attrition plus political bet. Plan B was to win a war of attrition both on the battlefield and in the diplomatic corridors of power, and hope that Donald Trump returned to the White House. Everything rested on the 2024 US election.

Trump's return changed the strategic calculus but not in the way Moscow assumed. For the Trump team, the Indo-Pacific region was the focus and Europe was secondary. Trump wanted to end the war to save money, replenish the US military arsenal, meet the rising challenge from China, and force the Europeans to take ownership of the defence of Europe.

The risk that breaks the framework: if Trump threatens to weaken or even leave NATO, the Europeans cannot be sure he is bluffing. With the USA, NATO is the most powerful military force in the world. Without it, NATO is a regional entity playing catch-up in funding, munitions and missile defence. Moscow watches with interest.

Marshall's residual worry: in the unlikely but possible event that NATO fractures, the Baltic states could be next on Russia's list of territories it would risk war for. Moldova is also flagged as a likely next geographic target, since the plain south of the Carpathians functions as another invasion corridor that Russia would prefer to control at its narrow point. The same flatland logic that drove the 2022 invasion remains active.
The takeaway

Russian foreign policy is not driven by ideology, individual leaders, or post-Soviet revanchism alone. It is driven by a permanent geographic weakness: a flat western frontier, a frozen coastline, and a need to keep aggressive powers as far from Moscow as possible.
Russia chose the geographically rational war and lost it operationally, economically, and diplomatically.

The structural Russian position is worse in 2025 than it was in 2021 on every measurable axis: NATO is closer, the Baltic is enclosed, the Black Sea Fleet is depleted, the Mediterranean foothold is gone, the Central Asian periphery has drifted, energy customers have substituted, and economic dependence on China has deepened.
Chapter 2 — China
The Han heartland

Han Chinese civilisation grew up in the cradle between the Yellow River (Huang He) and the Yangtze. Roughly 90% of Chinese live east of the line drawn from Heilongjiang in the northeast to Yunnan in the southwest.
The west and southwest (Tibet, Xinjiang) are vast, mountainous, sparsely populated, and ethnically non-Han. They are buffers, not heartland.
This split between dense Han core and thinly populated buffer regions is the underlying structure of modern Chinese geopolitics.
Tibet as strategic depth

Tibet is not just a religious-cultural appendage. It is the source of the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Mekong, the Brahmaputra, and the Indus. Whoever controls Tibet controls the water supply for much of Asia. Tibet is known as "China's Water Tower."

Tibet also sits on the high plateau immediately north of India. If India controlled Tibet, Indian forces would look down on the Chinese heartland. From the Chinese view, Tibet is non-negotiable strategic depth.
The 1950 invasion is  geographically inevitable for any Chinese government, not as a Maoist outlier.
Xinjiang and the western corridor
Xinjiang ("New Frontier") is the gateway to Central Asia and contains substantial oil, gas, and rare earths.

The Uighur population is Turkic and Muslim, ethnically distinct from the Han, and the source of persistent unrest. China responds with Han migration into the region (the Bingtuan production-construction corps) and heavy security.
A non-Han buffer secured at any political cost because losing it would expose the heartland.
Xinjiang is also the land bridge for the overland part of the Belt and Road Initiative, the route that lets China reach Central Asia and Europe without crossing maritime chokepoints.
The land borders, finally calm
China shares land borders with 14 countries, more than any other state.
For most of its history these borders were sources of vulnerability (Mongol invasions, Manchu conquest, Japanese invasion).

Today, for the first time in centuries, all major land threats are managed. Russia is a partner of convenience, India is deterred by the Himalayas, the Stans are locked into Chinese economic gravity through the Belt and Road Initiative, Vietnam and Myanmar are too small to threaten.
This is the precondition for the pivot to sea.
The First and Second Island Chains
China's Pacific coastline faces a string of islands controlled by hostile or unfriendly powers: Japan, Taiwan, the Philippines, Indonesia. This is the First Island Chain.
Beyond it, the Second Island Chain (Guam, Mariana Islands) is a US-dominated zone.
Chinese commercial sea trade, especially energy imports through the Malacca Strait, must transit waters that the US Navy could close in a crisis. This is the Malacca Dilemma.

Reading the South China Sea reclamation (artificial islands at Mischief Reef, Subi Reef, Fiery Cross Reef) through this lens — it is not territorial greed, it is an attempt to push the perimeter outward and create a defended buffer for sea trade.
The string of pearls

A series of port investments encircling the Indian Ocean: Gwadar (Pakistan), Hambantota (Sri Lanka), Chittagong (Bangladesh), Kyaukpyu (Myanmar), Djibouti (first Chinese overseas military base, 2017).
Combined with overland pipelines and rail corridors through Pakistan, this is China hedging against the Malacca chokepoint.

China also intends to become a two-ocean power, projecting through the Pacific and the Indian Ocean simultaneously. The deep-water ports in Burma, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka are the logistical spine of this ambition.
The internal constraint
1.4 billion people, mostly packed into the eastern third. Massive urbanization, rising middle class, single-party rule.
If growth falters, the social compact (party legitimacy in exchange for prosperity) breaks. The biggest threat to China is internal, not external.
China is locked into the global economy. "If we don't buy, they don't make. And if they don't make there will be mass unemployment."
Taiwan: the strategic center of gravity
The First Island Chain is no longer just a buffer concept; Taiwan is its keystone, and its political direction has become Beijing's most pressing operational question.

The 2024 election cycle in Taipei changed the tempo. After William Lai's inauguration in May 2024, the PLA conducted Joint Sword 2024A and 2024B large-scale exercises around the island. From May 2024 to December 2025, average monthly PLA air incursions into Taiwan's air defense identification zone reached 319, a 129 per cent increase from the prior 28-month baseline. Monthly incursions never dipped below 209 sorties after May 2024, whereas before that they had occasionally fallen as low as 64.

2025 set new operational records. PLA aircraft conducted 3,764 ADIZ incursions over the year. Two named exercises (Strait Thunder-2025A and Justice Mission 2025) circled the island. December 2025 brought another large-scale exercise framed as a response to a US arms sale package of more than $11 billion, the largest single Taiwan arms deal ever.

The political signaling around peaceful unification has hardened. The 2025 Taiwan Affairs Work Conference and the March 2025 National People's Congress work report both omitted the phrase "peaceful reunification" that had appeared in nearly every prior version. The omission is read across Western intelligence agencies as Beijing repositioning from deterring independence to compelling unification.

For the geographic framework, Taiwan is the keystone arch in the First Island Chain. With Taiwan controlled, the PLA Navy can break out of the East China Sea and into the open Pacific with no chokepoint to transit. Without Taiwan, the chain holds and the Malacca Dilemma is permanent.
The 2027 milestone
The PLA has been instructed to be capable of "strategic decisive victory" over Taiwan by 2027. US defense assessments now treat this as the planning timeline rather than the speculative one.

The military build-up is on a scale that the post-Cold War order has not faced from a peer competitor. Since Xi Jinping became General Secretary, China's announced defense budget has nearly doubled. The undeclared portion is widely believed to add a substantial further increment.

The PLA Rocket Force operates a missile arsenal designed for one specific scenario: saturating Taiwan and US forward bases at the start of a Taiwan conflict. Strikes could potentially range up to 1,500 to 2,000 nautical miles from China.

The DF-21D anti-ship ballistic missile, often called the "carrier killer," is a medium-range weapon designed to strike moving ships at sea, targeting US carrier groups. The DF-26 intermediate-range ballistic missile extends that envelope to Guam.

Most consequentially, the 2025 Pentagon report disclosed the DF-27, an intercontinental ballistic missile with both land-attack and anti-ship capability and a range of 5,000 to 8,000 km. The 8,000 km figure covers Alaska, Hawaii, and parts of the continental United States. This is the first time China's anti-ship capability extends beyond regional waters into transoceanic distances.

The nuclear arsenal has expanded faster than US analysts projected. Beijing held an estimated 200-300 warheads in 2020. By mid-2024 the figure was over 600. The Pentagon now projects over 1,000 by 2030 and 1,500 by 2035. Hundreds of new ICBM silos have been constructed in the western desert.
The naval transformation

China's shipbuilding industrial capacity is now estimated at roughly 230 times that of the United States in gross tonnage output. The PLA Navy is adding modern warships at a rate the US Navy cannot match with current shipyard infrastructure.

The carrier program has progressed in three steps. The Liaoning (Type 001, commissioned 2012) was a refurbished Soviet hull with a ski-jump ramp. The Shandong (Type 002, commissioned 2019) was the first domestically built carrier, still ski-jump. The Fujian (Type 003, launched 2022, sea trials 2025-26) is a generational leap: it features electromagnetic aircraft launch systems, the same technology used on the latest US Ford-class carriers. A fourth carrier, possibly nuclear-powered, is in early construction.

Submarines, destroyers, frigates, and amphibious assault ships are being built simultaneously across multiple yards. The amphibious build-up is the most operationally significant, since it addresses the transport bottleneck for any Taiwan landing force.

In any Western Pacific contingency, the PLA operates close to its bases, supply lines, and land-based air and missile cover. US forces must project across thousands of miles of ocean from a limited number of forward bases that are themselves vulnerable to Chinese missile strikes. The geography of the theatre favours the defender, and Beijing is the defender on its own coast.
South China Sea: the pressure campaign continues
The artificial-island campaign was the 2010s phase. The 2020s phase is constant kinetic harassment of neighbors, particularly the Philippines.
The PLA conducted a record 163 recorded operations in the South China Sea in 2025, including a record number of live-fire drills.

The geographic focus shifted from Second Thomas Shoal to Scarborough Shoal during 2025. The China Coast Guard more than doubled its presence around Scarborough year over year. This is consistent with the buffer-extension logic of the original chapter: pushing the perimeter outward in deniable, non-kinetic increments.

AUKUS (Australia, United Kingdom, United States, 2021) is the structural Western response. Marshall in 2025 reads it as a counter-encirclement of the Chinese maritime perimeter, with Australian nuclear-powered submarines as the strategic bet that matters.

The Quad (US, Japan, India, Australia) is the diplomatic overlay. India's involvement is the geographically novel piece, since it brings the Indian Ocean perimeter into the same strategic frame as the Pacific.
The chip chokepoint
Semiconductors are now a geographic resource as critical as oil, and they happen to be concentrated on a single contested island.

Taiwan, through TSMC, fabricates roughly 90 per cent of the world's most advanced chips. Whoever controls TSMC, or whoever can deny others access to it, controls the inputs to AI, defense systems, automotive electronics, and consumer technology globally.

This makes Taiwan simultaneously more valuable and more dangerous to invade. A successful invasion gives China the chip industry. A failed or destructive invasion destroys it for everyone, including China.

The "silicon shield" thesis (the chip industry deters invasion because everyone needs it intact) is contested — It raises the cost but does not change the geographic logic. Taiwan is in the First Island Chain whether it makes chips or not.
TSMC's diversification (Arizona fabs, Japan fabs, Germany fabs) is the global hedge. The Arizona projects in particular are an explicit US bet that the silicon shield cannot hold indefinitely.
Internal stress

First, the PLA is undergoing visible top-level corruption purges. CMC Political Work Department Director Admiral Miao Hua was placed under investigation and suspended in November 2024. CMC Vice Chairman General He Weidong was absent from key 2025 meetings, presumed suspended. These are unusually senior figures to be removed within a single year.

Second, the economy is decelerating in ways that strain the post-1989 social compact. Real estate is in multi-year contraction. Youth unemployment hit historic highs in 2023-24 before the publication of the metric was restricted. Local government finances depend heavily on land sales that have collapsed. The growth-for-legitimacy bargain is under structural strain.

Third, demographics have turned. China's working-age population peaked around 2014. The total population began declining in 2022. The country will get old before it gets fully rich, a constraint Japan navigated with established institutions and which China must navigate without them.

The 2024 reorganization of the Strategic Support Force into separate Aerospace Force, Cyberspace Force, and Information Support Force units is read as Xi consolidating personal command over the new domains of warfare while loosening the autonomy of mid-tier military structures. This is centralization, not delegation.
The Russia partnership of convenience

The Russia chapter described Russia's growing dependence on China after 2022. The China chapter describes the same relationship from the other side: Russia is now a discounted hydrocarbon supplier and a junior strategic partner, not a peer.

China conducted six joint exercises with Russia in 2025, the lowest count since 2020 and down from 14 in 2024. The headline development was the first joint Sino-Russian submarine patrol, which signals quiet alignment without strategic dependence.

The geographic bet is asymmetric. China gains a buffered northern frontier and discounted energy. Russia gains a market and a balancing power against the West. But the demographic and economic asymmetry across the Sino-Russian Far East border is so extreme (the 24:1 population ratio in Manchuria) that the long-run direction is Chinese cultural and eventually political influence over Russian territory, not the reverse.
Marshall's ironic framing carries through both chapters: Putin's irredentism in Ukraine writes the eventual case for Chinese irredentism in Russia's east.
The takeaway
China's geography forced it to spend two thousand years securing land borders. Having done so, it is now executing the only available next move to become a sea power.

This is not aggression. It is strategic sequencing dictated by the map. The question for the rest of the world is no longer whether China will project naval power but how, and within what rules, and against what timetable.

The Russia chapter showed a state behaving as the map predicted and failing operationally. The China chapter shows a state behaving as the map predicts and succeeding so far, with an explicit 2027 milestone for the most consequential single test of geography against deterrence in the post-Cold War era.

China's strategic position is strengthening on most measurable axes: naval tonnage, missile range, chip-input leverage, regional alliances, and economic gravitational pull on the periphery. The vulnerabilities are internal: demographics, debt, leadership purges, and the deflationary risk of a real-estate workout that has no historical precedent at this scale.

The framework's predictive power is highest when geography and capability point in the same direction. For China in 2025, they do. The risk to the framework is that when capability accelerates faster than expected, the timeline shortens and the planning horizon for everyone else compresses. Taiwan in 2027 is the operational expression of this. Whether or not Beijing acts on the 2027 timeline, every other actor in the region must price the option as if it could.
Chapter 3 — United States
The Mississippi system
The single most important geographic feature of the continental US.
The Mississippi-Missouri-Ohio river network drains 41% of the contiguous US and provides 17,500 miles of navigable inland waterway.
This is more navigable river mileage than the rest of the world combined. River transport is roughly 10 to 30 times cheaper per ton-mile than rail.
Combined with the fertile heartland soil, this network creates the most productive integrated agricultural-industrial zone on earth.

Crucially, the Mississippi mouth (New Orleans) is the world's busiest port complex by tonnage. Whoever controls it controls American commerce. Hence the Louisiana Purchase (1803), the most important real estate transaction in US history.
Manifest Destiny as geographic strategy
The 19th-century westward expansion was the systematic acquisition of geographic depth.

Louisiana Purchase (1803) doubled the country and secured the Mississippi, Florida (1819) closed the Gulf coast, Texas (1845) and the Mexican Cession (1848) brought the southwest, California, and Pacific access. Alaska (1867) bought the northern flank for two cents an acre, Hawaii (1898) gave Pacific projection.
Cumulative effect: the US now spans temperate latitudes from Atlantic to Pacific with no peer rival on the continent.
The two-ocean fortress
The Atlantic and Pacific are vast moats. Invasion of the continental US is essentially impossible by any conventional power.
Mexico to the south is non-threatening. Canada to the north is a willing ally with a population one-tenth the size.
The US is the only great power in history that can be both a continental power and a maritime power simultaneously.
This frees the US Navy to project globally rather than defend home waters. Eleven supercarrier groups, more than the rest of the world combined.
The chokepoints and the global commons

The US Navy underwrites freedom of navigation through the world's chokepoints: Hormuz (oil), Malacca (Asian trade), Suez and Bab-el-Mandeb (Europe-Asia), Panama (two-ocean transit), Bosphorus and the Danish Straits (Russian access).
This is the structural basis of the post-1945 global trading order. Countries trade because the US Navy guarantees the sea lanes.
The Panama Canal is critical. It cuts the Atlantic-Pacific journey by around 8,000 miles. The 1999 handover to Panama is in a sense nominal: passage depends on US goodwill.
The shale revolution
Emphasized that fracking made the US an energy near-superpower. Roughly self-sufficient in gas, decreasingly dependent on Middle East oil.
Strategic implication: declining US interest in policing the Persian Gulf, with knock-on consequences for Saudi-Iranian rivalry, Israeli security calculations, and European energy strategy.
The "American decline" question
Marshall is skeptical. The geographic endowment is unchanged. The river system, the two oceans, the friendly neighbors, the fertile heartland, the energy reserves, all remain.
Decline, if it happens, will be self-inflicted: institutional dysfunction, polarization, infrastructure neglect. Not geographic.
The map says the US should be the dominant power for generations. Unless Americans choose otherwise.
The Pacific pivot becomes structural

The original chapter described the US as a globally engaged hegemon. Now, it describes a country that has consciously narrowed its geographic focus to the Indo-Pacific and is forcing other regions to absorb the consequences.

For the Trump team the Indo-Pacific region was the focus, Europe was secondary, and to some it was just an afterthought. President Trump wanted to end the Ukraine war to save money, replenish the US military arsenal, meet the rising challenge from China, and force the Europeans to take ownership of the defense of Europe.

The framing is geographically coherent. Since the First World War, US foreign policy in Europe has tried to ensure no single power dominates the continent. Marshall's update notes that this argument was bought by Joe Biden but rejected by Donald Trump. The new doctrine treats Europe as solvable by Europeans and reserves US capacity for the Pacific theatre where the geographic stakes are higher.

The pivot has a hardware dimension. AUKUS (Australia, UK, US, 2021) routes nuclear-powered submarine technology to Australia for the first time outside Britain, embedding a forward US naval capability in the Indian Ocean and the Pacific approaches to the South China Sea.

The pivot also has a regional alliance dimension. The US-Japan-Philippines trilateral (2024), the strengthened US-South Korea posture, the Quad with India, and the new defense cooperation agreements with Pacific Island states (Marshall Islands, Palau, Micronesia) form a layered architecture aimed at one geography: the First Island Chain and its approaches.
Hemispheric defense and the Trump Corollary

The December 2025 US National Security Strategy explicitly identified protection of US territory and the Western Hemisphere as the central tasks of American foreign policy. This is a return to the geographic logic of the Monroe Doctrine, formally extended into what commentators have called the Trump Corollary.

The hemisphere is being defined unusually broadly: from the Aleutian Islands to Greenland and the North American Arctic to Antarctica, with Central and South America and the Caribbean in between, and the Pacific and Atlantic approaches included.

The strategic logic: deny the hemisphere to extra-hemispheric powers (China, Russia, Iran). This is the inverse of the global-policeman doctrine. Rather than the US Navy securing the world's chokepoints, the US is fortifying the chokepoints and approaches that immediately threaten its own territory.
The 19th-century US was a hemispheric power that became a global one. The 21st-century US is reverting to type. The two-ocean fortress is being re-fortified.
The Panama Canal question

Panama is now contested for the first time since 1999. Trump in January 2025 stated he would not rule out using military force to take the canal. Marco Rubio's first overseas trip as Secretary of State was to Panama, demanding reduced Chinese influence.

The geographic sensitivity: the canal cuts the Atlantic-Pacific journey by about 8,000 miles. Two ports at either end of the canal were operated by CK Hutchison, the Hong Kong conglomerate. Their 2025 sale to a BlackRock-led consortium was widely read as a forced asset transfer engineered by US pressure on the basis that Chinese commercial control of the canal's terminals was strategically intolerable.

The Pentagon was ordered to prepare contingency plans ranging from closer cooperation with Panama's military to the less likely option of a full US invasion. The doctrine is consistent with the original chapter: passage through Panama depends on US goodwill, and if the goodwill condition is not met, the US reasserts physical control.
The wider point: the 1999 handover always was nominal sovereignty over an asset of US strategic interest. The 2025 administration is making explicit what was previously implicit.
Greenland and the Arctic flank

Greenland is the new strategic prize, not a Trumpian eccentricity. It sits across the GIUK Gap (Greenland-Iceland-UK), the historical bottleneck for Russian submarine access to the North Atlantic. Its location matters more, not less, as Arctic shipping routes open and Russian Arctic militarisation accelerates.

The 1951 US-Denmark defence agreement already provides for US basing rights at Thule (now Pituffik). The 2025 push is to expand that footprint, deploy anti-submarine warfare assets, and prepare Arctic training infrastructure.

The economic dimension: Greenland holds substantial rare earth deposits at a time when China dominates global processing of rare earths and has used export restrictions as a strategic lever. Securing alternative supply is a defence-industrial priority.

The Greenland question is the High North equivalent of the Panama Canal question: the US re-asserting strategic primacy over a chokepoint or resource zone where soft sovereignty no longer feels sufficient.
Energy: from near-self-sufficiency to global dominance

Russia, second-largest gas supplier globally before 2022, has lost most of its European market. US LNG filled the gap. By 2023 Russian pipeline gas accounted for around 8 per cent of EU pipeline gas, down from over 25 per cent. The shift is structural and difficult to reverse.

This gives the US energy diplomacy leverage it has not held since the early 20th century. Europe's energy security now runs through US ports (Sabine Pass, Corpus Christi, Plaquemines) and US tanker fleets.

The geographic implication folds back into Marshall's broader argument: the US is now the supply-side actor in global energy as well as the demand-side actor in global trade. Both flows are routed through US-controlled chokepoints and US-owned infrastructure.
The Pacific alliance architecture

AUKUS is the single most consequential alliance restructuring of the 2020s. The Australian nuclear-powered submarine programme will, when delivered, place an additional six to twelve attack submarines in the Pacific theatre under US-allied command.

Japan has begun a serious remilitarisation, lifting the long-standing 1 per cent of GDP defence spending cap toward 2 per cent and acquiring offensive long-range strike capability for the first time since 1945.
The Philippines has expanded the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement to grant US forces access to additional bases, several of them facing Taiwan and the South China Sea.
South Korea is increasing defence spending and discussing extended deterrence arrangements that include the possibility of a more visible US nuclear umbrella.

The Pacific Islands cooperation network (Marshall Islands, Palau, Micronesia under Compacts of Free Association) has been extended and upgraded. New cooperation conversations are happening with Costa Rica.
Dense alliance presence around the First Island Chain to deter or, if necessary, contest Chinese action against Taiwan within the Pentagon's 2027 planning horizon.
The economic statecraft turn
Tariffs, export controls (especially on advanced semiconductors), entity-list restrictions, and secondary sanctions are now used routinely against allies and adversaries alike.

The CHIPS Act (2022) and the broader industrial policy turn aim to relocate semiconductor manufacturing onto US territory. TSMC's Arizona fabs are the most concrete result. Intel's Chandler and Ohio expansions, Samsung's Texas plant, and Micron's New York facility are part of the same logic.
