The geographic concentration of advanced chip fabrication on a single contested island (Taiwan) is a strategic vulnerability comparable to the pre-1973 concentration of oil refining capacity in the Gulf. The US response is the same in shape: domestic alternative supply, friend-shoring (Japan, Korea), and physical proximity to demand.

The trade war with China is now structural rather than cyclical. Tariffs on Chinese goods, restrictions on Chinese investment, and the unwinding of cross-border tech and capital flows form the new background condition.
Chapter 4 — Western Europe
Theme:
The productive accident. Climate, navigable rivers, varied but interconnected terrain, and the fragmentation that paradoxically generated competition, innovation, and the modern world.
The northern flatland
Same North European Plain that haunts Russia, but viewed from the western end. Flat, fertile, well-watered, traversed by the Rhine, the Danube, the Elbe, the Vistula.

Germany sits at the centre, with no natural defensive boundaries east or west. Hence the recurring strategic problem of German power, "too big for the European balance, too small for global hegemony."
The Rhine is critical: navigable from the North Sea deep into Switzerland, draining one of the most industrialised valleys on earth (Ruhr, Rotterdam).
Why Europe industrialised first: navigable rivers + temperate climate + coal deposits + small distances, all overlapping.
The Mediterranean periphery

Spain, Italy, Greece face south to a different geographic logic. Warmer, drier, more peripheral to the new economic core that emerged in the north after the discovery of the Americas shifted trade to the Atlantic.

The Pyrenees and the Alps separate the Mediterranean nations from the northern industrial core. Geography part-explains the persistent north-south economic gap inside the EU and the strain that gap puts on the eurozone.
Greece is "geographically European, economically Balkan, politically peripheral." Marshall reads its 2010-15 debt crisis as in part a geographic mismatch with the German-led eurozone.
Why fragmentation produced power

Compare with China: same continental scale, opposite political outcome. China unified under one empire for most of its history, Europe never did despite repeated attempts (Rome, Charlemagne, Napoleon, Hitler).
The Channel kept Britain separate. The Pyrenees, the Alps, the Carpathians, the Balkans created politically defensible regions. Multiple competing powers could survive simultaneously.
This forced competition: military, technological, commercial. Diamond and others have argued (and Marshall echoes) that European fragmentation was a hidden engine of innovation.
The European Union as geographic project
The EU is, on Marshall's read, an attempt to overcome geography through institutions: combine the fragmented states into a single economic and (partly) political bloc.
It works least well at the geographic edges (Greece, Spain, Portugal, the periphery) and best in the integrated Rhine corridor and adjacent zones.
The 2008 financial crisis and the 2010-12 sovereign debt crisis exposed the gap between geography and institutional design: a single currency for economies that did not converge structurally.
Brexit (Marshall writes around the time of the early debate) is foreshadowed as a Channel-driven political fact. Britain has always been geographically half-detached.
The northern question
Scandinavia, Finland, the Baltic states sit on a separate sub-geography: cold, peripheral, but increasingly central as Arctic shipping opens.
Russia's western frontier presses on this zone. Finland and Sweden's eventual NATO membership (post-2022, after Marshall's writing) is the predictable answer to the geographic position.
The takeaway

Western Europe is the case where geography produced both prosperity and political fragmentation simultaneously. Same continent, same climate, but the rivers and terrain shaped many states rather than one.
This is the chapter that complicates the framework. Geography is not a single output. It is a structure of incentives, and the European structure rewarded plurality.
Chapter 5 — Africa
Theme:

The inverse continent. Same continental scale as Eurasia, opposite outcomes. Coast without harbours, rivers without navigability, axis without diffusion. Marshall's most direct application of Jared Diamond.
The coastline curse

Africa has the longest coastline of any continent relative to land area, but very few natural harbours. The continental shelf drops sharply, surf is heavy, and the coast lacks the deep bays and estuaries that produced Hamburg, Rotterdam, Boston, Shanghai.
Marshall: "Great beaches, really, really lovely beaches, but terrible natural harbours."
This is why Africa never developed a large maritime trading civilisation comparable to the Mediterranean or East Asia.
Rivers that go nowhere
Africa has enormous rivers: the Nile, the Congo, the Zambezi, the Niger.

Almost none of them are navigable from coast to interior. Most are interrupted by waterfalls (the Congo's Livingstone Falls a few miles inland, the Zambezi's Victoria Falls, the Nile's cataracts) within a short distance of the sea.
Compare the Mississippi, the Rhine, the Yangtze, all of which carry shipping deep into the agricultural heartland. African rivers are barriers, not arteries.
The Nile is the partial exception, but it flows through desert and is politically contested across 11 countries.
The continental axis problem (borrowed from Diamond)
Eurasia runs east-west across temperate latitudes. Crops, livestock, technologies, and ideas diffuse easily across similar climates. Wheat from the Fertile Crescent reached China and Britain.
Africa runs north-south, crossing tropical, equatorial, and southern temperate zones. Crops and livestock that work in one zone fail in another. The Sahara is a massive diffusion barrier.
Result: Africa originated humanity (around 200,000 years ago) but its agricultural and technological development was slowed by an unforgiving structural feature of the map.
The Sahara as continental divider
North Africa is geographically Mediterranean. Its history, politics, and trade have been linked more to Europe and the Middle East than to sub-Saharan Africa.
The Sahara physically separates the two zones. Trans-Saharan trade existed (gold, salt, slaves) but at small scale relative to maritime trade elsewhere.
This explains why Egypt, Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia feel more like the "Middle East" in policy terms while sub-Saharan Africa is treated as a separate strategic zone.
The colonial border problem
The 1884-85 Berlin Conference partitioned Africa among European powers using straight lines drawn on a map without reference to terrain, ethnicity, or pre-colonial state boundaries.

Result: many African states contain hostile ethnic groups packed inside borders that ignore tribal geography (Nigeria with around 250 ethnic groups, Sudan splitting in 2011, the DRC's ungovernable scale).

Marshall returns to this theme in the Middle East chapter. Both regions suffer from the same colonial cartography failure, with the same long-term consequences: weak states, civil conflict, secessionist pressure.
Resource curse and resource endowment
Africa is rich in minerals, hydrocarbons, and arable land. It is also poorly equipped, structurally, to convert these into broad development without strong institutions.
Examples: Nigeria (oil-dependent, Niger Delta strife), DRC (cobalt, coltan, diamonds, perpetual conflict), Angola (oil, Luanda's extreme inequality).
Botswana is offered as the counter-example: diamonds plus stable institutions plus small homogeneous population produced consistent growth.
The China factor

Marshall (writing in 2015) emphasises Chinese investment across Africa as the new colonial overlay: infrastructure for resources, often with conditions on diplomatic alignment (the "One China" policy).

Chinese-built roads, rail, ports across the continent (Mombasa-Nairobi rail, Djibouti port, Lagos-Kano rail) are partially overcoming the navigability problem with overland infrastructure for the first time.
The takeaway

Africa shows that geography can be the primary structural disadvantage, separable from colonialism, governance, and culture. The continent has a head start as the cradle of humanity but the wrong shape, the wrong rivers, the wrong axis, and the wrong borders.
This is the chapter where the framework's explanatory range becomes clear: it is not just about strong powers, it is about why some regions structurally cannot become strong.
Chapter 6 — The Middle East
Theme:
The artificial-borders case study. Sykes-Picot, the colonial cartography failure, the post-2011 unravelling, and why ignoring geography produces multi-generational state failure.
Sykes-Picot (1916)
Secret Anglo-French agreement during WWI that divided the Ottoman Arab provinces into spheres of influence, formalised in mandates after WWI.

Lines were drawn on a map without reference to topography, sectarian distribution, or tribal geography. Iraq merged Sunni Arab, Shia Arab, and Kurd into one state. Syria merged Alawite, Sunni, Christian, Druze, Kurd. Lebanon was carved as a Christian-majority enclave with a built-in confessional power-sharing system.
Marshall's claim: every major Middle Eastern conflict since traces back to this cartography. The borders never matched the people or the terrain.
The sectarian map
The Sunni-Shia split (originating in the 7th-century succession crisis after Muhammad) is the deepest structural divide.

Shia majorities or large minorities: Iran (overwhelmingly Shia), Iraq (around 60%), Bahrain (around 70%), Lebanon (around 30%), Yemen (the Houthis are Zaidi Shia), eastern Saudi Arabia (the oil-bearing province).
Sunni majorities everywhere else.
The Shia crescent (Iran, Iraq, Syria via Alawite rule, Hezbollah in Lebanon) is the strategic axis Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states fear and seek to disrupt.
Iraq as exhibit A
Three regions, three peoples: Kurdish north (mountainous), Sunni Arab centre (the historic Baghdad heartland), Shia Arab south (the rice and oil belt around Basra).
Saddam held it together by force. The 2003 US invasion removed the binding force. The country effectively fragmented along its three historic geographic-ethnic lines.

ISIS in 2014 captured the Sunni heartland (Mosul, Raqqa across the border in Syria) and declared a caliphate. Marshall (writing in 2015) reads this as the sectarian-geographic logic asserting itself against the Sykes-Picot state.
Syria as exhibit B
The Alawite heartland (a Shia offshoot) is on the coast around Latakia and Tartus. The Sunni majority is in the interior. Druze are in the south. Kurds are in the north and northeast.
Assad's regime is built on the Alawite minority controlling the security state. The 2011 uprising split the country along these geographic-sectarian fault lines.
The Russian intervention (2015) is partly about preserving the Tartus naval base, the only Russian Mediterranean port. Geography reaches across chapters.
Israel and the geography of survival
A small country surrounded by larger Arab states. Strategic depth is minimal: Tel Aviv to the West Bank is around 15 miles.

Geography drives the obsession with the Golan Heights (Syrian high ground overlooking northern Israel), the Jordan Valley (eastern defensive line), and the Sinai buffer (demilitarised after Camp David).
The 1967 borders and the post-1967 occupation are read through the geographic-defence lens.
The Gulf and Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz, between Iran and Oman, is the world's most important oil chokepoint. Roughly 20% of global oil supply passes through it.
Iran sits along the entire northern coast, giving it the geographic capacity to disrupt traffic in a crisis.
This is the structural reason for the persistent US naval presence (Fifth Fleet, Bahrain) and for the Saudi-Iranian regional competition.
The Kurdish question
The Kurds, around 30 million, are the world's largest stateless people, divided across Turkey, Iraq, Syria, and Iran by Sykes-Picot.
They live mostly in mountainous terrain that has historically protected their identity but blocked unification.
Marshall: a Kurdish state remains the most plausible redrawing of the Middle East map. It would also be the most destabilising, since Turkey, Iran, Syria, and Iraq would all lose territory.
The takeaway

This is the chapter where the book's argument turns prescriptive. Drawing political lines that disregard topography and the geographic distribution of culture is not just analytically flawed, it produces state failure on a multi-decade timescale.

For investors and policymakers, the practical implication is that sovereign credit, security risk, and political stability in artificial-border states should carry a structural risk premium. The borders are not finished; they are unfinished.
Chapter 7 — India and Pakistan
Theme:
The subcontinent's geographic complexity, the partition trauma, Kashmir as a geographic flashpoint, and nuclear stakes overlaid on ancient terrain.
The subcontinent as fortress
Hemmed in by the Himalayas to the north (the world's highest range, and the reason India and China have fought only one significant war despite being the two largest countries by population).
The Hindu Kush in the northwest is the historic invasion corridor. Every major land invasion of India (Aryans, Greeks, Turks, Mughals) came through the Khyber and Bolan passes.
The Indian Ocean to the south is a moat, but it is also a maritime arena where Indian and Chinese naval competition is now intensifying.

Internally, the subcontinent is fragmented by language (around 20 official, hundreds of dialects), religion (Hindu majority, large Muslim minority, Sikh, Christian, Jain, Buddhist), and geography (the Punjab plains, the Bengal delta, the Deccan plateau, the Western and Eastern Ghats).
Partition (1947)
Britain partitioned India into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan along confessional lines drawn by Cyril Radcliffe in five weeks, with no field knowledge of the regions.
Result: around 14 million displaced, between several hundred thousand and over a million dead in communal violence.

Pakistan was created in two non-contiguous wings (West Pakistan and East Pakistan, separated by 1,000 miles of Indian territory). Geographic absurdity. East Pakistan seceded in 1971 to become Bangladesh.
Kashmir
Mountainous, strategically located between India, Pakistan, and China. Muslim-majority population but ruled by a Hindu maharaja at partition who acceded to India under contested circumstances.
Three Indo-Pakistani wars and a continuing low-intensity conflict. The Line of Control runs through some of the highest-altitude military positions in the world (Siachen Glacier, around 20,000 feet).

For Pakistan, control of Kashmir would secure the headwaters of the Indus, on which Pakistani agriculture depends. For India, ceding Kashmir would be a precedent for further territorial fragmentation. For China, it borders Aksai Chin and Tibet. Three nuclear powers contest the same valley.
The water wars overlay
The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) divides the river system between India and Pakistan. It has held through three wars but is under stress as both countries grow and climate change reduces glacier melt.
The Brahmaputra rises in Tibet, flows through India and Bangladesh. China's upstream dam-building creates a slow-moving dispute with India.
The next subcontinental crisis may be over water rather than territory.
Pakistan's geographic incoherence

Marshall reads Pakistan as a country still searching for a geographic identity. It has Punjab (the demographic and political core), Sindh (the Indus delta), Balochistan (the resource-rich, sparsely populated, restive west), and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (the Pashtun belt bleeding into Afghanistan).
The Pashtun region has never been firmly controlled by any central power. The Durand Line (the Afghan-Pakistani border) cuts through Pashtun lands and is rejected by Afghanistan.
The military-ISI complex's strategic depth doctrine treats Afghanistan as Pakistan's hinterland, which partly explains support for the Taliban historically.
India's strategic position

Demographically the world's largest country (now exceeding China). Economically growing but unevenly. Geographically secure on its land borders but vulnerable in the Indian Ocean to potential Chinese sea power.
Indian foreign policy, traditionally non-aligned, is shifting toward a quiet alignment with the US, Japan, and Australia (the Quad) as a hedge against Chinese expansion.
Nuclear overlay
Both India and Pakistan are nuclear states. Pakistan's doctrine is "first use." India's is "no first use" but with calibrated retaliation.
The geographic compression (short flight times, dense population centres near the border) means escalation timelines in any crisis would be measured in minutes, not hours.
The takeaway

Same lesson as the Middle East with different mechanism (partition, not colonial cartography) and higher stakes (nuclear weapons). Imposing political geometry on geographic complexity produces persistent instability, even when the populations are largely settled and the states are functional.
The chapter reinforces that the Middle East's problems are not Middle East exceptionalism. Wherever borders ignore geography, the same pattern emerges.
Chapter 8 — Korea and Japan
Theme:
The homogeneity case. What happens when geography produces ethnic and cultural unity rather than fragmentation? Different problems: resource scarcity, peninsula politics, demographic decline.
Japan's island geography
An archipelago of around 6,800 islands, four main ones (Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, Shikoku). Mountainous, with only around 12% of the land arable.
Devoid of significant natural resources: minimal oil, gas, or industrial minerals. This is the structural fact behind 20th-century Japanese imperialism. Resource access required colonial expansion.
The 1941 attack on Pearl Harbour was provoked, on Marshall's read, partly by the US oil embargo. Japan saw itself with months of strategic petroleum left and chose pre-emptive war.
Japan's modern strategic problem
Same resource dependency, now solved through trade rather than empire. Japan imports almost all of its energy and most of its industrial inputs.
Strategic vulnerability: sea lanes from the Persian Gulf through Malacca to Japan can be interdicted. Hence the deep US-Japan alliance and the slow remilitarisation of the Self-Defense Forces.
The dispute with China over the Senkaku/Diaoyu islands is read through this lens. The islands are tiny, but they sit on potential gas fields and along key sea lanes.
Demographic decline
Japan's population is aging and shrinking. By 2050 it may be around 100 million from a 2010 peak of around 128 million.
Geographic constraint plus cultural homogeneity plus immigration restriction equals a slow demographic crisis with no easy answer.
Marshall's broader point: even ideal homogeneity does not insulate a state from geographic limits. The map still binds.
The Korean peninsula as cockpit
Korea is the geographic bridge between continental Asia and Japan. Whoever controls the peninsula has a dagger pointed at Japan, or a forward base against China.
This is why every great power in northeast Asia (China, Russia, Japan, the US) has had a stake in the peninsula's status for over a century.

The 1950-53 war and the resulting partition along the 38th parallel are products of this geographic logic. Stalin and Mao backed the North; the US backed the South. The peninsula was divided not because the Koreans wanted it divided but because the surrounding powers needed a buffer.
North Korea's geography of survival
Mountainous, with a long border with China that complicates any external pressure. Most of the population, industry, and the regime sit close to the DMZ.
Nuclear weapons compensate for conventional weakness. The regime's calculation is that visible nuclear capability deters intervention while extracting concessions.
China tolerates North Korea's existence because regime collapse would produce a unified Korea allied with the US sitting directly on the Yalu River. Geography, not ideology, drives Chinese support.
South Korea's success and exposure
One of the post-WWII economic success stories. Highly educated, technologically advanced, strong export sector.

Geographically vulnerable: Seoul sits within artillery range of the DMZ. Around half the population lives in the Greater Seoul area, exposed to a first-strike artillery barrage that no missile defence could fully neutralise.
This is the structural reason South Korea has not pre-emptively struck the North despite the provocations: the cost of a war would fall first and heaviest on Seoul.
The takeaway
This chapter stress-tests the framework against the homogeneity case. If geography matters, it should matter even where ethnic and cultural complexity does not.
It does. Japan is bound by its resource scarcity; Korea is bound by its peninsular position between great powers. Different geographic problems, same fundamental constraint.
Chapter 9 — Latin America
Theme:
The overlooked continent. Why Latin America never produced an EU, why its interior is empty, and why geography blocks both internal integration and full participation in global trade.
The hollow interior
South America is shaped like an inverted triangle, with most of its population on the coasts.

The interior is dominated by the Amazon (rainforest, rivers that flow east to the Atlantic but mostly through ungovernable terrain) and the Andes (the world's longest mountain range, running the entire length of the continent).

Unlike the Mississippi system in North America, the Amazon does not link populated agricultural zones to each other. It runs through some of the least developed areas and exits at Belem, far from the Andean population centres.
Result: the continent's largest cities (Sao Paulo, Buenos Aires, Lima, Bogota, Caracas) are coastal or near-coastal, separated from each other by mountains, jungle, or distance.
The Andes as continental wall
Run for around 4,500 miles from Venezuela to the southern tip of Chile.
Block east-west commerce across the continent. Chile is essentially walled off from Argentina by the Andes.
The high altitudes (above 12,000 feet on the altiplano) created the great pre-Columbian civilisations (Inca, Tiwanaku) but in environments unsuited to large modern industrial economies.
Why no Latin American EU
Marshall poses the question directly: why is there no continental integration comparable to Europe's?

Geographic answers: no internal navigable river network connecting the major populated zones; mountains separating Pacific and Atlantic coasts; vast distances; Amazonian void; persistent infrastructure gaps.
Mercosur, the Andean Community, and other initiatives exist but remain shallow. The geographic friction is too high.
Mexico and Central America
Mexico is partly North American (NAFTA-integrated, US-bordered, manufacturing-linked) and partly Latin American (cultural and historical ties south).

The Mexican plateau is rugged. Major cities (Mexico City, Guadalajara, Monterrey) sit on a high interior plateau separated from the coasts by mountains. This historically slowed Mexican industrial integration with the global economy until the late 20th century.

Central America is an isthmus narrow enough to permit a canal at Panama. The canal's strategic and economic importance has been understood since Vasco Nunez de Balboa crossed the isthmus in 1513. The canal opened in 1914.
Brazil's potential and limits
The continent's largest country by population and area. Resource-rich (iron ore, soybeans, oil, hydropower).

Geographic constraint: most of the population sits on a narrow coastal strip backed by the Brazilian Highlands. The interior (the cerrado, the Amazon) is being developed but with high logistical costs.

Sao Paulo's port, Santos, is overburdened. The country lacks the integrated transport network that would make it a true global industrial power. This is partly a policy failure and partly a geographic challenge.
Argentina's curse
The Pampas are among the most fertile soils in the world. Argentina was, around 1900, one of the ten richest countries on earth.
Yet the country is far from major world markets. Buenos Aires to London is around 7,000 miles by sea. Buenos Aires to Tokyo is around 11,000 miles.
Distance compounds policy mistakes. Geography did not cause Argentine decline, but it left no margin for the policy choices that did.
The Pacific Alliance

A subset of states (Chile, Peru, Colombia, Mexico) attempting closer integration with each other and with Asia across the Pacific. Marshall reads this as a geographic-pragmatic answer to the failure of pan-Latin integration: bypass the Andes-Amazon problem and trade with East Asia directly.
The takeaway
Latin America closes the continental-scale loop in the book. Europe integrated, Africa fragmented, Latin America stalled. Three different geographic outcomes from three different physical structures.

The chapter is also where Marshall is most cautious about prediction. Latin America has the resources and the educated populations. Whether it can overcome its internal geography through infrastructure and institutions is open.
Chapter 10 — The Arctic
Theme:
The forward-looking chapter. Climate change is creating new geography. The 21st century will see a contested Arctic, with the same old rules of geopolitics applied to a thawing map.
The new geography
The Arctic ice cap is shrinking. Summer minimum sea ice extent has declined by around 40% since 1979.
Two new shipping routes are opening seasonally:
The Northwest Passage (through the Canadian archipelago), shortening Asia-Europe transit by around 7,000 miles compared to the Panama Canal route.
The Northern Sea Route (along the Russian Arctic coast), shortening Asia-Europe transit by around 5,000 miles compared to the Suez route.
New territory becomes accessible for resource extraction: the US Geological Survey estimates the Arctic holds around 13% of undiscovered oil and 30% of undiscovered gas globally.
The Arctic Eight
Eight states have Arctic Council membership: USA (Alaska), Canada, Russia, Norway, Denmark (via Greenland), Iceland, Sweden, Finland.
Sovereignty claims overlap. Russia in 2007 planted a titanium flag on the seabed at the North Pole to assert its claim to the Lomonosov Ridge.
China is not an Arctic state but has declared itself a "near-Arctic" power and obtained observer status on the Arctic Council in 2013. It has Arctic ambitions tied to its Polar Silk Road strategy.
Russia's Arctic priority
Russia has the longest Arctic coastline of any state. Its 40 icebreakers (the US has 2) reflect a long-term strategic commitment.
The Northern Sea Route along the Russian coast could become a major shipping artery, with Russia as gatekeeper. Tariff revenue and strategic leverage flow from this.
New Russian military bases along the Arctic coast (refurbished Soviet facilities, new airfields) signal that Russia treats the Arctic as a future theatre, not a frozen frontier.
The resource race
Hydrocarbons under the Arctic shelf are technically extractable but expensive. The economics depend on global oil prices and the cost of operating in extreme conditions.
Rare earth deposits in Greenland have attracted Chinese interest, complicated by US security concerns (Trump's 2019 Greenland purchase proposal made geopolitical sense, even if it sounded absurd).
Fisheries, currently limited by ice, may become accessible. The Central Arctic Ocean Fisheries Agreement (2018) is an early attempt to regulate this.
The overlap with conventional geopolitics

NATO's northern flank (Norway, the Nordics) is increasingly important as Russian Arctic capability grows. Sweden and Finland's NATO accession (post-Marshall's writing) is partly an Arctic strategic move.
US-Canadian sovereignty differences (the US views the Northwest Passage as international waters; Canada claims it as internal waters) become more pressing as the route becomes navigable.
China-Russia Arctic cooperation (financing, infrastructure) is growing but remains transactional rather than strategic. Their interests align in the medium term but diverge in the long term.
Why Marshall closes here
The Arctic chapter closes the book by demonstrating that geography is not static. Climate change creates new sea lanes, new resource zones, new chokepoints, new sovereignty disputes.

But the rules of the game remain unchanged: states compete for resources, sea lanes, and strategic position. The cast of actors is set by who happens to have Arctic coastline, Arctic capability, or Arctic ambition.
The framework is generative, not just descriptive. As the world changes, the analysis travels.
The takeaway

New geography, old logic. The 21st-century Arctic will be contested for the same reasons the 19th-century Mediterranean and the 20th-century South China Sea were contested: because the map creates incentives that no rational state can ignore.
Cross-Chapter Synthesis
A few patterns emerge once the chapters are laid side by side:
Land powers versus sea powers
: Russia and China sit on the land-power side, the USA and Britain (and historically Japan) on the sea-power side. The strategic doctrine of each follows from the underlying geographic position.
Buffer states recur
: Ukraine for Russia, Tibet and Xinjiang for China, the Caucasus for Russia again, the Korean peninsula for everyone in northeast Asia. Buffer logic is universal.
Chokepoints concentrate power
: Hormuz, Malacca, Suez, Panama, the Bosphorus, the Danish Straits. Whoever controls a chokepoint taxes the world that depends on it. This is the structural reason for sustained US naval dominance.
Artificial borders fail

: Sykes-Picot (Middle East), Berlin Conference (Africa), Radcliffe Line (India-Pakistan). When political lines ignore physical and cultural geography, the long-run outcome is state failure or chronic conflict.
Rivers and harbours determine economic geography

: navigable rivers (Mississippi, Rhine, Yangtze) create wealth, blocked rivers (Congo, Zambezi) prevent it. Natural harbours (Hong Kong, Rotterdam, Singapore) generate trade hubs, their absence (most of Africa) prevents them.
Climate sets demographic ceilings
: Russia's Siberian emptiness, Canada's northern void, Australia's interior, Greenland's near-uninhabitability. Cold and aridity are structural population limiters.
Geography ages well

: Marshall's 2015 forecasts have largely held up. China did expand naval power, the Middle East did continue to fragment, the Arctic did become contested, Russia did invade Ukraine again (2022). The framework's predictive power is the main reason the book is still in print and selling.
Chapter 3 — United States
Theme:

The geographic lottery winner. Two oceans, a navigable river network, fertile heartland, weak neighbours, and the structural reasons American hegemony is hard to displace. The 2025 update is the most strategically consequential rewrite of the original chapter. Marshall reframes the US not as a globally engaged hegemon but as a Pacific-focused continental power that is consciously withdrawing from one geographic theatre (Europe) to concentrate on another (the Indo-Pacific), while reasserting hemispheric primacy in ways not seen since the Monroe Doctrine.
The Mississippi system
The single most important geographic feature of the continental US, in Marshall's account.
The Mississippi-Missouri-Ohio river network drains 41% of the contiguous US and provides 17,500 miles of navigable inland waterway.
This is more navigable river mileage than the rest of the world combined. River transport is roughly 10 to 30 times cheaper per ton-mile than rail.
Combined with the fertile heartland soil, this network creates the most productive integrated agricultural-industrial zone on earth.

Crucially, the Mississippi mouth (New Orleans) is the world's busiest port complex by tonnage. Whoever controls it controls American commerce. Hence the Louisiana Purchase (1803), the most important real estate transaction in US history.
Manifest Destiny as geographic strategy
The 19th-century westward expansion was not just ideology, it was the systematic acquisition of geographic depth.
Louisiana Purchase (1803) doubled the country and secured the Mississippi.
Florida (1819) closed the Gulf coast.
Texas (1845) and the Mexican Cession (1848) brought the southwest, California, and Pacific access.
Alaska (1867) bought the northern flank for two cents an acre.
Hawaii (1898) gave Pacific projection.
Cumulative effect: the US now spans temperate latitudes from Atlantic to Pacific with no peer rival on the continent.
The two-ocean fortress
The Atlantic and Pacific are vast moats. Invasion of the continental US is essentially impossible by any conventional power.
Mexico to the south is non-threatening. Canada to the north is a willing ally with a population one-tenth the size.
The US is the only great power in history that can be both a continental power and a maritime power simultaneously.
This frees the US Navy to project globally rather than defend home waters. Eleven supercarrier groups, more than the rest of the world combined.
The chokepoints and the global commons

The US Navy underwrites freedom of navigation through the world's chokepoints: Hormuz (oil), Malacca (Asian trade), Suez and Bab-el-Mandeb (Europe-Asia), Panama (two-ocean transit), Bosphorus and the Danish Straits (Russian access).
This is the structural basis of the post-1945 global trading order. Marshall: countries trade because the US Navy guarantees the sea lanes.
The Panama Canal is critical. It cuts the Atlantic-Pacific journey by around 8,000 miles. The 1999 handover to Panama is in a sense nominal: passage depends on US goodwill.
The shale revolution
Marshall (writing in 2015) emphasised that fracking made the US an energy near-superpower. Roughly self-sufficient in gas, decreasingly dependent on Middle East oil.
Strategic implication: declining US interest in policing the Persian Gulf, with knock-on consequences for Saudi-Iranian rivalry, Israeli security calculations, and European energy strategy.
This is one of Marshall's forward forecasts that has aged reasonably well.
The "American decline" question
Marshall is sceptical. The geographic endowment is unchanged. The river system, the two oceans, the friendly neighbours, the fertile heartland, the energy reserves, all remain.
Decline, if it happens, will be self-inflicted: institutional dysfunction, polarisation, infrastructure neglect. Not geographic.
The map says the US should be the dominant power for generations. Unless Americans choose otherwise.
The Pacific pivot becomes structural (2025 update)

The original chapter described the US as a globally engaged hegemon. The 2025 chapter describes a country that has consciously narrowed its geographic focus to the Indo-Pacific and is forcing other regions to absorb the consequences.

Marshall is explicit on this in the new edition: for the Trump team the Indo-Pacific region was the focus, Europe was secondary, and to some it was just an afterthought. President Trump wanted to end the Ukraine war to save money, replenish the US military arsenal, meet the rising challenge from China, and force the Europeans to take ownership of the defence of Europe.

The framing is geographically coherent. Since the First World War, US foreign policy in Europe has tried to ensure no single power dominates the continent. Marshall's update notes that this argument was bought by Joe Biden but rejected by Donald Trump. The new doctrine treats Europe as solvable by Europeans and reserves US capacity for the Pacific theatre where the geographic stakes are higher.

The pivot has a hardware dimension. AUKUS (Australia, UK, US, 2021) routes nuclear-powered submarine technology to Australia for the first time outside Britain, embedding a forward US naval capability in the Indian Ocean and the Pacific approaches to the South China Sea.

The pivot also has a regional alliance dimension. The US-Japan-Philippines trilateral (2024), the strengthened US-South Korea posture, the Quad with India, and the new defence cooperation agreements with Pacific Island states (Marshall Islands, Palau, Micronesia) form a layered architecture aimed at one geography: the First Island Chain and its approaches.
Hemispheric defence and the Trump Corollary (2025 update)

The December 2025 US National Security Strategy explicitly identified protection of US territory and the Western Hemisphere as the central tasks of American foreign policy. This is a return to the geographic logic of the Monroe Doctrine, formally extended into what commentators have called the Trump Corollary.

The hemisphere is being defined unusually broadly: from the Aleutian Islands to Greenland and the North American Arctic to Antarctica, with Central and South America and the Caribbean in between, and the Pacific and Atlantic approaches included.

The strategic logic: deny the hemisphere to extra-hemispheric powers (China, Russia, Iran). This is the inverse of the global-policeman doctrine. Rather than the US Navy securing the world's chokepoints, the US is fortifying the chokepoints and approaches that immediately threaten its own territory.

Marshall's framework absorbs this cleanly. The 19th-century US was a hemispheric power that became a global one. The 21st-century US is reverting to type. The two-ocean fortress is being re-fortified.
The Panama Canal question (2025 update)

Panama is now contested for the first time since 1999. Trump in January 2025 stated he would not rule out using military force to take the canal. Marco Rubio's first overseas trip as Secretary of State was to Panama, demanding reduced Chinese influence.

The geographic sensitivity: the canal cuts the Atlantic-Pacific journey by about 8,000 miles. Two ports at either end of the canal were operated by CK Hutchison, the Hong Kong conglomerate. Their 2025 sale to a BlackRock-led consortium was widely read as a forced asset transfer engineered by US pressure on the basis that Chinese commercial control of the canal's terminals was strategically intolerable.

The Pentagon was ordered to prepare contingency plans ranging from closer cooperation with Panama's military to the less likely option of a full US invasion. The doctrine is consistent with the original chapter: passage through Panama depends on US goodwill, and if the goodwill condition is not met, the US reasserts physical control.

The wider point: the 1999 handover always was, in Marshall's framing, nominal sovereignty over an asset of US strategic interest. The 2025 administration is making explicit what was previously implicit.
Greenland and the Arctic flank (2025 update)

Greenland is the new strategic prize, not a Trumpian eccentricity. It sits across the GIUK Gap (Greenland-Iceland-UK), the historical bottleneck for Russian submarine access to the North Atlantic. Its location matters more, not less, as Arctic shipping routes open and Russian Arctic militarisation accelerates.

The 1951 US-Denmark defence agreement already provides for US basing rights at Thule (now Pituffik). The 2025 push is to expand that footprint, deploy anti-submarine warfare assets, and prepare Arctic training infrastructure.

The economic dimension: Greenland holds substantial rare earth deposits at a time when China dominates global processing of rare earths and has used export restrictions as a strategic lever. Securing alternative supply is a defence-industrial priority.

The Greenland question is the High North equivalent of the Panama Canal question: the US re-asserting strategic primacy over a chokepoint or resource zone where soft sovereignty no longer feels sufficient.
The southern border and the cartels (2025 update)

Mexico is the geographic sub-theatre that Marshall's 2015 chapter understated. The 2025 update treats the southern border and the cartel networks beyond it as a national security problem on the scale of an external rival.

In early 2025 the administration designated multiple Latin American criminal organisations as Foreign Terrorist Organisations: the Sinaloa Cartel, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, the Northeast Cartel, the Gulf Cartel, the Michoacan Family, the United Cartels, plus Mara Salvatrucha (MS-13) and Venezuela's Tren de Aragua.

The US authorised the military to control land on the Mexican border, deployed additional troops, and reportedly expanded a Biden-era CIA programme of secret drone flights over Mexico to identify fentanyl laboratories. CIA boundary crossings of this scale into Mexico's airspace have not been publicly acknowledged in modern times.

The Caribbean dimension: an increased US naval presence in the southern Caribbean, fighter jets to Puerto Rico in response to Venezuelan aircraft incidents, and strikes on Venezuelan-flagged vessels suspected of drug trafficking. Venezuela and Bolivia were both decertified as cooperating partners on counter-narcotics.

The geographic point is that the US is treating the Caribbean and northern Mexico as the inner perimeter of homeland defence in a way that 2015 Marshall would not have anticipated. The Mississippi system's southern outflow runs through these waters. So does roughly half of US LNG export traffic.
Energy: from near-self-sufficiency to global dominance (2025 update)

The 2015 chapter's forecast aged better than almost any other prediction in the book. The shale revolution did not just make the US self-sufficient. It made the US the world's largest oil and gas producer.

Russia, second-largest gas supplier globally before 2022, has lost most of its European market. US LNG filled the gap. By 2023 Russian pipeline gas accounted for around 8 per cent of EU pipeline gas, down from over 25 per cent. The shift is structural and difficult to reverse.

This gives the US energy diplomacy leverage it has not held since the early 20th century. Europe's energy security now runs through US ports (Sabine Pass, Corpus Christi, Plaquemines) and US tanker fleets.

The geographic implication folds back into Marshall's broader argument: the US is now the supply-side actor in global energy as well as the demand-side actor in global trade. Both flows are routed through US-controlled chokepoints and US-owned infrastructure.
The Pacific alliance architecture (2025 update)

AUKUS is the single most consequential alliance restructuring of the 2020s. The Australian nuclear-powered submarine programme will, when delivered, place an additional six to twelve attack submarines in the Pacific theatre under US-allied command.

Japan has begun a serious remilitarisation, lifting the long-standing 1 per cent of GDP defence spending cap toward 2 per cent and acquiring offensive long-range strike capability for the first time since 1945.
The Philippines has expanded the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement to grant US forces access to additional bases, several of them facing Taiwan and the South China Sea.
South Korea is increasing defence spending and discussing extended deterrence arrangements that include the possibility of a more visible US nuclear umbrella.

The Pacific Islands cooperation network (Marshall Islands, Palau, Micronesia under Compacts of Free Association) has been extended and upgraded. New cooperation conversations are happening with Costa Rica.

The geographic logic of all of this is the same: dense alliance presence around the First Island Chain to deter or, if necessary, contest Chinese action against Taiwan within the Pentagon's 2027 planning horizon.
The economic statecraft turn (2025 update)
The 2025 update reflects a broader US shift from military primacy to economic coercion as the primary foreign policy lever.
Tariffs, export controls (especially on advanced semiconductors), entity-list restrictions, and secondary sanctions are now used routinely against allies and adversaries alike.

The CHIPS Act (2022) and the broader industrial policy turn aim to relocate semiconductor manufacturing onto US territory. TSMC's Arizona fabs are the most concrete result. Intel's Chandler and Ohio expansions, Samsung's Texas plant, and Micron's New York facility are part of the same logic.

Marshall's framing in the 2025 edition: the geographic concentration of advanced chip fabrication on a single contested island (Taiwan) is a strategic vulnerability comparable to the pre-1973 concentration of oil refining capacity in the Gulf. The US response is the same in shape: domestic alternative supply, friend-shoring (Japan, Korea), and physical proximity to demand.

The trade war with China is now structural rather than cyclical. Tariffs on Chinese goods, restrictions on Chinese investment, and the unwinding of cross-border tech and capital flows form the new background condition.
The takeaway

The original chapter argued the US was the example of what perfect geography buys you: hegemony. The 2025 update argues the US is now choosing how to use that hegemony in a more focused, less universal way.

The geographic endowment remains unchanged. What has changed is the policy choice about which parts of the global commons the US still wishes to underwrite. The Pacific yes. Latin America and the hemisphere yes, more so than for decades. Europe much less. The Middle East selectively, mostly for energy chokepoints and Israeli security.

For investors and policy analysts, the practical takeaway is the inverse of the Russia chapter. Russia behaved as the map predicted and got weaker. The US behaved as the map predicted (concentrate on the home theatre and the most contested foreign one) and is getting stronger relative to its closest peer competitor.

The structural risk to the US position is what Marshall identified in 2015: self-inflicted institutional dysfunction. The 2025 update layers on a second risk: that the withdrawal from non-Pacific theatres creates power vacuums that the US later must re-enter at higher cost. The Middle East after 2011 is the cautionary template.

The framework's predictive power is highest when geographic constraints are dominant. The US case in 2025 shows the inverse is also informative: when geographic constraints are loose (because the endowment is so favourable), domestic political choices matter more, not less. The US is the country where geography most clearly enables a wide range of policy options. Which option the country selects is now the single most consequential variable in global affairs.

Exploration vs. Exploitation

As a university student, it often feels like everyone around me is trapped in a hyper-competitive bubble, where we are blindly gunning for the next prestigious internship — an Investment Banking (IB) stint, or a Private Equity (PE) role for instance has been the talk lately.
We measure our worth by our LinkedIn updates and our proximity to high-paying and high-status careers. Reading Mitch Albom’s
Tuesdays with Morrie
in this environment felt relatable and refreshing.

The book chronicles Albom’s final conversations with his former college professor, Morrie Schwartz, who is dying of ALS. For students caught in the relentless pursuit of corporate prestige, the parallels between Mitch’s early career obsession and our current campus culture are similar. This is exactly why we need Morrie’s wisdom.

Early in the book, we learn about Mitch’s turning point. After his uncle passed away, Mitch felt a sudden and desperate urge to achieve everything, believing that if he could just take control of his life and career, everything would be good.
How many of us in this track operate on the exact same anxiety?
We sacrifice sleep, relationships, and our own well-being to secure a sense of control through a job offer.
"Most of us all walk around as if we're sleepwalking. We really don't experience the world fully, because we're half-asleep, doing things we automatically think we have to do.”
We spend our days chasing the wrong things, caught in what Morrie calls the "opposite tensions" of life—the tearing conflict between who we
ought
to be and who we are
expected
to be by our peers and parents. Our culture does not make people feel good about themselves, and we need to be strong enough to say that if the culture doesn’t work, don’t buy it.

Morrie then points out the absurdity of how we idealize other people’s lives. Mitch uses the O.J. Simpson trial as an example, but today, it translates to how students idolize billionaire CEOs, finance moguls, or even just seniors who landed top-tier roles. We obsess over people who do not care about us in return. We do this, Morrie argues, because we are starved for real connection.

"Whenever I went in my life, I met people wanting to gobble up something new... These were people so hungry for love that they were accepting substitutes. They were embracing material things and expecting a sort of hug back."

In the pursuit of the best grades and our next role, we are often guilty of substituting prestige and future wealth for genuine tenderness, comradeship, and love. As Morrie bluntly states, it never works.
Perhaps the most striking contrast Morrie draws for a student, like myself, is the difference between corporate survival and genuine human connection.

"In business, people negotiate to win. They negotiate to get what they want. Maybe you are too used to that. Love is different. Love is when you are as concerned about someone else’s situation as you are about your own."

When your entire day is spent networking transactionally, trying to figure out what you can extract from a coffee chat to get an interview, you risk wiring your brain for business. Morrie reminds us that real security doesn't come from money or fame, but from "spiritual security.” What does he mean? It means knowing your family is watching out for you. He emphasizes the unparalleled weight of raising children and the necessity of shared values, open communication, and compromise in marriage. You cannot build a meaningful life with a "negotiate to win" mindset.   

Ultimately, Morrie’s terminal ALS forces a perspective shift that cuts through the noise of recruiting seasons and exams (something that even stresses me out!). Instead of hiding from his mortality, Morrie treats his final days as a celebration, even holding "living funerals" so he can hear what he means to people while he is still alive.
"Learn how to die, and you learn how to live,"
Morrie says.
When you strip away the resume building and the artificial timelines we set for ourselves, you are left with the essentials. That doesn’t mean we shouldn't feel the weight of our struggles.
"I give myself a good cry if I need it. But then I concentrate on all the good things still in my life... Because we're Tuesday people."
It’s a profound lesson in resilience for any student facing rejection letters or burnout. Feel the disappointment, shed a tear, and then immediately pivot back to gratitude for the people around you.
Tuesdays with Morrie
is a reminder that a life spent chasing a prestigious logo on a resume is often a meaningless one. True legacy isn't an offer letter. As Morrie says,
"Death ends a life, not a relationship."
You live on in the hearts of everyone you have touched and nurtured.
If you want to inject actual meaning into your life, Morrie gives us the formula:
"Devote yourself to loving others, devote yourself to your community around you, and devote yourself to creating something that gives you purpose and meaning."

After reading so many complex philosophical takes on the meaning of life throughout my book review page, Morrie’s practical wisdom cuts straight to the point, without sacrificing any of its depth. It is an easy to read book, especially after a hectic day.
